In the AdS/CFT context, the form is dual to Berry curvature in the boundary theory.
arxiv-2510-20039:
Yuyang Jiang and five co-authors study how opinions shift on both sides during long conversations between people and large language model chatbots. Earlier work mostly asked how chatbots change users, not how users change chatbots. The team ran fifty discussions on controversial topics with two hundred sixty-six participants under three conditions, including a personalized chatbot.

Human opinions barely moved, while model outputs shifted more and narrowed the gap with the human stance. Personalization made those shifts larger in both directions. Exchanges built around personal stories were most likely to trigger a stance change for either side. The authors warn that over-alignment is a real risk for personalized chatbot design.
arxiv-2510-20139:
A. V. Kotikov and A. V. Lipatov summarize a simple model for parton distribution functions in protons and in nuclei. Parton distributions describe how a proton momentum is shared among its quarks and gluons, and they evolve with energy through QCD equations. The authors derived an analytical solution of those evolution equations in their recent papers.

Their solution respects known sum rules for valence and non-singlet quarks and conserves momentum for singlet quarks and gluons. Parameters came from a combined fit to nine hundred thirty-three precision data points from BCDMS, H1, and ZEUS. A rescaling model with Fermi motion then predicts how parton densities change inside nuclear targets, fitted to deep inelastic scattering ratios.
arxiv-2510-20239:
Filippo Cenacchi, Deborah Richards, and Longbing Cao grade how bad two health states are at once: low mood disorder and post-traumatic stress. The two states often come as a pair with shared signs. Most tools give a yes or no call for one state at a time. Their frame fuses three streams from a talk: the words, the voice, and the face.

Each stream is put in a shared form, then joined by a late fusion step with tuned weights. The output gives graded scores for both states, plus which traits drove the call. In split tests, fusion ties the best single stream on raw scores. It adds a clear gain in use for care choices and stays strong when one stream is noisy or lost.
arxiv-2510-20339:
D. Kucharski and eleven co-authors set out a deep learning frame for surface metrology that gives texture scores plus their error bars. Their data span touch and light-based tools from many sources. Tasks join tool type calls with linked fits of the Ra, Rz, and RONt scores and their error marks. Doubt is shaped with quantile and spread heads, then tuned with conformal steps.

On held-out data, one-score fits hit the main texture marks with high truth rates. Two of three error marks fit well too, while the RONt error mark stays hard. The tool type call is right in most cases, near 93 in 100. Plain multi-output nets lose skill, so the team backs one-score nets.
arxiv-2510-20439:
Quannian Zhang and four co-authors argue for explainable benchmarking, a way of evaluating competing systems that automatically explains why each system performs as it does. Standard benchmarking sums performance up in a few metrics, leaving the detailed analysis and the lessons for developers as slow, manual, and often biased work. Their first example of the approach targets knowledge-graph-based question answering systems.

Explanations are computed with PruneCEL, a new concept learning method designed for large knowledge graphs. It beats leading concept learners on the explainable benchmarking task by a wide margin on the F1 measure. In a study with forty-one participants, the majority could correctly predict a system behavior from the explanations in eighty percent of cases, showing the explanations carry real insight.
arxiv-2510-20639:
Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci and nine co-authors tackle vision and language models for three dimensional CT scans, where large volumes and long slice stacks often blur fine anatomy. Their team builds BTB3D, an encoder and decoder that turns scans into compact tokens that keep local detail and work for both still images and full volumes.

Training runs in three stages, from local repair to wide window tiling and long scan decoding, so the model can handle scans of more than three hundred slices. On report writing and text to scan tasks, the system beats prior tools by wide margins. The gains suggest careful token design matters more than a larger language model alone.
arxiv-2510-20739:
Ronghao Ni and seven co-authors test whether machine learning can sort the flood of flaw reports from program analysis tools so human reviewers see the most likely real flaws first. Their test bed is Node.js packages, where taint style flaws can let hostile input reach dangerous code.

The benchmark holds close to two thousand packages, each with one reported flaw of the studied types, drawn from a real analysis tool output. Classical models, graph networks, large language models, and hybrids are all trained and scored. The best language model leads by a small margin. At a setting that keeps ninety percent of real flaws it clears away three quarters of the harmless reports, a large saving in review time.
arxiv-2510-20839:
Warisa Sritriratanarak and Paulo Garcia sidestep the usual fight over whether machines can be conscious and ask a narrower question, whether machines need felt awareness at all. Views on machine consciousness carry heavy ethical weight, yet scholars lack even a shared account of what consciousness is.

Focusing on felt awareness alone, the pair trace why it arose in living beings in computing terms. Inherited automatic nerve reactions in evolved brains make felt awareness necessary before higher reasoning can run on top of them. Built systems carry no such legacy baggage, so in principle they can reach any level of intelligence without felt awareness. That separation could ease some ethical puzzles and reshape how artificial consciousness is judged.
arxiv-2510-21539:
Johannes Lohmann tests a warning-signal idea for climate tipping points against the abrupt climate jumps of the last ice age. Theory says a system near a tipping point recovers ever more slowly from shocks. Rising wobble in records is often taken as an indirect alarm, though that inference leans on fragile assumptions about noise.

His direct test uses volcanoes as the shock. By averaging the climate response to hundreds of eruptions in ice core records, he measures recovery speed as the great Dansgaard-Oeschger warmings and coolings approach. Before warmings, recovery stays unchanged, arguing against slowing down. Before coolings, several key records do show larger, slower responses. Statistical alarms, meanwhile, flash before nearly all transitions, so the mismatch warns that single-record alarms deserve careful reading.
arxiv-2510-21639:
Pankaj K. Agarwal, Benjamin Holmgren, and Alex Steiger plan coordinated moves for a team of square robots. The robots share a flat polygonal room. The plan minimizes the total distance traveled. Each robot must glide from its start to its target. It cannot leave the room or touch a teammate. Even finding any valid plan for many robots is famously hard in the worst case.

Their algorithm settles for near-perfection with a twist. It may judge the optimum using robots very slightly larger than the true ones. That is a bicriteria bargain. For any fixed number of robots above two, it runs in polynomial time in the room's complexity. It returns a plan within a factor arbitrarily close to the best possible. A small additive slack vanishes when the optimal cost is at least one. No earlier optimal multi-robot planning method had achieved such a guarantee.
arxiv-2510-21739:
Liangqi Yuan and five co-authors chart how large language models can run drone operations end to end, from a spoken order to a flown mission. Research so far has toyed with small drones and isolated pieces like path planning. Real medium and long-range aircraft bring airport procedures and dense regulations. They also carry unforgiving mission standards that toys never face.

Their NeLV system chains five components. A language model parses the instruction, and a route planner picks points of interest. A path planner lays waypoints, and a control platform flies the trajectory. Monitoring watches the execution. Demonstrations cover multi-drone patrol, multi-stop delivery, and multi-hop relocation. Beyond the working system, a five-level taxonomy maps the road from today's parser role to a fully autonomous autopilot. It names the technical prerequisites and open challenges at each rung.
arxiv-2510-21839:
Pragna Prahallad and Pranathi Prahallad test whether a general chatbot can sort chest X-rays into normal or pneumonia cases without any medical training on the task. They gave the gpt-4o model a balanced set of four hundred images, half from each class, and tried four prompt styles ranging from bare instructions to detailed reasoning requests.

The simplest, feature-focused prompts did best, reaching seventy-four percent accuracy, while prompts asking for step-by-step reasoning scored lower. The authors read the result as early promise rather than readiness: a general model shows some feel for the images, but its reliability falls well short of clinical use. Better visual reasoning and domain-specific adaptation would be needed before such tools could assist diagnosis safely.
arxiv-2510-22039:
Po-Chen Kuo, Han Hou, Will Dabney, and Edgar Y. Walker borrow a brain idea to help agents track a hidden world. An agent that sees only part of its world needs a compact memory of the past. That memory should match the true odds over hidden states. It is the Bayes-optimal belief. Agents that adapt across tasks often act well without forming that clean picture.

The team adds self-supervised prediction modules. The modules constantly forecast the next sensory input. The idea comes from predictive coding in neuroscience. In simulated tasks, agents with the add-on formed clearer internal pictures. Their states sat much closer to true belief states. Standard agents did not, even when both solved the tasks equally well. The benefit held across many task types. Some tasks demanded active information seeking.
arxiv-2510-22439:
Ali Vosoughi and five co-authors present PromptReverb, a system that creates room impulse responses, the acoustic fingerprints that make virtual sound feel like a real room. Good training data at full bandwidth is scarce, and older methods cannot take varied inputs. Their two stage design first expands limited recordings to full band quality and then generates new responses from plain text descriptions.

Tests show the generated responses beat widely used baselines on echo time error and sound more realistic in room measures. The method suits virtual reality, building acoustics, and audio production, where flexible high quality room sound is needed.
arxiv-2510-22539:
Slow workers can hold up training that is split across many machines. Such slow workers are called stragglers. Heekang Song and Wan Choi wrote a 2025 paper on this flaw. Their plan is a coding scheme for gradients. Gradients are the step signals used in training. Each worker has its own chance to lag.

Coded shares of the data go to each worker. The main machine can then rebuild the full step. It needs shares from only some of the workers. The pair find the best code weights in closed form. Tests show the method settles fast. It also cuts the harm done by slow workers.
arxiv-2510-23039:
Ved Danait, Srijan Das, and Sujoy Bhore design compact sketches for two core tasks on massive data streams: finding near neighbors and estimating kernel density. Data arrives fast and changes over time, so storing it all is not an option. A good sketch keeps the structure needed to answer queries while using far less than linear space.

The authors give new sketching algorithms with sublinear space and query time for both tasks in a dynamic stream. Their guarantees hold as items come and go. Such sketches could help search and monitoring systems stay fast without keeping full copies of huge live data.
arxiv-2510-23839:
John C. Howell and two co-authors show how to rebuild a full spectrum of reflected light using only a handful of blinking LEDs. The setup flashes an object with random patterns from light-emitting diodes, each with a known Gaussian spectrum overlapping its neighbors. From the measured responses, digital signal processing recovers the object's continuous reflectance curve.

The authors gauge the information in the patterns using singular value decomposition. Spectra are rebuilt through its pseudoinverse and tested on hemoglobin and green vegetation at a set noise level. Sparse plant spectra came back with under one percent error using as few as twenty-five LEDs. The point is economic: random structured lighting lets cheap LED cameras match expensive spectrometers for dedicated jobs. That trade could put spectral imaging into settings where cost has kept it out.
arxiv-2510-24039:
Nikolaos Karalias and six co-authors build a neural method for hard choice problems that must obey strict limits. Such problems appear in planning and design, but teaching a network to respect discrete rules is tough. A network may give a near answer that breaks the rules and cannot be used.

Their framework uses ideas from convex geometry to split a network output into a mix of corner points from a shape that marks all valid answers. That mix can then be rounded to a valid answer with little loss in quality. In tests on problems with limits on how many items can be picked, the method beat prior approaches and kept its answers valid.
arxiv-2510-24239:
Zhen-Hao Gong and three co-authors build a framework to identify which mechanisms drive third order nonlinear transport in disordered materials. In such transport, quantum geometric effects can create higher harmonic voltages from a driving current, a fast growing field. In real materials, disorder scattering also contributes, so telling the mechanisms apart is hard.

Treating geometric and disorder effects on equal footing, the team finds twenty mechanisms for third order transport in total. More importantly, they give a symmetry guided method to resolve which mechanisms are at work in measured data. No general analysis framework existed before for nonlinear transport at any order, so this fills a basic gap for experiments.
arxiv-2510-24639:
Pedro P Sanchez, Damian Machlanski, Steven McDonagh, and Sotirios A Tsaftaris study how to find cause links in data that change over time. Such links matter in the body, the brain, the weather, and markets. A common shortcut picks one time order of the parts, but that choice cuts what the final map can show.

Their method, DOTS, uses more than one valid order at once. By joining the orders, it can rebuild more of the true cause map and dodge fake links. It uses a spread based score trick to gauge curve shape fast. Broad tests back the claim and show gains over one order ways.
arxiv-2510-24739:
Mario Angelelli, Morena Oliva, Serena Arima, and Enrico Ciavolino check if AI made survey forms can match a human made one. They took a known form on body sense and had a chat model make two new forms of it. One AI form had more plain cues on what each part should tap than the other.

Though the words looked close to the source, the forms split in key ways. Their shape in terms of traits tapped, and where they gave the most facts across trait levels, both shifted. A Bayes graded model was used to gauge the forms. The lesson is that word feel is not enough; stat checks must back AI forms.
arxiv-2510-25239:
Moritz Lucas, Hamid Ebrahimy, Viacheslav Barkov, Ralf Pecenka, Kai-Uwe Kuhnberger, and Bjorn Waske use deep learning to map trees that stand out of woods, in farm lands. Lone and lined trees hold life, store carbon, and cool the air, yet past maps lumped them as one class or used fixed cuts. Their set is new, built from high grade air shots of four farm zones.

Six net forms were tried, from coil nets to vision transformers and mixes of both. Four kinds were mapped: woods, patch, line, and lone tree. The best mix form scored well on both shared area and class marks. Such maps can guide farm and land care with more fine kinds.
arxiv-2510-25439:
Kristoffer Eggestad led four co-authors on ferroelectric phase transitions. Ida C Skogvoll, Oystein Gullbrekken, and Benjamin A D Williamson helped. Sverre M Selbach closes the five-author team. First-principles run of such transitions is computationally hard. Machine-learned force fields offer a new avenue.

Force fields were generated with on-the-fly training. Only zero-kelvin ground state forms supplied training input. Four well-studied ferroelectric oxides were investigated here. They are barium titanate, lead titanate, lithium niobate, bismuth ferrite. PBEsol proved more robust than other functionals tested. Abrupt first-order transitions appeared for two oxides correctly. Lithium niobate showed mixed displacive and order-disorder character. Likely and limitations of the method are discussed.
arxiv-2510-25539:
Marcus V Marinho and Eric C Andrade study quantum spin liquids. Their 2025 physics paper studies disordered non-Kramers pyrochlores. Pyrochlore oxides host ions with special magnetic traits. Structural randomness acts as a transverse field. That presents quantum fluctuations on spin ice manifold. Naively, disorder might favor short-range entangled phases instead.

They study a minimal disordered quantum spin ice model. The transverse-field Ising model supplies that minimal model. A real-space gauge mean-field theory is used. Stability of spin-liquid phase against disorder is assessed. Quantum spin ice remains remarkably stable against disorder. It persists until the polarized phase transition. A Griffiths region of enhanced fluctuations appears nearby. Average disorder descriptions capture actions well elsewhere. Inhomogeneous spin ice behaves close to homogeneous counterpart.
arxiv-2510-25939:
Robert A. Bridges, Thomas R. Mitchell, Mauricio Munoz, and Ted Henriksson survey what happens when large language models meet honeypots. A honeypot is a decoy computer system set up to lure attackers and study them. Designers have long faced a trade off between rich deception and low running risk, and models promised to ease that trade off.

Bridges and the team give the first broad overview of the new field since work took off in late twenty twenty two. They classify ways attackers can detect a honeypot, map how model based simulation helps or fails for each, and trace a common system design and test pattern. Their roadmap argues the real gain lies in autonomous systems, not single tricks.
arxiv-2510-26439:
Hongliang Lai, Mengyu Luo, and Jie Zhang settle a question left open since 1983 by Schweizer and Sklar. The question concerns an operation, written tau with subscripts T and L, built from two simpler operations on distribution functions. The trio ask when that operation counts as a triangle function, a kind of generalised addition for such functions, on a set written Delta-plus.

Lai and his two co-authors prove the operation qualifies exactly when three conditions hold at once. First, L must be a continuous t-conorm, a generalised or, with an extra stated trait. Second, T must be a t-norm, a generalised and. Third, T must be weakly left continuous, with full left continuity when L is of a certain kind. Closing a forty-year-old gap gives this corner of probability theory a firm answer.
arxiv-2510-26839:
Jonathan Chan explores how proof assistants can track their own extensions from inside the type system. Proof assistants let users add features and axioms that boost expressive power, but some combinations clash and break logic. Existing tools track which extensions a proof uses, yet that tracking sits outside the type system, so a definition cannot state exactly which extensions it needs.

Chan studies the Dependent Calculus of Indistinguishability, a dependent type system where terms carry dependency levels arranged in a lattice. He maps each set of extensions to a level, so the lattice describes how extensions may interact. That promises precise specifications, wider reuse of definitions, and even the chance to reason about one extension using another as a metatheory. The report is an exploration of that route.
arxiv-2510-26939:
Mihai Prunescu and Joseph Shunia present formulas that give a non-trivial divisor, meaning a divisor larger than one and smaller than the number itself, for every composite integer. Each formula uses only a fixed count of basic steps such as addition, multiplication, and integer division. One family comes from the hypercube method and yields the smallest prime divisor and related quantities.

A second formula avoids a hard step called factorial unwinding by joining two counts, one for squared divisors and one for distinct prime divisors, with root taking. The formulas need very long run times, yet the count of steps stays fixed. That contrast with normal search methods is the main point for readers in number theory.
arxiv-2510-27639:
Cynthia S. Froning and nine co-authors report ultraviolet views of the young star HIP 67522 in 2025. The star is seventeen million years old and much like a young Sun. Its outer layers glow strongly in lines that trace hot gas. Light levels wobbled by about fifteen percent, with two small flares seen during the watch.

High-energy light at a planet-like distance far exceeds what the Sun gives Earth today, by huge factors at short wavelengths. Tries to rebuild a key hydrogen line gave unreal results. Extra hydrogen inside the system itself seems to block that line over a wide speed range. The gas could flow from a planet losing air or from the star, a point that needs sharper views.
arxiv-2511-00039:
Krishna Kumar Neelakanta Pillai Santha Kumari Amma — the byline as recorded — studies multi-agent reinforcement learning for dynamic retail pricing. Prices must adapt to shifting demand and coordinate across related products. A strong MAPPO baseline is compared with a graph-attention variant that learns interactions among products. The test environment is simulated from real transaction data.

Profit, stability across random seeds, fairness across products, and training efficiency are all measured under a standardized protocol. Retail analytics readers get an empirical comparison rather than a single showcase run. Coordinated pricing matters because raising one product's price can move demand for its neighbors.
arxiv-2511-00839:
John Yang and colleagues introduce CodeClash, a benchmark that tests language models the way real software work happens: chasing broad goals over many rounds, not fixing one named bug. Models compete in tournaments, editing their code in one phase and then facing rival codebases head to head in arenas scored on goals like resource gain or survival.

Across many tournaments with eight models in six arenas, the team finds wide differences in development style but shared weaknesses. Models reason poorly about long term strategy, and their codebases grow messy and redundant over time. The results suggest current models handle isolated coding tasks far better than the open ended, self directed upkeep that real projects demand.
arxiv-2511-00939: Jurgen Muller revisits the projective cover of the trivial module for the sporadic simple Janko group J4 in characteristic eleven. The paper is a sequel to his earlier preprint, where the modular projective indecomposable summands of a permutation character for J4 were determined up to one remaining parameter. Here that parameter is fixed, using a new condensation method for induced modules that enumerates long orbits to make the computation feasible. The result completes the identification of this basic building block in the modular representation theory of the group.
arxiv-2511-01239:
Dipan Dey and Telikepalli Kavitha build data structures that answer distance queries fast even when an edge of the graph fails. Given an undirected weighted graph and a chosen source set, the structure must, for any source, target. One faulty edge, quickly estimate the source to target distance in the damaged graph, within a small multiplicative error.

Earlier work implied an oracle with stretch at most three but slower queries. Their construction answers in constant time, with stretch at most five and near compact size, leaning on a known single edge fault tolerant distance oracle between two terminals. A second construction trades stretch up to thirteen for a smaller structure. Both serve settings like road and communication networks that must route around failures.
arxiv-2511-01739:
Florian Nortier explores classicalization, an unconventional answer to a standard problem. Light scalar fields in effective field theories usually need protection from quantum corrections. Yet inventing new high-energy particles to save them may not be nature's way. In classicalization, strong self-interactions instead reorganize the theory's own low-energy degrees of freedom into extended semi-classical objects, classicalons, which decay into many soft particles.

Reviewing the mechanism with a simple k-essence model, Nortier argues a little hierarchy must remain. It must hold between the scalar's mass and the first new resonances. This is a direct consequence of the ultraviolet-infrared mixing the mechanism creates. Black hole physics mixes scales in a like way. He then examines how a scalar potential and couplings to fermions affect the Vainshtein screening at the theory's core, and how a chameleon-like screening can act in synergy with it.
arxiv-2511-01839:
Nelusha Nugegoda, Marium-E-Jannat, Khalad Hasan, and Patricia Lasserre explore how remote partners should see each other's work in mobile augmented reality. Phones can overlay digital objects on the real world for distant collaborators. But many design choices were untested for remote tasks. Among them: viewing angles, how manipulations are synchronized, and whether a small secondary screen shows the partner's current view.

The team designed five techniques mixing those attributes and ran a user study across two remote modes, one collaborative and one competitive. In both modes, one technique won on performance and preference. It let users view the partner's object manipulations asynchronously on the small screen. It did not force a shared live view. The study closes with recommendations for designing mobile AR tools that support remote work on shared objects.
arxiv-2511-02139:
Jonas Sauer, a mathematician in harmonic analysis, extends a powerful bootstrapping technique called extrapolation to a much wider setting. Extrapolation takes an estimate known for one family of weighted function spaces and spreads it to many others. Sauer's version is multilinear, works off the diagonal, and restricts attention to limited ranges, all at once, in mixed-norm Lebesgue spaces over general measure spaces.

The integrability exponents are allowed to run over the full range from zero to infinity. The weight classes are decoupled from the spaces being extrapolated between, apart from one basic consistency requirement. This separation yields new insight into how the bounds depend on the weight, and some endpoint results are new even in ordinary Euclidean space. A weighted transference principle for compact abelian groups completes the picture.
arxiv-2511-02339:
Omar Alehyane, Chinh Lu, and Mohammed Salouf work on a class of fully nonlinear equations that sit at the heart of complex geometry. Monge-Ampère equations on a compact complex manifold can degenerate, and their weak solutions may need to have prescribed singularities, meaning the solution's blow-up profile is fixed in advance. The setting here is a Hermitian, not necessarily Kähler, manifold whose reference form is semipositive and big, with a general positive measure on the right-hand side.

The authors prove such weak solutions exist and are unique. The result extends their own earlier work in two directions at once: from Kähler to more general Hermitian manifolds, and from usual finite-energy solutions to solutions whose singularities are prescribed in advance. Questions of this type feed into the broader programme of learning which geometric structures a complex manifold can support.
arxiv-2511-02439:
Xiang Liu, Mengwei Xu, and Liwei Zhang derive the sharpest possible tests for whether a candidate solution of a nonsmooth optimisation problem is truly optimal. In nonsmooth problems the objective and constraints are merely Lipschitz continuous, though twice directionally differentiable, so classical second-order conditions need reworking. Their conditions are no-gap, meaning the necessary and sufficient versions meet, and they require no convexity of the constraint set.

The key device is a new notion, second-order gph-regularity of the constraint functions, which controls the geometry of the feasible region and lets the conditions be stated through parabolic curves. The headline application is bilevel programming, where one optimisation problem is nested inside another. For that setting they derive second-order conditions for locally optimal solutions of the whole problem under standard constraint qualifications, carefully avoiding any assumption that the lower level's multipliers are unique.
arxiv-2511-02639:
Vieri Benci develops the theory of numerosity, a way to assign sizes to infinite sets that keeps more detail than the usual notions of infinity. His 2025 paper stresses how numerosity relates to ordinal numbers, cardinal numbers, hyperreal numbers, and surreal numbers, four frameworks that each extend counting in a different direction.

By joining numerosity with the idea of a continuum, Benci arrives at a definition of the Euclidean line, the straight line of classical geometry. That line, in his construction, contains all of the infinite number systems named above at once. The work is foundational rather than applied. It probes what a number system must look like if it is to host counting, ordering, and the continuum together, without giving up any of them.
arxiv-2511-03539:
Julia Ahlvind, Josefin Larsson, and Dennis Alp hunt late X-rays from old nearby supernovae to learn what dead cores they left behind. Years after a massive star explodes, its thinning debris should let hard X-rays from a newborn neutron star or black hole escape. The team studies two hundred forty-two nearby events across six hundred seven telescope observations.

Absorption is modeled with three-dimensional simulations of neutrino-driven blasts, since lopsided debris hides the center unevenly. Emission turns up in twelve supernovae, four of them for the first time, and several at later ages than before. Spectra fit interaction stories better in many cases. Upper limits on the silent majority still bound how many compact objects shine at late times.
arxiv-2511-03739:
Eugenius Mario Situmorang, Adila Alfa Krisnadhi, and Ari Wibisono add step-by-step verification to TextGrad, a system that optimizes text-based artificial intelligence pipelines by verbal feedback. TextGrad treats text like a differentiable quantity, yet it cannot check whether its own reasoning steps are valid. TextualVerifier fills that gap without rebuilding the host system.

Four stages do the checking: break the reasoning into steps, spawn variants, vote among them with a language model jury, and merge the consensus. Hooks attach at both the loss stage and the final result stage. Tests with a leading commercial model run in two phases, first standalone, then inside live optimization. Verified steps could keep long text pipelines from compounding one early slip into a confident wrong answer.
arxiv-2511-04139:
Dazhong Chen is the lead author among eight authors on CantoASR, a collaborative system for recognizing Cantonese speech, a low-resource language with six lexical tones, tone sandhi, and wide accent variation. General models such as Whisper post high error rates on spontaneous Cantonese, while large audio-language models reason better but need explicit tone and prosody cues.

Forced alignment extracts acoustic features, a lightly fine-tuned Whisper improves tone discrimination, and an instruction-tuned audio model then corrects errors with prosody awareness. Tests on spontaneous Cantonese data showed substantial character error gains over a large Whisper baseline. Combining acoustic detail with model reasoning offers a scalable route for tonal, dialectal recognition.
arxiv-2511-04339:
Federico Settimo and Bassano Vacchini study phase synchronization in a periodically driven two-level system coupled to a non-Markovian bosonic bath. Treatment avoids the rotating-wave approximation for both drive and coupling, and numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion supply the dynamics, a demanding but trustworthy route.

Robust phase-locking develops, and the synchronization measure quickly reaches a finite value at a special resonant-ratio condition: when drive amplitude over frequency hits a zero of the Bessel function of order zero. A static approximation from Fourier analysis of the driven Hamiltonian explains the effect. The condition gives experimenters a concrete tuning rule for locking a qubit-like system to its drive.
arxiv-2511-04439:
Anisha Garg and five colleagues fix a flaw in how language models learn to reason. The standard method, GRPO, scores each answer against its group's average reward. That can give credit to wrong answers that merely beat a weak group.

Their variant, CoRPO, clips the baseline at a fixed correctness threshold. Wrong answers can no longer gain an edge just by standing in poor company. The change is small, but it stops training from reinforcing incorrect behavior. The authors report better generalization from the corrected objective, a useful step for reward-based training of reasoning models.
arxiv-2511-04539:
Subati Abulikemu and three colleagues learn geometry-guided representations of functional brain graphs. Brain connectivity graphs are dense and weighted, and each person varies a little. The authors expect these graphs to lie near a low-dimensional latent geometry.

Along that geometry, both network structure and spectral traits should shift smoothly. Their generative approach aims to capture graph-level patterns, not just node-level features. That matters because labeled brain data are scarce, so supervised tools stall. A compact shared representation could help compare brains across people and conditions without needing large labeled sets for each study.
arxiv-2511-04639:
Alberto Merino and three colleagues improve congestion isolation in data-center networks. Distributed AI jobs can trigger sudden incast floods that choke shared links. Rate throttling at end nodes reacts slowly, while isolation in switches needs extra hardware logic.

Used together, the two tools misread some congestion and throttle too hard. Resources then sit idle while flows wait needlessly. The team's proposal targets that false detection and signaling directly. Better isolation should keep healthy flows moving at full speed while truly congesting flows are set aside, a growing need as AI clusters scale.
arxiv-2511-04939:
Harshit Nainwani and his co-author argue that search is not retrieval in AI pipelines. Most systems blur two jobs: finding relevant text and supplying enough context to reason. Their SINR framework splits those jobs into two linked layers.

Fine-grained chunks serve the search layer, where semantic accuracy matters most. Coarse, complete chunks serve retrieval, where reasoning needs the full picture. Direct links join each small chunk to its larger home context. The design adds no extra processing cost, the authors stress. Retrieval becomes an active assembly step, closer to how people gather and then read evidence.
arxiv-2511-05339:
Lars Grüne and co-authors study when compositional neural networks keep convexity in high-dimensional optimal control tasks. Neural nets help beat the curse of dimensionality in such tasks, and their layered form fits functions built from nested parts.

They build on a 2022 frame by Kang and Gong for net approximations of compositional maps in control. The authors check which convexity and strict convexity traits pass through those nets. Keeping convexity matters, since it can make the control task solvable to a true best rather than a local one, a key point for safe use.
arxiv-2511-05439:
Aayush Saxena applies variational autoencoders to find galaxy groups on his own, from public JWST spectra of distant galaxies, with no labels given in advance. Large surveys now gather more spectra than humans can sort by eye, so blind discovery tools are in demand.

The unsupervised method sorts the spectra into distinct classes of galaxy types. Saxena reports that the classes match real astrophysical kinds, some of them rare and prized. The work tests how far a learned latent space can act as a first scout for big sky surveys, flagging odd groups for human study.
arxiv-2511-05639:
Bobae Kim and a team of co-authors report test results for AstroPix, a pixel sensor built for gamma-ray telescopes and a future collider detector. The chip packs amplification and digitization into each pixel, uses little power, and can tile large areas. It began as a tool for imaging medium-energy gamma rays in space.

The team tested single chips, a four-chip assembly, a three-layer stack, and a nine-chip module. The module is the smallest prototype unit for an imaging layer in a collider calorimeter at the planned Electron-Ion Collider. In space, the sensor is headed for rocket and balloon payloads. The tests check whether the design meets the needs of both settings.
arxiv-2511-06039:
Mehul Srivastava and co-authors design a mechanical device that can click its stiffness between rigid and free. Compliant mechanisms move by bending their own parts rather than using joints. Adding an engage-disengage ability lets one mechanism lock or release its elastic segments on demand.

Their design rests on bistable arches, which snap between two stable shapes, plus a locking mechanism. The authors explain the working, list the design parameters, and size the parts with analytical formulas. A 3D-printed prototype passed both finite element checks and physical experiments. Three earlier design attempts that led to the final one are also described. The team frames the device as a building block for mechanisms that must switch roles.
arxiv-2511-07339:
Reza Marzban, Ashkan Zandi, and Ali Adibi redesign how large optical metasurfaces are invented. Designing surfaces with nonlocal optical effects by standard optimization means searching an immense design space under build constraints. Their system, GiBS, instead describes an entire device with a compact set of coefficients drawn from smooth bases like Fourier or Chebyshev functions. That shrinks the design space by more than an order of magnitude while guaranteeing the smoothness building needs.

An autoencoder-based manifold learning workflow maps the relationship between geometry and optical response, enabling rapid exploration and sensitivity analysis. The team validated the approach experimentally with a PEDOT:PSS broadband scattering metasurface whose measured response closely matched full-wave simulations across the 500 to 1100 nanometer range. They present GiBS as a scalable, build-aware platform for multifunctional metasurface design.
arxiv-2511-07539:
Bart van Baal and Anders Jerkstrand present ExTraSS, a code for the fading phase of supernovae and similar transients. Late on, radioactive decay powers the glow while thinning debris turns mostly transparent. Spectra then carry fingerprints of the whole explosion, not just its surface.

ExTraSS splits its three-dimensional domain across processors and solves non-equilibrium radiation transfer directly. That physics matters because atoms in thin gas depart strongly from equilibrium. Asymmetric explosion models feed the code, producing spectra observers can compare line by line. The tool helps turn late telescope data into verdicts on how stars exploded.
arxiv-2511-07939:
Aurelien Perera bridges two theories of how liquids organize between molecular and larger scales. Aqueous amine mixtures sit between simple solutions and microemulsions, with hydrogen bonding weaving local structure. Site-site liquid theory loses orientational links that field theory keeps, so each sees half the picture.

The bridge formalism reconnects the two frameworks. Local orientational order, dropped by the liquid closure, reappears as effective long-range behavior. X-ray scattering from simulations and experiments shows the unified account. Complex fluids in industry and biology are organized across scales the same way, so a bridge theory has wide reach.
arxiv-2511-08039:
David Ellerman contrasts marginal productivity theory with the labor theory of property using vector valued marginal products. Textbook economics uses single number marginal products and links competitive pay to a slogan about each person receiving what they and their tools produce. Ellerman shows an equivalent formulation where each added input changes a whole vector of outputs and liabilities.

In that vector view, the simple distributive shares picture breaks down. Legally, one party receives all outputs of a productive opportunity and also bears all liabilities for used up inputs. Property rights then follow the normal legal rule for assigning responsibility, which supports the labor theory of property.
arxiv-2511-08139:
Kushal Tatariya, Wessel Poelman, and Miryam de Lhoneux test whether positional encodings in language models interact with a language grammar. Languages rich in word endings can allow flexible word order, while simpler morphology often needs stricter order. Since models are usually designed for English first, an encoding choice might quietly favor English like structures.

The team pretrained monolingual models with absolute, relative, and no positional encodings for seven diverse languages. Four downstream tasks measured the effect across morphology and word order measures. No clear interaction appeared, contrary to earlier findings. Task, language, and metric choices strongly shaped conclusions, warning against broad claims from narrow tests.
arxiv-2511-08339:
Ruiyu Qiu and co-authors present LPPG-RL, a reinforcement learning method for tasks with several objectives ranked in a strict priority order. Lexicographic problems appear wherever a main goal must never be traded against lesser ones. Earlier lexicographic methods need hand tuned thresholds with prior knowledge or work only in discrete settings, leaving continuous control poorly served.

Sequential gradient projections find policy updates that respect the priority order, and the projection step is reformulated as an optimization solved fast by Dykstra method. A subproblem exploration component prevents gradients from vanishing, speeds convergence, and steadies training. Theory supplies convergence guarantees and a lower bound on policy improvement for the framework.
arxiv-2511-08439:
Alireza Abbaspour and co-authors lay out a structured framework for building safe data sets for autonomous driving AI, aligned with the ISO PAS 8800 guidelines. Perception systems learn from data, so flaws in collection, annotation, curation, or maintenance become safety hazards on the road. The paper introduces an AI data flywheel view of the data set lifecycle and pairs it with rigorous safety analysis to find where insufficiencies create risk.

Processes define data set safety requirements, and verification and validation strategies check compliance with standards. Best practices are set alongside a review of recent research and emerging trends in data set safety. The framework aims at robust, safety assured AI development for self driving applications.
arxiv-2511-08739:
Chiara Paulsen works on a density question in harmonic analysis that grows out of a classical theorem of Szegő about orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle. Szegő's result gives a clean condition on a measure that decides whether polynomials fill the whole square-integrable function space.

The sharper question asks whether monomials using only exponents from a chosen subset can already span that space under the same condition. Earlier work by Olevskii and Ulanovskii answered the question for a class of absolutely continuous measures. Paulsen takes up the same problem for Markoff measures, a different and less understood family. The paper sits in pure analysis, where such spanning results govern how well functions can be approximated by restricted polynomial systems.
arxiv-2511-08939:
Yingtong Dou and twenty-eight co-authors present TransactionGPT, a base model trained on the payment streams of one of the world's largest payment networks. The model learns to read and generate sequences of consumer payments. At the same time it serves prediction and classification jobs such as anomaly detection.

A purpose-built 3D-Transformer design handles the payment data's structure, with design changes that improve how data types fuse and how fast the model computes, while allowing joint training with downstream goals. Trained on billions of real payments, the model beats a strong production system at spotting odd payments and out-generates baselines on future payment prediction. It also outperforms fine-tuned large language models in accuracy while training and running faster, and the authors draw practical guidelines for base models over payment-like data.
arxiv-2511-09139:
Zijian Chen and four co-authors replace the fixed exam with a living one for large AI models. Hundreds of benchmarks exist, but most are closed-ended, vulnerable to overfitting as their contents leak into training data, and dependent on slow human curation that cannot keep pace with the models.

MACEval runs evaluation as a network of cooperating agents. Roles are assigned across the network, fresh test data is generated during the process itself, and evaluation is routed through a cascade, making the whole assessment interactive and autonomous. New longitudinal metrics quantify performance over time rather than in one snapshot. Experiments across twenty-three large models show the network works and trims a considerable amount of the usual evaluation overhead. The authors hope continual, agent-run evaluation becomes a standard direction for the field.
arxiv-2511-09339:
Arka Mukherjee and Shreya Ghosh build a tougher benchmark for judging whether vision-language models truly reason through science problems. Existing benchmarks report high scores that may reflect pattern matching more than articulated reasoning. Their test draws on one of the world's hardest entrance exams.

mmJEE-Eval holds 1,460 questions from India's JEE Advanced papers of 2019 to 2025, in English and Hindi, across physics, chemistry, and mathematics. Seventeen leading models were evaluated: closed frontier systems scored far ahead, while open models plateaued far lower despite huge sizes. When the reasoning load was raised meta-cognitively, even the best model fixed only about five percent of its errors. Ablations show the difficulty comes from reasoning depth, not memorization.
arxiv-2511-09539:
Mohamed Elaraby and Jyoti Prakash Maheswari build a framework for judging when synthetic data helps verify claims against long documents. Long-context language models promise direct fact-checking over whole texts, but hand-labeled training resources are costly. Synthetic examples could fill the gap, if their usefulness can be judged honestly.

Their framework varies three dimensions. Inputs change in length and domain, synthesis varies claim complexity and error types, and explanation quality is scored. Tests across benchmarks show long-context synthesis can improve verification in base instruction-tuned models, notably when augmenting human-written data sets. Synthesis also raised explanation quality even where verification scores stalled. The framework helps builders decide which synthetic data earns its place.
arxiv-2511-09839:
Xiaomeng Ding, Simon Weidenholzer, and Boyu Zhang study how firms in a Cournot oligopoly change not just their output but the very rules they use to revise output. Two principles guide rule revision, No-Birth and Survival-of-the-Fittest, both rooted in imitation. The model is symmetric, so differences come from the learning rules themselves rather than from firm size or cost.

Under these principles, all firms eventually adopt the same behavioral rule. Long-run outcomes include everyone using myopic best response at the Nash equilibrium quantities, and states where everyone imitates and produces specific symmetric quantities, including Walrasian ones. Rule revision thus shapes which equilibrium the market reaches, and the results extend to more general aggregative games.
arxiv-2511-10139:
Indranil Biswas and Sorin Dumitrescu study holomorphic geometric structures on compact complex manifolds that are non-Kähler yet have trivial canonical bundle, a non-Kähler Calabi-Yau setting. For the Vaisman subclass, they prove that every holomorphic geometric structure of affine type is locally homogeneous, meaning the geometry looks the same from point to point. The proof uses a decomposition theorem together with a weak Bochner principle proved in the paper.

If such a structure is rigid, the Vaisman manifold must in fact be a Kodaira manifold, a strong classification consequence. Related results give infinite fundamental groups for manifolds carrying rigid affine-type structures under self-duality or semistability conditions. The authors also exhibit simply connected examples with trivial canonical bundle that carry non-closed holomorphic one-forms.
arxiv-2511-10339:
Tomáš Čížek, Martin Balko, and Martin Schmid massively parallelize proof-number search, a best-first algorithm used to solve games, and aim it at the Sprouts conjecture. Earlier parallel versions scaled poorly across many cores. Their design parallelizes at two levels and shares information among workers, and it uses Grundy numbers to shrink impartial game trees before searching them.

On 1,024 cores the solver ran more than three hundred times faster than serial, beating the state-of-the-art Sprouts solver GLOP by four orders of magnitude while generating far more complex proofs. Despite exponential tree growth, the team verified the Sprouts conjecture for forty-two new positions, nearly doubling the number of known outcomes. The method is presented as useful beyond impartial games.
arxiv-2511-10639:
Vitor Gelsleichter Probst Curtarelli, Stephan Paul, and Anderson Wedderhoff Spengler propose a joint method for estimating where sounds come from and the noise around them. Beamforming systems need such a pairing to steer their listening. Estimating the direction of arrival and the noise covariance matrix separately is standard but wasteful, since each informs the other.

Building on an existing covariance framework, their approach finds a quasi-linear answer instead of the classic full search, simplifying the procedure. A new direction estimator works across all frequency bins at once, which helps in reverberant rooms. In simulations, the method beat classic techniques such as MUSIC at mid to high angles. It had lower angular errors, a stronger signal boost, and better noise rejection and interference blocking.
arxiv-2511-10739:
Naixin Liang and Damiano Caprioli model what happens when layers of gas slide past each other faster than sound. Such supersonic shear flows are common in warm and cool interstellar gas. How they shed energy controls heating, magnetic field growth, and the making of energetic particles.

Their two-dimensional hybrid runs, which treat ions kinetically and electrons as a fluid, follow decaying shear flows across the subsonic-to-supersonic transition. In subsonic cases the classic Kelvin-Helmholtz instability dominates, but supersonic shears instead form shocklets, shed energy faster, and make nonthermal particles. The paper examines how particle acceleration, kinetically induced viscosity, and magnetic turbulence depend on the flow's Mach number. It also weighs what follows for the warm interstellar medium, molecular clouds, and accretion disks.
arxiv-2511-10839:
Ivan H. C. Shum and Angela Capel design hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for preparing Gibbs states, the thermal equilibrium states of quantum systems, for two important error-correcting codes. Their targets are the Hamiltonians of the rotated surface code and the toric code, workhorses of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

The samplers use only local quantum algorithms. Preparing the rotated surface code's Gibbs state takes circuit depth of roughly half the lattice side, while the toric code takes depth equal to the side. The authors further show that with non-local gates allowed, the Gibbs state of the one-dimensional Ising model with periodic boundaries can be prepared in logarithmic depth. The preparation uses linearly many simultaneous measurements, a striking shortcut for a basic model.
arxiv-2511-11139:
Yiming Rong, Yixin Zhang, and their colleagues present a method that helps speech recognition use long background context, such as a full talk's slides, without drowning in noise. Standard systems miss domain terms when context is long and the useful words are sparse inside a large window. Their SAP-squared method prunes and merges context keywords in two stages.

Each stage uses a speech-driven pooling step that squeezes context vectors while keeping the parts the speech itself highlights. On slide-talk and audiobook data sets, the method reached top error scores and cut errors on biased keywords by a large share over plain baselines. It also held up as context grew.
arxiv-2511-11239:
Zhongbin Guo, Jiahe Liu, and their colleagues present GEODE, an architecture that gives vision-language models real 3D spatial skill by splitting reasoning from number output. Such models grew up on flat images, so they miss depth and layout, and their token outputs cannot state precise continuous values. Costly geometric encoders at the input stage clash with shallow 2D features as well.

GEODE adds two plug-in modules. One acts as a spatial co-processor, aligning explicit 3D data with image features and distilling spatial step-by-step logic into tokens the main model can use. The other routes special tokens to a small network that regresses exact values and 3D boxes.
arxiv-2511-11339:
Davood Momeni argues that puzzling shifts in cosmic distance measures may come from gravity that changes with environment, rather than from faulty calibration or new particles. Recent checks of supernova and Cepheid data show localized shifts in the distance modulus, the gap between true and apparent brightness. His candidate is Starobinsky gravity, which adds a squared curvature term and a scalar field tied to local matter density.

He derives how that field alters light travel in sparse regions and thus the luminosity distance. The corrections reproduce the observed shifts without pasted-on step functions. Standard model comparison scores favor the Starobinsky frame over ad hoc models, casting it as a minimal geometric account.
arxiv-2511-11439:
Yiling He, Junchi Lei, and their colleagues propose RETROFIT, a continual learning method for binary security analysis that forgets in a controlled way and needs no stored old data. Deep learning now supports malware reasoning, but shifting threats and code styles erode accuracy over time, and replaying old data is often barred in sensitive security settings. RETROFIT instead merges the previously trained model and the newly tuned one, which act as teachers of old and new knowledge.

Forgetting is steered by keeping changes inside low-rank, sparse directions that stay near-orthogonal to past knowledge. A confidence-guided rule then blends the two teachers case by case. Tests on malware detection under drift and a second application show strong retention with adaptability kept.
arxiv-2511-11539:
Diptarka Chakraborty, Kushagra Chatterjee, Debarati Das, and Tien-Long Nguyen extend fair clustering to many groups at once. People in real data belong to many protected groups at once. Age, ethnicity, and gender all define groups. Plain clustering can underrepresent some communities. The fix should change the first clustering as little as possible.

Past work on closest fair clustering handled just two groups. Here, methods seek the nearest clustering that treats many groups fairly. The methods can run as a post-processing step. Fairness gains are weighed against how far the result moves from the natural grouping. The extension matters wherever clustering feeds choices about real people.
arxiv-2511-11739:
Christina Schenk and four co-authors build decision tools for fleets of near-identical machines. Each machine in a fleet behaves a little differently. In high-throughput work, such as fleets of 3D printers, this device noise quietly harms repeatability. At the scale of building-sized printing, it can cause real damage or loss.

Their method profiles the noise of each device. It then uses divergence measures and clustering to pick a strategy. The choice is between tuning on one device and tuning robustly across several. Standard methods assume the machines are all the same. Here, the differences are measured and managed head-on. Fleets can then grow without losing trust in their output.
arxiv-2511-11839:
Milena Piotrowska and Francesco Giacosa define a weak decay constant for positronium. Positronium is a bound state of an electron and a positron. It is the lightest purely leptonic atom-like system. Its annihilation through light is well understood. Its weak side is heavily suppressed and largely unexplored.

A composite field theory frame, built for two-photon decay, is extended here. The new constant plays the role that decay constants play for mesons. It measures how the bound state couples to the weak axial current. That coupling reveals internal structure. A concrete numeric estimate is given. The system's simplicity makes it an ideal test bed for field theory of composite systems.
arxiv-2511-11939:
Manya Bansal and four co-authors present Prism, a language that restores modularity to GPU code. Low-level control is kept intact. Peak GPU performance needs two mindsets at once. One is per-thread control of behavior. The other is collective action by groups of threads, as in tensor core instructions.

Functions that hide collective operations are treacherous today. They look per-thread but must run cooperatively. Typed perspectives fix the mismatch. The type system records the granularity at which each code piece operates. The compiler then enforces the cooperation contract. A persistent source of GPU bugs is attacked at its root.
arxiv-2511-12039:
S. Mahmoud Mousawi and Sandra Zilles study how a language can be identified from positive examples alone. In language learning, a characteristic set is a small set of labeled words that lets an algorithm pin down the target language within a class. Their new notion keeps only the positive examples, the words that do belong.

They examine this idea for relational pattern languages, a family used in string processing tasks. Positive-only sets matter because in many settings no reliable negative examples are given. The work sets out when such small positive sets exist and what they must contain for a learner to identify the target language efficiently within its class.
arxiv-2511-12239:
Tarun Gupta and Danish Pruthi question whether having a world model is the right test for whether an AI system understands. World models are inner representations that track objects and causes and predict what will happen next. Many researchers hope that finding such models in AI would signal human-like understanding.

Drawing on case studies from the philosophy of science, the authors examine where world model ability and human understanding come apart most clearly. They stress that these cases reflect particular views of understanding, not a single agreed definition. Still, the contrast helps show limits of the world model frame for judging what a system truly grasps.
arxiv-2511-13439:
Sarah Klanderman and 4 co-authors characterize transfer systems for non-abelian groups. For a finite group, a transfer system gives homotopy theorists a combinatorial way to track equivariant structure. The non-abelian case is richer and less fully mapped than the abelian one.

The authors compute the width of transfer systems for all dihedral, quaternion, and dicyclic groups in explicit terms. They also grow the catalog of known transfer system lattices, adding dihedral, dicyclic, Frobenius, and alternating groups. Those lattices help combinatorialists spot patterns and test conjectures. Each new family turns scattered examples into a chart that later work can extend.
arxiv-2511-13739:
Byung-Kwan Ko, Soowon Kim, and Seo-Hyun Lee study how to decode imagined speech from brain signals for people the system has never seen. Brain patterns vary hugely between individuals, so a decoder trained on others often fails on a new user. Their work tests training rhythm and tiny personal calibration as two cheap remedies.

Cycling quickly between subjects in short training segments gave modest but steady gains on unseen users. Adding just a tenth of the new user's data for calibration lifted accuracy and discrimination scores sharply under a leave-one-subject-out test. The pairing of cyclic training with light calibration offers a scalable route to brain-computer interfaces that adapt without long personal training sessions.
arxiv-2511-13839:
A. de Oliveira Junior, Rafael A. Macedo, Jakub Czartowski, Jonatan Bohr Brask, and one co-author ask where a key quantum resource comes from. Quantum advantage needs states with nonstabiliserness, a property that makes them hard to mimic on ordinary computers. The team studies whether simply putting a well-behaved starting state in contact with a heat bath can create that property.

Under mild assumptions about heat and work, they find an exact condition for when such thermal contact can do the job. For single qubits they list every reachable state of this kind and bound how much of the resource can appear. They also name the Hamiltonians and threshold temperatures that work best, and prove a general trade-off with the system's starting free energy.
arxiv-2511-14239:
Sourav Ghosh grows a classic tool of operator theory from one operator to a pair. The Sz.-Nagy-Foias theory treats a single contraction, a map that shrinks lengths, by placing it in a larger space where its acts become clear. Ghosh's note builds the same kind of theory for two such maps at once, both their dilation side and their model side.

The pair does not swap order in the plain way. The two maps obey a twisted swap rule, scaled by a phase factor q of length one, a rule called q-commutation. Results in that twisted case widen the known one-map picture. They let the same model tools treat pairs whose swap rule is braided rather than plain.
arxiv-2511-14639:
Marco Acerbis and three co-authors present SLAM-AGS, a pretraining framework for computational cytology. Cell level labels are costly and often unreliable, while abnormal cells can be extremely rare. Their method learns from slide level labels only. It mixes a weakly supervised similarity task on negative patches with a contrastive task on positive patches.

Adaptive gradient surgery resolves conflicts between the two training tasks. The pretrained encoder feeds an attention based system for slide level prediction. That system also retrieves the most abnormal cells in a slide. On a public bone marrow data set, the method improves detection and retrieval. Gains hold even when abnormal cells are simulated as very rare.
arxiv-2511-14739:
Sourabh Magare, Abhinav Roy, and three co-authors forecast what space-based gravitational wave detectors will learn from merging massive black holes. Such mergers, expected to be heard by the future LISA mission, can probe the distant universe and show how galaxies grow. The team draws its merger population from a large cosmological simulation suite.

They check how simulation resolution and box size limit the lightest mergers that can be counted. The heaviest detectable pairs top out at a set total mass, and adding realistic delays from friction and stellar hardening shifts the expected signals. The forecasts help planners know what LISA-class missions should and should not expect to find.
arxiv-2511-14939:
Daniel Oliveira de Brito, Letícia Gabriella de Souza, and three co-authors test whether pretrained audio models can spot COVID-19 from coughs and speech. The team fine-tunes an audio masked-autoencoder model and three sizes of a popular audio network family on two public benchmark collections. Careful splits by age and gender block the models from cheating on demographic clues.

Within one collection, results are moderate, with the autoencoder model clearly ahead on the stronger set. Across collections, though, every model fails badly, sometimes scoring near chance. That collapse is the real finding: cough-based screening tools trained on one data set do not yet travel safely to another, a warning for health deployment.
arxiv-2511-15039:
Kousuke Kuto and Yaping Wu examine extreme steady patterns in a classic two-species competition model with cross-diffusion. In that model, each species spreads partly in response to the other's density, which can drive striking segregation. When one cross-diffusion rate grows without bound, the steady states are described by simpler shadow systems of three known types.

Building on earlier work on one shadow type, the authors prove that a branch of coexistence states exists whose one component blows up as a key parameter nears a threshold eigenvalue. They also prove the blow-up states are unstable. The analysis clarifies how intense cross-diffusion forces one species toward a singular, spiked profile.
arxiv-2511-15239:
Tomoki Nakao, Kazumi Kasaura, and Tadashi Kozuno solve a social problem for robots: how head-on agents should step aside for each other. When independent agents plan without sharing goals, mirror-image setups cause deadlock, since neither side has a reason to pick left over right. Each agent here sees the others' positions, speeds, and sizes, but not their intentions.

Their method, WNumMPC, pairs agents' winding numbers, a topological count of how they loop around each other, with learned passing strategies. A reinforcement-learned planner outputs target winding numbers and urgency weights, while a predictive controller executes the motion safely. Learning the passing convention, rather than hand-coding it, lets swarms break symmetry the way crowds do.
arxiv-2511-15439:
Pei-Yao Song, Jin-Lei Wu, Weibin Li, and Shi-Lei Su propose a protected way to turn a single microwave photon into an optical photon. Such conversion links devices that work at very different light energies, a key need for quantum networks. Their setting joins a microwave cavity and an optical cavity through a group of Rydberg atoms, which are atoms boosted to very large, sensitive states.

The setup forms a lattice whose links depend on photon number, with a special dark state at zero energy. That state lets one photon travel between the two cavities with strong protection from noise. The math also shows a winding number that changes smoothly, a new feature for this kind of system.
arxiv-2511-15539:
Deeponjit Bose and Andrzej Sitarz compute geometric quantities for a noncommutative torus, a space where the order of multiplication matters, unlike ordinary geometry. They work with a spectral triple, a package of algebra, space, and a Dirac operator that encodes geometry in this setting. Their Dirac operator differs from a standard symmetric one by a partial rescaling that varies across the space.

Carrying out the calculation explicitly, they obtain the spectral metric, the torsion, and the Einstein tensor for this nontrivial example. Both the torsion and the Einstein tensor turn out to vanish identically. That flat outcome, despite the rescaling, makes the example a useful test case for theories of noncommutative gravity.
arxiv-2511-15639:
Mark T. Lusk derives an exact formula for gravitational Faraday rotation, the twisting of light polarization as light passes through curved space-time near a rotating mass. The formula is written for observers in the ADM split, a way of slicing space-time into space evolving over time, applied to the Kerr solution for a spinning black hole. The reference frame is a triad carried along without extra rotation, aligned with the light direction.

The closed-form rate is implemented and checked against numerical predictions. Because the sliced coordinates avoid a known singularity at the ergosphere, the boundary where space itself is dragged around, predictions can be made for light paths that pierce that region. One observer can compare measured twist against the formula directly.
arxiv-2511-15739:
Floyd Creevey and Lloyd Hollenberg use genetically engineered quantum circuits to encode financial market indicators. Quantum finance needs fast loading of real data into quantum states. Their approach applies a genetic algorithm framework for state preparation to stock price data. Optimization targets both encoding quality and efficiency on current noisy hardware.

Encoded prices are processed on both a simulator and a real quantum computer. The team compute a singular value decomposition entropy as a market indicator. Results show improved quality over prior encodings and promise for more precise analysis. The demonstration uses real world data rather than toy inputs. Fast state preparation remains a gate to practical quantum advantage in finance.
arxiv-2511-16139:
Yongnan Jin and four co-authors introduce a multidimensional rubric oriented reward model for aligning medical language models. Medical use demands more than static benchmark scores. Standards evolve, come from many sources, and span nuanced quality dimensions. Conventional reward models flatten those dimensions into one score. Their framework structures medical standards into a multi perspective matrix that guides data generation and optimization.

Geometric projection reference constraints anchor the reward model to that rubric structure. Three alignment failures motivate the design: benchmark mismatch, evolving standards, and one dimensional rewards. Early results are framed around learning rewards that reflect real medical criteria. Better reward models could make medical assistants safer and more faithful to professional guidelines in practice.
arxiv-2511-16339:
Miquel Noguer i Alonso lays out a framework he calls Financial Information Theory, applying entropy, divergence, mutual information, and transfer entropy to financial time series. The goal is a set of principled tools for spotting regime changes, testing market efficiency, and building portfolios.

Each measure is derived with full proofs and paired with a practical estimation algorithm. Tests on S&P 500 data from 2000 to 2025 show normalized mutual information flagging structural breaks such as the 2008 crisis and the COVID shock more clearly than autocorrelation or volatility tools. The paper also gives an entropy-adjusted Value at Risk, an information-based diversification rule, and a market efficiency test built on the same measure.
arxiv-2511-16439:
Idan Fonea, Amir Peles, Sivan Niv, Goren Gordon, and Amir Natan present a black-box way to estimate uncertainty in neural networks that predict atomistic properties. Their ensemble-based signal works without opening or altering the multi-headed regression network, which suits sealed models that users cannot retrain or inspect inside.

Tested on sodium and aluminum systems across temperatures, the method scales its uncertainty signal to handle data whose noise level varies, a property called heteroscedasticity. The scaled signal reliably flagged out-of-distribution inputs in several test scenarios. It also tracked how well the model was converging during training, giving practitioners a second use for the same signal. It is a live diagnostic for when training has settled and when predictions should not be trusted.
arxiv-2511-16539:
L. Caussou and eight co-authors probe moiré excitons in stacked layers of molybdenum diselenide and tungsten diselenide, combining light emission measurements with lateral force microscopy. Interlayer excitons, bound electron-hole pairs split across the two layers, feel the moiré pattern formed where the twisted crystals overlap.

The microscopy maps the moiré superlattice's spatial profile while the spectroscopy records which optical states the excitons can reach. In samples twisted by a few degrees, a continuous moiré lattice extends over areas near the optical resolution limit. There the emission collapses to a few narrow lines whose energies match the moiré geometry. The match shows excitons moving in a controlled periodic trap, a step toward realizing Bose-Hubbard models with light-matter particles.
arxiv-2511-16639:
Wei-Cheng Tseng and David Harwath introduce Codec2Vec, the first speech representation learning framework built entirely on discrete neural codec units instead of raw waveforms or spectrograms. Codec tokens promise smaller storage, faster training, and better privacy, since the stored units are one step removed from the original audio.

The method trains with masked prediction, and the authors compare several ways of deriving the prediction targets from codec sequences. On the SUPERB benchmark, Codec2Vec performed competitively with continuous-input models while cutting storage needs by up to a factor of about sixteen and training time by more than half. The result suggests discrete codec units can serve as a general acoustic front end for speech processing.
arxiv-2511-16839:
Falk Dippel and seven co-authors build a discharge planning tool for heart failure that reads a patient's whole hospital trajectory instead of a snapshot of variables. Their method, TGDS-HF, runs diagnoses, vitals, labs, medications, and procedures through a compact short-context autoregressive transformer, then stratifies one-year risk of clinical instability or death.

Three design choices carry the method: category-level tokenization, recency-weighted time representation, and the sequence model configuration, each validated by ablation. On a Swedish cohort of nearly forty-three thousand patients, the system beat gradient boosting and BERT-style baselines on precision-recall area, with sound calibration. It held up when clinical concepts were scarce and training data limited. A daily aggregation refinement improved mortality prediction further, supporting discharge choices from primary care follow-up to palliative referral.
arxiv-2511-16939:
Yongtao Ma and Wenjie Dou fix detailed balance in orbital surface hopping, a mixed quantum-classical method for molecules hitting metal surfaces. Representing the metal's electronic continuum with finitely many states makes the simulated system closed, while the real process is open. The mismatch corrupts the dynamics and breaks the balance between forward and reverse rates.

Their remedy adds an electronic thermostat into the hopping framework, built to handle many discrete states efficiently, with the thermostat's amplitude derived rather than assumed. Simulations then reproduce the true dynamics and hold detailed balance over long times, where the thermostat-free version visibly violates it. The method gives surface scientists a reliable tool for nonadiabatic dynamics at metal interfaces, from scattering to energy transfer.
arxiv-2511-17439:
Patryk Krukowski and five co-authors present InTAct, a continual learning method with a mathematical promise: a network can learn new tasks without its behavior on old ones drifting. Most continual learning methods fight catastrophic forgetting heuristically; the few with guarantees constrain the weights themselves, which is expensive in high dimensions. InTAct instead works at the level of neuron activations, which are far fewer than weights.

The method identifies the activation intervals where earlier tasks live and constrains updates inside those intervals, while letting the network adapt freely elsewhere. Because predictions stay stable within the nested intervals, functional invariance is guaranteed in a tractable way. The approach is architecture-agnostic, and combined with prompt-based methods it reached state-of-the-art results on challenging continual learning benchmarks. The authors argue activation space is the right place to buy guarantees cheaply.
arxiv-2511-18039:
Thong Bach, Thanh Nguyen-Tang, Dung Nguyen, Thao Minh Le, and Truyen Tran restore safety in language models after fine tuning, which often weakens safety alignment even with light methods. They find that fine tuned models keep the geometric shape of their loss landscape for harmful content, so safety behavior is shifted rather than erased.

Their restoration method uses curvature information and influence functions to raise the loss on harmful inputs selectively, steering the model back without undoing task learning. Across model families and adversarial tests, harmful responses drop while utility and few shot performance hold or improve. The updates are precise and low impact by design.
arxiv-2511-18339:
Han Cao proves global solutions exist for a model of a viscous gas star that pulls itself together by gravity. The model joins gas flow equations with a Poisson equation for gravity, in a ball with a free edge. Gas pressure follows a power law in density, with the power in a set range tied to star models.

For the top power in the range, the start mass must sit below that of the classic Lane-Emden star. For lower powers the start data must lie in a guarded set near those stars, a set Cao shows holds cases past work barred. He also proves any strong solution's support grows without bound in time. That growth marks the Lane-Emden stars as strongly unstable in this model.
arxiv-2511-18439:
Debapratim Banerjee and Debabrata Jana probe how two draws from a spin glass settle in like or unlike states. A spin glass is a magnet with mixed bonds that freeze spins in a tangled way. The spread of overlaps between two copies tells if the system has one main state or many split states.

Their model uses a round spin form with a general spread of bond strengths. Two large outlier strengths sit close, at a gap that shrinks with system size. In that setup they prove the overlap spread has a smooth density at low heat, a mark of full state splitting. With one outlier the twin model stays in a single state. The edge of the bond spectrum thus decides the phase.
arxiv-2511-18639:
Predrag Janičić builds a SAT based frame to state, test, and justify reductions between hard problems. A reduction turns one problem into another, and for NP-complete problems it proves both share the same hard core. Textbook sketches of reductions leave a gap to formal proof that students and researchers must cross by hand.

Powered by the URSA constraint solver, the frame lets a user state a reduction in a checkable form. The solver then tests claims and helps justify each step. The flow backs human insight in place of replacing it, an interactive aid for exploring how hard problems relate. Teachers and researchers gain a workbench for reduction craft. Formal care here guards a core skill of computing theory.
