It detects which spectral regions the adulterant affects most, giving deeper insight into each case. That detail could guide portable, faster instruments for authenticity testing. Tests on synthetic and real honey mid-infrared data gave precise adulteration estimates. The model also correctly identified the parts of the spectra most changed by the adulterant.
arxiv-2512-14139:
Julian Speith and coauthors describe HAL in a 2025 paper on gate level netlist analysis, a key step in hardware reverse engineering. A netlist lists the logic gates in a chip and how they connect, and analysts study it to learn what a chip does.

HAL gives analysts an interactive visual interface, a plugin system that can be extended, and programming interfaces in C++ and Python. Built in plugins cover word level grouping, cryptographic analysis, simulation, and graph based search. Since its 2019 release, HAL has supported at least 23 academic papers and is used in teaching, industry, and government. The authors argue it makes this research more open and repeatable.
arxiv-2512-14239:
Juan Jose Guzman Landa and five coauthors present two context free grammars for Nawatl in a 2025 paper. Nawatl, also spelled Nahuatl, is a national language of Mexico with very few digital resources. Almost no text exists to train large language models or word embeddings for it.

A context free grammar is a set of rules that can generate valid sentences. Used in generative mode, the two grammars produce many syntactically valid artificial Nawatl sentences, which expand the corpus a lot. Word embeddings learned from the expanded corpus beat those from the original corpus alone on a semantic similarity task. The authors also note that cheap embeddings often beat some large language models there.
arxiv-2512-14339:
Natalia Gorobey, Alexander Lukyanenko, and A Goltsev study the no boundary wave function of the universe in a 2025 paper. The no boundary idea describes the quantum state of a closed universe with a Euclidean functional integral, a sum over possible histories with no starting edge.

The authors find a discrete class of privileged reference frames in which the equations of motion for physical degrees of freedom stay identical. In such a frame they obtain the quantum state with no boundary conditions. A condition at the pole makes the Hubble parameter grow without bound, which lets them regularize the integral by flipping the sign of the expansion energy. Their construction also allows a nonzero proper mass of the universe.
arxiv-2512-14539:
Dan Song, Ayfer Özgür, and Tsachy Weissman analyze an unusual way to clean noise from data: compress it. Their denoiser squeezes the noisy samples with a lossy compressor, and the reconstruction doubles as the cleaned signal. Earlier theory covered only noise that adds onto the signal. Their version handles any memoryless channel, where each symbol is corrupted on its own.

The trick is choosing the compressor's distortion measure to mirror the channel's own behavior. With that match, they bound how far the observed statistics stray from a Markov property and derive an exact formula for the denoiser's loss. Worked examples cover squared error and Hamming loss, with a comparison to rate-distortion theory.
arxiv-2512-14839:
Antonio Herrero-Brocal, Javier Perez-Soler, and Avelino Vicente push a core rule of particle physics to its limit. The gauge principle builds forces from symmetries, yet many models leave some U(1) symmetries ungauged, as mere global rules. The authors instead promote every SU(N) symmetry to a full U(N) gauge symmetry.

Their test case uses a U(3) by U(2) symmetry for the strong and electroweak forces together. In this frame, electric charge quantization and the observed hypercharge values stop being inputs and come out as unique predictions. The model also forces right handed neutrinos to exist and adds a U(1) factor tied to baryon minus lepton number. That addition gives neutrinos small masses in a natural way, and the authors suggest this symmetry may be the true base of both forces.
arxiv-2512-15239:
M. Lemoine reviews how magnetized turbulent plasmas can fling particles to extreme energies. This proceedings paper reports theory work backed by fully kinetic simulations of strong turbulence, from mildly to fully relativistic. Such turbulence may power some of the most energetic particles seen in the cosmos.

The findings fit a generalized Fermi picture of stochastic acceleration, which the paper summarizes. The biggest boosts come where particles meet sharp, moving bends in magnetic field lines and zones where the flow compresses. The acceleration rate varies strongly from place to place, with a broken power law spread that reaches very large values. That spread makes such turbulence an extreme accelerator. The paper also discusses what this means for particle transport and for the shape of energy spectra when radiative losses act over long times.
arxiv-2512-15339:
Peili Mao and four coauthors place virtual network functions inside huge data centers without wasting power. Data centers hold thousands of servers and consume vast electricity, so packing their workloads well is an environmental as well as a cost issue. The placement problem is multi objective and large scale, which defeats exact methods.

Their routing led evolutionary algorithm searches placements in parallel, guided by fast heuristic scores for quality of service. New memory efficient data structures keep the problem tractable on very large networks. The team also finds a simple, fast heuristic that stays competitive even on the biggest instances. Together the methods produce high quality placements for data centers with up to 64,000 servers. The work targets operators who must place network functions at a scale where naive search drowns.
arxiv-2512-15539:
Timothy Parsons and co authors measure how much massive star winds vary at low metallicity in a 2025 paper. Mass loss from massive stars shapes stellar and galactic evolution, but wind structure adds uncertainty to any single measurement of the loss rate. Most hard numbers so far came from stars in our own galaxy.

The team uses ultraviolet spectra of 20 OB stars in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. Comparing repeat observations, they find single observation uncertainty of up to 45 percent for cooler OB stars, similar to galactic values. Varying narrow absorption features are unlikely to be handled well by current mass loss models. Evidence for a binary companion to one star is also reported.
arxiv-2512-15739:
Sharif Al Mamun and co authors build a Bayesian framework for uncertainty management in financial risk work in a 2025 paper, dated December 6. Risk teams must forecast market volatility, catch fraud, and watch compliance, and point estimates alone hide how unsure each call is. Bayesian models quantify that doubt directly.

The team tests one day ahead 95 percent Value at Risk forecasts on S&P 500 returns, training on 2000 to 2019 and testing on 2020 to 2024. An LSTM baseline calibrates near nominal coverage, while a GARCH model understates tail risk and their dynamic linear model runs slightly liberal. Bayesian logistic regression improves fraud detection recall, and a hierarchical model gives transparent compliance scoring. GPU acceleration speeds analysis up to 50 fold.
arxiv-2512-16139:
Mengqi Xue, Yuchao Xiong, and Yue Song study groups of agents that come and go in a control paper published on arXiv in 2025. In an open multi-agent system, members migrate in and out, so the network keeps changing size and shape. Worse, some agents repel each other instead of cooperating, and disturbances never fully fade.

The authors recast the system as a multi-mode model where hostile interactions can create unstable modes. They extend stability theory for such systems and apply it to the open network. Their result: bounded consensus tracking, where agents follow a target with limited error, is achievable when network switching is slow enough on average. If the disturbances vanish, exact tracking follows under weaker conditions. The work guides designers of swarms and sensor networks with shifting membership.
arxiv-2512-16239:
Bohan Wu, Eli N Weinstein, and David M Blei generalize a classic statistics idea in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. Empirical Bayes sharpens many estimates at once by learning a shared prior from the data itself, famously described as learning from the experience of others. Classic theory assumes the hidden quantities are independent draws from that prior.

Real data has structure: arrays, space, and covariates. The authors pair each inference problem with a symmetry of the hidden variables' joint distribution, then derive the matching empirical Bayes method from that symmetry's decomposition. Classical empirical Bayes falls out as the exchangeable case. New versions cover matrix recovery, covariate-informed problems, and spatial regression. In simulations the methods beat existing denoisers, and real tests cover cancer gene expression, brain connectivity, and New York City air quality.
arxiv-2512-17539:
A. Madathil-Pottayil and coauthors study X ray spectra of PG 1535+547, a narrow line Seyfert 1 galaxy whose central black hole sits at redshift 0.038. They combine XMM Newton and NuSTAR data from 2002, 2006, and 2016, spanning 0.3 to 60 keV in the last epoch.

The spectra need several layers of neutral and ionized gas between us and the source. In 2016 the flux in the 2 to 10 keV band had dropped by a factor of about seven from 2006. The light was then dominated by reflection, with the X ray source sitting no higher than 1.72 gravitational radii above the hole. A joint fit of all three epochs puts the black hole spin above 0.99, close to the fastest spin allowed.
arxiv-2512-17739:
Johanna T Malle and a large team ask a money question for climate science: how sharp must climate data be before sharper stops helping? Impact models predict floods, crop losses, and heat harm from climate inputs, and finer grids cost dearly to compute. The team ran shared impact models across many sectors at grid sizes from 60 kilometers down to 1.

Most of the gain arrived in the first step, from 60 down to 10 kilometers. Finer grids helped only modestly, and unevenly. Temperature-driven impacts and mountain regions gained the most; rain-driven models on flat land sometimes got worse past 10 kilometers. The advice for data providers is blunt: fund the resolution jump that pays, and fix model physics before buying pixels.
arxiv-2512-18139:
Benjamin Teo and Cécile Ané work on fitting models of trait evolution to phylogenetic networks, the branching diagrams that allow hybridization alongside descent. Exact likelihood fitting on large, complex networks can grow too slow to use, so the paper looks for a sound shortcut.

The shortcut is loopy belief propagation on cluster graphs, which optimizes an approximation to the log likelihood built from factored energies. Through simulations with their Julia package PhyloGaussianBeliefProp, the authors vary the largest cluster size. They track the trade between accuracy and run time for Gaussian trait models. They close with advice on choosing that size, plus a proof about the Brownian motion model. For that model, likelihood based and factored energy based estimates agree exactly.
arxiv-2512-18239:
Yueqiao Jin leads a six author team testing what a hidden AI teammate does to student teamwork. Agentic systems now join group work in set roles, either warm and supportive or prickly and contrarian. The team placed 224 students in 97 online trios, some with a secret AI member in one of those roles, to draft a movie plot in ten minutes of chat.

The contrarian AI stirred debate and second thoughts, a kind of helpful friction, while the supportive one kept talk smooth and agreeable. Yet the prickly groups felt less safe and less pleased, with no gain in the quality of the final plot. Designers, the team warns, must weigh sharper thinking against group mood.
arxiv-2512-18439:
C. Swastik and a large team of astronomers present new images of LkCa 15, a young star surrounded by a disk of gas and dust about 160 astronomical units wide. Earlier reports claimed candidate planets forming inside the disk at 15 to 18 astronomical units from the star. The team's images, posted to arXiv in December 2025, were taken with the SPHERE instrument in the Ks band.

They used a star-hopping technique that avoids the self-subtraction artefacts which blur fine detail in standard imaging. Modeling the disk with both SPHERE and ALMA data, they found the dust behaves like porous aggregates rather than compact spheres. No new planets turned up; the team sets upper mass limits of about 1.5 Jupiter masses beyond 200 astronomical units. The results sharpen what astronomers know about dust in planet-forming disks.
arxiv-2512-18639:
Davide Brioschi and eight coauthors at the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics study fusion plasma turbulence in a 2025 paper. Using global nonlinear gyrokinetic simulations, they examine how fast ions interact with rational surfaces of the safety factor. Fast ions strengthen shearing structures born from the turbulence itself, and the team weighs this against competing effects such as profile dilution and quasi-resonant interaction.

The key finding is that fast ions lower the threshold for zonal modes, which then suppress turbulence strongly. In some regions turbulent transport drops to about a tenth of its original value. An n=m=1 fishbone mode also grows unstable, and its beat-driven zonal structure cuts turbulence further, unless it flattens the thermal profiles too much.
arxiv-2512-18739:
Y. N. Lima and three co-authors forecast a measurement the LHC will soon make: how many charm particles a single proton-proton collision produces. As data volumes grow, counting charm events by multiplicity becomes feasible. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, simulates the distribution with the PYTHIA-8 event generator.

They generate charm multiplicities across detector acceptance ranges and collision energies from 0.9 to 13.0 TeV, and probe how multiple parton interactions and color reconnection shape the counts. Comparing D meson counts with the underlying charm quark counts, they find the quark-hadron duality hypothesis holds. They test Koba-Nielsen-Olesen scaling on the distributions and fit them with Poisson and negative binomial forms. The results give experimenters a tuned expectation before the real data arrives.
arxiv-2512-19039:
Li Yan and Derek Teaney study paired-particle patterns seen when heavy nuclei collide at near light speed. Such collisions make a hot fluid, and its flow leaves marks on particles that fly out close together. The authors ask how much of that short-range pattern comes from fluid behavior itself.

Working from the Boltzmann-Langevin equation, they derive and solve an equation for equal-time two-point correlations. The answer splits into local and non-local parts, both scaled by transport coefficients of the fluid. The non-local part comes from two-to-two scattering. It gives experimenters a clear fluid signature to look for in short-range data.
arxiv-2512-19239:
Muhammad Raihannafi Fadhel and Chalis Setyadi use HERA collider data to map where matter sits across the proton's face. Coherent J/psi production, where the proton stays whole, carries a momentum-transfer pattern that encodes the transverse layout. They model the proton as three hot spots, one per valence quark.

Each spot has a width, a distance from the center, and an angle, arranged in a symmetric triangle. Changing those geometric knobs moves the slope of the cross-section in clear ways. The angle matters most at larger momentum transfer, while the small-transfer region barely reacts. The study shows which features of the proton's shape such data can actually pin down.
arxiv-2512-19439:
Rixin Yu borrows an old soliton trick to keep neural PDE solvers stable over long runs. Fourier neural operators forecast fluid and wave equations well for a few steps, yet errors pile up on chaotic or stiff systems. The classical inverse scattering transform, by contrast, is built on reversible spectral motion.

His IS-FNO ties its lifting and projection maps into a near-reversible pair through an explicitly invertible transform. Latent time steps then run through exponential Fourier layers that mirror spectral evolution. Benchmarks include the Michelson-Sivashinsky and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations in one and two dimensions, against plain and Koopman-style rivals.
arxiv-2512-19839:
Orlando Oliveira and Paulo Silva use a known lattice QCD object to solve a calibration task. The object is the Landau gauge gluon propagator. Lattice runs compute in grid units. Each real-world call needs the grid step turned into real units. That step is called scale setting. The team sets scales between runs at unlike couplings. They use propagators computed with large sets of runs.

Once the scales are fixed, finite-size effects show up at high momenta. The authors treat them with an effective picture drawn from perturbation theory. The method links the lattice results to continuum theory at high momenta with ease. They note the same plan can serve other Green functions from lattice runs. That widens its use for the field.
arxiv-2512-19939:
Rayan Ibrahim and Allison Moore give RNA pseudoknots a graph-based yardstick. RNA strands fold into complex shapes. Pseudoknots form when paired parts interleave. They resist strict counting and sorting. Chord diagrams picture such shapes, with arcs for paired bases. The method builds the diagram's intersection graph. It adds a distance-based metric on that graph.

In this frame, a pseudoknot gets a formal definition. It rests on a weighted vertex cover of the graph, built from a split of the diagram. The method yields a strict algorithm. It counts pseudoknots and sorts secondary structures. It stays alert to three-dimensional traits as well. The code runs in MATLAB. Tests used structures from the bpRNA-1m database. They confirmed that genus is a robust gauge of pseudoknot complexity.
arxiv-2512-20039:
Shubhanshu Shekhar designs stats tests that can peek at streaming data with no cheating. The setting is anytime-valid testing against a composite null. Data arrive one by one. The test must hold its error level at each stop. It must also reject false nulls in the end, for sure. Past theory sets a speed limit on such tests. It is a log term over the minimum divergence from the null class.

Shekhar shows a test that meets that bound, for finite alphabets. It rests on a universal e-process. That is the ratio of a universal predictor to the running null fit. The proof uses a saddle-point form and a minimax theorem. A general build extends the recipe to any observation space. Its optimality is checked for compact convex nulls and smooth density models.
arxiv-2512-20139:
I. A. Pshenichnov, S. D. Savenkov, and A. O. Svetlichnyi calculate how collider beams transmute into other nuclei. When heavy ions collide, nuclei break apart. Hadronic fragmentation and electromagnetic dissociation both do the breaking. The debris can form secondary species, which may contaminate event samples. The study covers neon-20 beams at the LHC and xenon-124 beams at NICA.

For light nuclei at LHC energies, hadronic hits dominate the transmutation. That reverses the electromagnetic dominance found for lead on lead. For neon collisions, cross sections and momentum spreads are given for the products. They span helium-4, carbon-12, nitrogen-14, and oxygen-16. Xenon beams at NICA will shed secondary nuclei by dissociation too. The authors find those will not contaminate the xenon-xenon data.
arxiv-2512-20239:
Josef Grus and co-authors formalize hierarchical rectangle packing, a layout problem found in chip design, facilities, and logistics. Rectangles must be packed into containers whose sizes are not fixed in advance. Some items are blocks whose own dimensions come from solving a smaller packing problem, creating up to seven levels of nesting.

The authors give exact formulations using mixed-integer programming and constraint programming. Because direct solving scales badly, they design a multi-level logic-based Benders decomposition that refines block dimensions on the fly. On synthetic tests with up to eighty items per block, their method beat both the monolithic formulations and a bottom-up benchmark. The gains matter most for large, deeply nested instances.
arxiv-2512-20339:
Ye Tao and co-authors built MMEdit, a system that edits audio following plain text instructions. A good edit changes only the target sound and leaves the rest untouched. Earlier training-free methods hurt the signal, while trained systems suffered from scarce paired data and narrow task coverage.

MMEdit widens the task list to addition, replacement, removal, reordering, and attribute changes. A scalable synthesis pipeline builds large paired data sets with event-level labels to train on. The design pairs a Qwen2-Audio encoder with a diffusion-style generator so instructions align tightly with acoustic context. Experiments show stronger edit placement, better command following, and cleaner keeping of unedited regions than prior approaches.
arxiv-2512-20539:
Sai Cui, Yi-Jie Li, Guang-Zhi Xu, and Kui-Yong Liu push a standard calculation two orders further. When a heavy quark fragments into S-wave quarkonium, nonrelativistic QCD organizes the answer as an expansion in the quarks' relative velocity. Earlier work stopped at the second power; this team reaches the fourth.

Using the Collins-Soper definition of the fragmentation function, they first reproduce the known lower-order results for the two colour-singlet spin states. The new fourth-order correction comes out positive across a wide range of the momentum fraction, yet stays much smaller than the second-order term. That hierarchy signals healthy convergence of the expansion. Analytical expressions for the unequal-mass case are also obtained, covering mixed-flavour quarkonia.
arxiv-2512-20839:
Putu Indah Githa Cahyani, Komang David Dananjaya Suartana, and Novanto Yudistira speed up vision-language models by slimming the pictures before the model sees them. High-resolution images make these models slow and costly, yet most pipelines shrink every image the same fixed way. Simple images then waste computing effort on needless detail.

Their method inspects each image first, then picks a resolution and crop suited to its content. It plugs into the FastVLM model with no redesign and no retraining. On document-question data, per-image time fell by more than half, and the count of visual tokens dropped by over fifty-five percent. Preparation, not the model, delivered the savings.
arxiv-2512-20939:
James Aspnes pins down exactly what a broad family of simple distributed systems can compute once randomness enters the scheduling. He extends well-structured transition systems with a probabilistic rule for which interaction happens next. The resulting class covers population protocols, chemical reaction networks, and common gossip models, including versions given an oracle that ranks agents or sorts them into equivalence classes.

Two limits drive the results: any phase clock in these systems either stalls or races after polynomially many expected steps, and every terminating computation finishes or fails in expected polynomial time. From those bounds comes a clean characterization. With the ranking or grouping oracle, the systems compute exactly the languages in the class BPP; without it, only the symmetric languages in BPL. A whole zoo of models gets one shared measure of power.
arxiv-2512-21039:
Roopa Bukke, Chandranath Adak, and three co-authors staff a fake-news detector like a newsroom. Their framework, AMPEND-LS, assigns multiple agent personas to examine a story's text, images, and context through a structured reasoning pipeline. It is backed by reverse image search, knowledge-graph paths, and an analysis of persuasion strategy. A credibility fusion step weighs semantic similarity, source trustworthiness, and timing before anyone reaches a verdict.

Because large models hallucinate, a smaller language model classifier works alongside as a check on uncertainty. Across three benchmark datasets the system beat state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, F1 score, and robustness, and case studies show reasoning a human can inspect. Explainability is a design goal here, since a bare fake-or-real label rarely persuades anyone.
arxiv-2512-21439:
Geoffroy Morlat, Mehdi Khamassi, Raja Chatila, and their co-authors ask how machines can learn that morality depends on context. The same action can be judged very differently depending on the situation around it. Their framework, called COMETH, learns moral contexts from human judgments instead of fixed rules.

The team built a dataset of three hundred scenarios covering six core actions measured against three moral rules: do not kill, do not deceive, and do not break the law. One hundred and one participants rated each scenario as blame, neutral, or support. COMETH clusters scenarios by the pattern of human judgments, then extracts simple yes-or-no contextual features and learns their weights in a transparent model. It matched the majority human judgment about twice as often as prompting a large language model end to end. Its predictions can also be explained by the features that drove them.
arxiv-2512-21939:
Two Néel-type skyrmions in an ultrathin ferromagnetic film interact in ways that matter for skyrmion-based spintronic devices. M. Al Busaidi, F. Al Ma'Mari, and R. Sbiaa study the pair with micromagnetic simulations backed by a Thiele collective-coordinate model, tracking how separation, damping, and internal oscillation shape the motion.

When the initial separation exceeds twice the skyrmion radius, the pair repels along an outward spiral whose radial and angular parts depend sensitively on Gilbert damping. The out-of-plane magnetization oscillates in two components: a fast intrinsic breathing mode under a slower interaction-induced modulation. The model yields formulas for radial drift, angular decay, and logarithmic separation growth, matching the simulations. A tail analysis explains the exponential decay of the interaction.
arxiv-2512-22139:
Amur Saqib Pal and four co-authors present HLS4PC, a system that moves 3D point cloud neural networks from power-hungry graphics cards onto FPGA chips. Point cloud models, used for tasks like recognizing objects from laser scans, demand heavy computation and memory. Their sparse, scattered data leaves graphics processors underused, which hurts real-time safety-critical uses.

HLS4PC uses high-level synthesis with tunable settings to build efficient fixed-point hardware for both the mapping steps and the network layers. The team also compressed a leading model into PointMLP-Lite, four times less complex with only a small accuracy drop on ModelNet40. Their FPGA build delivers higher throughput than earlier work, and beats graphics-card and processor implementations by wide margins.
arxiv-2512-22339:
Debasish Borah and Indrajit Saha explore how collapsing domain walls could broadcast gravitational waves with help from the seesaw mechanism. When a discrete symmetry breaks, stable domain walls form, and if they lingered they would clash with cosmic data. A small explicit bias makes the walls annihilate, releasing a random gravitational wave background. The authors source that bias from heavy right-handed neutrinos of the type-I seesaw.

Quantum corrections from those neutrinos generate the bias term, tying the seesaw scale to the gravitational wave peak's amplitude and frequency. Both could be probed by gravitational wave tests and precision microwave background readings. In flavor-symmetric setups, the same tiny couplings can split the neutrino masses slightly, letting resonant leptogenesis explain the universe's matter surplus.
arxiv-2512-22439:
Khalfalla Awedat, Mohamed Abidalrekab, Gurcan Comert, and Mustafa Ayad present SuperiorGAT, a network that fills in missing slices of LiDAR scans for self-driving systems. Spinning LiDAR has fixed vertical resolution, and beams drop out when the environment blocks them, leaving holes in the point cloud. SuperiorGAT models each scan as a beam-aware graph and rebuilds the missing elevation information with graph attention.

Gated residual fusion and feed-forward refinement let the design stay shallow while staying accurate. To test it, the team simulated structured dropout by deleting every fourth vertical beam. Across KITTI driving sequences covering people, roads, campuses, and city streets, SuperiorGAT achieved lower reconstruction error than its rivals. It also showed better geometric consistency than PointNet-based models and deeper graph attention baselines, with minimal vertical distortion.
arxiv-2512-23039:
Laura Baudis reviews the hunt for dark matter particles through direct detection, the strategy of waiting underground for a galactic dark matter particle to bump into an ordinary nucleus. Her overview starts with the principles: what signals such collisions should produce, what backgrounds mimic them, and the main experimental techniques built to tell the two apart at extremely low rates.

The survey then turns to the current generation of experiments, which search for new particles across a mass range running from kilo-electron-volt to tera-electron-volt scales. Ongoing projects, their present status and results, and the sensitivity expected from future detectors are all covered. As a review, the piece maps where the field stands after decades of increasingly quiet detectors and null results. It also weighs what an eventual discovery, or continued silence, would mean for dark matter theories.
arxiv-2512-23339:
Subrata Majumdar and Debanjit Mondal prove controllability results for fourth-order parabolic equations steered by bilinear controls. The system lives on a one-dimensional torus. The controls vary only in time, acting through fixed spatial profiles. They multiply the state rather than adding to it, which is what bilinear means. Fourth-order equations model thin films and phase separation, and whether scalar knobs can drive them anywhere was open.

Two results are established. First, small-time global approximate controllability using three controls, between states sharing the same sign, obtained by adapting control methods with a family of frequency-localized controls. Second, small-time exact controllability to nonzero constant states. That comes from proving null controllability of a linearized system, then lifting it to the nonlinear one with a fixed-point argument. The authors note this opens the study of bilinear control for fourth-order parabolic problems.
arxiv-2512-23739:
Michaela Levi-Richter, Reuth Mirsky, and Oren Glickman set a homely test for household robots: someone says bring me a plate. The robot must guess where plates are kept, usually hidden in a drawer or cabinet. Robots can see and grasp, but they lack the everyday commonsense that tells humans where things belong. The authors formalize this as the Stored Household Item Challenge.

Their benchmark combines a small real-world set of one hundred item photographs with human-annotated answers from participants' kitchens, and a larger development set of thousands of annotated public kitchen images. Their system, NOAM, turns the visual scene into a language description of the space and its visible containers, then asks a large language model to infer the hidden item's likely home. NOAM beat vision-language baselines by a wide margin and approached human accuracy.
arxiv-2512-23839:
Kalina Mincheva and Naufil Sakran settle a conjecture in semiring algebra, by refuting it. Their object is the polynomial semiring in one variable over the Boolean semifield. A stripped-down arithmetic with only zero and one where addition and multiplication behave like logical OR and AND. Alarcón and Anderson had conjectured a description of its prime ideals.

The authors disprove that conjecture and replace it with a complete classification. Every prime ideal of the Boolean polynomial semiring falls into one of three classes, and the classes are indexed by the integers. Classification results of this completeness are valuable because prime ideals are the basic building blocks for the geometry-like study of semirings. A field where intuition imported from ordinary rings often fails and precise structure theorems are scarce.
arxiv-2512-24439:
Nimrod Sherf and five colleagues ask how wiring symmetry shapes the dynamics of neural networks. Real circuits overrepresent two-way links between neuron pairs. A random recurrent network models that bias. The knob is how strongly the two directions of each pair track each other. Complexity is measured by how fast the count of fixed points grows with network size.

A striking pattern emerges. Partial anti-symmetry strongly raises complexity. Partial symmetry lowers it. Other measures track the same split. Path length, chaos rates, and the spread of activity all follow. Two-way links that agree favor low, slow activity patterns. Links that disagree favor fast, chaotic, high-spread activity. Fixed-point structure looks like a key driver of dynamics. The results yield testable predictions about real circuits.
arxiv-2512-24639:
Siyang Wang, Hanting Li, Wei Li, Jie Hu, Xinghao Chen, and Feng Zhao present RadAR, a faster way to generate images with autoregressive models. Standard models build an image token by token in scan order, which is slow. RadAR instead starts from one token and grows outward in rings.

Grouping tokens into concentric rings lets many tokens be predicted in parallel while keeping local spatial links. The team reports that the reordering speeds up visual generation without giving up the strength of the original models. Readers interested in efficient image generation get both the radial design and the reasoning behind it.
arxiv-2512-25039:
Rina Anno, Vladimir Baranovsky, and Timothy Logvinenko prove an orbifold-style splitting for the Hochschild homology of symmetric powers of a small graded category. In noncommutative geometry, those symmetric powers act as symmetric quotient stacks. Their splitting shows the total homology of all symmetric powers matches a symmetric algebra built from the starting homology.

Methods are clear: both ways inverse homotopy matches between the standard Hochschild complexes are built, not just claimed. Algebra and geometry readers get formulas they can compute. Hochschild homology is a central object, so a symmetric-power formula lets new cases be read off old ones.
arxiv-2601-00139:
Brady Zhou and coauthor Philipp Krähenbühl give self driving vision a memory of roads already traveled. Their 2026 study notes a simple fact. Most streets a car meets have been driven many times before. Yet most vision systems treat each place as brand new. Their framework learns spatial priors from past trips. It stores them in a compact binary hash map.

The stored map is tiny for each area covered. It uses twenty times less space than dense storage. The priors plug into leading 3D perception systems. Extra computing cost stays small or zero. On the nuScenes dataset, object detection improves in a steady way. Gains appear across several model designs. For builders of driving systems, the lesson is cheap and clear. Past trips are useful data, not waste.
arxiv-2601-00239:
Ioannis Papastathopoulos and coauthor Jennifer Wadsworth build a geometric frame for modeling extreme events on graphs. Multivariate extremes ask how big values move together. Their approach uses the gauge function of a limit set. Scaled random vectors with light tails define that set. The result is a class of extremal graphical models.

Block graphs get the deepest treatment here. The authors prove how dependence measures travel along the graph. Some measures link to conditional extreme value theory. Those matter when variables peak at different times. Other results cover joint extremes, when variables peak together. A recent shift recasts geometry as statistical modeling. That shift lets these models fit real data. High dimensional extremes with tangled dependence gain a new tool. Risk modelers in finance and climate may benefit.
arxiv-2601-00339:
Alaa Saleh leads eight coauthors in copying the body healing playbook to keep sprawling computer systems alive. A distributed computing continuum links tiny sensors to big clouds. Faults strike often in such a mixed, moving fabric. Service breaks follow unless the system heals itself. Their framework maps four body phases onto four computing layers.

Containment echoes blood clotting at a wound site. Diagnosis echoes the inflammation response that follows. A meta cognitive layer plans adaptive recovery steps. A knowledge layer stores lessons for the long term. Language model agents power each of those layers. They read mixed logs and infer root causes. Recovery runs with little human help at all. Public fault data test the design across several models. Healing lands within tens of seconds in tests. Agent cost stays modest while depth of analysis grows.
arxiv-2601-00939:
Feng Luo and five co-authors present ShadowGS in 2026, a method that rebuilds 3D scenes from satellite photos despite shifting shadows. Photos taken on different days have shadows that fall in new places. Standard 3D splatting, which builds scenes from soft blobs, trips on those shifts. ShadowGS adds a physics-based rendering step drawn from remote sensing. A ray march then casts shadows that match the scene's true shape.

The method splits light into parts, so shadow and shine are not confused. A consistency rule forces the cast shadows to agree with the built shape. A prior shadow map helps when few photos are on hand. Tests beat the best current methods on shadow handling and on shape accuracy. They also won on the quality of new views built from the scene. Training took only a few minutes. The method held up on colour, sharpened, and sparse photo sets.
arxiv-2601-01939:
Robots that share space with people must learn social behavior, and training them needs a safe, flexible simulator. Victor Sanchez, Chris Reinke, Ahamed Mohamed, and Xavier Alameda-Pineda present OpenSocInt, an open-source package that simulates multi-modal social interaction and provides a modular architecture for training social agents.

The paper describes the software and demonstrates it through social navigation, the task of moving through human spaces without causing discomfort. Researchers can swap perceptual features, their encodings and fusion, and the agent design itself, making controlled comparisons possible. Released publicly under the GPL, the environment gives the human-aware navigation community shared ground for experiments that real-world trials cannot easily repeat.
arxiv-2601-02039:
Broadcasting rights are the biggest revenue source in professional sport. Leagues often sell those rights collectively. Splitting the money then becomes a problem of fairness and incentives. Gustavo Bergantiños and Juan Moreno-Ternero survey the economics literature on sportscast revenue sharing.

The survey stresses the allocation problem at the heart of collective selling. A jointly raised pot must be divided among clubs of unequal drawing power. The split must not distort competition or investment. Sports carry huge weight in television and platform viewing. The question is commercially large. The surveyed work connects two fields. One is cooperative game theory, where sharing rules are studied as axioms. The other is the practical design of league contracts. The paper serves as a map of what economists know and still debate about paying teams for a shared product.
arxiv-2601-02239:
Quantum steering, measurement mismatch, and instrument mismatch look like separate effects. They are now understood as faces of one resource: quantum incompatibility. Kuan-Yi Lee and three co-authors build a general way to certify that resource. Their nonlinear witnesses need no tuning step.

The witnesses come from convex functions. They are nontrivial exactly when the function is non-affine on extremal points such as pure states. For pure bipartite states, they lower-bound entanglement measures. They beat most linear steering bounds in that regime. The same construction certifies measurement and instrument mismatch too. There, the witnesses behave as genuine monotones of the resource. Two examples show the framework at work: a skew-information function and a coherence function.
arxiv-2601-02339:
Jingming He, Chongyi Li, Shiqi Wang, and Sam Kwong improve 3D Gaussian modeling. A method that builds a scene from many soft three dimensional blobs so it can be rendered and labeled at the same time. Recent versions attach meaning features to each blob for segmentation, but they train meaning and appearance separately. Guided only by flat images, and they add blobs based only on rendering errors, which misses faint regions.

Their framework joins the two branches. A shape descriptor built from the Laplace Beltrami operator captures fine three dimensional shape, helping separate objects that look alike. Blob placement and color detail then adapt using local meaning and shape signals, not rendering alone. The result is sharper rendering and cleaner labels with resources spent where they matter.
arxiv-2601-02739:
Jinbo Hao and five co authors reduce hallucinations that the prompt itself induces in a large language model. A misleading or thin prompt can push a model toward confident invention. Their method builds on a knowledge distillation chain style model and adds a code module that guides exploration of a knowledge graph. With the code itself woven into the chain of thought prompt. The model then reasons with accurate, structured external information instead of free association.

The improved distillation chain model is used to analyze and constrain the model's reasoning process, raising inference accuracy. Tests with two leading model families on several public data sets show the code module markedly improves how well the model captures context and cuts prompt induced hallucination. Scores on standard hit rate measures rose by roughly thirteen to sixteen percent.
arxiv-2601-02839:
Erika Kuno, Rin Kuramochi, and Kento Sakai study the large scale geometry of two families of graphs that interpolate between the curve graph and the pants graph of a surface. Both graphs encode how curves sit on a surface, at opposite levels of detail, and the interpolating families were invented independently. By Erlandsson and Fanoni in one case and by Mahan Mj in the other, for different purposes.

For each family the authors give explicit formulas for the quasi flat rank, a number that measures how large a flat grid like piece the geometry contains. The formulas depend on the genus of the surface, its number of boundary components, and the interpolation parameter. They also sort the geometries into three types, hyperbolic, relatively hyperbolic, and thick. The approach rests on a theory of twist free graphs of multicurves developed by Vokes and Russel.
arxiv-2601-02939:
Tomasz Downarowicz, Jean-Paul Thouvenot, and Benjamin Weiss prove a version of a theorem of Dan Rudolph for actions of countable amenable groups. Rudolph's original result concerns a single transformation and its invariant measures sorted by entropy. Loosely, among measures with entropy at least some value c, a typical one has entropy exactly c and is Bernoulli, meaning it behaves like a sequence of independent coin flips.

The authors extend that picture from one transformation to actions of any countable amenable group on a shift space. Their theorem says a typical invariant measure above the entropy threshold again has entropy exactly c and is Bernoulli. They also prove a relative version of the theorem, where the comparison happens over a fixed factor of the system.
arxiv-2601-03339:
Marloes van Asselt, Francesca Rizzo, and Luca Di Mascolo measure how thick the stellar discs of distant galaxies are, to test how discs assemble. Nearby spirals have thin and thick components, which may record an early turbulent phase or later heating of an originally thin disc. The authors fit full three-dimensional models to edge-on galaxies, explicitly allowing for slight departures from a perfectly edge-on view, which older methods ignored and biased thickness high.

Applied to JWST imaging of galaxies between redshifts one and three, the method gives a median scale height of about a quarter of a kiloparsec. Those values match the Milky Way and local thin discs, and run about one point six times smaller than estimates for local galaxies made the old way. Thin discs, it seems, were already in place early.
arxiv-2601-03439:
Vijay Singh and Shraddha Singh wrote lecture notes that teach a classic many-body physics method first set out by D. N. Zubarev in 1960. The method uses double time Green functions to study systems with very many interacting particles. Leading solid state physicists such as John Hubbard used it widely in the 1960s, yet clear teaching material is scarce.

The notes apply the method step by step, starting with free electron and boson gases that do not interact. They then treat the Hubbard model and show how the Stoner rule for ferromagnetism, the onset of magnetism in metals, follows from it. The approach extends to superconductivity as well. Readers need only basic second quantization, the math language for many-particle systems.
arxiv-2601-03539:
A. L. Wallace and A. R. Casey ask whether the famous brown dwarf desert is real. Brown dwarfs are objects between planets and stars in mass, and few have been found orbiting Sun-like stars with periods under five years. That gap led many to think such companions rarely form or survive there. The Gaia space telescope is well suited to check, since it is sensitive in exactly that period range.

Using Bayesian inference on nearby Sun-like stars from the Gaia DR3 catalog, the pair found thousands of systems whose data fit a brown dwarf companion. After correcting for observation biases, about ten percent of nearby Sun-like stars fit that picture, far above earlier rates under one percent. The authors note limits to their method, but the desert may be far less empty than believed.
arxiv-2601-03639:
Kecheng Zhang, Weijie Yuan, and Maria Sabrina Greco work on systems that communicate and sense targets with the same signal, using a waveform design suited to fast-moving users. The setting is bistatic sensing, where transmitter and receiver sit apart, inside channels that smear signals in both delay and Doppler shift. Accurate channel estimates are the bottleneck for both jobs at once.

Their semi-blind scheme frames channel estimation and data detection together as an atomic norm denoising problem, a method that recovers signals from few clean components. A custom penalty handles the awkward discrete symbol constraints, and an accelerated iterative algorithm solves the problem efficiently. Progress here supports sixth-generation networks that could track vehicles and drones while carrying their data.
arxiv-2601-03739:
Fabio Ancona, Elio Marconi, and Luca Talamini study entropy dissipation for a relaxed class of solutions to conservation laws, the equations governing flows like traffic and gas dynamics. Their quasi-entropy solutions allow more general behavior than classic ones. The authors first build a Lagrangian representation for such solutions in several space dimensions, tracking the flow's structure along particle paths.

In one dimension, for fluxes obeying a general non-degeneracy condition, they prove the entropy dissipation measures bunch on a thin, well-behaved set called one-rectifiable. The same result holds for the isentropic Euler system with a set pressure power, where they also slightly improve known fractional smoothness by using the sign of certain kinetic measures. Knowing where dissipation bunches is a step toward proving when rough flow solutions are physically allowed.
arxiv-2601-03839:
Nijesh Upreti and Vaishak Belle combine two neural frameworks so generated data obeys stated rules. Generative adversarial networks make realistic samples but have no built-in respect for prior knowledge or logical consistency, which limits them where rules are not optional. Logic Tensor Networks, by contrast, fuse first-order logic with neural learning, letting a model reason about and satisfy logical constraints during training.

Their combined system, LTN-GAN, enforces domain-specific logical constraints while samples are generated, rather than filtering bad outputs afterward. Evaluating across multiple datasets, they study how the constraints shape the generative process and report gains in both diversity and logical consistency of the samples. Rule-aware generation could serve fields like medicine, engineering, and finance, where a plausible-looking but rule-breaking sample is worse than useless.
arxiv-2601-04039:
Jie Gu, as sole author, disproves a guessed ranking between two ways to bound hidden entropy production. Both bounds apply to jump processes watched only in part. One uses the mean and spread of a current, the other uses waiting times and the one-way look of seen transitions.

It had been guessed that the waiting-time bound is always at least as tight as the current bound when both come from the same watched link. Gu gives four-state counterexamples in a steady state away from equilibrium where the waiting-time bound is the weaker one. No universal ranking exists under partial watching. The result warns researchers to compute both bounds rather than assume one always wins.
arxiv-2601-06739:
Daniel Munoz George and co-authors study random monomial ideals from large graphs in 2026. Their model is inspired by the Erdos-Renyi model of random graphs. They propose a new model for squarefree random monomial ideals.

The ideals are generated by edges and covers of a graph, they explain. This permits investigating conditions of normality for such random ideals. For those conditions they obtain asymptotic results in the paper. As graphs grow large, probabilities settle into patterns they compute. Random ideals connect combinatorics, probability, and commutative algebra in one object. Their edge-and-cover generation ties ideal theory tightly to graph structure. Algebraists get limit theorems for when random ideals stay normal. The work extends random graph thinking into polynomial ring territory.
arxiv-2601-06939:
David D. Dai and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers essentially no energy barrier between independent fermionic neural quantum state minima. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Neural quantum states (NQS) have proven highly effective in representing quantum many-body wavefunctions, but their loss landscape remains poorly understood and debated.

Here, we show that the NQS loss landscape is more benign and similar to conventional deep learning than previously thought. Exhibiting mode connectivity: independently trained NQS are connected by paths in parameter space with essentially no energy barrier. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07039:
Lihong Guo, Harry Ip, and Mingyang Wang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a swinging system with a lag in its spring. The system is a bilinear oscillator, driven by white noise. Such a model sees wide use in design and build work. It can show strong bends in how a metal acts, such as the Bauschinger effect.

Most teams find the long-run spread of the swing by Monte Carlo runs, which test the model with random draws again and again. The authors take a new path based on a PDE, an equation for how a spread shifts over time. Their path builds on the elasto-plastic frame set out by Bensoussan and co-authors. For a reader in this field, the paper gives a direct way to get the long-run spread. It skips the cost of vast numbers of random runs.
arxiv-2601-07139:
Junhong Zou and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers AdaField. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The surface pressure field of transportation systems, including cars, trains, and aircraft, is critical for aerodynamic analysis and design. In recent years, deep neural networks have emerged as promising and efficient methods for modeling surface pressure field.

Being alternatives to computationally expensive CFD simulations. Currently, large-scale public datasets are available for domains such as automotive aerodynamics. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07339: Victoria Motsch and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers impact of boundary conditions on the Double-Kicked quantum rotor. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors study the on-resonance Spin-1/2 Double Kicked Rotor, a periodically driven quantum system that hosts topological phases. Motivated by experimental constraints, the authors analyze the effects of open and periodic boundary conditions. In contrast to the idealized case of infinite momentum space. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07439:
Julián Garrido and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with advanced computing for reproducibility of astronomy big data science, with a showcase. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) faces unprecedented technological challenges due to the vast scale and complexity of its data. The work provides an overview of research by the AMIGA group to address these computing and reproducibility challenges.

The authors present advancements in semantic data models. Analysis services integrated into federated infrastructures, and the application to astronomy studies of techniques that enhance research transparency. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07539:
Ryo Okano and Daisuke Kurisu extend a popular causal method to outcomes that live in abstract spaces. The synthetic control method estimates the effect of a policy by building a weighted copy of the treated unit. Recent work lets outcomes be distributions, functions, networks, or covariance matrices rather than single numbers. Their 2026 preprint develops functional synthetic control methods for such metric space-valued outcomes.

When outcomes are curves or distributions, ordinary averaging and fitting need rethinking. Functional versions must respect the geometry of the outcome space. Sound methods here matter for policy studies where the outcome is a whole distribution, like income or health profiles. The paper speaks to econometricians and statisticians evaluating interventions with complex outcomes. It aims to give the method a firmer theoretical base.
arxiv-2601-07639:
Norm Levenberg and Sione Ma'u develop potential theory on algebraic curves, in a 2026 mathematics preprint. Earlier work by the second author defined directional Robin constants for a compact, nonpolar subset of a curve. The curve sits inside complex space of several dimensions. Robin constants measure how a set interacts with growth of analytic functions. The authors relate these constants to a natural class of Chebyshev constants for the same set.

Chebyshev constants govern best polynomial approximation on a set. Linking two kinds of constants lets results pass between potential theory and approximation theory. Algebraic curves give the theory concrete, structured sets to work on. The paper is aimed at specialists in pluripotential theory and complex analysis. It continues a line of work the authors have built over several papers.
arxiv-2601-07839:
Pawan Kumar and Aditi Gupta compress large language models with a two-stage scheme that respects their weight structure. Modern LLMs strain memory and compute budgets, for both deployment and further training. Their method, Hierarchical Sparse Plus Low-Rank compression, first removes the largest-magnitude weights into a sparse matrix. It then factorizes the remaining dense matrix with a recursive hierarchical low-rank method. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

Splitting weights this way keeps the few big weights exact while compressing the many small ones. Hierarchical factorization exploits structure at several scales. Principled compression decides whether a model can run on available hardware at all. The paper speaks to machine learning engineers facing deployment limits. It offers compression as a designed procedure, not a blunt cut.
arxiv-2601-07939:
Shireesh Reddy Pyreddy and colleagues present SECite, a tool that reads how later papers treat an earlier one. Judging a paper's strengths and limits is core to any literature review. Standard summaries only reflect the authors' own view of their work. Citations reveal how the community actually used, praised, or criticized it. Their 2026 preprint builds analysis and summarization around those citations in software engineering literature.

A citation can signal endorsement, routine use, or disagreement. Telling these apart gives a deeper, more practical picture of a paper. SECite aims to summarize that reception automatically. Scholars drowning in reading lists could triage papers faster. The tool also exposes limitations that authors would not advertise. The paper serves software engineering scholars and tool builders. It treats citations as evidence, not just counts.
arxiv-2601-08539: Jeffrey Spaan, Kuan-Hsun Chen, and Ana-Lucia Varbanescu cut compute waste in language models with kernel-level frequency scaling. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that AI growth has expanded GPU data centers fast. Rising operational energy use has become a critical bottleneck and sustainability concern. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers energy use with existing hardware and little effort. Applying it at kernel level targets the moments when full GPU speed is wasted. Such tuning could trim data center bills without slowing model serving.
arxiv-2601-08639:
Six authors, led by Tanmay Inamdar, study a hard choice problem on graphs. A graph here is a set of points joined by lines. The task is to pick a small set of red points that cover many blue points. The picked set must also stay joined as one piece. Past work treats each part of this task on its own.

The team gives one shared model for the whole task. They then look for fast methods that get close to the best pick. The methods run in time that stays fixed for a key size in the task. Such work helps when a network must serve many users but can build links at only a few hubs. A reader gets both the model and the near best methods.
arxiv-2601-08739:
Xingyu Tan and six co-authors work on safe use of fact graphs by chat models. A fact graph stores facts as linked triples, such as a name, a link, and a value. Such graphs can ground a model and cut made up claims. But many graphs hold private facts that must not leak to a closed model host.

Their tool is called PrivGemo. It uses two towers, one on the user side and one for search. The private graph stays on the safe side while the model still gets the facts it needs. No raw triples need to cross to the host. A reader who must guard data gets a plan for strong search with less leak risk.
arxiv-2601-08839:
Toshiyuki Shigemura builds a team of three chat models that check each other in a loop. One model drafts text. A next model checks if the draft holds up. A third model checks if the work is clear and can be traced. The loop runs more than once, so each round can fix the last.

He calls this loop Recursive Knowledge Synthesis. The claim is that the loop makes a whole that no one model can match on its own. He also gives ways to test if the loop stays stable, or if it drifts with each round. A reader who builds model teams gets both a plan and a test frame. It helps judge when a team loop helps, and when it just adds cost.
arxiv-2601-08939:
B. Moreschini and a large team warn that one cloud form can skew chem counts in far galaxies. The Webb scope lets us read the gas in such galaxies with tools honed nearby. Near tools rest on calm gas states. Far gas is far more wild, with strong light and low metal counts. A calm form may not fit it at all.

The team shows how wild states shift the lines we read. If we force a one cloud form, the chem counts we get can be off by much. More than one cloud state must be let in the fit. A reader who reads far gas gets a clear warn. Old near tools need a fresh check at high range.
arxiv-2601-09239:
Hanlin Zhang and eight co-authors split speech into two code streams: sense and sound. A speech code turns a wave into a short list of codes a chat model can use. Past codes mix what was said with how it sounds. That mix makes it hard to swap voice yet keep words, or to keep voice and change words.

Their code tool is called DSA-Tokenizer. It holds sense codes and sound codes apart by set rules in train. A flow match step then joins the two in a ranked way for the next stage. A reader in speech tech gets a split code that may serve voice swap and text true tasks at once.
arxiv-2601-09539:
Nataniel Marquis works on deep conjectures that link two sides of the p-adic Langlands program. His 2026 arXiv paper weighs what conjectures by Breuil, Herzig, Hu, Morra, and Schraen imply for Zábrádi's functor. On one side sit representations of the p-adic Galois group; on the other, representations of GL_n over the p-adic numbers. When a Galois representation is generic and well placed, a notion of compatibility ties the two sides. Papers like this one test whether the grand conjectures of the field fit together without clashes.

The paper is a work of pure mathematics. It sits in the p-adic Langlands program, a long effort to link Galois groups with linear groups.
arxiv-2601-09639:
Y. Kilic and a large team pin down the size and shape of Ixion, a large world beyond Neptune. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses multi-chord stellar occultations of the trans-Neptunian object (28978) Ixion. When such a body crosses a star, its shadow gives a sharp outline.

Trans-Neptunian objects are among the most primitive leftovers of the early solar system. Occultations give accurate sizes and shapes, while photometry constrains albedo and surface colors. Several chords across the shadow trace Ixion's true outline. Knowing one large body's form in detail anchors models of how the outer system was built.
arxiv-2601-10039:
C. R. Skolar and B. Srinivasan study the thin layer that forms near a wall in a plasma. The work is set in a Z-pinch, a fusion test bed. In such a bed, plasma is held in a tube. A bias is set on the end plates.

The field lines run along the wall, not across it. That case has had few past tests. The pair run a full sim of a cut through the pinch. They solve for the grains and the field as one. The sim shows how the layer forms when hits are rife and the field runs flat to the wall.
arxiv-2601-10339:
Xue-Nan Chen tests if gravity can tell quantum stuffs apart. The weak equivalence rule says all stuff falls the same. Its quantum form is still an open ask. In quantum work, chance is part of each claim. A test must code that chance in full.

Chen sets the rule in terms of a scatter spread. At tree level, that spread is worked out for a light grain off a heavy one. The claim is that the spread does not rest on the grain's mass or kind. The heavy mass cap makes the test sharp. The work gives a form for the quantum rule.
arxiv-2601-10639:
Ranajoy Sadhukhan and co-authors present STEM, a way to scale transformer models with less compute per token. Sparse designs promise more capacity without a matching rise in cost. In practice they often suffer unstable training, poor load balance, and heavy traffic between chips. STEM takes a static, token-indexed route instead.

The method swaps the up-projection in each feed-forward block for a lookup in a local embedding table. The gate and down-projection stay dense, as before. Lookups are cheap, so capacity can grow while token cost stays low. The design targets teams that train large language models and want size without runaway bills.
arxiv-2601-10939:
Christopher J. Butler and co-authors report liquid-crystal-like electronic order living alongside superconductivity in NaAlSi. Electronic nematic and smectic phases break symmetry in the electron fluid itself. They often appear near or inside unconventional superconducting states. NaAlSi is a semimetal with a silicon square net, and its superconductivity is thought to be unconventional.

Using scanning tunneling microscopy, the team observed short-range charge stripe order, the smectic pattern. The stripes coexist with superconductivity in the same material. That coexistence is a clue about how the two orders relate: rivals, partners, or two faces of one cause. The work adds a clean case to the study of quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-11339:
Shangjie Tian and nine coauthors name a new topological insulator in this work. Their 2026 preprint studies the compound Ge2Bi2Te5 in layered form. Topological insulators pass current on their surface only. Their bulk stays inert, which makes them rare and prized.

Most known cases are binary compounds of two elements. The search has moved to ternary mixes for new physics. This compound joins germanium, bismuth, and tellurium in one stack. The team identifies it as a 3D topological insulator. New members of this class feed both physics and devices. They may host exotic states that future chips can use.
arxiv-2601-11539:
Dinanath Padhya and four coauthors build a low-cost sensor glove for sign language. Their 2026 preprint reports the design and implementation in full. Severe hearing loss affects over 430 million people worldwide. Access to sign language interpretation stays critically scarce.

The gap bites hardest in low-resource settings like Nepal. Assistive tools split into two flawed camps today. Commercial gloves often cost more than 3,000 dollars. Research gloves use flex sensors that degrade fast under stress. The team's glove uses Hall-effect sensors instead of flex ones. Hall sensors read magnetic fields as fingers move. The aim is a cheap, tough glove that lasts.
arxiv-2601-11739:
Xinyu Pi, Qisen Yang, Chuong Nguyen, and Hua Shen map how large language models are now used in work with words and themes. Such work, called qualitative analysis, reads texts to find sense and themes. Model output can range from plain sums of what was said to full models of a system.

To make these gaps clear, they build a grid with four rows and four cols. One axis lists four levels of sense making, from plain facts to full theory. The other lists four levels of form, from fixed maps to loops that feed back. The grid helps teams state what a tool does and does not do.
arxiv-2601-12939:
Kaleem Arshid and four co authors plan flight paths for swarms of drones by a method called active inference. Their frame joins chance based reasoning with self learning in one system. It hands out jobs across the swarm with no single lead drone. It also sets the order of routes and plans the moves of each craft.

Trained world models guide the swarm at three levels: the job, the route, and the move. The training paths come from a genetic search that adds a push apart force. That force keeps drones from crowding one spot. A swarm that can re-plan in flight can serve search, mapping, and aid work. The study shows one way to build that skill.
arxiv-2601-13139:
Alessandro Midolo, Emiliano Tramontana, and Massimiliano Di Penta test if GPT-4 can clean up Python code well. Code clean up, called refactoring, aims to lift code grade with no change in what the code does. Old auto tools for it exist, but their use in real work stays thin.

Large language models open a fresh path for the task. The team asks how class level code in Python fares when GPT-4 does the clean up. They check both grade and how easy the code is to read. For dev teams, the study helps judge when a model can be trusted with clean up and when a human eye must lead.
arxiv-2601-13339:
B. J. Chen, Z. Deng, C. Q. Jin, and co-authors report huge low field magnet drag in a layered diluted magnetic semiconductor. Such stuff is a semiconductor spiked with magnetic atoms. Their host has a CaAl2Si2 type plan, with barium and potassium on one site and cadmium and manganese on a next.

They vary the manganese share across a wide span, from five per cent to half. They track magnet traits and how charge moves in a field. At low field the drag on charge flow drops by a huge span, a colossal effect. Such a big reply at low field is apt for sensors and spin based tools. The team maps how the effect grows with the spike share.
arxiv-2601-13439:
Sonu Kumar and co-authors report weak magnetism in a rare earth crystal with a triangle grid. The crystal is SmMgAl11O19. Its samarium ions sit on a triangular lattice, a grid prone to magnetic frustration. Each ion forms a Kramers doublet, a pair of states kept by time symmetry.

Lab reads span three tools. The team tracks magnet pull, field curves, and heat held. They find the doublet is strongly quenched, with its pull cut far below the free ion mark. The net swap scale is very weak. A weak scale on a triangle grid makes the stuff a clean case for odd magnet states.
arxiv-2601-13839:
Aisha Al-Mohannadi and co-authors build a test set for AI questions on disaster photos in 2026. Social media images give fast, low-latency clues during natural and human-made disasters. Visual question answering, or VQA, lets users ask a model about an image. Strong results on plain photos do not prove skill in disaster scenes.

Their benchmark, DisasterVQA, targets damage assessment and response needs. Disaster reasoning is complex and safety-critical, unlike most VQA tasks. A firm test set shows where models fail when lives are at stake. Responders could then trust, or avoid, model help with clear eyes.
arxiv-2601-14039:
Wesam Moustafa and co-authors help medical image models cope with wrong labels in 2026. Label noise is a critical problem in medical image segmentation. Manual annotation is hard, so errors creep into training data. Models trained on noisy data are prone to overfitting, which degrades generalization.

Many methods try to mitigate noisy labels in segmentation. The area remains largely under-explored, the team notes. Their work generalizes abstention, where a model can decline to learn from suspect labels. Safer learning from flawed labels could improve tools that outline tumors and organs.
arxiv-2601-14239:
Roberto Sussman and co-authors derive odd velocity fields from exact relativity solutions in 2026. Peculiar velocities are motions beyond the smooth cosmic expansion. They analyze them through cosmological perturbations in the Newtonian longitudinal gauge. The setup uses irrotational, shear-free congruences in an Eulerian frame.

They show non-trivial peculiar velocity fields can arise through Lorentzian boosts. The boosts act in the non-relativistic limit of analytic Einstein equation solutions. The fluid source is irrotational and shear-free, with nonzero energy flux. Exact solutions give clean tests for cosmic flow models. Exact forms give a rare check on code that tracks cosmic flows. Codes that pass such checks can be used with more trust.
arxiv-2601-14439:
Maria Chatzieleftheriou, Jonas B. Profe, Ying Li, and Roser Valentí study a kagome superconductor under pressure in this 2026 paper. The material is CsCr3Sb5, a newly identified strongly correlated superconductor. At higher temperatures it shows non-Fermi-liquid behavior. Below about 54 kelvin, charge- and spin-density-wave order sets in, in intertwined form.

Under external pressure, that order is suppressed. A superconducting phase then emerges. The team studies how pressure tunes the electronic correlations and the flat bands in this material. Flat bands are energy levels where electrons barely move, which can amplify odd effects. Readers get a map of a new material's phases as pressure squeezes it.
arxiv-2601-14639:
Yuheng Shao and five co-authors build a co-design tool for fashion in this 2026 paper, set for the Intelligent User Interfaces conference. Effective collaboration between designers and users matters for fashion design. It can increase user acceptance of fashion products and thereby create value. The authors' system is DesignBridge, named in their title.

DesignBridge bridges designer expertise and user preferences through AI-enhanced co-design. In co-design, users shape the product alongside the professional. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off early in that setup. Readers get a system aimed at fashion work where expert craft and wearer taste must meet in one draft.
arxiv-2601-14839:
Daizhan Cheng studies control systems whose state space can change size over time. His 2026 arXiv paper calls these dimension varying systems. Each mode of such a system lives in its own space, with its own number of dimensions.

Cheng proposes one shared space that can hold all of these modes at once. He calls it a cross-dimensional Euclidean space. The paper shows that the shape of this space fits well with each mode's own space. That gives all the modes a single shared home for study and for control work.
arxiv-2601-15939:
Yo Ikeda builds a lattice version of a gauge theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chern-Simons theory is a topological theory with deep math ties. Defining it on a lattice needs care with gauge structure. Ikeda defines Deligne-Beilinson cohomology on a cubic lattice. He uses it to formulate lattice U(1) Chern-Simons theory at even levels. In the continuum, that cohomology refines how U(1) connections are built patch by patch.

A good lattice definition must keep the theory's topological traits. Patchwise constructions handle connections that no single chart can describe. This paper carries that care onto the lattice. Lattice formulations let physicists compute with such theories. They also test whether continuum ideas survive discretization. The work is mathematical physics, aimed at gauge theory specialists.
arxiv-2601-16039:
Hector Buffière and four coauthors sort a class of sparse graphs with tree order. Their 2026 preprint sits in pure maths and logic. A class counts as tied in a weak sense if one fixed rule can not read all graphs from its tinted forms. The team adds a tree order to the base form. They then ask which such forms stay weak and sparse.

The authors give clear tests that mark out these classes. The tests link tree order, sparsity and logic in one frame. Such marks help maths teams sort new graph classes fast. They also show where strong graph reading must fail. The work is a step in the study of sparse graph types and their logic.
arxiv-2601-16239:
Li Huang, Bertrand Meyer and Manuel Oriol argue that tests and proofs work best as a pair. Their 2026 preprint deals with how to check that code is right. Tests run the code and watch what it does. Proofs read the code text and show it must hold. The two ways have long been cast as foes in the field.

The team shows the pair as mates, not foes. Each way catches faults the other can miss. Joined use can thus lift trust in code at less cost. The view shapes how teams plan checks for big code. It draws on long work by the group in this field.
arxiv-2601-16339:
Naoki Endo and three coauthors ask when Rees rings of closed ideals are Cohen Macaulay. Their 2026 preprint deals with ideals in a plain local ring. The ideal is closed in the whole sense and tied to the top ideal. Its Rees ring spreads the ideal powers in a new ring. In two dims that ring is always of the sought type.

In high dims the trait can fail in plain cases. The team seeks terms that force the trait to hold. Terms of that kind sort good ideals from bad ones. The sort aids work in ring sums and blow up maths. The work is a step in local ring theory.
arxiv-2601-16439:
Geethika Santhosh and coauthors study star birth in rings and tails cast off star systems. Their 2026 preprint deals with systems bent by pulls or gas hits. Such hits throw off rings and tails far from the main disk. New stars can be born in those far thrown zones. Dust in those zones dims and bends the light they shed.

The team weighs dust dim and birth pace in the far zones. Dim must be fixed ere birth pace can be read true. True pace tells if far zones add much to star counts. It also tests if birth needs a dense disk to start. The work maps birth past the bright disk edge.
arxiv-2601-16839:
Anwar Ghammam and Mohamed Almukhtar check the build code that AI tools write. Build files tell how source code turns into apps. They are a key part of the software life span. Yet past checks of AI code skipped build files. Their 2026 preprint fills that gap with a broad check.

The team grades bot-made build code for flaws and upkeep cost. Weak build code can break whole teams' work. It can also hide flaws in shipped apps. Their grades show where bots need a human eye. That helps firms set rules for bot use in build tasks.
arxiv-2601-16939:
Andrei Agrachev and Bettina Kazandjian ask how far control can steer a class of flows. Their stage is the group of volume-keeping maps of a torus. A fixed swirl field drives the flow on it. A steady push, set in time, adds the steer. Their 2026 preprint tests near-full reach for that steer.

Near-full reach means most states can be got close to. Folks who quit one good for the next shape such flows. Proofs of reach bound what control can do in fluids. They guide steer plans for mix and flow tasks. The torus stage keeps the math clean and sharp.
arxiv-2601-17339:
Payel Santra, Partha Basuchowdhuri, and Debasis Ganguly question how search quality tools are judged. Query performance prediction, or QPP, guesses how well a search worked. The usual test checks set-level correlation. It compares guessed quality ranks with true ranks across a query set. The authors say that test is too coarse.

It does not show how QPP works for one query at a time. It also does not link scores to real downstream use. Their framework judges QPP by what it helps users do next. That shift can change which methods look best. Search teams gain a test that tracks real value, not just neat rank match.
arxiv-2601-17439:
Dieu D. Nguyen and co-authors weigh the black hole at the heart of galaxy M81. M81 is a near spiral galaxy, also called NGC 3031. Its central mass stayed unsure for years. Past measures clashed and none was robust. The team uses JWST NIRSpec data for a fresh measure. They map star motion in the central three arcseconds in fine detail.

From that stellar dynamics map, they derive a robust mass. A firm mass anchors study of how galaxies and black holes grow together. Near galaxies are the best labs for that link. JWST sharpness made the new map possible. The work sets a firmer base for M81 research.
arxiv-2601-17539:
Pawan Singh Mehta and Biswajyoti Saha study multiple polylogarithms near integer points. Polylogarithms are special functions with deep ties to number theory. Their local behavior in the s-aspect is the focus. The authors write a Laurent type expansion at integer points. The expansion uses power series and rational functions.
