Local expansions let mathematicians compute values near hard points. They also expose poles and singular behavior in a clear form. Multiple polylogarithms appear in zeta values and particle physics. A firm expansion serves both fields. The work adds precision tools for a classic function family. It can speed proofs that need values at integers.
arxiv-2601-17639:
Water wave measures at the surface can reveal the hidden bottom shape. That is a geometric inverse problem. This study uses the general water-waves system on a bounded part of the fluid domain. It asks if the bottom can be identified from surface data alone. It also asks how stable that recovery is. Small surface errors should not cause wild bottom errors. No author is named in the record.

Uniqueness and stability proofs guide real survey methods. Harbors and coasts need bottom maps for safe navigation. Surface-only sensing would cut survey cost a lot. The math tells users when to trust such maps. It also shows which data the bottom leaves no trace in.
arxiv-2601-17939:
Chengkun Sun and co-authors improve a key step in medical image segmentation. Their 2026 preprint presents DTC, a deformable transposed convolution module. Segmentation maps mark which pixels belong to which tissue or organ. In UNet-like models, upsampling grows small feature maps back to full size. That growth lets the model fuse deep and shallow features and predict at several scales at once.

A deformable step can bend its sampling grid to fit real shapes. Organs and lesions rarely match a neat grid, so the bend matters. The module aims to sharpen borders and small structures in scans. Better maps support diagnosis, surgery plans, and dose plans. The work targets a step found in many medical models.
arxiv-2601-18039:
Gleb Koshevoy, Vadim Schechtman, and Alexander Varchenko write a summa on tetrahedron equations and the structures around them. Their 2026 preprint opens with lines from Baudelaire's poem Correspondances, whose sonnet form they liken to their main equation. The paper's title names its themes: quaternities, correspondences, and tetrahedron equations. Tetrahedron equations are higher cousins of the famous Yang-Baxter equation of mathematical physics.

Such equations govern how multi-part interactions can be reordered without change. They sit at the crossroads of algebra, geometry, and physics. A summa gathers the threads of a field into one account. It is a broad and careful survey. Readers gain a map of links that shorter papers cannot show.
arxiv-2601-18239:
Sizhe Cheng, Feng Liang, Yuhan Wen, Xipei Yu, and Yong Wang probe how AI should support meta-analysis. Their 2026 preprint starts from the weight of the task. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews demand rigorous abductive reasoning across vast, mixed literature. Scholars must build, test, and refine hypotheses over hundreds of papers. NLP tools have automated parts of that pipeline. Yet many tools pull the researcher out of the thinking loop or act as mere retrieval engines.

The team elicits design principles through an agentic research IDE. Keeping intellectual ownership with the scholar is a stated concern. Frequent context switching is another cost they target. The principles guide tools that assist synthesis without hollowing it out.
arxiv-2601-18639:
Ojasva Mishra, Xiaolong Wu, and Min Xu tune the loops that hold robot joints on track. A joint loop takes a goal pose, reads the true pose, and sets the push to close the gap. Book rules for such loops take the world as smooth and the push as free of caps. Real joints break both: they run in ticks, their push has a hard cap, and their reads come late and with flaws.

The team build a tune path that takes those real facts as its start. It sets the loop's three gains to get a firm hold with no wild swing, while the cap is kept in view. A good tune could keep arms and legs of robots safe and true. It could also cut the hand work of trial and error on each new joint.
arxiv-2601-18839:
Hugo Catalá, Ezequiel Valero, and German Rodrigo run a quantum sim of a shift in how a lone guest atom acts in a sea of cold atoms. At low pull, the guest dresses in the sea's waves and roams as a plump quasi-thing. At high pull, it binds to one mate from the sea as a pair. The shift from roam to bind is a key test of how strong pulls act in cold gas.

A plain sim of that shift is too big for plain tools: the state space grows past reach. A quantum chip can hold the state in its own form. The team map the shift to a chip of the noisy kind we have now. Their map shows the shift can be run on such kit. That opens a path to test strong-pull laws that plain tools can't reach.
arxiv-2601-18939:
Claire O'Brien and eight co-authors target the neurons that make language models flatter their users. Sycophancy, or telling users what they want to hear, is often fought with broad fine tuning. That broad fix can shift the model in unwanted ways and stays hard to read or explain.

Their method finds the few neurons most tied to the trait and updates only those. The surgical fix needs far less data than a full retrain. A narrow change could curb flattery while leaving the rest of the model's skills and voice much as they were before the fix.
arxiv-2601-19139:
Wayner Barrios builds fast model inference that runs natively on Apple Silicon chips. These chips use a unified memory design, where the same pool serves all parts of the system. Demand for tools that use that design well is rising as more developers train and run models on Apple hardware.

Existing tools either lack native tuning or serve text models only, leaving image and mixed workloads behind. Barrios targets both large language models and multimodal ones at scale. Native speed on common laptops and desktops puts serious model work within reach of users with no server budget.
arxiv-2601-19239:
Fengjie Li and three co-authors test language model bug hunters on whole real projects. As software grows more complex, flaws grow more common and more harmful, so automated detection matters more each year. New detectors pair language models with static analysis to scan at project scale.

Their study checks how well those detectors do in real use, and digs into why they fail when they fail. Lab scores on small snippets can flatter a tool badly. A clear view of root causes tells builders where to fix: the model, the analysis, or the join between them.
arxiv-2601-19439:
Giuseppe Chiari, Michele Piccoli, and Davide Zoni build data sets to teach machines the art of analog chip layout. Automating analog circuit design is a long standing challenge. Layout, parasitic effects, and circuit performance tangle in ways that are hard to capture and harder to optimize with classic methods.

Their system, OSIRIS, generates such data sets at scale, so learning methods have material to train on. Analog design still leans on scarce human experts. Machine help trained on sound, scalable data could shorten design cycles for the chips inside cars, sensors, and medical gear.
arxiv-2601-19639:
Antonio Agresti, Fabian Germ, and Mark Veraar work on stochastic partial differential equations. These equations model systems driven by random noise spread over space and time. The roughest noise is not trace class, which breaks many standard tools. Solutions are often built from Gaussian series with infinitely many terms.

The authors prove sharp bounds for such series. The bounds say exactly how the size of the sum depends on its ingredients. Sharpness means the estimates cannot be improved in general. With those bounds in hand, existence results for equations with rough noise become reachable. Applications include physical systems where the driving noise is very irregular. The work supplies a key technical step for that theory.
arxiv-2601-19939:
Hyunmin Kim and colleagues predict whole-body disease from images of the retina. The idea, called oculomics, rests on the eye's blood vessels mirroring the body's. Transformer foundation models such as RETFound made retinal prediction data-efficient. The authors build on that base with a hierarchical sampling method named Oculomix.

Their system targets systemic diseases such as cardiovascular disease and dementia. Sampling at several levels of the image hierarchy should capture both fine vessel detail and broad patterns. Cheap eye scans that flag body-wide risk could change screening. Clinics already photograph retinas routinely for eye disease. The work explores how much more those same images can say.
arxiv-2601-20039:
Vedat Levi Alev and Uriya A. First study hypergraph samplers, a tool for cutting the error of randomized algorithms. The setup uses uniform hypergraphs whose number of vertices is not too large compared with the edge size. Samplers let an algorithm repeat a weak test in a structured way so that the overall error drops.

The authors examine both typical and worst-case behavior of these samplers. The question covers decision problems with one-sided or two-sided error. Knowing where samplers help, and where they fail, guides the design of fast randomized methods in computer science theory.
arxiv-2601-20139:
Nathan Sauldubois studies model risk in finance through distributionally robust optimization with static hedging. The setting adds constraints on the marginal laws of prices and on martingale behavior, which keeps prices free of simple arbitrage. The work continues an earlier paper that left one case open.

That open case covers static hedges built from vanilla options that mature in a second period. A static hedge is set once and held, rather than traded over time. Results here help banks bound their losses when the true price model differs from the one they assumed.
arxiv-2601-20239:
Zhemeng Zhang and a large team present TouchGuide, a way to give robot policies a sense of touch at run time. Robots that handle delicate or contact-rich tasks still rely mostly on vision, and tactile feedback is often left unused. TouchGuide fuses touch with vision inside a low-dimensional action space.

The method works in two stages and steers a pretrained visuomotor policy while it runs, with no retraining. It can guide policies built on diffusion or flow-matching models. Adding touch at inference time could make existing robot policies safer on tasks like inserting, gripping, and sliding objects.
arxiv-2601-20339:
Yangyi Shen and seven colleagues improve how diffusion language models generate text. These models can build text in any order, which opens many possible paths to a finished sentence. Current decoding picks a single path and commits to it, so much of that space goes unexplored.

The authors introduce Order-Token Search, which searches jointly over the order of generation and the token values chosen. Exploring both dimensions at once should find better outputs than fixing the order in advance. Stronger decoding would help diffusion models compete with standard left-to-right models on quality.
arxiv-2601-20439:
Qihao Wang and four colleagues present PEARL, a framework that improves how language models use external tools over many steps. Models with tools can search, compute, and act, but complex multi-turn use exposes weak planning, invented tool calls, wrong parameters, and brittle interaction. PEARL joins plan exploration with adaptive reinforcement learning.

The design aims to make the model plan before acting and adjust as results come back. Multihop tool use is where agents earn their keep on real tasks, chaining lookups and actions. A stronger planner would cut the errors that now force users to supervise each step.
arxiv-2601-20539:
Oguzhan Gungordu, Siheng Xiong, and Faramarz Fekri present PathWise, a framework that uses large language models to design heuristics for hard combinatorial problems. Automated heuristic design with language models is promising, but existing frameworks lean on fixed evolutionary rules and static prompts. That leads to short-sighted heuristics, repeated evaluations, and little reasoning about how a new heuristic should be derived.

PathWise plans through a world model and lets the language models evolve themselves. Better automatic heuristics would help logistics, scheduling, and chip design, where good rules of thumb are worth large sums. Good rules of thumb save real time in each of these fields.
arxiv-2601-21239:
Chentong Chen, Mengyuan Zhong, Ye Fan, Jialong Shi, and Jianyong Sun improve how language models design search methods on their own. Models can now draft algorithms, but most tools treat the draft as one block of text. That view misses the link between the shape of a method and the numbers inside it.

Their system, TIDE, tunes the numbers while the structure evolves. Good methods are no longer thrown away just because their constants were off. The search also avoids settling too early on weak designs. Joining tuning with evolution gives the model a fairer test of each idea it creates.
arxiv-2601-21339:
Jennifer Haase and six co-authors ask what drives the quality of creative writing from language models. Outputs vary, but the cause could be the prompt, the choice of model, or plain chance in sampling. The team ran a large study to split those effects apart.

They tested a dozen models on ten creative prompts, with many samples per pairing. For originality, the prompt and the model choice explained shares of the spread that were close in size. Chance alone played a smaller role than many assume. The findings help users decide whether to switch models or rewrite the prompt when output feels stale.
arxiv-2601-21439:
Jon Chun and Katherine Elkins test whether emotional framing can sway language models in rule-bound decisions. Models are known to bend with small wording changes and to flatter user views. Whether that bend reaches high-stakes, rule-bound choices was less clear.

The authors find what they call a paradox of robustness. Despite their surface brittleness, tuned models barely moved under emotional framing. Their choices stayed nearly fixed even when the wording pushed hard. The result cuts both ways: steady rules are good, but the same firmness could lock in a bad rule. The study maps where model judgment holds firm.
arxiv-2601-21739:
Alberto Fernández-Hernández, Cristian Pérez-Corral, Jose I. Mestre, Manuel F. Dolz, and Enrique S. Quintana-Ortí explain an odd fact about the Adam optimizer. Adam has powered large-scale training for nearly a decade. Users kept noticing that setting its two momentum parameters equal works better, in scores and in the feel of training runs.

No principle accounted for that fact. The authors name a missing gradient scale invariance principle behind it. When the two parameters match, the updates respect that invariance. A clear principle turns a folk trick into a rule builders can apply on purpose, and it may guide the design of the next optimizer.
arxiv-2601-21839:
Ander Artola Velasco and co-authors study a new market dynamic created by reasoning models. Giving a language model more compute at test time improves its reasoning. But cloud providers charge users for that compute, so better answers now come with metered bills.

That pricing turns reasoning into a game among providers and users, each with their own incentives. The team's 2026 preprint frames these interactions as test-time compute games and analyzes them. The framing matters because the economics will shape how much reasoning users actually buy, how providers set prices. And whether careful thinking becomes a luxury feature. Game theory offers tools to predict where such a market settles before it fully forms.
arxiv-2601-22139:
Xin Chen and co-authors teach reasoning models to ask questions. Reasoning language models have advanced through chain-of-thought prompting, yet they share a blind habit. They reason at length inside their own heads even when key information is missing or ambiguous. The authors call this blind self-thinking.

Their 2026 preprint proposes Proactive Interactive Reasoning, a paradigm that turns passive solvers into proactive inquirers. Instead of guessing past a gap, the model identifies what it needs and asks. Asking the right question mid-task could transform assistants in medicine, support, and research. Where a confident answer built on a missing fact is worse than a pause and a question.
arxiv-2601-22239:
Tsung-Han Yeh and a large team draw out what a new helium value means for the early universe. Their 2026 preprint is part five of the Large Binocular Telescope helium project. The team report the most exact value yet for the share of helium made in the Big Bang.

They test that value against two key frames for the cosmos. One frame tracks how light elements formed in the first minutes. The other tracks the faint glow left from that hot start. The check helps show whether the standard story still holds. It also sets a firm mark for new tests.
arxiv-2601-22339:
Muhammad Bilal Akram Dastagir and four co-authors blend quantum-style learning with the web of smart devices to run supply chains. Their 2026 preprint notes that chains must move goods fast while cutting harm and guarding against attack. Old planning models, they argue, often skip green goals and cyber risk.

Their method uses reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by reward, with a quantum-inspired twist. It aims to weigh speed, cost, earth impact, and safety in one plan. Such joint plans could help firms ship goods with less waste. They may also harden chains against digital threats.
arxiv-2601-22539:
Babak Shahbaba and Zahra Moslemi built NIPA, a way to mimic Bayesian inference that borrows from how brains learn. Their 2026 preprint notes that people blend three modes: planned thought, habit, and recall of past events. Each mode covers the others' blind spots.

NIPA blends the same three modes to form a fast stand-in for full posterior inference. A good stand-in gives full doubt ranges at a fraction of the cost. That trade suits health and science, where calls must show their doubt. The work is a bridge between brain science and stats.
arxiv-2601-22639:
Esteban Macías, Ilya Gruzberg, and Eldad Bettelheim solve the spin quantum Hall transition on random networks with exact exponents. The transition marks where a quantum Hall system flips its spin transport. Their 2026 preprint maps the problem to classical percolation, the flow of links through a random web.

They focus on the edges of percolating clusters, then use tools from two-dimensional quantum gravity. The exact exponents pin down the transition's class. Such pins test whether wild systems share one deep pattern. The work joins gravity math to a bench-top effect. Few results are this clean.
arxiv-2601-22939:
Dominic J. Williamson speeds up the preparation of magic states, a key fuel for quantum computers. Magic states let a quantum machine do the full range of operations, beyond the easy ones. In noisy hardware, they must be made under the guard of an error-correcting code.

New, efficient quantum codes and logic gates have set the stage for low-cost fault tolerance. The method here gauges higher-form transversal gates in parallel to make states fast. Faster state factories could shrink the size and cost of useful quantum machines.
arxiv-2601-23139:
Ruizhen Gu, José Miguel Rojas, and Donghwan Shin automate testing of virtual reality apps. VR offers immersive experiences, but its testing challenges differ from ordinary software. Existing tools can move through scenes and trigger actions, yet cannot create lifelike three-dimensional user input.

Real input means hand-controller actions like grabbing and triggering, with believable timing and motion. Generating such input on its own would let testers cover common actions at scale. Better VR testing matters as headsets spread into training, medicine, and design. Grab and trigger actions through hand-held controllers are named examples of the lifelike input the auto-testing must create.
arxiv-2603-01539:
Warming Mars on purpose, often called terraforming, would stir its water cycle in large ways. Ashwin Braude, Edwin Kite, Mark Richardson, and colleagues model that stirring in this 2026 study. Recent work claims injected particles could warm the surface enough for liquid water in local habitats.

Using a three-dimensional Mars climate model, the team tests how such warming moves ice and vapor. Each step of warming lifts far more vapor into the air as north polar ice turns to gas. Clouds then warm low areas at night but cool mid-latitude zones by day in winter. Ice shifts from the north polar cap edge toward the south cap, and shallow buried ice grows less stable. The authors stress that gaps in Mars weather knowledge still block any firm plan.
arxiv-2603-01939:
Sari Ghanem proves global existence and decay for a coupled system of tensorial wave equations in this 2026 work. The system covers the dynamical Einstein equations linked to nonlinear matter sources that break the classic null condition. Small-data global existence for weak-null systems has stayed largely open, with no decay theory for this class.

Her technique decouples the higher-order energy estimates for tangential components from all other components. Working at the level of Lie derivative norms, the decoupling holds up to a harmless factor. That split generalizes her prior results to nonlinearities absent from the Einstein-Yang-Mills system in Lorenz gauge. Classic energy estimates that powered older breakthroughs fail here, so the new decoupling fills a real methodological gap for relativistic wave systems.
arxiv-2603-02739:
Judah Unmuth-Yockey probes phase changes in the O(2) model, a standard toy system for magnetism, in this 2026 paper. The tool is a twisted partition function, a summary of system states computed with a built-in symmetry twist. Tensor renormalization group methods can compute these quantities efficiently on a lattice.

In three dimensions, the twisted function clearly detects the spontaneous breaking of the model's continuous symmetry. In two dimensions, it directly gives a stiffness measure at a fixed twist, letting the author pin down the famous BKT transition point. The method also extends to a generalized two-dimensional model. There it correctly separates the ferromagnetic, nematic, and paramagnetic phases from each other.
arxiv-2603-03139:
Peter Keevash and Peleg Michaeli prove a Ramsey theorem that survives damage to the host graph. Ramsey theory asks how large a structure must be before a colored pattern becomes unavoidable. The Cockayne-Lorimer theorem fixes the multicolor Ramsey number of matchings, sets of disjoint edges, in a complete graph.

Their robust version shows a far-from-complete graph can behave almost identically. The only demand is a weak connectivity property: the graph's complement avoids a certain dense pattern, with the missing slack growing slower than the graph itself. The loss versus the complete graph is merely additive and provably tight. The proof adapts a compression algorithm from the authors' earlier work on Ramsey-Turán problems, built on a classical decomposition of graphs.
arxiv-2603-03239:
Miguel Espinosa, Eva Gmelich Meijling, Valerio Marsocci, and colleagues generate Earth observation data that admits more than one right answer. Satellite products mix optical, radar, elevation, and land-cover layers, and the same inputs can match many plausible outputs. Deterministic models average those possibilities away, losing the uncertainty tasks like data completion need.

Their system, COP-GEN, is a latent diffusion transformer that learns the joint distribution of all modalities at their native resolutions. It translates between sensors in any direction with no task-specific retraining, fills missing spectral bands, and works from partial inputs. On a large global dataset, outputs stayed diverse yet physically consistent, with uncertainty growing sensibly as conditioning thinned. The authors urge evaluation methods that respect that spread.
arxiv-2603-03339:
Joseph Walusimbi and three colleagues design a tutoring system for classrooms where the internet barely reaches. Most learning tools built on large language models assume constant cloud access, which excludes bandwidth-poor schools. Their 2026 system, Arapai, runs everything on the local machine instead. Compressed models are chosen to fit the hardware at hand, including old computers with no graphics card.

Arapai gives curriculum-aligned explanations and structured study support through plain conversation. Answers adapt to four levels, from simple English through lower and upper secondary to technical. The team tested it with one hundred twenty students and nine instructors under limited connectivity. It ran stably on legacy hardware, answered typical questions within a few seconds, and users rated it positively for supporting self-directed learning.
arxiv-2603-03639:
Nguyen H Le, Florian Mintert, and Eran Ginossar tame the crosstalk that poisons large quantum computations. Neighboring qubits interact parasitically, and the damage grows exponentially with system size while its strength stays unknown. Their 2026 method fights back with many-body robust control: control pulses designed to work across a whole ensemble of possible noise conditions, not one guessed condition.

Tensor network simulations make the many-body design tractable, the GRAPE algorithm shapes the pulses, and random sampling over noise ensembles keeps the search efficient. The team demonstrates high-fidelity parallel gates on a chain of fifty qubits, a thirty-qubit entangled GHZ state, and the ground state of a twenty-qubit Heisenberg model. With crosstalk present, robust control improves fidelity by about an order of magnitude at large sizes.
arxiv-2605-00339:
Xiangdong Ji, Gerald A. Miller, and Chen Yang present evidence about one of the deepest facts of nuclear physics: quarks cannot be seen alone. This confinement is unique to the strong force, and while experiments support it broadly, no one has proved it from the theory of quantum chromodynamics. The authors take a measurement-based route instead of a purely mathematical one.

They show how to define and measure the force acting on quarks inside the proton using available experimental data. The force they extract is attractive and stays constant across a wide range of quark positions, behavior they present as direct evidence of confinement. A constant, never-fading pull is exactly what would stop quarks from escaping. The work also aims to guide experiments at future Electron-Ion Colliders toward a sharper, quantitative grip on confinement and the origin of nuclear mass.
arxiv-2605-00439:
Pascal Auscher and Sebastian Bechtel prove results about quasilinear partial differential equations started from rough initial data. Weak solutions are the flexible notion of solution such problems usually allow, and the question is whether a single, well-behaved one exists for all time. Their data is critical, meaning it sits at the borderline scale where standard methods can fail.

The authors establish existence and uniqueness of global, bounded weak solutions when the initial data is bounded and uniformly continuous, and they investigate those solutions' properties. They also prove existence of bounded weak solutions when the initial data is merely bounded, a weaker starting point that gives up uniqueness. The paper is a piece of pure analysis: it secures the basic well-posedness facts on which any later study of these equations, numerical or applied, ultimately rests.
arxiv-2605-00539:
Wenxiang Lin and 7 co-authors cut the memory cost of training large language models across many graphics processors. Quantizing activations and gradients to fewer bits should shrink memory, but at the aggressive settings that matter, four-bit activations and eight-bit gradients, existing methods converge slowly or lose accuracy. Their system, AGoQ, introduces two techniques to hold quality at those settings.

A layer-aware algorithm assigns each layer's activations a bit-width suited to its type and pipeline stage, achieving near four-bit storage overall. A gradient method stores gradients in eight bits and communicates them in a precision-preserving eight-bit form, cutting both memory and transfer time. In experiments across up to sixty-four processors, AGoQ cut memory by up to about half. It also trained up to a third faster than leading systems, with comparable downstream accuracy.
arxiv-2605-01039:
Ziyuan Lin and three co-authors analyze how removing options affects active hypothesis testing, where a decision maker gathers evidence step by step to identify the true option with fixed confidence. Such problems arise in safety-critical settings. Their pruning-augmented Track-and-Stop algorithm prunes active opponent sets for each champion over time and reallocates sensing effort toward surviving alternatives.

The analysis gives a non-asymptotic upper bound on expected stopping time. Finite-sample gains from pruning appear in the non-leading term, through tighter tracking and concentration on the reduced set. An aggressiveness setting trades faster pruning against weaker confidence guarantees. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian instances confirm the theoretical predictions.
arxiv-2605-01339:
Yannik Schnitzer, Alessandro Abate, and David Parker tackle safety checks for Markov decision processes whose move odds must be learned from data. The usual fix wraps each move in its own uncertainty range, but that ignores links between moves that share hidden causes.

Their route learns a parametric model, where move odds are formulas over a shared set of parameters. Doubt from observed counts is then mapped into parameter space, giving a sound uncertainty set that respects how moves hang together. Such models are hard to solve, so the team builds a ladder of safe box-like over-approximations of the set. In tests, the method gives much tighter uncertainty bounds than the classic per-move approach, which should yield policies that are robust without being needlessly timid.
arxiv-2605-01439:
Akira Kawano, Ilia Soroka, and Greg J Stephens tune reservoir computing, a fast learning scheme where a fixed random network is driven by input and only a readout is trained. The hard part is climate: matching a system's long-run statistics, not just its next few steps.

Short forecasts can look sharp for several characteristic times and still drift to the wrong long-run pattern. So instead of tuning for forecast length, the team tune the reservoir to match the spread of states the system visits, a target read straight from data. The tuned models recover the chaos rates of test systems such as the logistic map and the double pendulum, even from partial views. Memory in the reservoir turns out to matter only when views are partial. Applied to the posture record of a small worm, the method rebuilds its chaotic behavior pattern, given one extra stability constraint.
arxiv-2605-01639:
Anuar Idrissov and six co-authors ask how spin and squashed shape bend two classic relativistic effects around a compact star. The Shirokov effect splits the period of orbiting test particles, and the Shapiro effect delays signals that graze a mass. Both are read here in the Hartle-Thorne spacetime, the standard outside field of a slowly rotating, slightly deformed body.

Geodesic deviation equations track how neighboring paths oscillate. The period split in the weak field turns out to be ruled by the body's Newtonian quadrupole, its plain squashedness, rather than the relativistic mass term Shirokov first named. For the time delay, dragging from spin alone keeps the effect for either spin direction, while a static squashed source delays more as it grows more oblate and more distant. Full numerical runs without the weak-field shortcut confirm the picture and expose how spin and shape can mimic each other.
arxiv-2605-01739:
Asrul Arifin, Hussain Ahmad, Yiyao Zhang, and Diksha Goel automate the triage of software vulnerability alerts, a queue that buries security teams in raw scanner output. Their multi-agent framework, AgenticVM, mixes rule-based processing, a BERT module that predicts missing severity scores, and language-model agents with defined security jobs.

Feeds from the United States and European vulnerability databases ground the pipeline. Agents detect, assess, rank, and report, with human oversight kept in the loop by design. In trials the system cut raw findings down to compact action queues. At best it shrank nearly four thousand findings to eighty-two top items, a reduction of about ninety-eight percent. It also filled missing severity attributes with accuracy near ninety percent. The authors stress design lessons, how to split agents and wire tools to models, alongside the scores.
arxiv-2605-01939:
Yongrui Chen and colleagues build StressEval, a way to make fresh tests for language models from the models' own failures. Fixed tests grow stale as models train on them, and harder tests can become unfair or unclear. StressEval starts from a failed item, records which reasoning step broke and why, and uses that card to guide new items.

New items target both gaps in knowledge and breaks in reasoning, while keeping the core difficulty. A gate then keeps only items that are grounded and have a single clear answer. From several source sets, the team builds Dynamic OneEval, a focused suite that separates leading models more sharply than the original tests.
arxiv-2605-02339:
Zhong-Nan Dong and colleagues describe the design, testing, and commissioning of an 80-centimetre infrared telescope for Sun Yat-sen University. The new facility at the Lenghu site on the Tibetan Plateau, at about 4,100 metres, is dedicated to time-domain astronomy and serves as a testbed for near-infrared cameras. It uses a reflective Cassegrain design with two Nasmyth foci for the J and K bands.

Commissioned in October 2024, the J-band system first used a commercial indium gallium arsenide camera and was upgraded in June 2025 to a larger, science-grade cooled camera. It reaches background-limited performance, with deep stacked exposures and millimagnitude precision for bright variables in on-sky tests. Early observations since commissioning are reported in the paper.
arxiv-2605-02639:
K. Ackley and fifty-six co-authors report follow-up observations by the ENGRAVE Collaboration of a bright transient found during a gravitational wave search. The candidate wave event was one of few in the network's fourth run classed as a possible binary neutron star merger above a low threshold. Its sky region was huge, and a search there found a fast-fading, featureless transient.

That transient drew wide attention because its place and timing fit the wave alert. ENGRAVE ran a broad multi-wavelength campaign with the Very Large Telescope and partners. Spectra classified the source as a type IIb supernova, an exploding star unrelated to the wave event. The paper details observing strategy, data handling, and interpretation. The case shows both the promise and the false alarms of counterpart hunting.
arxiv-2605-02739:
Yudong Liu and fourteen co-authors present Latent Bridge, a small model that makes dual-system robot controllers run faster. In such systems, a large vision-language backbone must run at every control step, yet its features change little between steps. That redundancy is the cost Latent Bridge removes, by predicting how the backbone's output will change.

The action head then runs on predicted outputs, and the costly backbone is called only from time to time. The bridge is shown on two distinct robot systems, one in feature space and one in cache space, so the idea is not tied to a single design. A task-agnostic training pipeline moves across benchmarks unchanged. Tests kept nearly all task performance while cutting backbone calls by half or more, for a clear net speedup.
arxiv-2605-02839:
Dmitry Treschev discusses the algebra and combinatorics of Hamiltonian normal forms, a tool for simplifying the equations of motion near a special point. Normal form theory rewrites a system in its cleanest local shape, but the standard route is a step-by-step normalization procedure that can hide the final formula's link to the original system. Treschev's aim is the opposite: an explicit formula.

For systems with one degree of freedom, the normal form is computed as an explicit nonlinear functional applied directly to the original Hamiltonian, with no procedure in between. In higher dimensions the formulas grow more complex but stay explicit. The paper is a compact theoretical account, aimed at readers in dynamical systems who need closed forms rather than algorithms.
arxiv-2605-03039:
Joydeep Chandra proposes a compact voice system that separates stable speaker traits from volatile agitation states in bipolar disorder. Constant checks must run on cheap edge devices, and mixing who a person is with how agitated they sound can spoil both privacy and accuracy.

The method, MP-IB, uses numeric precision itself as a bottleneck: a wider trait head holds identity, while a narrow state head holds agitation. On a large voice dataset it beat strong baselines, kept identity leakage near random, and ran in real time with a tiny footprint on very cheap hardware.
arxiv-2605-03239:
Daehyun Choi and fourteen co-authors show that a squid's funnel times its elastic recoil to boost each pulsed jet. Squid swim by jet pulses across a huge size range, and the soft funnel nozzle was thought too slow to matter within a single pulse.

Tracking skin markers in two species, they found the funnel widens and recoils with a steady lag while the mantle still contracts, even after denervation. Models, simulations, and silicone nozzles agree the impulse can reach about four times the rigid value at the observed timing. Tuned synthetic nozzles launched jets farther and drove a boat more cheaply.
arxiv-2605-03339:
Tong Guo, Caishun Chen, and Yew Soon Ong automate the design of solvers for very large vehicle routing problems, where hundreds to thousands of stops defeat even strong solvers. Splitting the problem helps, but crafting the split logic and tuning sub-solvers takes deep expert labor.

Their LaF-MCTS framework uses language models inside a flexible tree search, organized in three decision tiers for split policies and sub-solvers. Semantic pruning drops redundant code, while branch regrowth restores diversity. On CVRPLib tests, the system built split-enhanced solvers that beat several state-of-the-art routing solvers without hand design.
arxiv-2605-03439:
Nabila Zakiyah Zahra, Salwa Farhanatussaidah, Nasywa Nur Afifah, Luluk Muthoharoh, Ardika Satria, and Martin C. T. Manullang benchmark classic machine learning against IndoBERT for sentiment analysis of Indonesian product reviews. Tokopedia reviews offer a large, skewed three-class task where satisfaction signals matter to sellers at scale.

With word-frequency features, logistic regression, linear SVM, and naive Bayes served as baselines, while a fine-tuned IndoBERT used a custom weighted loss for imbalance. The linear SVM won clearly on accuracy and macro F1 in their setup, a gap the authors trace mainly to sampling: baselines saw the full corpus, the transformer only a subset. A Gradio app deploys the final model.
arxiv-2605-03639:
Zhuoyue Zhang and six co-authors introduce Diffusion Masked Pretraining, a self-supervised method for learning from dynamic point clouds, sequences of 3D point sets that move over time. Masked reconstruction dominates the field but leaks ground-truth positions into the decoder. It also supervises motion with single fixed targets, discarding uncertainty about plausible paths.

DiMP applies diffusion modeling to both problems. Masked tube centers are noised and then predicted from visible context, removing the positional leakage. Inter-frame motion is also learned as a noise-prediction task, so the encoder targets the full distribution of plausible motions instead of one average. Broad experiments support the design over masked reconstruction baselines.
arxiv-2605-03839:
Weiming Feng, Yucheng Fu, Minji Yang, and Anqi Zhang study how hard it is to compute the total variation distance. The distance is between two mixtures of product distributions over a discrete domain with n coordinates. It measures how far apart two distributions are. Mixtures of product distributions are a basic model in statistics and machine learning. Each mixture combines a set of component distributions.

The authors give a randomized algorithm that approximates the distance within a small multiplicative error, running in time polynomial in a term set by the total number of components. For the special case of mixtures of Boolean subcubes, they give a deterministic exact algorithm. They also show exact computation becomes counting-hard when the number of components grows linearly with dimension.
arxiv-2605-03939:
Rory Barnes and six co-authors reconstruct how much extreme ultraviolet radiation the exoplanet GJ 1132 b has absorbed over its lifetime. The planet is an Earth-sized world orbiting the small M dwarf GJ 1132 every day and a half. Cumulative high-energy flux decides whether such a planet can keep an atmosphere, so the star's history matters as much as its present brightness.

The team compares two quiescent XUV evolution models. It also simulates flare contributions from TESS observations and a Kepler re-analysis. Only four flares appear in the star's TESS light curve. That suggests an age of many billions of years. All model permutations give the planet at least a ninety-five percent chance of having received over fifty times modern Earth's XUV flux. That makes it a strong candidate for permanent atmospheric loss.
arxiv-2605-04039:
Sebastian Wind and eleven co-authors show that safety and accuracy follow different scaling laws in clinical large language models. Medicine punishes a few confident, high-risk errors more than average benchmark scores suggest, so the common assumption that bigger, more accurate models are safer by default is incomplete. The authors introduce SaFE-Scale, a framework for measuring how safety changes with model scale, evidence quality, retrieval strategy, context exposure, and inference-time compute.

Its testbed, RadSaFE-200, is a radiology safety benchmark of two hundred multiple-choice questions with clinician-defined clean and conflicting evidence and option-level labels for high-risk errors. Thirty-four locally deployed models were evaluated under six conditions. Clean evidence gave the strongest improvement, raising mean accuracy a lot while sharply reducing high-risk errors, evidence conflicts, and dangerous overconfidence.
arxiv-2605-04239:
Véronique Defonte and three co-authors tackle gaps in satellite image records caused by clouds and the edges of a satellite's path. Their focus is the Sentinel-2 mission, whose optical images are widely used for farming, climate, and land studies.

Most methods only fill gaps inside the time already observed. Their learning framework can also forecast images at future dates, by combining optical data with radar data from Sentinel-1, which sees through cloud. They pay special attention to how unsure each generated image is, so users know how much trust to place in a filled or forecast view.
arxiv-2605-04339:
Hossein Nemati and four co-authors ask how a varied environment changes the fate of a beneficial mutant in a population spread over a lattice. Depending on the setup, variation can either help the mutant take over or hold it back, and past results seemed to conflict.

Their unified framework lets the fitness of mutants and residents depend on the local environment. Two principles emerge: which genotype the environment affects decides the direction of the effect, while how mixed or clustered the environments are decides its size. Together these principles reconcile earlier findings and give criteria for predicting outcomes in new settings.
arxiv-2605-04539:
Qiming Bao and three co-authors tackle a weakness in a popular fine-tuning method for language models: the preference signals it learns from tend to reward fluent, lengthy answers over logically correct ones. In knowledge-heavy subjects, that leaves models that sound good while their answers are rarely entailed by the facts.

Their system builds preferences automatically by fusing a natural-language inference model's signal with a verifier model's score, needing no human annotation. Across five academic domains and three base models, it raised entailment scores substantially over standard fine-tuning in most settings. It also improved answer coverage. On one compact model it ran faster at inference time as well.
arxiv-2605-04939:
Erel Shtossel and Gal Kaminka propose a modular way for cooperative robot swarms to learn how to work together. Each small robot can only interact with a few neighbours and cannot see how its choices affect the whole group's goal. Earlier learning methods forced each robot to track a huge number of combined interaction states, straining tiny memories.

Their alternative splits the spatial state into features, with a separate learning procedure handling each feature and the results combined afterwards. Simulated swarms carrying out foraging tasks show the approach works well across many experiments. It offers swarm designers a memory-light route to coordinated behaviour in simple robots.
arxiv-2605-05039:
Akinari Hoshi and Kazuki Kanai study generalised Jacobi sums and cyclotomic numbers inside Thaine's framework, proving new multiplicative identities between them. Their main result extends a classical lifting theorem of Davenport and Hasse from single prime powers to products of prime powers. Jacobi sums are basic objects in number theory with deep links to counting points on curves.

As applications, the authors construct multiplicative forms of higher degree on complete intersections of such forms in algebraic geometry. That places a classical theory of multiplicative quadratic forms inside a broader setting on affine varieties, where new phenomena appear. On a dense open part of the variety, the form also fits an algebraic torus structure and its group law.
arxiv-2605-05239:
Jianhao Yang builds a variational framework for quantising gravitational fields based on an entropy-based action principle, aiming to avoid a classic puzzle of canonical quantum gravity. The usual route turns momentum into an operator, which creates ordering ambiguities. Yang instead extends the stationary action principle with an added term built from the relative entropy of field fluctuations.

An ensemble version on superspace carries that added term, and the refined scheme treats the quantum step and constraints together, settling the long-standing ordering question between them. The Wheeler-DeWitt equation emerges without operator promotion. Applied to gravity coupled to a massless scalar field, it yields a Schrödinger equation for the scalar wave function with an extra small quantum term.
arxiv-2605-05339:
When several drones carry one load on cables, a snapped cable can doom the flight. Hadi Hajieghrary and Paul Schmitt study that failure for teams of unmanned aircraft flying a shared slung load. The load shifts at once, and there is little time to diagnose the fault or plan a fix.

Their answer is a passive design that feeds each drone's measured cable tension straight into its thrust command. Control layers around it keep the load steady and limit swing. In simulations with five vehicles and a ten-kilogram load, the system recovered within one swing period, even when two cables broke.
arxiv-2605-05839: Maxim N. Demchenko studies the characteristic problem for the ultrahyperbolic equation, a wave-like equation with extra time-type directions, posed in Euclidean space. The data are given on a characteristic hyperplane, a surface aligned with the equation's own wave directions. He asks how smooth the solution is and how it behaves far away, tracing it along lines that cross the starting plane at an angle. The work connects to scattering questions: what a solution looks like at infinity records how it met the starting data.
arxiv-2605-06239:
Masatsugu Yamada and Mahito Sugiyama ask whether graph language models learn real structural rules or just memorize training graphs. Standard fidelity scores cannot separate the two, since a model that copies can score as well as one that generalizes. The authors build a calibrated diagnostic protocol to pull memorization and structural alignment apart.

Their method joins frequent subgraph mining, a graph level bootstrap baseline, and three level frequency stratification. At small scale, fidelity proved largely indistinguishable from verbatim recall under the diagnostic. At large scale, with millions of graphs, verbatim memorization dropped sharply while rank correlation stayed near ceiling. High frequency patterns were reproduced well at every scale, while rare patterns stayed poorly covered.
arxiv-2605-06339:
Zhaoyang Jiang and six co-authors develop a regime theory for choosing how a deployed model should decide what to do with each input. On every request, a language or vision language system can answer directly, fetch evidence, defer to a stronger model, or abstain. Common sense says more expressive per input controllers should win, but strict cross validation shows different benchmarks preferring different controller classes, a finite sample effect the paper sets out to explain.

Controllers form a nested lattice of four classes, from fixed actions up to prior gated designs. The theory converts three measurable bottlenecks into a class choice, with matching lower bounds on what any method can achieve. Across four benchmarks the predicted class matched the empirical winner. A prior gated controller also won a visual question task where OCR text supplied a free prior.
arxiv-2605-06639:
Apurva Gandhi, Satyaki Chakraborty, Xiangjun Wang, Aviral Kumar, and Graham Neubig introduce Recursive Agent Optimization, a reinforcement learning method for agents that can spawn copies of themselves. A recursive agent delegates sub-tasks to fresh instances of itself, giving a divide-and-conquer way to scale past one context window and toward harder problems at inference time.

RAO trains models to use that ability well: when to delegate, how to split work, and how to communicate results back. Agents trained this way learn more efficiently, handle tasks longer than a single context, and generalize to problems much harder than their training tasks. They can also finish faster in wall-clock time than single-agent systems by working branches in parallel.
arxiv-2605-06939: James Fiedler does bias and uncertainty in LLM-as-a-judge estimation. The doing does. Their doing is bias uncertainty LLM-as-a-judge estimation. The doing does. It is AI evaluation. The doing in. The estimation estimates LLM-judge-bias-uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-07039:
Minghao Yan and thirteen co-authors improve how language-model search agents learn during a search itself. Most evolutionary search systems sample new candidates from a fixed policy, which adapts poorly when evaluations are costly. PACEvolve++ instead trains a smaller advisor model at test time to guide the search.

The advisor proposes, judges, and selects hypotheses, while a stronger frontier model turns chosen ideas into working candidates. Training shifts strategy as the search matures, from broad group feedback early to frontier-focused feedback later. Across load balancing, recommendation, and protein tasks, the system converges faster than a leading framework and keeps test-time training stable.
arxiv-2605-07139:
Jialin Yang and five co-authors fix a quiet problem in teaching small language models to reason: teacher examples are inconsistent. For similar problems, a large teacher may show wildly different solution styles, burdening the student with noisy supervision. Their method constrains the teacher to a small bank of reusable reasoning paths.

For each question, the system retrieves the closest path and has the teacher follow it, keeping style consistent yet varied across problem types. Theory ties bank size to coverage, pointing to a best middle size that experiments confirm. Across five reasoning benchmarks and two student models, the method beats standard distillation approaches while using fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-07239:
Hongyu Cheng and three co-authors count how many samples stochastic optimization needs when variables must be whole numbers. Intuition might say integer problems are always harder than their continuous versions, but the picture depends on the objective's shape and the constraint set. The authors map out where each direction holds.

For Lipschitz objectives over box-shaped regions, mixed-integer complexity exactly matches plain linear optimization. Over round regions, integer problems can need strictly fewer samples in one regime. For strongly convex, smooth objectives, they need far more, with a lower bound that beats the classic continuous rate. New continuous results fill gaps along the way.
arxiv-2605-07439:
Mutian He and six co-authors release CA-DEL, a public benchmark for learning drug activity from DNA-encoded library screens. Such screens generate huge datasets, but their main signal, sequencing read counts, is a noisy stand-in for true binding strength. The benchmark covers screens against three closely related carbonic anhydrase enzymes, focusing on selectivity among near-identical targets.

Unlike benchmarks built only on noisy enrichment scores, CA-DEL adds a validation set of experimentally measured binding affinities from a public database. Models train on the noisy screens and are tested on high-fidelity measurements, a sim-to-real setup. The authors present it as a tougher, more realistic test for drug-discovery models.
arxiv-2605-07639:
Lorenzo Lamazzi and six co-authors address a stubborn problem in knowledge engineering: much of expert know-how is tacit, held in habits and judgments that never get written down. Procedural work runs on such knowledge, so pipelines that only handle explicit instructions miss what makes experts succeed. Their goal is machine-readable knowledge graphs that capture it.

They propose a neuro-symbolic framework pairing logic-augmented generation with an active-inference-inspired method for ontology-grounded graph construction. In a manufacturing case study, assembly-style repair procedures drawn from instructional videos served as the test domain. The approach improved both the completeness and the semantic quality of the extracted knowledge, a step toward knowledge engineering that can reuse real industrial expertise.
arxiv-2605-07739:
Eric Jacob and eight co-authors revisit the Emery model, the standard theoretical description of cuprate superconductors. Emery's original version included only one hopping term between oxygen and copper sites; later work added nearest and next-nearest oxygen-oxygen hoppings. Whether those three parameters suffice for a quantitatively correct picture was the open question.

Using the dynamical vertex approximation, the team does find a superconducting dome consistent with real cuprates. But matching the phase diagram quantitatively, and getting a proper d-wave order parameter, required long-range hoppings beyond the three conventional parameters. The result says the textbook model is qualitatively right but quantitatively incomplete, and names the missing ingredient.
arxiv-2605-07839:
François Pachet generates sequences that obey hard structural rules exactly, joining variable-order Markov models with regular constraints. The Markov side conditions each symbol on the longest matching stretch of history; the constraint side is an automaton expressing fixed positions, forced endings, metrical patterns, or banned copied fragments. Exact belief propagation already handled constraints for first-order chains, but not for variable-order generators.

Pachet pinpoints why: a first-order layer merges histories that a variable-order generator deliberately keeps separate, corrupting the future probabilities. The fix is to run the machinery on the observed context state instead, then take the product with the constraint automaton. Inference stays linear in sequence length for a fixed setup, and the same interface supports reversible data augmentation by inverse count lookup.
arxiv-2605-08139:
Gopal Krishna Shyam and Priyanka Bharti propose a stability-first autoscaler for distributed cloud systems. Ordinary scaling rules react to load spikes and can oscillate, repeatedly adding and removing virtual machines because network delays hide the true state. That flapping wastes money and hurts performance.

Their framework, C-SAS, converts noisy telemetry into a safety envelope on the complex plane using the argument principle and Rouché's theorem, and computes a real-time analytic stability index. Operations that would push the system toward oscillation are suppressed. In experiments, the method cut virtual machine flapping by ninety-four percent and reached ninety-six percent resource efficiency, beating PID and learned baselines.
arxiv-2605-08239:
Viktor Danchev, Alex Dyer, Sebastian Grau, and Guillaume Vazeille make the case for building particle colliders in space. The Large Hadron Collider has confirmed the Standard Model to high precision, yet dark matter, the hierarchy problem, and force unification stay open. Planned ground machines reach about one hundred teraelectronvolts, far below the scales where grand unified theories should show themselves.

From the scaling law for circular proton colliders, the authors estimate that rings thousands to hundreds of thousands of kilometers across are needed for the next energy frontier. Only orbital infrastructure offers that room, they argue, and space machines bring further practical benefits for reaching unification energies.
arxiv-2605-08339:
Shivam Singh Kushwah computes charge transport in a holographic model of hot quark-gluon plasma. The setup is a top-down M-theory background with quartic curvature corrections, extending the usual gauge-gravity dictionary into a non-conformal, higher-derivative regime closer to real thermal plasma.

Direct-current and Hall conductivities come from the Dirac-Born-Infeld action of probe flavor branes, using a reality condition method from earlier literature. Kushwah also works out pair production with and without an external magnetic field and identifies where thermal pair creation outweighs transport by existing charge carriers. The results carry earlier AdS/CFT transport findings into a richer class of plasma-like theories.
arxiv-2605-08439:
Natalie Seah, Danielle Bitterman, Daphna Spiegel, and Thomas Hartvigsen test whether language models can list the side effects of breast cancer radiation accurately enough for survivorship care. Patients deserve complete, clear toxicity information at consent and beyond, but clinician knowledge gaps and fragmented records make that hard in practice.

The team built paired clinical scenarios for twenty-one patient profiles that differ only in the radiotherapy regimen, then asked seven instruction-tuned models for side effect lists under several prompting styles. Comparing the outputs against the regimen differences forms a deployment-oriented stress test. The study probes how much trust oncology teams can place in model-generated counseling material.
arxiv-2605-08539:
Annan Yu, Dongwei Lyu, and N. Benjamin Erichson ask whether sequence models that claim roots in continuous time actually behave smoothly as time steps shrink. A model counts as continuous when its outputs settle toward one smooth path under finer time sampling. They also build a score for how continuous a dataset's own time structure is.

One state space model, S4, behaves steadily, while Mamba's core can react sharply to input size and selective dynamics. Across test sets, matching model continuity to task continuity tracks better results. Finer sampling tricks can then boost both speed and quality. Sequence modeling gains a clear law linking smooth time behavior to real gains.
arxiv-2605-08839:
Zhen-Hao Xie and five coauthors unify two hard learning problems: adapting to new domains and learning new classes without forgetting old ones. A driving system trained on sunny city roads may later face rural highways in rain, needing both shifts handled at once. Their CORF framework refines training samples by spatial contribution maps that highlight informative regions, and weighs samples by prediction confidence to favor domain agnostic features.

For memory, a cascaded distillation scheme transfers relational knowledge between samples across several feature levels from earlier tasks. The framework plugs into existing incremental learning methods and lifts their results across benchmarks. Systems that must keep growing in changing worlds gain one tool for both pressures.
arxiv-2605-09039:
Timo Kleger and four co-authors build SeasonScapes, a way to make large 3D landscapes that change with the seasons and can be lit anew. Their data comes from webcams in the Swiss mountains: more than eighty-five thousand images from thirty-two spots, taken at thirteen times across a full year.

The team projects the webcam images onto a 3D mesh of the terrain, which spans over fifty by sixty kilometers. Gaps from blocked views and missing data are filled with a diffusion model that paints directly on the mesh. The finished seasonal landscapes can then be rendered again under new lighting with standard tools, giving researchers a rare record of how a whole region changes through the year.
arxiv-2605-09239: Ask a model to count repeated tokens and something odd appears: what it represents internally dissociates from what it outputs. Sohan Venkatesh uses this simple task to reveal the gap between representations and outputs. The 2026 paper is a crisp experiment in interpretability.
arxiv-2605-09439: Matching a conditional distribution — generating the right outputs for each input — can be framed as inverse design. Ori Meidler, Shaul Tolkovsky, and Or Zuk take that route, designing backwards from the desired distribution. The 2026 paper is generative modeling through the lens of design.

Singh and co-authors examine how text-to-image models reproduce caste discrimination in this 2026 arXiv paper for a fairness and accountability conference. Prior work documented caste stereotypes in images but treated caste as a simple identity category, often a binary split. The authors study caste as a relation: how hierarchy and moral ordering operate between groups. Their audit combines algorithmic testing of generated images with discourse analysis, guided by a frame challenging Brahminical normativity, the assumption that upper-caste norms define the default.

In their corpus, prompts about people in particular places produced images where caste appeared outright and through an invisible order shaping cleanliness, dress, and setting. Bias thus outlived simple categorical representation. The gains are twofold: showing the mechanics of caste bias, and proposing an anti-caste approach to fairness efforts in AI. The authors argue that fixing representation counts will not undo the normative patterns.
