The United States delegation circulated this memorandum at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. With two days left, staff papers carried urgent weight. A memo could lock a position before a plenary session began. This one was filed with the conference papers and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Final-week memoranda reward close reading. They often mark the last point where a view could still change. Writers stated their case in short, plain terms. For readers today, the memo is a dated marker of American thinking at the brink of the final deal. It adds grit to the smooth surface of the agreed texts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-39:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record the approval of their 196th meeting's conclusions, held July 19, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. It settles the rules for passing war information to the Russians, the dispute aired in volume one.

Two rules were written into the conclusions. On operational information and intelligence, each side may pass the Russians what it wishes, without bargaining. That covers the theaters for which each staff is responsible. On all other information, the two staffs must consult together first. Neither party may pass Moscow anything drawn wholly or partly from the other's sources without that party's consent. The chiefs then took up a draft directive to the Supreme Commander in Southeast Asia, proposed by the British chiefs.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d739:
Benjamin Gerig, the American alternate delegate to the United Nations Preparatory Commission, wrote to Leo Pasvolsky and Alger Hiss on July 26, 1945. Document 739 comes from the building of the new world body. The Commission, seated in London, was readying the first General Assembly. Gerig reported to two of the Department's top planners.

Letters like this one wired Potsdam to the United Nations' birth. The men addressed had shaped the charter at San Francisco. Readers see postwar planning as a single web: summit talks in Germany, organization work in London. The document shows staff keeping both efforts in step during a crowded week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d839:
Document 839 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 22, 1945. Staff drafted it as the conference closed its first week. Working papers at this stage answered points raised in the early sessions. The paper was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A week's-end draft shows learning in progress. The writers had heard the other sides and adjusted. Readers can track the change from the opening papers. The document also shows the staff's rhythm: sessions by day, drafting by night. That rhythm produced the mountain of paper from which the final protocol was cut.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d939:
Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov presented this second definition of war trophies at Potsdam on July 27, 1945. It restates the Soviet claim in two parts. War trophies mean all German military property. That includes gear meant for use by enemy military and paramilitary units, or by their members.

The second part reaches beyond the battlefield. It covers property the enemy used for military purposes. Such property counts even when it was removed from Germany during the war to serve Allied military needs. A later letter in the Pauley Files notes that no formal action was taken on either Soviet definition.
fundamental-orders-connecticut-1639:
Settlers from Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield adopted the Fundamental Orders in 1639 to govern their Connecticut towns. The document lays out a frame of government made by the settlers themselves. No royal charter stood behind it, which made the act bold for its time.

The orders provide for a general court, elected magistrates, and a governor chosen each year. They set rules for meetings, voting, and the duties of town deputies. Because the plan is written, general, and based on consent, many call it the first written constitution in America. It guided Connecticut until a royal charter arrived in 1662.
gao-gaoreports-b-296239: PPCSC/RAC Benning JV took its July 2005 contract fight to GAO as a joint venture, and this ruling is the verdict. The venture said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Joint ventures get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298239: PPG-CMS-PSI JV doubled its July 2006 protest — two case numbers, one joint-venture fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The venture challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299539: Moore's Cafeteria Services, doing business as MCS Management, took its June 2007 food-service fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims. Chow-hall contracts get the full fair-play treatment too.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-139: The young homeland shop's merger needed staying power in 2005, and GAO's report says the long game was required. The review calls for the patient build. The young department deserved the integration. The build had to last. The haul was long.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-239: Germ-fight grant spending got a GAO accounting in 2005, and the report tracks what the locals spent and owed. The review follows the money trail. The ready crews deserved the count. The trail was followed. The money was followed. The count was complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-339: The nuclear cops needed to do more in 2005, and GAO's report says the NRC had to ensure plants controlled spent fuel effectively. The review demands the vigilance. The glowing rods deserved the guard. The commission had to act. The glowing rods deserved the guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-539: Job training scorecards needed a rethink in 2005, and GAO's report says Labor should try fresh ways to grade the programs. The findings demand the rethink. The report warns that the trainees deserved workable rules. The trainees deserved workable rules. The rethink had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-639: The Global Fund's AIDS fight got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the fund responded to challenges, though better information was needed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the dying deserved honest aid. The information had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-239: The SEC's 2005 financial statements got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines the books for fiscal years 2005 and 2004. The findings grade the accounting. The report shows the market cop's own money was checked. The statements had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-639: Oil spills in the St. Clair-Detroit waterway needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says better information and targeted prevention could help. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the shared waters deserved guarding. The management had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-839: Weapon buying needed better data rights in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon should strengthen policies for assessing technical data needs. The findings demand the rules. The report warns that the military's toys needed their blueprints secured. The policies had to be strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-139: FEMA's day-to-day money needed better tracking in 2007, and GAO's report says the agency needed adequate data, plans, and systems. The findings demand the tools. The report warns that the disaster agency should not be a disaster of bookkeeping. The books had to match the mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-39: Guarding critical infrastructure was uneven in 2007, and GAO's report says progress in coordinating public and private efforts varied by sector. The findings map the gaps. The report warns that the power grid and water plants needed steadier guarding. The coordination had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-839: Iraq's oil money moved through Pentagon deals in 2007 — and GAO's report says the contracting rules got bent. Skipping key bidding principles on the oil contract put the government at risk. The findings read as a wartime cautionary tale: haste in contracting invites waste, or worse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-39: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at stabilization and Reconstruction: Actions Are Needed to Develop a Planning and Coordination Framework and Establish the Civilian Reserve Corps. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-539: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at influenza Pandemic: Federal Agencies Should Continue to Assist States to Address Gaps in Pandemic Planning. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-939: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at federal Real Property: Progress Made in Reducing Unneeded Property, but VA Needs Better Information to Make Further Reductions. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
great-bible-1539:
Myles Coverdale prepared the Great Bible, printed in 1539 as the first English Bible authorized for public use. King Henry VIII ordered a copy placed in every parish church in England. Its huge page size gave it the name Great, and copies were chained to lecterns so anyone could hear or read them.

Coverdale built the text by revising Matthew's Bible, drawing on Latin and German sources where older English ran out. The volume holds the complete Old and New Testaments. It put one shared English Scripture in front of the whole country, and later translators, including the Geneva team, worked from it.
ioannis-aurelij-augurelli-p-ariminensis-: Ioannis Aurelii Augurelli Chrysopoeia et Vellus aureum, 1639. The gold-making poem. This book preserves that alchemy. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machado-10239:
Machado, the name of a Marano family that crossed to America, is traced in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The name appears early in Mexico and the West Indies. In 1600 the Mexican Inquisition charged Isabel Machado and her father Antonio with being Jews. Machados also surface in Martinique and Surinam.

The article centers on the New York branch of the family. David Mendez Machado fled the Inquisition from Lisbon to England, then sailed to Savannah in 1733. He married Zipporah, daughter of Dr. Samuel Nunez, and moved to New York. There he served as cantor of Shearith Israel from 1734 until his death in 1753. His descendants, the entry notes, include Commodore Uriah P. Levy and Mordecai M. Noah. A family tree closes the piece. It preserves the path of one refugee family into American Jewish leadership.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mamon-mammon-10:
Mamon, or Mammon, is examined as a word in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The term is Mishnaic Hebrew and Aramaic for riches. It is the word Jesus uses in the Sermon on the Mount. You cannot serve God and mammon, the saying runs. The article is signed simply by Joseph Jacobs.

The entry clears away a popular error. No evidence shows that Mammon was ever a Syrian god, the writers state. That idea comes from Milton, who personified Mammon in Paradise Lost as a fallen spirit. The word appears in the Mishnah tractate Abot, where almsgiving is called the salt of riches. Gesenius derived it from matmon, meaning treasure, with a letter assimilated. Scholars also debate the spelling, since the Greek form with two m's is held correct. The short piece is a model of separating a word's real history from poetry's inventions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marshall-louis-:
Louis Marshall was an American lawyer and a Jewish communal leader. Cyrus Adler wrote his profile for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Syracuse, New York, on December 14, 1856. He studied at Columbia College Law School and began practice in Syracuse in 1878. He moved his practice to New York City in 1894.

The entry traces his rise at the bar. In 1890 he sat on the commission to revise the judiciary article of the New York constitution. He also played a part in the state constitutional convention of 1894. The entry then turns to his communal work. It names the Jewish Theological Seminary, Congregation Emanu-El, and the Educational Alliance, plus his push for a protectory for delinquent Jewish children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medals-10539:
Cyrus Adler and Albert Wolf catalogue Jewish medals in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The medals run from the fifteenth century to the day of the encyclopedia. The art of engraving medals revived in Italy about 1450, and a few Jewish pieces survive from that age. Their numbers were kept small, the authors say, by the general oppression of the Jews. As conditions improved through the eighteenth century the medals multiplied, and after emancipation they appeared nearly every year.

What follows is a dated list, each item describing obverse and reverse and giving the size in millimeters. It opens with a portrait medal of 1503 and one for Gracia Nasi in 1556. It turns to events: the defense of Buda in 1686 and the Frankfort ghetto fire of 1711. It goes on to the execution of Süss Oppenheimer in 1738 and the Prague expulsion edict of 1745. Private and cabalistic medals are left out by design.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millaud-moise-p:
Moïse Polydore Millaud, born at Bordeaux on August 27, 1813, was the French journalist and banker who built a press empire from almost nothing. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A poor Jewish tradesman's son with little schooling, he started as a bailiff's clerk and was publishing his own paper at twenty.

His early Paris ventures failed but taught him the trade, and his court-news paper L'Audience prospered from 1839 until 1845 against the official Gazette des Tribunaux. His La Liberté backed Louis Napoleon and was suppressed after the June rising of 1848. With Mirès he then launched the Journal des Chemins de Fer, which became a power in railway finance and speculation across France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mommsen-christi:
Theodor Mommsen, the great historian of Rome, was born at Garding on November 30, 1817. He earns his Jewish Encyclopedia entry on two grounds, as Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer explain in 1906. His Römische Geschichte treats the Jews of the Roman empire at length. Its fifth volume has a whole chapter on Judaea and the Jews. In German politics, too, he fought the anti-Semites.

Mommsen sat in the Prussian Diet and the Reichstag as a Liberal. He answered Treitschke's attack with his own pamphlet of 1881. In it he pleaded tolerance. He called the Jewish element in the empire a wholesome one. He was among the first to sign the notables' declaration of November 1880. That declaration branded Jew-baiting a national disgrace. He died at Charlottenburg in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moscheles-ignaz:
Ignaz Moscheles was an Austrian pianist ranked, in his entry's words, the greatest player between Hummel and Chopin. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Prague on May 30, 1794, he played a concerto of his own in public in 1808. After his father's death he made his living in Vienna as a teacher and player.

In Vienna, Moscheles knew Beethoven and helped prepare the piano arrangement of Fidelio. Ten years of concert tours followed, and in London in 1824 he gave lessons to the young Felix Mendelssohn. He settled in London, led the Philharmonic Society, and in 1846 became the first piano professor at the new Leipzig Conservatorium. He died at Leipzig in 1870, leaving concertos, studies, and a school of playing of his own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-samue:
Moses ben Samuel ben Asher was a French Talmudist of Perpignan in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He and his father held great influence in the city. They won from King James of Majorca leave for Jews expelled from France in 1306 to settle at Perpignan.

Moses was a close friend of Abba Mari of Lunel, and his daughter married Abba Mari's son. During the Montpellier controversy over philosophy, the two men corresponded steadily. Moses, the more liberal and peaceable of the two, refused to take his friend's hard line. He defended Abba Mari locally while pressing him for facts, and worked to calm all parties in Perpignan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mourning-10639:
Mourning, the show of grief for the dead, is covered at length in this Jewish Encyclopedia article by Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein. It treats grief for a relative, a friend, a leader, or a whole nation. The Bible's first mourner is Abraham, weeping for Sarah.

The article sorts the customs by period and source. Biblical mourners threw dust on their heads, wore sackcloth, and sat in ashes, though self-wounding was forbidden. Public mourning among the Hebrews never passed thirty days, while the anniversary of the Temple's fall is mourned yearly. Rabbinic law then divides grief into stages of three days, seven days, thirty days, and a year for parents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nataf-isaac-b-s: Isaac b. Solomon Nataf was a rabbi at Tunis around the year 1800. His short entry was written by Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nataf wrote a book on oaths, printed at Leghorn in 1820. The book treats twenty kinds of oaths and the duties they place on man. The entry also points readers to notes on Tunisian Jewish books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-night-11539:
Night, in the Bible, runs from sunset to sunrise. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Landsberg wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The older phrase for a full day was day and night. Later speech used evening and morning instead. Israel, like Greece, reckoned days from sunset.

The Gauls and old Germans kept the same custom. It likely grew out of the cult of the moon. Yet sacrifice law counts some nights with the day before. Time had no exact measure in early Israel. Stages were named by light: dawn, midday heat, evening breeze. Between the lights named the hour of the evening sacrifice. Three night watches divided the dark in the Temple. Roman practice later made the watches four in number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oath-11639:
Oath treats the sworn pledge in Jewish law and court use. The entry was written for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its authors were the Editorial Board and Julius Rappoport. Two Hebrew words, alah and shebuah, name the oath. In the Bible the two words are used as one.

Under old Jewish law, courts used oaths in civil suits only. They were not used in crime cases at all. An oath came when proof was weak or lacking. It was laid on the one who was sued, not the one who sued. The oath called God to witness the truth told. A man thought prone to lie was not sworn. The piece traces how later rabbis widened these rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheimer-fra:
Franz Oppenheimer was a German doctor who turned to writing. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berlin on March 30, 1864. His father was rabbi of the Berlin Reform flock. Franz read cures at Freiburg and at Berlin. He took his medical degree in the year 1885.

In 1887 Franz set up a practice in Berlin. He made throat and nose ills his chief field there. Soon he gave up the work of a doctor in full. He turned to books, to wealth in lands, and to groups. He wrote verse and a drama in his first years. His chief works treat land held in common by men. One treats the great land owners and the needs of the poor. One treats the law of growth in the count of souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pacifico-case-1:
The Pacifico Case was a clash of states over one man's claim. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. David Pacifico was born a British subject at Gibraltar. He was born there in the year 1784. He died in London on April 12, 1854.

Pacifico first set up in trade at Lagos, in Portugal. His goods were seized for his lean to the Liberal side. In time he was made consul of Portugal in Greece. He was cast out of that post in the year 1842. He stayed on at Athens, the chief town of Greece. In 1847 a mob burnt his house down in that town. He claimed a huge sum for his loss in goods. Greece would not treat that great claim with care. So Lord Palmerston sent a British fleet to Piraeus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paternity-11939:
Paternity in Jewish law is the subject of this legal article. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote it. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The stakes are high, since fatherhood fixes inheritance and priestly rank.

The Bible traced descent through the father alone. Census lists were kept by the house of the fathers. A man could deny a child born outside marriage. He could also claim such a child and give him full rights. The rules set a three month wait before a widow remarried. That wait kept a child's father clear in most cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-periodicals-100:
Jewish periodicals, as this long survey defines them, serve Jewish readers. Richard Gottheil and William Popper wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The term covers both newspapers and magazines. Some are marked Jewish by language, others by subject alone.

Daily papers report the general news of the world. Jewish weeklies focus on matters of Jewish concern. They range from world politics to local community gossip. Magazines split into literary and scientific kinds. Most scientific ones serve the Jewish sciences, like history and philology. Special papers serve cantors, students, and societies too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perles-12039:
Perles is a family of rabbis and scholars from Prague. Gotthard Deutsch and Isidore Singer wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its members spread from Bohemia into Hungary and Germany. Many of them served as rabbis for generations.

Aaron Perles edited a classic work on meat porging. His edition came out at Offenbach in 1722. Baruch Asher Perles taught at Baja in Hungary. He favored plain sense over clever pilpul in study. He sent his son Joseph to the new Breslau seminary. Joseph's son Felix became a rabbi at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pico-de-mirando:
Giovanni Pico de Mirandola was an Italian thinker and cabalist. He was born in 1463 and died at Florence in 1494. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At twenty-three he stunned the learned world.

In 1486 Pico printed nine hundred bold new theses at Rome. One held that Kabbalah best proves Christ divine. Johanan Aleman had taught him the Kabbalah himself. Pico rendered three Hebrew cabalistic books into Latin. He tried to wed Plato, Aristotle, and Jewish mysticism. Charged with heresy, he was cleared and retired.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-police-laws-122:
Police laws are laws that guard public peace, health, safety, and morals. The Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their main aim, they say, is to stop crime before it starts. The article asks how far back such laws go in Jewish life.

The writers first ask if Bible towns had a true police force. They note that the book of Deuteronomy orders officers in every town. These officers, called shoterim, worked beside the judges. They made public calls to the people, above all in war. They guarded the king and watched over public works. Later parts of the article trace such rules in later Jewish law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-preexistence-12:
Preexistence means that a thing or soul lived before earthly life. Kaufmann Kohler and Ludwig Blau wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Old Jewish books give such early life to key persons and things. These are things that form part of God's plan. They serve the saving of man or the rule of the world.

One teaching tells of the souls of the righteous. God took counsel with them before he made the world. The writers trace this view to a foreign source. They find it in the Zend-Avesta of Persia. There the holy souls of heroes hold a cosmic place. Their god holds council with them before creation as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahmer-moritz-1:
Moritz Rahmer was a German rabbi born on December 12, 1837. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Rybnik in Prussian Silesia. He died at Magdeburg on March 2, 1904.

The article traces his study at the Breslau seminary from 1854 to 1862. He then served at Thorn and, from 1867, at Magdeburg. His books treat Maimonides, Jerome, prayer, and the twelve minor prophets. He also edited Jewish papers for many years. Those papers included the Jüdisches Litteraturblatt and the Israelitische Wochenschrift. The entry shows a rabbi who also shaped Jewish reading week by week.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rice-isaac-leop:
Isaac Leopold Rice was an American lawyer, author, and chess player. Cyrus Adler and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born on February 22, 1850, at Wachenheim. His mother brought him to America at age six.

The article says he studied literature and music in Paris. He reported for a Philadelphia paper while there. Back in New York he won fame as a music teacher. He took a law degree from Columbia in 1880. He practiced law and worked in railway affairs. In 1885 he founded the Forum magazine. Later he led an electric storage battery company. He founded America's electric car and boat industries, they say. He also led the Manhattan Chess Club.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomons-sir-ju:
Sir Julian Emanuel Salomons was an Australian statesman born in Birmingham in 1834. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Called to the English bar in 1861, he emigrated to New South Wales.

Salomons practised with much success before Sydney's Supreme Court, becoming Queen's Counsel. He defended O'Farrel, the Fenian who shot the Duke of Edinburgh in 1868. He served as solicitor-general in two ministries, in 1869 and 1870. Offered the chief justiceship in 1886, he resigned it after a few days. Twice he served as the colony's agent-general in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-phoebus-:
Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel Phoebus ben Nathan Feitel, an Austrian writer of history. He lived in Vienna across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. His book Ṭiṭ ha-Yawen tells of the Cossack uprising under Bogdan Chmielnicki. That revolt swept the Ukraine and Galicia in the seventeenth century.

The book names the cities that suffered in the rising. It lists 140 synagogues that were destroyed. It states that some 600,070 Jews were thought to have been killed. The work first appeared at Venice after 1649. A second edition came out at Cracow in 1892. There it formed part of Gurland's collection on the persecutions of Israel. It remains a grim firsthand-style record of the disaster.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saxon-duchies-1:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Saxon duchies. The four duchies are Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, Saxe-Meiningen, and Saxe-Weimar. All lie in Thuringia, within the German empire. Saxe-Altenburg held only forty Jews among some 195,000 people. Saxe-Coburg-Gotha held 580 Jews, split between Coburg and Gotha.

Saxe-Meiningen carries the darkest history here. On Good Friday in 1349, a girl claimed she heard Jews plotting an attack. Jews were jailed on her word. On July 17 they were burned at the stake with their families. Their synagogue stood closed for twenty-two years. It then became a chapel. By 1904 the duchy held 1,487 Jews again. Saxe-Weimar's edict of 1823 ended the body tax on Jews. It still barred them from brewing, butchering, baking, and innkeeping.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-anton-1:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Anton Schwarz. He was an Austrian chemist. Schwarz was born at Polna, in Bohemia, on February 2, 1839. He died in New York City on September 24, 1895. He studied law at Vienna, then chemistry at Prague. In 1868 he emigrated to the United States.

In New York, Schwarz joined the staff of Der Amerikanische Bierbrauer, The American Brewer. He soon became its editor and then its owner. He did much to improve brewing methods in America. In 1880 he founded the Brewers' Academy of the United States. His son Max succeeded him at both the journal and the academy. Max championed the cause of pure beer in America. He died in New York in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-serene-serenus-:
Serene, also called Serenus, was a false messiah in Syria early in the eighth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. A responsum by Natronai Gaon preserves much of what is known. Serene set up rites that broke rabbinic law in many ways.

He dropped set prayer and loosened rules on food, wine, and marriage. He also let people work on the second holy day. His rise is dated to about 720, under the caliph Yazid II. In Spain, many Jews sold all they owned and made ready to follow him. The entry shows how hope for redemption could sweep whole communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shelah-13539: Shelah was the youngest son of Judah, by a Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shuah. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Chezib, in Judah's lowland country. When his brother Onan died, Shelah was still very young. Judah used that youth as his reason for delay. He would not let Shelah marry his sister-in-law Tamar, as custom required. Shelah later became ancestor of many families, as Chronicles records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sidon-simon-136:
Simon Sidon was a Hungarian rabbi and author born at Nadas in 1815. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied at the yeshivah of Moses Sofer, the famed Hatam Sofer. Settling in his native town, he opened a yeshivah there.

In 1845 Sidon became rabbi of Cziffer in Hungary. In 1856 he moved to the rabbinate of Tyrnau. He held that post until his death in 1891. Though strictly conservative, he tolerated modern ideas in others. In 1860 he sent his son to Breslau's seminary. That choice drew strong opposition from traditionalists around him. His Ot Berit covers circumcision, proselytes, and firstborn redemption. His Shebet Shim'on adds legal notes and special sermons in three parts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-cephas-be:
Simon Cephas, better known as Peter, was the first of the Twelve Apostles. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Peter was the chief disciple of Jesus and head of the early Church. His second name, Kaipha, means rock in Aramaic. Latin Petrus comes from petra, also meaning rock.

Peter was a fisherman of Capernaum, like his brother Andrew. The Gospels tell of Jesus calling both men from their nets. Peter's house became a center of Jesus' work in Galilee. The sick were brought there to be healed on the Sabbath evening. The article follows these Gospel accounts and the legends that grew around his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solis-sometimes:
Solis was a Spanish and Portuguese family of crypto-Jews. Joseph Jacobs and Emily Solis-Cohen Jr wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Some members served as inquisitors, while others suffered under the Inquisition. Those who escaped to Holland, France, and England professed Judaism openly. In the eighteenth century some crossed to America.

The American branch traced its line to Solomon da Silva Solis. He emigrated from Spain to Amsterdam in the seventeenth century. David Hays Solis aided schools and charities in Philadelphia and New York. He backed Isaac Leeser and the anti-slavery movement as well. Other members served as merchants, lawyers, and soldiers across three continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-victor-14:
Victor Stern was an Austrian dramatist born at Vienna on May 5, 1837. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He spent a short time in commercial work first. Then he turned to literature as his calling. The playwright Friedrich Hebbel encouraged him from 1861.

Under Hebbel's support, Stern wrote some of his best work. His tragedies include Valentin, printed in 1868. Das Kronenhaus followed in 1872. Calas appeared in 1889, late in his career. Schloss Arnheim came out in 1893. The brief entry lists four stage tragedies across twenty-five years. It gives readers a quick map of a Viennese playwright's output. His work belongs to the German theater of his century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sutro-adolph-he:
Adolph Sutro was an American engineer born in Prussia in 1830. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Aix-la-Chapelle on April 29. The revolution of 1848 ruined his family's woolen mills. They emigrated to Baltimore in 1850.

Gold drew Sutro to San Francisco that same year. Nevada silver mines next pulled him east to Dayton. His stamping mill there proved a technical success. Deep Comstock shafts grew too hot for miners to work. Sutro planned a tunnel to drain and cool the lode. Congress approved his tunnel company in 1866. Digging began in 1869 at the Carson River valley. He died at San Francisco in 1898. The entry follows the tunnel that bears his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmud-10739:
The Talmud is the great record of Jewish tradition after the Bible. Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Two Talmuds survive from the amoraic age. One comes from Palestinian schools, the other from Babylonian ones. Scholars call them the Yerushalmi and the Babli.

Used alone, the word Talmud usually means the Babylonian work. The name itself comes from a verb meaning to teach. It can mean teaching or learning in older usage. The amoraic period ran from the third to fifth centuries. In that span the schools built both compilations. The Talmud crowns the writings of Jewish tradition. Bacher calls it tradition's most important production historically. The long entry unpacks its name, making, and contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanna-debe-eliy:
Tanna debe Eliyahu is a midrash in two linked parts. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its final editing came at the end of the tenth century. Part one, the Greater Order of Elijah, holds thirty-one chapters. Part two, the Lesser Order, holds fifteen.

The Talmud ties the work to the prophet Elijah himself. Elijah used to visit Rabbi Anan and recite it. After one ruling by Anan, the prophet stopped coming. Anan fasted and begged forgiveness until he returned. Fear then made Anan hear it from inside a box. Rashi explains the two names from those visits. The greater book holds the earlier lectures. The entry blends textual history with a prophet's legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tugendhold-jaco:
Jacob Tugendhold was a Russian educator who modernized Jewish schooling in Warsaw. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Breslau in 1791, he died at Warsaw in 1871. In 1819 he founded a school for Jewish children there. Its teaching used modern methods and broad subjects.

Conservative teachers fought his plan at every step. In 1820 Russia made him censor of Warsaw's Jewish books. He directed the city's rabbinical school from 1853 to 1862. He also led the Warsaw kahal for years. His efforts built a home for aged and invalid Jews. His books include a Polish defense against the blood accusation. He translated Mendelssohn's Phaedon into Polish as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-van-oven-abraha:
Abraham Van Oven was a doctor who settled in London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His grandfather had fled Spain early in the seventeen hundreds. The family name came from Oven, in Holland. Van Oven earned his medical diploma at Leyden in 1759.

After some time at Hamburg, he moved to England. In London he built a large practice among Jewish patients. He also knew Hebrew well. He translated Congreve's play The Mourning Bride into Hebrew. Van Oven died in England in 1778. His son Joshua and grandson Barnard appear in later entries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vulgate-14739:
The Vulgate is the Latin Bible of the Roman Catholic Church. Crawford Howell Toy and Ira Maurice Price wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Council of Trent authorized it in 1546. Most of the work came from Jerome. He was among the most learned of the early church leaders.

Earlier Latin versions came from North Africa, not Rome. They were translated from Greek, not Hebrew. Jerome did not revise every book in the Latin Bible. Old Latin text fills those gaps. Books like Wisdom and Maccabees kept the older wording. The Psalms also survive in a revised older form. The entry traces how these layers joined into one Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-windows-hallon-:
Windows in ancient Hebrew houses were few and small. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew words are hallon and arubbah. Climate and custom made houses mere sleeping places. Work and life went on outdoors. Many windows would admit heat, rain, and cold.

Street windows sat small and high in the wall. Solomon's Temple windows followed that pattern. Wide windows belonged to rich men's palaces only. Glass existed in the ancient East but never glazed windows. Openings stayed bare or took wooden shutters. Lattices, some fixed in place, served the Temple itself. The entry compares Hebrew, Egyptian, and Babylonian practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-xanten-15039:
Xanten is a town in Rhenish Prussia on the Rhine. Joseph Jacobs and Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Like most Rhine towns, it had Jews in early medieval times. Two mass killings struck its Jews in the First Crusade.

Both blows fell in June of the year 1096. Some Jews took their own lives to escape the mob. In 1187 the slain of Neuss were brought there for burial. They were laid by the side of the dead of 1096. Late in the 1800s the town drew the eyes of world Jewry. A blood charge rose there in the year 1891. A boy of five was found dead with his throat cut. Mob press blamed a Jewish butcher for the crime.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zabim-sufferers:
Zabim is the ninth tract in the order on purity laws. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in both the Mishnah and the Tosefta. It treats the foul state caused by flux from the body.

Those rules rest on the fifteenth part of Leviticus. A man or a woman with such a flux is unclean. All that such a one sits or lies on is unclean. A man who shares that seat or bed is unclean till night. He must wash his flesh and his clothes in water. A clay pot touched by such a one must be smashed. A wood pot so touched must be rinsed in water. When the flux stops, the sick one counts seven days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zemirot-songs-1:
Zemirot, which means songs, names two sets of hymns in Jewish rite. Joseph Jacobs and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Sephardic Jews use the word for the Psalms at dawn rite. Those psalms stand in the first parts of that rite.

North rite Jews use the word in a more tight sense. For them it names the hymns sung at the home board. Those hymns come ere or after grace at the chief meal. That meal is the feast of Sabbath eve and day. Song at board was a set part of old Jewish life. The Mishnah says it stopped as a sign of woe. That woe was for the fall of the great court of old. Late rabbis had to press men to shun board song still. No ban stood on songs of a devout cast in that rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zionism-14339:
Zionism is the movement to gather the Jewish people as a nation in a home of their own. Richard Gottheil wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its modern form, he explains, seeks a publicly and legally assured home in Palestine. Theodor Herzl started that modern movement in 1896, and it soon came to lead Jewish public life.

Gottheil traces the idea first to the Bible, where return from exile fills many passages. He then links it with belief in the Messiah, who would gather the scattered people. The article also sets modern Zionism apart from the earlier Chovevei Zion groups. Written while the movement was still young, it shows how its supporters grounded a new politics in old texts.
journal-of-a-residence-on-a-georgian-pla:
Frances Anne Kemble's Journal of a Residence on a Georgian Plantation records her stay in Georgia in 1838 and 1839. Kemble was an English actress who married into a slaveholding family. The journal's front matter quotes Alexander H. Stephens, vice-president of the Confederacy. He called slavery the chief cornerstone of the new Confederate edifice, in his 1861 speech.

That quotation, printed as the book's motto, frames Kemble's pages as an answer. Her journal describes daily life on the plantation as she saw it, written by a woman who came to oppose slavery. Published in the Civil War era, it gave Northern readers a firsthand account from inside a slaveholder's household. It remains a sharp witness to the system Stephens praised.
la-psychologie-et-la-phrenologie-compare:
Adolphe Garnier published La Psychologie et la Phrénologie Comparées in Paris in 1839. Garnier taught philosophy at the Faculty of Letters there. The publisher was L. Hachette, bookseller to the royal university.

Garnier compares two ways of explaining the mind. Psychology studies inner life by reflection and reason. Phrenology claims character sits in organs of the brain. His book weighs those rival claims side by side, at a time when phrenology drew crowds and critics alike. The comparison itself is the book's main event. Garnier asks what each method can prove, and what it cannot.
lakhovsky-secret-of-life-1939:
Georges Lakhovsky, a Russian-born engineer working in France, set out his theory of life and health in Le Secret de la Vie. Mark Clement's English version, The Secret of Life, came out in 1939. Its subject is cosmic rays and the unseen waves given off by living things.

Lakhovsky held that each cell works like a tiny radio set, tuned to waves from space. Sickness, in his view, is a cell out of tune. His Multiple Wave Oscillator was built to retune the body. Mainstream science never took the theory up, but the book led the fringe field of wave healing. His name still turns up wherever wave cures are sold.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-4:
Books eight to ten close Laplace's Mecanique Celeste, and Bowditch's fourth volume appeared in 1839. Satellites and comets take up much of this final part. Laplace also surveys the system of the world as a whole. A treatment of capillary attraction, the pull seen in narrow tubes, ends the work.

Bowditch's commentary runs alongside the text to the last page. With this volume the English set stands complete at four. The project took him a decade of spare hours. It carried the summit of French celestial mechanics to America. Readers who finish it have crossed the whole system. The feat still anchors his fame.
morton-crania-americana-1839:
Samuel George Morton, a Philadelphia physician, published Crania Americana in 1839. He measured hundreds of skulls from Indigenous peoples across North and South America. From those measurements he ranked human groups by supposed mental worth.

The plates and tables present his skull collection in careful detail. Later scholars, most famously Stephen Jay Gould, showed how bias warped the work. It became a founding text of American physical anthropology and of scientific racism. Readers today study it to see how prejudice can dress itself as measurement. Its large plates made it a reference work in American museums for decades.
openalex-w2009068239:
Claudio Lanata, Christa Fischer-Walker, Ana Olascoaga and colleagues estimated what kills young children through diarrhoea. Their review appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Knowing which germs cause deaths guides vaccine work. It also guides other prevention plans. The team focused on children under five.

They reviewed studies from 1990 to 2011 on thirteen germs. The studies covered hospital patients in many countries. They also used world rotavirus survey data for 2011. Rotavirus came out as the leading cause of deaths. Two forms of E. coli and calicivirus followed. Together these germs caused over half of diarrhoea deaths. In many cases no germ could be identified at all.
openalex-w2073832139:
Adam Riess, Alexei Filippenko, Peter Challis and colleagues found signs that cosmic expansion is speeding up. Their paper appeared in The Astronomical Journal in 1998. They observed exploding stars called Type Ia supernovae. Such blasts shine with a known brightness pattern. That makes them markers of cosmic distance.

The team measured ten of these stars at large distances. Their light curves gave the distance to each one. Combined with nearer star data, a pattern emerged. Distant blasts looked dimmer than a slowing cosmos predicts. The expansion of space appears to speed up. A steady push, called the cosmological constant, can explain it. The finding reshaped how scientists view the cosmos.
openalex-w2105942939:
Jan Suchodolski, Melissa Markel, Jose Francisco Garcia-Mazcorro and colleagues compared gut microbes in healthy and sick dogs. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. A complex bacterial community lives in the dog gut. Its role in gut disease was growing clearer. The team profiled stool samples by gene sequencing.

Healthy dogs were compared with dogs with diarrhoea. Dogs with bowel inflammation were also included. Acute diarrhoea dogs showed the strongest microbe shifts. Bloody diarrhoea brought the deepest changes of all. Several helpful bacterial groups fell sharply. One harmful species rose in those dogs. Inactive bowel disease looked closer to healthy patterns. Microbe profiles may guide future dog gut treatments.
openalex-w2132089139:
João Paulo Souza, A. Metin Gülmezoglu, Pisake Lumbiganon, and colleagues published this study in BMC Medicine in 2010. They used the World Health Organization global survey on maternal and perinatal health. Their question was whether caesarean births done without a medical reason are linked to worse short-term outcomes for mothers.

The survey covered twenty-four countries and hundreds of health facilities, with records for over two hundred eighty thousand births. About one in a hundred births was a caesarean without recorded medical indication. Compared with spontaneous vaginal birth, these caesareans were associated with higher risk of death, intensive care, transfusion, and hysterectomy. The link looked strongest in Africa.
openalex-w2168608639:
Li-Jun Ma, Ashraf Ibrahim, Christopher Skory, and colleagues published this genome study in PLoS Genetics in 2009. They sequenced Rhizopus oryzae, the main cause of mucormycosis, a fast, vessel-invading fungal infection that kills over half its victims. The fungus also serves as a model for an early-branching group in the fungal kingdom.

The strain came from a fatal human case. Full analysis of its genome revealed a surprise: an ancient doubling of the entire genome. Such wholesale duplication helps explain the fungus's gene richness and adaptability. The sequence gives researchers a reference for studying both this dangerous infection and how the earliest fungal lineages evolved their complex traits.
openalex-w2256016639:
Monkol Lek, Konrad Karczewski, Eric Minikel, and colleagues published this analysis in Nature in 2016. They built ExAC, a reference catalogue of protein-coding genetic variation in over sixty thousand people. Doctors reading a patient's genome need such a baseline to tell harmless differences from disease-causing mutations.

The team gathered exome sequences from over ninety thousand people and filtered them for quality. The final set spans sixty thousand seven hundred six individuals of diverse ancestry, mapped by genetic clustering. Protein-coding regions, though a small share of the genome, hold most known disease mutations. The catalogue shows how variation is distributed in the general population, sharpening medical and functional reading of DNA changes.
openalex-w2437571239:
B. Abbott and colleagues in the LIGO and Virgo collaborations published this letter in Physical Review Letters in 2016. It reports GW151226, the second gravitational-wave signal confirmed from merging black holes. The twin LIGO detectors caught it on December 26, 2015, during the first observing run.

An online search flagged the candidate within seventy seconds of the waves passing. The merging pair totaled about twenty-two times the Sun's mass, lighter than the first event. Its signal was fainter and stretched over more cycles, so template matching proved essential to dig it out. No other strong candidates appeared in that mass range all run. A third, weaker candidate is folded into the same analysis.
openalex-w2555590239:
Timothy J. Killeen, Anna Guerra, and Miki Calzada, with colleagues, documented land-use change in eastern Bolivia in this 2008 Ecology and Society paper. They asked who changed the land, where, when, and by how much. The team tracked forest, savanna, pasture, cropland, and other cover types below the mountain tree line. Their record runs from before 1976 through 2004, split into five periods.

The pace of change rose steeply, from modest yearly rates in the 1960s to far larger ones after 2000. Ten groups with shared traditions and production systems did the changing. Mechanized farmers and Andean indigenous colonists drove most early clearing. Colonist deforestation surged in the late 1980s, eased in the 1990s, then climbed again. Cattle ranchers and the forest products sector also played major roles. The history shows land change follows people and markets, not one single cause.
openalex-w2767215839:
Robert J. Zomer, Déborah Bossio, and Rolf Sommer, with Louis Vincent Verchot, estimated soil carbon's climate potential in Scientific Reports in 2017. Cropland soils have lost much of the organic carbon they once held. Winning some back could store carbon while improving farms. An international initiative launched in Paris aims to grow soil carbon steadily worldwide.

The authors used global soil grid data to map carbon in the top thirty centimeters of croplands. They then assessed how much extra carbon improved management could lock away. Because croplands are already actively managed, better practices can start without land-use upheaval. Their analysis supports the view that the technical potential is significant. It also gives the Paris initiative a quantitative footing. Soil carbon gains would pay farmers twice: richer soil and a cooler planet.
openalex-w3025100939:
Beatriz Schmidt, Maria Crepaldi, Simone Bolze, and colleagues published this review in Estudos de Psicologia in 2020. Written in Portuguese, it covers mental health and psychological care during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors call the pandemic the greatest public health emergency in decades.

Beyond physical illness, the pandemic stirred wide psychological distress among the public and health workers. The team reviewed technical and scientific writing from several countries. They summarize the mental health impacts reported, name the groups needing priority care, and give guidance on psychological interventions. Their advice weighs the needs of the general population and of health professionals. They close with the promise and strain of practicing psychology in Brazil.
openalex-w4411441839:
Hitoshi Yamaoka, Patrik Thunström, Naohito Tsujii, and colleagues map the electronic structures of two ytterbium compounds. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. The compounds, Yb3Si5 and Yb3Ge5, belong to a family with unstable electron counts. Such materials show unusual heat and charge behaviour.

The team combines three X-ray and electron spectroscopies. Each method views the electronic structure from a different angle. They also run calculations that treat strong electron forces. Comparing experiment and theory reveals how the ytterbium valence is shared between states. That picture helps explain the compounds' physical properties and guides work on related materials for energy conversion.
openalex-w7204235439:
Guilherme Silva do Carmo led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on oral health among hospitalized children. Hospital dentistry works to protect mouth health and prevent problems during a child's stay. Searching four sources for studies from 2016 to March 2026, the team kept eight observational studies and appraised their quality with a standard checklist. Looking at medical problems, caregivers, and the dental care actually delivered.

Hospitalized children showed frequent dental plaque, poor oral hygiene, cavities, and unmet treatment needs, alongside sugary foods and drugs and caregivers who knew little about oral health. Where ongoing dental follow-up existed, problems were better and preventive measures stronger. The authors argue for a dentist on the multiprofessional team and better caregiver schooling.
openalex-w7205010439:
Emilly de Azevedo Leite led a Portuguese-language epidemiological study, in Brazil in 2026, asking what changed in dengue incidence in Itabuna, Bahia, across the COVID-19 pandemic. The team studied notification system data for dengue cases from January 2019 to September 2025, comparing pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic periods and examining age, sex, medical evolution, hospitalizations, and deaths.

Incidence oscillated across the period, the analysis shows, with cases rising during and after the pandemic and a striking peak in 2022. Environmental factors and limits in epidemiological surveillance may have influenced the pattern, and the disease remains endemic in the municipality. The major variation between periods, the authors conclude, reinforces the need for ongoing stopping, monitoring, and stronger epidemiological surveillance.
openalex-w7206186239:
Julia Nicolau Barbieri and four colleagues count deaths from suppurative and unspecified otitis media across Brazil from 2016 to 2025. Ear infections are usually minor, so deaths are rare, but they do occur. The team used national mortality records kept by the health system, sorted deaths by sex and age group, and tracked how the totals moved year by year.

Just over one thousand deaths were recorded in the decade, a little over one hundred per year on average. Slightly more than half were men, and people aged fifty and older made up the largest share, with the oldest group, eighty and above, highest of all. Deaths rose sharply after 2021 and peaked in 2024. The authors urge continued monitoring and timely ear care, and caution in reading pandemic-era swings.
openalex-w7213541339:
Pedro Carlos Damasceno Neto leads a review on early diagnosis in Guillain-Barré syndrome. That acute autoimmune illness attacks peripheral nerves and can lead to breathing failure. Their 2026 review searches PubMed, SciELO, and Google Scholar for 2010 to 2025, keeping fourteen studies.

Diagnostic delay was linked consistently to worse outcomes. Risks kept breathing failure, mechanical ventilation, and lasting motor weakness. Intravenous immunoglobulin given in the first two weeks brought faster healing and less residual disability. Benefit fell when treatment was postponed. Nerve ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging helped early detection alongside medical and electrical tests. Certain subtypes needed longer ventilation and hospital care.
openalex-w7213556439:
Mariane Bezerra de Menezes and co-authors argue that law alone does not solve femicide study in Brazil. Their 2026 article reviews literature and papers, including national and Latin American study protocols. Brazil recorded its highest femicide count since the 2015 law in 2024, they note.

The dominant study model centres on physical evidence of the crime. That focus cannot rebuild the relational pattern behind lethal gender violence, the authors argue. A framework of twenty-three contextual and behavioural elements is proposed to strengthen evidence production. Feminist criminology, forensic victimology, and behavioural evidence analysis inform the model. Standard study, they conclude, protects victims insufficiently as currently practised.
openalex-w7214085939:
Suelen Cristina Vianna de Moraes and co-workers develop a polymer wound dressing for pressure injuries. Their 2026 study builds a sticky dressing from a chitosan and polyvinyl alcohol blend carrying aloe vera gel. Chitosan and aloe bring healing and germ-fighting traits, while the man-made polymer adds strength and grip.

Bench tests measured fluid uptake, fit, and germ load. The dressing stayed in place for over five hours in on-body testing. Germ counts sat below Brazil's official drug book limits, with none of three named dangerous organisms found. Working traits and safety looked sound, the authors conclude, giving the dressing real healing promise for pressure injury care.
phrenology-proved-illustrated-and-applie: What is hosted here shows only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages that precede this scan, with no page of the work itself visible. The catalogue record names the book Phrenology Proved, Illustrated, and Applied, accompanied by a chart, and dates it 1839. It credits three authors, Orson Squire Fowler, Lorenzo Niles Fowler, and Samuel Kirkham, the brothers and partner who built the Fowler phrenology business in America.
plos-pbio-0020139:
Adam Amsterdam, Kirsten C. Sadler, Kevin Lai, and a large team screened zebrafish genes in PLOS Biology in 2004. They broke genes one by one to see which ones cause cancer when lost. To their surprise, many of the hits were genes for ribosomal proteins, the parts of the cell's protein-making machines.

A broken ribosomal protein gene can lead to tumors, a link also seen in some human syndromes. The screen found this class again and again, far more than chance would suggest. That breadth makes the claim strong. The work raised a fresh question for cancer biology: how does a fault in the basic protein factory push a cell toward uncontrolled growth?
plos-pbio-0020239:
Michael J. Galko and Mark A. Krasnow analyzed wound healing in fruit fly larvae in PLOS Biology in 2004. A cut in the larva's skin closes as cells around the wound stretch and move. The authors used genetics to find which genes that closing process needs.

Their study breaks healing into steps and names genes for each step, from first response to final seal. Fly larvae are simple enough to watch cell by cell, yet their healing shares parts with our own. A clean parts list lets other labs test single genes and single steps. Wound healing gone wrong causes chronic sores in people, so basic maps like this one have long term medical value.
plos-pone-0000039:
Mel Slater, Angus Antley, Adam Davison, and co-authors restaged one of psychology's most troubling experiments inside virtual reality in 2006. Stanley Milgram had shown in the 1960s that ordinary people would deliver what they believed were painful shocks when an authority figure ordered it. Repeating that with real people and real-seeming pain is no longer acceptable.

Their virtual reprise replaced the victim with a computer character, and participants knew it was not real. Even so, the setup let the team watch obedience, hesitation, and stress in a setting no ethics board would allow with a human victim. The study opened a way to study harmful obedience safely, and raised fresh questions about how real virtual people feel.
plos-pone-0000139:
Nitchakarn Noranate, Rémy Durand, Adama Tall, and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tracks Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, and its growing resistance to antimalarial drugs. The worrying point, stated in the title, is that resistance spread fast even where drug use was strictly controlled.

Controlled use is supposed to slow resistance down. The authors document a case where it did not, at least not enough. That result warns malaria programs that careful prescribing alone may not save a failing drug. It also presses the case for monitoring resistance wherever these medicines are deployed.
plos-pone-0000239:
Ewan Thomas Macleod, Alistair Charles Darby, Ian Maudlin, and colleagues published this parasitology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Trypanosomes are the parasites behind sleeping sickness, carried by tsetse flies. The authors study factors affecting how the parasites mature inside the fly, a required stage before they can infect people.

Only mature parasites in the fly can pass to a human bite victim. Knowing what speeds or slows maturation helps predict transmission and may suggest ways to block it in the fly. The work is part of the long campaign against a disease that has shaped life across central Africa.
plos-pone-0000339:
Jeff Shrager, Richard Waldinger, Mark Stickel, and colleagues published this computing paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, introducing deductive biocomputing. The idea is to use formal deduction, step-by-step logical proof, as a computing method for biology. A system can then reason over biological knowledge and derive answers the way a theorem prover does.

Biology drowns in data but much of its knowledge sits in logical relationships. A deductive approach aims to chain those relationships automatically. The paper is a position and systems piece, arguing for logic-based tools alongside the statistics that dominate bioinformatics.
plos-pone-0000439:
Alberto Mazzoni and colleagues analyzed the chatter of neurons with no task at hand, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Even at rest, neuronal networks fire in spontaneous activity, patterns once dismissed as background noise. The team studied the dynamics of that activity, how the patterns form, spread, and change over time.

Spontaneous firing may rehearse the network's repertoire and keep its connections tuned. Its dynamics also reveal the network's built-in wiring rules, visible only when no stimulus is driving it. The study belongs to a shift in neuroscience toward treating rest activity as structured and meaningful rather than as static.
plos-pone-0000539:
Jordi Figuerola tracked how far shorebirds spread in dry versus wet years, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The birds are black-winged stilts, long-legged waders of shallow wetlands. Figuerola found that climate and dispersal are linked. Stilts disperse further in dry springs, when local wetlands shrink and young birds must travel on.

When local wetlands dry, young birds must travel farther to find breeding sites, spreading genes and colonizing new areas. Dispersal distance shapes how species respond to shifting climates. A clear year-to-year effect like this gives climate-change ecology a measured behavior, not just a projection, to build on.
plos-pone-0000639:
Craig R. White, Norman Day, Patrick J. Butler and colleagues asked how great cormorants actually find their food, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cormorants are pursuit-diving birds, widely seen as guided by vision while hunting underwater. They also post the highest known foraging yield of any marine predator. That success often puts them in conflict with human fishing interests.

The title poses the comparison sharply: more like herons than hawks? Herons strike from stillness, while hawks chase in open air. Testing what cormorant vision can and cannot do underwater reshapes which hunting style fits. Bird biologists and fisheries managers both have stakes in the answer.
plos-pone-0000739:
Tomas Knapen, Raymond van Ee and Randolph Blake watched the brain's visual tug-of-war move across the cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In binocular rivalry, the two eyes see conflicting images, and perception alternates between them. One percept replaces the other not all at once but as a traveling wave sweeping across space. Such waves are a general way nervous systems switch states.

Their title adds a driver: stimulus motion propels those traveling waves. Moving the images sets the waves in motion and steers them. Vision scientists care because rivalry waves expose how the brain settles competition between signals, a process at work in everyday seeing.
plos-pone-0000839:
Bernardo V. Alvarez, Gregory S. Gilmour, Silvina C. Mema and colleagues showed that losing an acid-handling protein in the eye causes blindness. Vision begins with phototransduction in the outer retina, where photoreceptors' high metabolic rate generates large carbon dioxide loads. Inner retina cells then process both the visual signal and that CO2. The AE3 gene encodes a chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that moves acid equivalents out of cells.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title states the consequence plainly: deficiency in the AE3 exchanger causes blindness. A waste-disposal failure in the retina is a surprising cause of vision loss. It points genetic screening for inherited blindness toward an ion transport gene.
plos-pone-0000939:
Christopher Beck and Daniel Promislow examined why females in some species prefer younger males, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Older theory said females should pick older males, since survivors ought to be fitter than average. Yet in humans and lab species, males lose quality as they age, through damage built up over life.

That decline flips the prediction. Beck and Promislow set out the case for a female preference for younger males. Mate choice shapes how traits evolve, so getting its direction right matters. The paper also shows how a neat theory can fail once aging itself is priced in.
plos-pone-0001039:
Frans Walther, Alan Waring, Jose Hernandez-Juviel and colleagues tested a fully synthetic lung surfactant, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Surfactant is the slippery coating that keeps air sacs open in the lungs. Natural versions can be broken down by phospholipase enzymes during lung injury.

Their synthetic version pairs a new phospholipid built to resist that breakdown with a short peptide modeled on surfactant protein B. The team examined its surface activity and resistance to degradation. A synthetic surfactant could be made in steady supply, unlike animal derived versions. Premature infants and injured lungs are the patients who need it most.
plos-pone-0001139:
When a stream is broken into fragments by barriers, the fish inside each piece live apart. Benjamin Letcher and colleagues studied that situation in a 2007 PLOS ONE article on stream-dwelling brook trout. Fragmentation can strongly shape whether a population persists and how its life history plays out.

The team directly estimated dispersal, growth, and survival by fish size within a stream network containing connected and isolated stretches. Measuring all three at once gives a fuller picture than tracking movement alone. Their work shows how a population responds, in concrete numbers, when its habitat is chopped into pieces.
plos-pone-0001239:
Sex determination in fruit flies of the tephritid family, which includes major crop pests, is governed by a gene called transformer. María Fernanda Ruiz and colleagues traced that gene's evolution across insects, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In the Mediterranean fruit fly and the olive fly, transformer acts as the memory device for sex determination. Working Tra protein is made only in females.

The authors investigate the Anastrepha fruit flies and compare the gene's history across insect groups. How a master sex switch evolves matters for pest control strategies that release sterile or all-male flies.
plos-pone-0001339:
Natural killer cells patrol the body for transformed cells, and receptors called NKp30 and NKp44 help switch on their attack. Andreina Byrd and colleagues analyzed expression of the ligands for these receptors, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ligands are the surface molecules the receptors recognize; knowing which cells display them matters for rational design of NK-based therapies.

The authors map where the ligands for the natural cytotoxicity receptors appear, on normal and neoplastic cells. If tumor cells display them more than healthy cells do, the receptors can be exploited. Their expression analysis is groundwork for immunotherapy design.
plos-pone-0001439:
Brian Huntley and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how climate change may shift where European breeding birds live. As climate shifts, species ranges are set to move. Plans to guard wild life need hard counts of how far and how fast. The team modeled range shifts for the region's breeding birds.

Their models give the scale, course, and pace of likely shifts bird by bird. Some birds gain ground while others lose it sharply. Such counts are of most value when they can guide real choices. Park and reserve plans can use them to keep guarding birds as their ranges move north or uphill.
plos-pone-0001539:
Delphine Pages and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a soil germ that shrugs off metals. The germ lives widely in soil and water and resists many germ drugs by nature. One strain also bears high levels of toxic metals, from a tenth to fifty units in tests. The team asked how it holds up under that load.

They probed the genes and traits that let the germ bear metals that kill most kin. Such grit makes the germ a survivor in harsh, tainted sites. It could serve in clean up of metal waste. It also warns that drug grit and metal grit can travel as a pair.
plos-pone-0001639:
Ji-Yeon Lee and co-authors studied how signals in the brain and pituitary gland control body weight, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The signals pass through a protein pair called STAT5, which carries messages from cytokines, a group of immune and hormone-like messengers. STAT5 is switched on in nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a brain region that helps set hunger and energy use.

When the team removed this signaling in the central nervous system and pituitary gland of mice, the animals' energy balance shifted and they became obese. The full text gives the weight and feeding data and the hormone changes they recorded. The results point to a brain pathway that drug and diet research on obesity needs to take into account.
plos-pone-0001739:
Mikael Åkesson, Staffan Bensch, Dennis Hasselquist, and their co-authors compared two ways to estimate heredity in wild animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Heritability and genetic correlations guide predictions of how traits evolve. The animal model, a statistical method using full pedigrees, had largely replaced parent-offspring regression, yet the two had rarely been tested on the same data.

Using data from a natural population, the team ran both methods on equivalent data sets and compared the estimates. The full text gives the trait values and where the methods agree or diverge. Field biologists stake evolutionary forecasts on these numbers, so knowing which method to trust, and when, is a practical result.
plos-pone-0001839:
Seyed M. Moghadas, Christopher S. Bowman, and Gergely Röst modeled antiviral resistance in a flu pandemic in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Resistance to the main flu drugs raised concerns about careful use of antiviral drugs in the next influenza pandemic. Resistant strains may start off weaker, but later mutations can restore much of that lost fitness.

The team modeled how resistance spreads during a pandemic under different drug use plans. The full text gives the scenarios and the timelines. Stockpiled antivirals are a central flu plan. If heavy use breeds resistance fast, planners must weigh treatment against prophylaxis with that risk included.
plos-pone-0001939:
Adam Wasserstrom and co-authors built family trees of cells inside mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Every cell in a body descends from the first cell, the zygote, by a long chain of divisions. That chain forms a lineage tree, which, if it could be read, would show how tissues are built.

A new method reads small mutations that pile up in cells over time and treats them like the marks used to build species trees. The team used it to rebuild parts of the cell tree in mice at fine detail. Such trees can reveal when lines split in growth, and where odd growth in disease begins.
plos-pone-0002039:
Benoit Smagghe, James Trent, and Mark Hargrove tested a chemical trick found across blood proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Genome work has turned up hundreds of new hemoglobins, found in nearly every kind of living thing. Lab tests of many of them show the same reactions, such as binding oxygen and a reaction that breaks down nitric oxide, called NO dioxygenation.

As the title states, that NO reaction is ubiquitous in the test tube. But in living cells it is limited by how fast the protein can be reset by reduction. A common talent, throttled in life: the gap warns against reading test-tube results as body truth.
plos-pone-0002139:
Seung-Chul Kim and co-authors traced how plant life spread and split into new species across Atlantic islands, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Macaronesia covers five island groups: the Azores, Canaries, Madeira, Cape Verde, and the Savage Islands. Its plant life is rich, with many species found nowhere else on Earth.

Island chains like these are natural labs for studying how new species arise. The team studied the timing and pace of adaptive radiations, bursts where one ancestor splits into many species fitted to local niches. Their timeline helps explain how a few arriving plants gave rise to whole floras across scattered islands.
plos-pone-0002239:
Sigal Rencus-Lazar, Yaniv Amir, Junetai Wu, and co-authors studied a cancer-linked gene in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The gene Int6 is a proto-oncogene, a normal gene that can help drive cancer when it misbehaves. Its protein is part of the machine that starts protein building, and it also interacts with the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder.

How Int6 does its work was unclear. The team reports that Int6 is essential for neddylation, a tagging process that activates two proteins, Cul1 and Cul3, in Drosophila. Those proteins help choose which cell proteins get destroyed. The link places Int6 at a control point for protein turnover.
plos-pone-0002339:
Huiyi Chen, Bin Liu, Thomas Lukas, and co-authors profiled the aging tissue at the back of the eye, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Age is the greatest risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness in older people. Yet the cellular and molecular reasons why age matters so much are not generally known.

The team studied the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid, the layers that feed and support the light-sensing retina, as they age. Changes there may form the substratum, the ground in which macular degeneration takes root. Mapping the aging of this support tissue tells drug hunters where the disease truly begins.
plos-pone-0002439:
Miozzi joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Laura Miozzi, Rosario Michael Piro, Fabio Rosa, among others. Its subject is functional Annotation and Identification of Candidate Disease Genes by Computational Analysis of Normal Tissue Gene Expression Data. High-throughput gene expression data can predict gene function through the “guilt by association” principle: coexpressed genes are likely to be functionally linked.

We analyzed publicly available expression data on normal human tissues. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002539:
Esposito led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Irene Esposito, Diana Born, Frank Bergmann, among others. Its subject is autoimmune Pancreatocholangitis, Non-Autoimmune Pancreatitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis: A Comparative Morphological and Immunological Analysis. Autoimmune pancreatocholangitis (AIPC) is an emerging, not completely characterized disease.

Aim of this study was the comprehensive evaluation of a series of AIPC patients. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002639:
Y. Jeffrey Chiang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was tankyrase 1 and tankyrase 2 are essential but redundant for mouse embryonic development. Authorship is credited in the record to Y. Jeffrey Chiang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Tankyrases are proteins with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase activity. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002739:
David T. S. Hayman and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on evidence of henipavirus infection in west african fruit bats. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David T. S. Hayman, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Henipaviruses are emerging RNA viruses of fruit bat origin that can cause fatal encephalitis in man. It goes on to note a further point. Ghanaian fruit bats (megachiroptera) were tested for antibodies to henipaviruses. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002839:
A 2008 study by Sheila G. Crewther and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up potassium channel and NKCC cotransporter involvement in ocular refractive control mechanisms. The catalog record names Sheila G. Crewther first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Myopia affects well over 30% of adult humans globally. It goes on to note a further point. However, the underlying physiological mechanism is little understood. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002939:
Mbemba Jabbi, Jojanneke Bastiaansen and Christian Keysers scanned brains around disgust in 2008. Similar areas light up when we act, watch an act, or picture one, and the team asked whether feelings behave the same way. They focused on gustatory disgust, the revolting taste response.

The same subjects were scanned while they felt disgust, watched another person feel it, and imagined it. A shared area in the front insula took part in all three, while its connections diverged by condition. Published in PLOS ONE, the study refines how shared feeling is built in the brain.
plos-pone-0003039:
