Nicholas Graham, Tim McClanahan, M. Aaron MacNeil and co-authors studied warming, protected areas, and coral reefs in 2008. Coral reefs are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change. Warming's role in loss of live coral cover was well documented at large scales, while effects on reef fish were less settled.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team assesses ocean-scale integrity of reef ecosystems and what marine protected areas can preserve under warming. Protection cannot stop heat, but it may keep food webs intact. The study helps managers judge what reserves can and cannot do.
plos-pone-0003139:
Corrado Di Natale, Eugenio Martinelli, Roberto Paolesse and colleagues describe a test platform for artificial smell in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Artificial olfactory systems had been studied for two decades, mostly through the response patterns of smell receptors. Other basic traits of natural smell had only rarely been built into such systems, leaving current devices limited.

The team present an experimental platform that copies biology more closely, a biomimetic approach. Readers see an attempt to close the gap between machine sensors and a real nose. Such work matters for chemical sensing, food checks, and medical breath tests, where better smell tools are still needed.
plos-pone-0003239:
Vicente Sentandreu, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández, Manuela Torres-Puente and colleagues look for recombination in hepatitis C virus in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C virus is a major cause of liver disease worldwide and a potential cause of substantial morbidity and mortality in the future. The virus is characterized by a high level of genetic heterogeneity. Homologous recombination had been demonstrated in many virus families.

The team present evidence of recombination in populations of the virus within a single patient. Readers see new viral variants arising not just by mutation but by mixing. Recombination can speed adaptation to drugs and immunity, which complicates treatment planning.
plos-pone-0003339:
Mai T. Q. Le, Heiman F. L. Wertheim, Hien D. Nguyen and colleagues report a virus shift in Vietnam in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prior to 2007, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 viruses isolated from poultry and humans in Vietnam were consistently reported to be clade 1 viruses, susceptible to oseltamivir but resistant to amantadine. The team describe re-emergence of human H5N1 virus with different traits.

Their title reports that clade 2.3.4 virus, with a different antiviral susceptibility profile, replaced clade 1 virus in humans in northern Vietnam. Readers see drug planning change with viral lineage. Surveillance of clades is essential for vaccine and stockpile decisions.
plos-pone-0003439:
Shih-Lei Lai and co-authors studied cell movement in early embryos in this 2008 paper. During gastrulation, embryo cells stream into new layers. That motion depends on actin, a protein that builds moving scaffolds inside cells. A regulator called Diaphanous helps direct actin assembly.

The team tested one formin, Diaphanous-related formin 2, plus profilin I. Both proved required for normal gastrulation cell movements. Without them, the embryo's early reshaping faltered. The work names key parts of the engine behind a basic step of life. Errors at this stage can end development before organs even form, which makes its machinery a basic research target.
plos-pone-0003539:
Matthew Heath, Anika Maraj, and Bryan Godbolt tested reaching without awareness in this 2008 study. Their title states the puzzle plainly: action without awareness. Volunteers reached for objects they did not remember seeing. Memory of the object and control of the hand came apart.

Accurate reaching showed the hand used visual data the mind forgot. Two visual streams may split knowing from doing. One stream serves conscious recognition, the other guides movement. The study catches that split in a simple lab task. Such tasks help map the split between seeing and doing in brain injury.
plos-pone-0003639:
Traci Mouw, Annemarie Koster, Margaret E. Wright, and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks whether the amount of schooling a person has relates to their risk of cancer. The authors used a large cohort of men and women in the United States.

They compared cancer rates across levels of education within that cohort. Education can stand in for income, work, habits, and access to care, all of which shape health. A study this size can show whether schooling tracks with cancer risk in the population as a whole.
plos-pone-0003739:
Jean N. Manirarora, Michele M. Kosiewicz, Sarah A. Parnell, and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2008. NOD mice develop diabetes much like human type 1 diabetes. Their antigen-presenting cells fail to switch on regulatory T cells properly, and those peacekeeper cells keep the immune system from attacking the body.

The team found that activating the antigen-presenting cells restores working regulatory T cells. The revived cells, marked CD4 and CD25, could prevent diabetes from developing in the mice. The rescue points to immune retraining as a path against this autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0003839:
Xu Wang, Qi Sun, Sean D. McGrath, and colleagues published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Imprinted genes are active from only one parent's copy, depending on which parent passed them down. The strength of imprinting varies by tissue and stage, and it can go wrong in disease. The newborn mouse brain was unmapped territory.

The team scanned the whole transcriptome of neonatal mouse brain for imprinted genes. They identified novel imprinted genes beyond those already known. The brain-wide map expands the catalog of genes where a mother's and a father's copies are not treated as equal.
plos-pone-0003939:
Andrew Gallagher rechecked claims of tiny ancient humans from Palau in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Recent finds on the Pacific islands of Palau were said to be small-bodied humans. Some claimed the bones show island shrinking of body size. That claim had not yet faced a statistical test.

Gallagher assessed sixteen published limb bone specimens from Palau. He compared them with recent small-bodied human samples. Careful measurement can separate true island dwarfing from normal variation. The study urges caution before naming a new kind of small human. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004039:
Lynne A. Murray, Tillie L. Hackett, Stephanie M. Warner, and co-authors tested a growth factor against scarring in 2008. BMP-7 belongs to a family of growth factors in the TGF-beta superfamily. It had been reported to block kidney scarring. It also reportedly blocked a cell change that drives tissue fibrosis.

Their PLOS ONE article reports BMP-7 did not protect lung or skin. The damage agent was bleomycin, a drug that induces fibrosis. Negative findings matter where hopes for a therapy run high. They caution against assuming one organ's result transfers to others. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004139:
Sandeep Kumar, Aisha Farhana, and Seyed Hasnain published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ that causes tuberculosis, can sit quietly in the body for years in a low-activity state before waking to cause disease. To copy itself, the germ must first unwind its DNA at a start site called oriC.

Working with purified parts in the lab, the team shows that the DnaA protein opens the DNA helix at one precise spot in oriC. They also show that a protein resembling IciA blocks that opening. The result pinpoints a first step in how the germ starts copying its DNA, a step drugs might one day target.
plos-pone-0004239:
Peng Xu, Min Shi, and Xue-xin Chen published this bee study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Asiatic honey bee, Apis cerana, is an important honey bee across Asia. It still lives wild yet is also one of the few bee species people can domesticate, and it carries genetic advantages over its western cousin.

The authors traced the evolution of its antimicrobial peptides, small proteins that kill microbes and form a first line of immune defence. Comparing these peptides across bees shows how the weapons changed as the species adapted. The work adds an Asian chapter to the study of insect immunity.
plos-pone-0004339:
Suhail Asrar and colleagues published this synaptic study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Calcium enters through GluR2-lacking AMPA receptors, a calcium-permeable form of the main excitatory receptor. It can trigger long-lasting changes in synaptic strength in both interneurons and principal neurons. How it works remained unknown. Interneurons are the local circuit cells between main neurons.

Using genetically altered mice with weak or missing versions of these receptors, the team mapped the needed pathways. They report that this long-term potentiation requires PI3 and MAP kinases but not CaMKII. Separating which enzymes are needed maps the chemistry of a memory-like change.
plos-pone-0004439:
Harm caused by medicines given in hospital is the subject of a 2009 PLOS ONE study by Emma Davies, Christopher Green, Stephen Taylor, and co-authors. Bad drug reactions are a major reason people end up in hospital. Less was known about reactions that start after a patient is already admitted.

The team followed patients on twelve wards over six months in 2005, covering thousands of patient episodes. They recorded each bad reaction, its cause, and its effect on care. Fresh counts like these show how large the problem is inside hospital walls, not just at the door. They also help hospitals target the drugs and habits that put in-patients most at risk.
plos-pone-0004539:
Yeast can be used to hunt for the toxic form of amyloid, the protein clumps tied to several diseases. Julien Couthouis, Karine Rebora, Francoise Immel, and co-authors show how in PLOS ONE in 2009. Since amyloid structures were found in different diseases, the link between the clumps and the toxic species has been a central problem. Despite intense work, the harmful species is still unknown at the molecular level.

One reason may be the lack of a structure-based way to find it. The authors set up a screen in yeast that exemplifies an alternative pathway responsible for cytotoxicity. Yeast is cheap and fast to screen in bulk. If its toxic species mirrors the one in human disease, the screen could point to what actually kills cells.
plos-pone-0004639:
Chains of signals travel through cells at speeds set by the chain's design, show Christopher Govern and Arup Chakraborty in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells are not mixed bags of signaling molecules. A signal must travel from its origin to distant locations inside the cell. Much is understood about purely diffusive propagation, signals drifting like scent in still air.

Many signals, however, propagate via signaling cascades, relay chains of proteins that activate each other. The authors show cascades modulate the speed of signal propagation through space. A relay can move a message faster, or hold it back, compared with diffusion alone. For cell engineering and drug design, knowing the speed rules helps predict how a cell will answer a signal in time.
plos-pone-0004739:
Ravi Akundi and Scott Rivkees showed that low oxygen changes cell cycle proteins and rushes early brain cell growth, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Injury to white matter is a common brain harm in babies born too early. Low oxygen is a major factor that sets up that injury in the newborn period.

Cells that later wrap nerve fibers in insulation are at risk in this window. The team found low oxygen shifts their cycle controls and pushes them to mature too soon. Early forced growth may leave insulation thin or flawed. The work helps explain lasting harm after early birth.
plos-pone-0004839:
Jacqueline Schmuckli-Maurer and colleagues analyzed output of the Theileria parva subtelomere encoded variable secreted protein family, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The intracellular protozoan parasite transforms bovine lymphocytes, inducing uncontrolled growth. Proteins released from the parasite are assumed to help to host cell changes and parasite persistence. With eighty five members in genes encoding secreted proteins representing a large variable family.

Output patterns vary across family members and stages. Variable secretion may aid immune evasion. The parasite causes East Coast fever in cattle. Knowledge transformation could yield control methods. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004939:
Biologists would love to read a cell's chemical wiring from measurements. That task is called reverse engineering. Edgar Delgado-Eckert examined its feasibility in PLOS ONE in 2009. He focused on models called time-discrete finite dynamical systems. Interest in the approach had grown with high-throughput profiling.

He stress-tested a top-down algorithm by Laubenbacher and Stigler. The algorithm rebuilds biochemical networks from data. His analysis maps where the method works and where it breaks. The verdict helps researchers judge rebuilt networks. It shows what extra information a reliable reconstruction needs.
plos-pone-0005039:
Candida albicans is a yeast that lives in human mouths. It turns harmful when immunity drops. Mouth candidiasis is a warning sign of AIDS. Timothy Meiller and colleagues found a new evasion trick in PLOS ONE in 2009. Saliva carries antimicrobial peptides that kill germs. Candida cuts one of them apart.

The yeast uses its own enzymes for the cutting. This proteolytic cleavage destroys the peptide's protection. The sabotage disarms the mouth's first line of defense. It helps explain how the fungus colonizes mucosal surfaces. The work names a fresh target for antifungal thinking. Blocking the cutting enzymes could restore saliva's natural guard.
plos-pone-0005139:
A good TB vaccine must rally the right T cells. Helper CD4 cells are crucial for defense. Whether killer CD8 cells are also needed was unclear. Tara Elvang and colleagues compared vaccine strategies in PLOS ONE in 2009. All carried two TB antigens, Ag85B and TB10.4. The strategies differed: adjuvanted subunit, adenovector, or heterologous prime-boost.

The team measured both CD4 and CD8 responses to the antigens. The comparison shows which approach builds the strongest balanced response. A balanced army may protect best. The work guides the design of next-generation TB vaccines. TB still kills over a million people yearly. Small design choices in trials like this one shape the vaccines that reach clinics.
plos-pone-0005239:
Coral reefs worldwide are degrading under warming seas, overfishing, disease, and nutrient pollution. Diaz-Pulido and colleagues followed one reef through damage and recovery, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 under the apt frame of doom and boom.

Warming caused bleaching, algae then overgrew the reef, and yet corals later recovered. A reef that bounces back shows which conditions favor resilience. Tracking the full cycle gives conservationists concrete lessons about what helps reefs survive the next warming event. Most reefs do not get a second chance in this way, so the few that do are worth close study while the recovery is still fresh.
plos-pone-0005339:
Foods that pack many calories into each gram can promote overeating in lab studies. Whether dietary energy density predicts long-term weight change in free-living people was less clear. Du and colleagues followed European men and women prospectively, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study related the energy density of people's diets to later changes in weight and waist size. Waist change matters because belly fat carries the highest health risk. Evidence from daily life, not just labs, is what dietary guidelines are built on. Waist size tracks the fat that does most harm, so a link to waist gain, not just to weight, gives food advice a sharper aim for men and women alike.
plos-pone-0005439:
Pauline Leclerc, Alan Matthews, and Michel Garenne modelled the HIV epidemic in Zambia in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier models of how HIV spreads in African countries often skipped the exact times when each person was at risk. That gap can blur who spreads the virus and when.

Their model follows single people, male and female, through their lives and risks. It was fitted to match the known course of the epidemic in Zambia. A model that tracks real risk periods can help planners judge which steps against HIV are most likely to work.
plos-pone-0005539:
Amy Murphy, Paul Guyre, and Charles Wira studied a hormone effect on immune cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Macrophages are front-line immune cells that release signals when they sense danger. The female hormone estradiol directly shapes how these cells behave.

The team studied how the hormone controls one form of its own receptor in human macrophages. That receptor form can change how strongly the hormone acts on immune responses. Knowing the control loop helps explain sex differences in infection and in diseases of inflammation. Sex differences in immunity are large and often unexplained, and hormone control loops like this one help explain them.
plos-pone-0005639:
Casey Greene, Nadia Penrod, and Scott Williams argued that failed replications in gene studies can still teach, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Genome-wide studies are judged by whether their findings repeat in new samples. That standard is strict, and real effects can be missed because of it.

The authors list the many reasons a true result may fail to repeat, from small samples to real differences between groups. They urge readers to mine failures for clues about how genes act. A failed repeat is data, not just disappointment. Their argument favours reporting failures openly, since hidden failures waste the next team's samples and funds.
plos-pone-0005739:
Ilana DeLuca and co-authors probed in 2009 why the immune system usually leaves a brain protein alone, until it suddenly does not. In the Hu syndrome, tumors trigger an immune attack on HuD, a protein found only in neurons. The attack can badly harm the nervous system.

Old experiments suggest the brain hides its proteins from immune patrols. The team tested how tolerance to HuD is kept, and how cancer breaks it. Their work uses the syndrome as a window on a broad question: how the body avoids attacking the brain. The answer bears on autoimmune disease and cancer care alike.
plos-pone-0005839:
Donald Anderson and Patrick Stover showed in 2009 that two related enzymes back each other up in making a DNA building block. Making thymidylate, the T of DNA, takes a three-enzyme pathway that moves into the nucleus during DNA copying. Two members of that team are near-twins, SHMT1 and SHMT2.

The team demonstrated the twins are functionally redundant for nuclear thymidylate synthesis. Losing one does not cripple DNA production because the other covers. Redundancy explains why single-gene faults here are rare in disease. It also tells drug designers that both enzymes may need blocking to starve fast-growing cells.
plos-pone-0005939:
About one ovarian cancer in ten is thought to run in families. Bamidele Tayo, Richard DiCioccio, Yulan Liang and colleagues asked how that risk passes down, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They used family records from the Gilda Radner registry, a collection built to study inherited ovarian cancer.

Their analysis of the family trees found a pattern that fits a dominant pattern of inheritance, as if one major gene copy can pass the risk on. That shape matters for how doctors counsel families and whom they watch most closely. The study gives the registry's rich records a clear use: sharper risk advice for the next generation.
plos-pone-0006039:
Clear cell cancer is the most common cancer of the adult kidney, yet its course varies wildly between patients. Hongjuan Zhao, Zongming Ma, Robert Tibshirani and colleagues hunted the gene patterns behind the worst cases in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper profiles gene activity in these tumors, building on a set of transcripts already known to predict survival after kidney removal.

In lethal tumors, two signature programs were altered: one for cortical differentiation, the kidney's mature identity, and one for wound response. A tumor that has lost its tissue identity and runs a wound program nonstop may be primed to kill. The patterns could guide prognosis and point treatment toward the programs that matter most.
plos-pone-0006139:
A pig pathogen must survive the lung's first wash of defenses to cause disease. Abdul Lone, Vincent Deslandes, John Nash and colleagues watched it adapt in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper exposes Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae, the cause of contagious pleuropneumonia in swine worldwide, to bronchoalveolar fluid, the liquid lining the lung, and measures how its gene expression shifts.

Genes that answer lung fluid are likely the tools of early infection. Reading that answer tells vets and vaccine makers where the germ is tender. Swine pneumonia costs farms heavily across the world, so a gene-level view of the first hours of infection has direct economic as well as scientific worth.
plos-pone-0006239:
Faces are hard to read, for people and machines alike, so psychologists use careful test tasks. Qi Zhu and colleagues put one such task under the microscope in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The part task, from the part-spacing paradigm, was meant to measure how much people use separate face parts.

The team shows the task is not a pure measure of part-based information. Other cues leak into the scores it gives. Impure measures can mislead theories of how faces are recognised. The paper helps labs choose and interpret face tests with more care.
plos-pone-0006339:
One enzyme both senses DNA damage and helps decide whether a stressed cell lives or dies. Ben Buelow and colleagues dissected PARP-1 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme responds to oxidative and nitrosative stress by building ADPR chains on proteins, and it also forms single ADPR units.

Their structure and function analysis maps which parts of PARP-1 produce the single-unit form under stress. Separating the two outputs clarifies the enzyme's fork-in-the-road role. PARP blockers are used in cancer care, so fine mechanism matters. The study guides how those drugs might be refined.
plos-pone-0006439:
Ruggero D'Anastasio and co-authors examined a very old skeleton from Sterkfontein, South Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The partial skeleton, known as Stw 431, belongs to Australopithecus africanus, a late Pliocene early human relative. An earlier study had read marks on its spine bones as a wear condition called spondylosis deformans. The new team re-examined the bones for signs of disease.

Their title raises a striking possibility: the lesions may reflect brucellosis, an infection still known today. If so, disease shaped life long before modern humans. Reading illness in fossil bones is hard, and the claim is framed as possible. The study shows how much care such claims require.
plos-pone-0006539:
George Cerniglia and co-authors studied a cancer drug and the tissue around tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Drugs that block the EGFR growth signal have shown only modest effects when used alone against cancer. The team asked how EGFR blockade changes the tumor microenvironment, the mix of cells and vessels around a tumor. They focused on blood vessels.

Blocking EGFR can make tumor vessels more normal, a change called vascular normalization. More normal vessels may carry drugs and oxygen to the tumor in a better way. That in turn can help radiation and other drugs work. The study looks past the cancer cell to its whole setting.
plos-pone-0006639:
Hendrik Wilking, Mario Ziller, Christoph Staubach, and colleagues evaluated wild bird monitoring for bird flu in PLOS ONE in 2009. Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1 proved remarkably mobile in migratory bird populations. It led to extensive outbreaks for which the true number of cases is unclear. Monitoring wild birds is a main surveillance strategy.

The authors assess chances and limitations of wild bird monitoring for H5N1. Detection of pathogens hides behind sampling biases: sick birds are easier to find than healthy carriers. Honest evaluation helps agencies spend surveillance money where it works. It also prevents false reassurance from weak monitoring.
plos-pone-0006739:
Gertjan S. Verhoeven and colleagues displayed short peptides on the surface of bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Displaying peptides on bacteria is a workhorse technique in biotechnology. Peptides sit inside a scaffold protein of the outer membrane. The scaffold here was OmpA, a common bacterial surface protein. The team inserted known antibody tags into its exposed loops.

They compared display using different parts of the OmpA membrane domain. The tags were the well-known 3xFLAG and 2xmyc epitopes. Some designs showed the peptides to antibodies better than others. Knowing which design displays best improves library screening. It also improves bacterial systems built to present antigens or bind targets.
plos-pone-0006839:
Polloneal Jymmiel R. Ocbina, Miquel Tuson, and Kathryn V. Anderson tested whether cilia are needed for a key embryo signal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Primary cilia are small antenna-like structures on cells. In mouse embryos, sonic hedgehog signaling requires the cilium. Cilia are built and maintained by intraflagellar transport proteins. Mutants lacking those proteins cannot answer hedgehog signals.

The authors asked whether canonical Wnt signaling also needs cilia. Their answer was no. Embryos without normal cilia still ran Wnt signaling properly. The negative result separates the two great developmental pathways. It tells researchers which signaling defects to expect in cilia disorders.
plos-pone-0006939:
Patrick Sénéchal, Geneviève Arseneault, Alexandre Leroux, and colleagues studied a yeast prion in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein chaperone Hsp104 helps yeast survive heat stress. Its disaggregase activity rescues misfolded proteins by pulling them apart. Hsp104 also helps propagate fungal prions, the self-copying protein states.

The team tested the fission yeast version of Hsp104 against a famous prion called [PSI+]. They found this Hsp104 unable to propagate that prion. The negative result is informative. It shows that prion propagation rules differ between yeast species, and it sharpens models of how chaperones handle misfolded proteins.
plos-pone-0007039:
M. Melissa Gilbert, Brian Robinson, and Kenneth Moberg studied tumor gene teamwork in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. The fly gene erupted is the counterpart of human TSG101. It helps run the ESCRT-1 complex, which routes proteins for disposal. Loss of such genes in fly tissues can grow into tumors of the imaginal discs.

The team tested how erupted interacts with two other genes, DaPKC and rbf1. Genetic teamwork can turn mild defects into strong growth. Their crosses map which combinations push discs toward tumors. Fly genetics like this often previews interactions later found in human cancer.
plos-pone-0007139:
Jeffrey Koehler, Michael Bolton, Amanda Rollins, and colleagues modelled dual infection in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria and HIV overlap across sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. Co-infection is therefore a real risk for millions. Studies of HIV with the main human malaria parasite had shown strong interactions. The team built an animal model for relapsing malaria instead.

Rhesus macaques were co-infected with SIV and Plasmodium cynomolgi. Their immune responses differed from single infections. A relapsing malaria model mirrors much African disease better. It lets researchers test vaccines and treatments under realistic dual pressure.
plos-pone-0007239:
Sylvie Rodrigues-Ferreira, Anne Di Tommaso, Ariane Dimitrov, and colleagues reported a protective protein in breast cancer in 2009. Breast cancer is varied, and current therapies do not fully eradicate it. Sorting tumors into molecular subtypes helps doctors predict outcomes and likely treatment responses for patients.

The authors study ATIP3, a product of the MTUS1 gene on chromosome region 8p22. They describe ATIP3 as a new anti-mitotic protein, meaning it restrains cell division. They report it is underexpressed in invasive breast cancers with poor prognosis. Low levels may mark tumors needing closer attention.
plos-pone-0007339:
Melody Tsui, Tiao Xie, James D. Orth, and colleagues screened for genes that modify a cancer drug's effects in 2009. Kinesin-5 is a motor protein required to assemble the bipolar mitotic spindle. Its inhibitors, developed as potential anti-cancer drugs, arrest cells in mitosis and promote cancer cell death in dividing cells.

The authors perform a genome-wide siRNA screen with live cell imaging. Imaging is intermittent, balancing detail against cell health. They search for enhancers and suppressors of a kinesin-5 inhibitor. Hits from the screen point to combination treatments and resistance mechanisms for this drug class.
plos-pone-0007439:
Kara Johnson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on BCR-ABL, the abnormal protein that defines chronic myeloid leukemia. BCR-ABL is an overactive enzyme, and its activity is required to start the disease. It was thought to work by gathering a team of adapter proteins into one complex. The team tested whether those direct partnerships are truly essential.

They built a mutant BCR-ABL that could no longer bind three adapters: GRB2, CBL, and CRKL. The altered protein kept its enzyme activity yet failed to cause leukemia in mice. That failure proves the direct connections are not decoration. They are required steps in how BCR-ABL triggers disease. The result points drug research toward the protein's binding surfaces as well as its enzyme pocket.
plos-pone-0007539:
Francesco Di Serio and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on viroids, the smallest known plant pathogens. A viroid is a naked loop of RNA with no protein coat and no genes for proteins. Infected plants fill with tiny RNAs copied from the viroid, signs of the plant's silencing defense. The team deep-sequenced those small RNAs from two disease-causing variants of a chloroplast viroid.

The sequences showed how the small RNAs arise from each variant. Their patterns also bear on how the viroids cause symptoms. Comparing a mild and a severe variant highlights which RNA pieces track with damage. Minimal pathogens leave few clues, so each pattern counts. The study uses the plant's own defense output as a window into viroid biology. It informs the broader question of how naked RNA can make a plant sick.
plos-pone-0007639:
Kelly Heim and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the rhythm of vitamin A signaling. Retinoic acid, the active form of vitamin A, works through nuclear receptors that switch genes on and off. Those receptors recruit helper complexes in rapid cycles. A coregulator called RIP140 represses receptor activity. The team examined how retinoic acid shapes receptor activity over longer stretches of time in their system.

They found evidence for long-paced oscillations in retinoid receptor activity. RIP140 appears to play a potential role in setting that slow rhythm. A timing layer in gene control means the same signal can mean different things at different hours. That matters for development, where retinoids pattern whole body regions. It also matters for drugs that mimic vitamin A. The study adds tempo to the usual picture of switches.
plos-pone-0007739:
Kevin Miller and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows how the pancreas builds its hormone-making clusters in newborn mice. Each cluster, an islet of Langerhans, mixes several cell types. Beta cells make insulin, while alpha cells make glucagon, among others.

How these mixed clusters assemble after birth was poorly mapped. The team traced islet formation through the neonatal period. Their account shows when and where the different cell types come together. Understanding normal islet growth matters for diabetes research, where working beta cells are lost or never form properly.
plos-pone-0007839:
Chin-Hsing Lin and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how the protein c-Myc reshapes mouse embryonic stem cells. Myc is a transcription regulator tied to many tumor types. It also plays an important role inside stem cells.

Whether Myc has unique targets in stem cells was unclear. The authors mapped its gene regulation there. They also tracked epigenetic remodeling, the chemical changes that open or close DNA. The picture shows Myc steering both gene activity and chromatin state. That dual grip may explain why Myc is so central to growth and cancer.
plos-pone-0007939:
Kouki Fujioka and colleagues tried a new way to sniff out yeast, writing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wine tasters name smells with rich comparisons, while machines that mimic the nose give plain numbers. The team joined the two styles, pairing true smell values with word pictures.

Blending the two kinds of data helped the system spot yeast more surely than either style alone. The trick borrows from human skill: a good metaphor can carry fine shades of scent that raw numbers miss. The method may help food and drink makers catch spoilage early with cheaper tools.
plos-pone-0008039:
Ragnvi Hagman and colleagues read gene activity in infected dog wombs for PLOS ONE in 2009. Severe womb infection is a common, dangerous illness in female dogs, and it can tip into sepsis, a whole-body crisis. The team compared sick tissue with healthy tissue.

Genes that chew up proteins ran hot in the sick wombs, while genes that pattern and regulate tissue ran cold. That tilt fits a tissue breaking down faster than it can hold form. The readout may help vets spot the worst cases early and may hint at new treatments.
plos-pone-0008139:
Maneesha Chhikara and colleagues showed how carbon monoxide quiets inflamed human blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The body makes small amounts of this gas itself, and it acts as a messenger that damps inflammation. The team exposed monocytes to a bacterial toxin that normally fires a storm of inflammatory genes.

With the gas present, the storm was cut short near its start. The break sat between the toxin sensor TLR4 and the command protein NF-kB. Genome-wide reads confirmed the cut. The precise break point may let drug makers copy the gas's calm without its poison risk.
plos-pone-0008239:
Géraldine Giraud and colleagues tested tumor samples for virus DNA in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some polyomaviruses can cause cancer, and older types had been linked loosely to brain tumors. Three new polyomaviruses, named KI, WU, and Merkel cell, had recently been found. The team asked whether their DNA appears in childhood tumors. They checked central nervous system tumors and neuroblastomas.

No DNA from the three viruses was detected in those samples. A clear negative result still matters in a field full of hints. It narrows the search for viral causes of these childhood cancers. Future work can focus on other candidates.
plos-pone-0008339:
Stefano Farioli-Vecchioli and colleagues studied memory in knockout mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. New neurons are born in the dentate gyrus of the adult hippocampus. This neurogenesis has been implicated in plasticity and memory. The molecular controls on newborn neurons remain largely unknown. The team removed a gene called PC3/Tis21 in mice.

Without it, hippocampal granule neurons failed to finish differentiating. The mice also showed defective contextual memory. Linking one gene to both cell maturation and memory is a strong result. It helps explain how new neurons join memory circuits.
plos-pone-0008439:
Cristina Cigana and co-authors wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on lung infection in cystic fibrosis. A germ called Pseudomonas aeruginosa can live in the airways for life. Strains found late in the disease differ from strains found at first. The team study parts of the germ that the immune system senses. Those parts include lipid A and bits of the cell wall.

They find the late strains change those parts. The changes make the germ less apt to trigger innate defense. In short, the germ learns to hide from the host. That helps explain why the infection lasts so long in these lungs.
plos-pone-0008539:
Silke Raffegerst and co-authors report blood cancers in transgenic mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their mice carry a chimeric MHC class II gene called DR4. MHC molecules present antigen fragments to immune cells. The homozygous mouse line spontaneously develops diverse hematological malignancies. That happens at a high frequency of about seventy percent. Tumors split evenly between T cell and B cell types.

The malignancies include lymphoblastic T cell lymphomas and Hodgkin-like lymphomas. Such variety in one mouse line is unusual. The model may reveal how a single immune gene change unleashes many cancer types. It offers a system for testing treatments across blood cancers.
plos-pone-0008639:
Frances Mercer and co-authors study receptors on regulatory T cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Regulatory T cells suppress immune activation and prevent autoimmune diseases. Their ability to inhibit proliferation of other T cells is well established. It was not yet clear whether they also modulate inflammatory cytokines during responses. TNF and IL-1 are two major inflammatory cytokines. The team examine expression and function of their receptors on human regulatory T cells.

They find those receptors are expressed and functional on the cells. Through them, inflammatory signals can tune regulatory cell behavior. That tuning may decide if suppression holds during infection or flare. The receptors become potential levers for autoimmune therapy.
plos-pone-0008739:
Changrui Lu, Fang Ding, and Ailong Ke solved the shape of an ancient RNA-shredding machine. Their structural study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The exosome chews up RNA messages that cells no longer need. In archaea, simple microbes, it has a cutting ring and a binding ring. Earlier work suggested both rings were neatly threefold. A sharper portrait was needed.

Their crystal structure, from the archaeon Sulfolobus solfataricus, broke that neat picture. The binding ring sat in an uneven, flexible arrangement. Flexibility may help the machine grip many RNA shapes. The portrait informs models of RNA cleanup in all complex cells.
plos-pone-0008839:
Marinus van Batenburg, Hualing Li, J. Annelies Polman, and colleagues predicted a hormone target gene from a DNA pattern. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glucocorticoids are stress hormones with wide medical use. They act when their receptor binds response elements near genes. Most direct target genes in the body were still unknown. The team proposed that paired elements close together mark real targets.

That rule pointed to caveolin-1, a membrane protein gene. Tests supported it as a true glucocorticoid target. A predictive rule speeds the hunt for hormone-controlled genes. Such genes explain both benefits and side effects of steroid drugs.
plos-pone-0008939:
Marie Benoit and colleagues read the gene activity of infected human heart valves for PLOS ONE in 2010. Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart's inner lining and valves. Bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus cause most cases. The infection grows crusty deposits on valves and can destroy them.

The team measured which genes were turned up or down in diseased valve tissue. The pattern traced how the disease unfolds, step by step, inside the valve. Genes tied to immune defence and blood clotting stood out in the picture. That map of the disease's course may point doctors toward better treatments.
plos-pone-0009039:
Andrew Crossett, Nick Lauter, and Tanzy Love built a better error bar for gene hunting, in PLOS ONE in 2010. QTL mapping finds chromosome stretches behind traits like yield or disease risk. Each find comes with a confidence interval, the range where the gene likely sits. Sequenced genomes now make chasing those genes realistic, so intervals must be honest.

Old support-interval methods can misstate the true uncertainty. The team derived intervals from the data themselves, tailored to composite interval mapping. Their empirical method was checked against known cases. Tighter, truer intervals save laboratories from hunting genes in the wrong stretch.
plos-pone-0009139:
Vidya Devi Negi and co-authors vaccinated pregnant mice against Salmonella, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pregnancy softens the mother's immune defences so the fetus is not rejected. That truce leaves pregnant mothers more open to invading germs. Salmonella infection during pregnancy can end in loss of the litter.

The vaccine strain, called DV-STM-07, was designed to be safe in pregnancy. Vaccinated mothers resisted Salmonella infection while carrying their young. Abortions were prevented, and the newborn mice carried protection too. A vaccine for mothers that shields two generations at once is a double gain.
plos-pone-0009239:
Ruhee Dere, Patricia Wilson, Richard Sandford, and co-authors published this kidney study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Polycystic kidney disease is a common inherited disorder that fills kidneys with cysts. It is a major cause of kidney failure, and treatment options are limited. The disease comes from faults in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes.

The study follows polycystin-1, the protein made by PKD1. Its tail end was found to guide another protein, TSC2, to the right place in the cell. Positioned there, TSC2 holds back mTOR, a growth signal that cysts seem to exploit. The finding links the cyst gene to a pathway doctors already hope to target.
plos-pone-0009339:
Young-Beob Yu and co-authors published this herbal medicine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cinnamon bark from Cinnamomum cassia appears in two traditional herbal formulas. Proving that such mixtures work, and how, is hard because they mix many herbs. The team used the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans to test the formulas cleanly.

Worms given the formulas lived longer than untreated worms. The gain ran through insulin signaling and stress response pathways, two known levers of aging. Showing a pathway gives herbal research a mechanism to test further, beyond simple claims. It also links a traditional remedy to the basic biology of lifespan.
plos-pone-0009439:
Leopoldo de Meis and co-authors wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about brown fat in rats. Brown fat burns fuel to make heat for the body. Its heat making is driven by its mitochondria, the cell's power units. The team looked at two compartments inside brown fat cells: the endoplasmic reticulum and the mitochondria.

They saw the outer coat of the mitochondria fuse with the reticulum. Calcium signals helped switch on heat making after that fusion. A calcium pump known as SERCA 1 was found at the site. The result shows that cell parts can join up in a direct way to turn on warmth.
plos-pone-0009539:
Savita Khanna and co-authors studied slow healing wounds in diabetic mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wounds in diabetes often stay open and inflamed for a long time. Healing needs inflammation to end once its job is done. A key step is the clearing of dead cells by macrophages, a clean up process called efferocytosis. The team tested that step at wound sites in diabetic animals.

Macrophages in the diabetic wounds cleared dead cells poorly. With dead cells left in place, inflammation dragged on. The work names a precise failure behind a common and serious problem. Fixing the clean up step could help wounds in diabetes finally close.
plos-pone-0009639:
Marisa King, Jeb Owen, and Hubert Schwabl questioned a cherished idea about baby birds in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mother birds pass antibodies to their chicks, supposedly giving vital early protection. House sparrow chicks are born helpless and grow up in the nest. The team tracked how the chicks' own immune systems developed. They measured whether maternal antibodies played the central role often assumed.

Their data test that assumption against real development patterns. Maternal antibodies mattered less, or for shorter times, than the standard story claims. Findings like these reshape how ecologists model disease in wild birds. They also show why field checks beat armchair claims about immunity.
plos-pone-0009739:
Virginia B. Kraus and co-authors published a medical study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks whether blood or urine markers can stand in for the total load of osteoarthritis in a body. Whole-body scans are too costly and give too much radiation for that task.

The team studied 461 women with hand arthritis and scored X-rays of hands, hips, knees, and spine. Three markers each rose with the total load of bony spurs across the body. Markers plus basic facts about the women predicted 35 to 38 percent of the spread in total disease load.
plos-pone-0009839:
Deep-diving seabirds must fight their own buoyancy on the way down. Timothée Cook and colleagues measured how one such bird manages that fight underwater. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Buoyancy is the upward push water gives to air-filled bodies.

The team recorded underwater locomotor performance during deep dives. The pattern suggested respiratory strategies, ways of handling air, that cut foraging effort. Air carried down adds lift, so managing breath saves energy. Smarter breathing lets the bird spend its dive hunting, not fighting to sink. Foraging effort decides whether a dive pays off.
plos-pone-0009939:
Parents are having children later than in past generations, and autism rates have climbed too. Jean Golding, Colin Steer, and Marcus Pembrey tested whether those trends connect. Their birth cohort study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The study covered autistic spectrum disorders across a whole birth cohort. A birth cohort follows everyone born in a set time and place. It weighed parental ages and, unusually, grandparental ages as well. Grandparents' ages can matter through effects passed down generations. Cohort data let the team test age effects without cherry-picking cases.
plos-pone-0010039:
Ole Norgaard and Jeffrey Lazarus wrote about searching medical literature during a crisis in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic produced thousands of papers and news items very fast. Finding the right studies in that flood was hard. Poor searching can leave decision makers using old or weak evidence.

Their PLOS ONE article used PubMed, the main medical database, as its test case. It considered how searches perform when a health emergency is moving quickly. The lessons apply to any outbreak where officials must find sound science under time pressure. Speed and accuracy both counted in their tests.
plos-pone-0010139:
The authors were Márcio Baptista, Carlos Melo, Mário Armelão, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used cultured rat brain neurons. They studied an enzyme that makes GABA, the brain's main calming signal molecule. Under excitotoxic conditions, when overexcited neurons are damaged, that enzyme gets cut into pieces.

The team tested whether the proteasome, the cell's main protein shredding machine, does that cutting. They worked with neurons from the hippocampus, a memory center. Understanding the cut could reveal how seizures and strokes disturb the brain's balance of signals. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010239:
Alessia Ligresti leads a 2010 PLOS ONE study of a disputed cell transporter for anandamide, a cannabis-like signal made in the body. Whether a dedicated carrier ferries it across cell membranes was argued, partly because the blocker drugs used to test uptake might act elsewhere.

The team used a pain and heat channel, TRPV1, inside cells as a sensor for anandamide entry. They also hid anandamide inside tiny plastic particles so it could enter without touching membrane proteins. Masked anandamide kept its normal action pattern but became much less sensitive to the blocker drugs. That supports the blockers' specificity, and the existence of the carrier route.
plos-pone-0010339:
Kevin Doherty, David Naugle and Jeffrey Evans wrote about sage-grouse and energy building in PLOS ONE in 2010. As the United States builds more energy projects at home, wild land is lost. Offsets try to balance that harm by funding protection elsewhere. Fans call offsets a useful way to pay for conservation. Critics fear the trade lets real damage slide.

The authors propose treating sage-grouse habitat like a currency that can be traded openly. A market price, they argue, could show what saving habitat is worth. Energy firms would buy credits; landowners who protect birds would earn them. The idea tries to make conservation compete in dollars. Whether such trading truly helps the bird is the debate the study joins.
plos-pone-0010439:
H. Christina Fan and Stephen Quake measured the true limits of a blood test for unborn babies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fragments of a fetus's DNA float in the mother's blood. Counting them by rapid sequencing can reveal extra chromosomes, as in Down syndrome. A quirk of the sequencer, favoring some DNA types, had capped the test's sensitivity. The authors asked what limits remain once that bias is handled.

They argue the ceiling is set by simple counting statistics. More counted fragments mean surer answers, in a predictable way. That clarity helps labs design tests with known reliability. A blood draw is far safer than sampling the womb directly. This analysis helped turn a lab feat into a dependable screening tool.
plos-pone-0010539:
Soo Chan Lee and colleagues traced the sex-related region and shared genome features of microsporidia and fungi in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microsporidia are tiny parasites that live inside cells of many animals, including humans. Evidence increasingly ties them closely to fungi, either inside that kingdom or beside it. Their genomes are stripped down by parasitic life. The team compared their sex locus and other genome features with true fungi.

Shared features support the fungal kinship with fresh detail. The sex-related locus shows how even mating machinery survives extreme genome shrinkage. Origins of parasite groups matter for predicting their biology and weaknesses. This study uses genome comparison as an ancestry test. It places an odd group more firmly on the tree of life.
plos-pone-0010639:
Hiromi Sawai and colleagues traced the family history of the domestic chicken, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chickens were tamed from wild junglefowl in Southeast Asia thousands of years ago. Which wild species contributed most was still debated among researchers.

The team compared DNA from many chicken breeds and two junglefowl species. The red junglefowl emerged as the main ancestor. The green junglefowl left smaller traces in some breeds. Genetic family trees like this one help breeders protect rare traits. They also show how human choices reshaped one wild bird into the world's most common farm animal.
plos-pone-0010739:
Wees Love and colleagues tested which immune sensor guards mouse lungs against mycoplasma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycoplasma pulmonis is a natural lung pathogen of mice, akin to germs that cause walking pneumonia in people. Mycoplasma surface fats are sensed by toll-like receptors, the body's early warning set.

Mice lacking the sensor TLR2 fought the infection far worse than normal mice. Lab cells with added TLR2 reacted strongly to the germ's surface fats. TLR2 thus carries most of the early defense in the lung. Knowing the key sensor focuses vaccine and drug work on the pathway that actually matters.
plos-pone-0010839:
Linda Douw, Marjolein de Groot, Edwin van Dellen and co-authors published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Epilepsy affects about one in a hundred people, but a first seizure is hard to judge because a standard EEG often shows no clear warning signs. The authors tested whether functional connectivity, a measure of how brain regions fire in sync, could do better.

They drew on hundreds of EEG records from patients seen after a first suspected seizure, then compared people later confirmed to have epilepsy with matched people who did not. A sync measure averaged across frequency bands separated the groups more sharply than the usual search for abnormal spikes. Douw and colleagues suggest that reading the EEG as a network, not just a trace, could make early epilepsy diagnosis more reliable.
plos-pone-0010939:
Nickolai Titov, Gavin Andrews, Matthew Davies and co-authors ran this trial of internet therapy for depression, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Online cognitive behavioral therapy works for depression when a clinician guides it, but clinician time is scarce and costly. The authors asked whether a trained technician, offering support without clinical advice, could guide patients just as well.

Community volunteers with major depression were assigned at random to clinician-guided treatment, technician-guided treatment, or a waiting group. Both guided groups worked through six online lessons with weekly homework and weekly contact over eight weeks. Titov and colleagues set the trial up as a fairness test: if technician support matches clinician support, effective therapy can reach far more people. Their question goes to the heart of scaling mental health care online.
plos-pone-0011039:
Caroline Kizilyaprak, Danièle Spehner, Didier Devys and co-authors published this retina chromatin study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rod photoreceptor nuclei are built inside-out compared with most cells: a dense central ball of silent chromatin wrapped in a thin rim of active chromatin. The authors used these natural extremes to correlate structure with chemical marks and gene activity in intact cells.

Using cryo-preserved tissue, electron tomography, and gold-tagged antibodies, they mapped where histone modifications and the gene-reading enzyme sit relative to the dense core. The central domain carried the marks of silenced chromatin, while the machinery of active reading occupied the rim. Kizilyaprak and colleagues turn an oddball nucleus into a clean test of how packing states relate to function, informing the wider effort to read the histone code.
plos-pone-0011139:
Marrazzo, Thomas, Fiedler and colleagues ran a cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a common vaginal infection caused by a shift in normal bacteria. They followed women who report sex with women and recorded who developed the condition and when.

The study mapped the risks tied to picking up the infection in this group. Such detail was lacking, since most past work focused on other groups. Clearer risk data leads to better advice in clinics and better care. It also corrects a gap in women's health research for a group often left out of studies.
plos-pone-0011239:
Yew, Zhao, Hong and colleagues treated obese mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. In obesity, the liver often stops responding well to insulin, a step toward diabetes. The team blocked an enzyme that builds a fatty molecule in cell membranes and measured insulin action in the liver.

Blocking that enzyme increased how well the liver responded to insulin in mice made obese by diet. The enzyme thus becomes a named drug target for insulin resistance. A treatment built on it would attack a root fault rather than manage blood sugar alone. The finding now needs study of safety and effects beyond the liver.
plos-pone-0011339:
Kelli Barr and colleagues asked in 2010 whether germs living inside a corn pest help the pest disarm the plant. The western corn rootworm is a beetle whose young chew corn roots across North America and Europe. Plants fight back by switching on defense genes, but the attack often still succeeds and harvests suffer.

The team found that microbes living with the rootworm lower the plant's defense response in roots. With those genes turned down, the plant mounts a weaker counterattack while feeding goes on. The result shifts how scientists think about crop pests. The real opponent may be a partnership of insect plus microbes, so protecting corn may require breaking up that partnership rather than targeting the beetle alone.
plos-pone-0011439:
Hye-Jung Kim and co-authors tested in 2010 whether two supposedly minor immune cell types do real cleanup work in the thymus. The thymus trains immune cells, and many trainee cells die there by design. Those dead cells must be cleared quietly, or their contents could trigger autoimmunity, an attack on the body's own tissue.

By selectively removing eosinophils or neutrophils in mice, the team showed that clearing dead cells in the thymus became less efficient. Cells often cast as allergy or infection players thus hold a housekeeping job where self-tolerance is learned. The finding widens the cast of cells that keep the thymus orderly. It also hints that when these cells are missing or faulty, leftover debris might help explain how tolerance breaks down.
plos-pone-0011539:
Carol Camlin, Victoria Hosegood, and Marie-Louise Newell examined in 2010 how gender and migration together shape HIV risk in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The province carries one of the world's heaviest HIV burdens, and its pattern is not random. Men often migrate for work, while women remain with limited power to negotiate safety in their relationships, and the team traced how those forces meet.

Their analysis grounds infection risk in lived structure: who moves, who decides, and who is left vulnerable by both. Prevention that ignores that structure, handing out identical messages to everyone, misses why risk concentrates where it does. The findings argue for programs that reach migrant men at work sites and strengthen women's bargaining power at home. Epidemiology that names the social machinery gives policy something it can actually change.
plos-pone-0011639:
Jörg Ritter and co-authors presented a new microscope method for watching single molecules in living tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seeing individual molecules at work promises detailed views of how the body functions. In thick living tissue, though, most microscopes are too slow, too blurry or too damaging to follow them.

Their technique pairs light sheet illumination, which lights only a thin slice, with ultra-sensitive detection. It tracks lone molecules while keeping tissue alive and largely unharmed. Biologists gain a gentler window onto molecular movement in its natural setting, opening studies that were not feasible before.
plos-pone-0011739:
Ciara Greene, Pooja Bahri and David Soto separated two emotional influences on memory, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mood and bodily arousal are both known to affect how well people think and remember. How much each one contributes, and how they interact, was poorly understood.

After a study phase with abstract shapes, the team altered participants' feeling states and measured recognition memory. Their design teased apart the effect of emotional tone from the effect of arousal. Finding two separate levers on what people remember helps explain conflicting results in earlier emotion research.
plos-pone-0011839:
Angela Kamps and co-workers studied fruit flies in 2010 to find out what the Tre1 receptor needs in order to guide moving cells. Tre1 belongs to the large receptor family that lets cells sense signals around them. In a fly embryo it helps germ cells, the future egg and sperm cells, travel to the right place.

The team pinpointed one building block, an arginine kept nearly unchanged across species, and showed that Tre1 fails without it. A single altered piece can therefore break a whole migration route. The result shows how finely built these receptors are, and it gives cell movement research a precise point where guidance can be switched off for study.
plos-pone-0011939:
Satyendra Tripathi and co-workers reported in 2010 a protein sign that marks the most risky cancers of the head and neck. The team set tumor tissue side by side with normal mouth lining and tagged proteins to find which ones differ. One stood out: a protein called S100A7, found in the core of tumor cells.

That core form of the protein was tied to poor outcomes for patients with this cancer type. A sign that sorts patients by how their disease is likely to run helps doctors choose who needs the strongest care and the closest watch. Since the test uses tissue that is already taken for diagnosis, it could slot into the checks patients now get.
plos-pone-0012039:
Sujoy Das and co-workers isolated in 2010 a factor from goat reproductive fluid that stops sperm from swimming. Several mammals carry sperm motility inhibiting factors in male reproductive fluids, but these proteins had not been adequately purified or characterized. The team worked with plasma from the caprine epididymis, the duct where sperm mature.

They purified the novel factor, called MIF-II, and characterized its properties. A natural, specific brake on sperm movement is scientifically interesting for how fertility is timed, and it hints at contraceptive ideas based on stopping sperm rather than hormones. Careful purification is the unglamorous step that makes any of that testable.
plos-pone-0012139:
Han Yan, Kavitha Venkatesan, John Beaver, and co-authors built a resource for predicting gene functions in the fruit fly, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fruit fly is one of biology's main model animals, yet the jobs of many of its genes remain unknown. Guessing each gene's role from large mixed datasets is a standing challenge for systems biology.

The team trained separate prediction programs for different functions, letting each data type count where it helps most, then combined the results into one public resource. Other researchers can look up a fly gene and get a ranked guess at its job, ready to test in the lab. Resources like this speed up genetics far beyond a single lab's reach.
plos-pone-0012239:
Takashi Saito, Akinori Nakamura, Yoshitsugu Aoki, and co-authors carried a gene therapy from dystrophic dogs toward a human patient, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Duchenne muscular dystrophy destroys muscle because the dystrophin message is broken; skipping the broken section during message assembly can restore a shorter but working protein. The team had treated dogs with a synthetic snippet that forces such skipping.

They then tested that same snippet in cells taken from a patient whose deletion pattern differs, and found it still worked. Showing one drug design can serve more than one deletion type widens the pool of boys it might help. Exon skipping remains one of the few strategies that treats this disease's root cause.
plos-pone-0012339:
Pawandeep Dhami, Peter Saffrey, Alexander Bruce, and co-authors examined the marks that outline genes' working segments, in PLOS ONE in 2010. As a gene is read, the cell must know which segments, exons, to keep in the final message and which to cut. Recent work had shown the protein spools along genes are placed and tagged in patterns that mirror those segments, as if chromatin itself keeps the outline.

Their analysis shows the outline is not explained by spool placement alone; the chemical tags carry independent information. That distinction matters for understanding splicing errors, which underlie many diseases. It also refines the picture of the gene as a text whose punctuation is written in several inks.
plos-pone-0012439:
Yoel Lubell, Anne Mills, Christopher Whitty and colleagues priced a policy of treating malaria at home in Uganda, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Home management teaches community workers to treat feverish children fast, before malaria turns deadly. The approach is widely promoted in Africa, but its cost per benefit needed a careful check.

Using an interactive Markov model that follows children through sickness and recovery states, the team weighed program costs against lives and health gained. Their analysis helps ministries decide whether home treatment deserves scarce funds next to clinics and bed nets. Models of this kind make policy trade-offs explicit instead of guessed.
plos-pone-0012539:
Bob Uttl and Kelly Kisinger examined what missing information means in witness statements and accident records, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Eyewitness reports and crash records often omit the very conditions researchers need — lighting, speed, attention — leaving gaps called missing values. Analysts usually treat a gap as no information, but Uttl and Kisinger question that habit.

They argue silence in a record often carries meaning: witnesses mention what struck them as notable, so what is absent was likely ordinary. Reading absence correctly changes conclusions in court cases and safety studies. The paper gives researchers rules for handling gaps without inventing data — or wasting real clues.
plos-pone-0012639:
Rodriguez, Aburjania, Priedigkeit and co-authors mapped the parts of a protein that decide whether it fights or feeds cancer. The protein KLF6 normally suppresses tumours, but a shortened variant made by splicing, called KLF6-SV1, does the opposite. The variant lacks the tail that helps the full protein work.

Their 2010 study found that regions guiding the protein into and out of the nucleus also control how fast it is destroyed. Place and lifespan together set whether the guard or its rival wins. That logic may help design drugs for cancers driven by this gene.
plos-pone-0012739:
Factor, Seo, Ishikawa and co-authors cut out a growth receptor in mice and watched liver regrowth stall late. After part of the liver is removed, the HGF and c-Met signal starts DNA copying for regrowth. Their 2010 study used mice lacking c-Met to see what happens after that start.

Without c-Met, a whole gene program needed for the late division step failed to run. Regrowing livers therefore need this signal twice, not once. The detail matters for liver surgery and for diseases where regrowth is weak.  Gene activity was read across the whole regrowth period.
plos-pone-0012839:
Agam, Yalcin, Bhomra and co-authors hunted for stretches of DNA that mice gain or lose compared with a reference genome. Such copy number variants can shift gene dosage and traits. Their 2010 study used array hybridisation, a chip method that spots gains and losses across the genome.

They found this class of variation oddly elusive in the mouse genome, with fewer clear cases than expected. Elusive does not mean absent, and the study probes the limits of the tool itself. Honest limits matter, since mouse genetics underpins much medical research.
plos-pone-0340539:
Hugo Charoud and four colleagues evaluate two programs that paid Colombian farmers to keep Amazon forest standing, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One was a government scheme offering cash across a wide area of Guaviare; the other, a four year charity project, worked closely with frontier farms on sustainable land use. Together the two covered different ground, and the authors measured how much deforestation each actually prevented.

Combined, the programs spared roughly fourteen hundred hectares of forest, a real but modest dent in regional clearing. The government scheme guarded larger, less threatened patches, while the charity targeted smaller farms at the sharp edge of clearing and added technical help such as tree dotted pasture systems. The authors argue the designs complement each other, yet payments alone cannot stop clearing without stronger measures behind them.
plos-pone-0341539:
Wengang Gan and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on roadbed material made from cement-stabilized phosphogypsum, an industrial byproduct, and how its springiness under traffic loading survives wetting and drying. That property, the resilient modulus, steers pavement design, yet codes still use a static version. The team ran dynamic triaxial tests varying confinement, repeated load, cement content, and wet-dry cycles, then examined microstructure to explain the changes.

The modulus rose with confining pressure and cement dose and fell as load and wet-dry cycles increased, with nearly all cycle damage done in the first four rounds. Microscopy and mineral analysis accounted for the decay. Dynamic values ran above static ones by a stable ratio, and a simple strength test predicted the modulus closely. A prediction model including cement content and cycle count, verified against experiments, is supplied for engineers designing with this recycled material.
plos-pone-0342639:
Masaru Sakai and co-authors grow edible mushrooms in Fukushima in 2026. Two species were grown on forest floor beds. Fourteen broad leaf forest sites took part in the work. The aim was to measure radioactive caesium uptake. That uptake has blocked outdoor growing since the accident. Air dose rates were checked at each site.

Both species stayed well below the food safety limit. That supports a return to outdoor growing in wide areas. Uptake tracked soil contamination in species specific ways. One species tracked litter and deep soil layers. The other tracked top soil and leaf mould more. Clean soil fill may help the first species. Clean litter cover may help the second one.
plos-pone-0344039:
Mohamed M Hassona and co-authors ran two seasons of field trials to see whether buckwheat, a gluten-free grain crop new to Egypt, can thrive there, and under what conditions. Two species, common buckwheat and the hardier Tartary type, were grown at a Nile Delta site and a desert fringe site. Each was sown in late autumn, midwinter, and early spring. Growth and yield were measured plant by plant.

The three-way interplay of species, place, and sowing date drove nearly every trait. Tartary buckwheat outperformed the common type at both sites, peaking with early spring sowing in the Delta at nearly a tonne of grain per hectare, while common buckwheat preferred an autumn sowing. The authors give Egyptian growers their first concrete calendar for a crop that could diversify farms under dry conditions.
plos-pone-0347739:
Funmito Omolola Fehintola and colleagues check teen smoking with a breath test. Their study from Osun State, Nigeria, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Teens often understate smoking on forms. So the team measured carbon monoxide in the breath of six hundred sixteen school students. A handheld meter did the reading. A standard WHO form was filled in as well.

Breath scores at or past the smoker line flagged current smokers. That gave an objective count to set against what students admitted. The team also hunted for factors linked to smoking. The gap between breath and self-report matters far beyond Nigeria. Health plans everywhere rest on surveys that may understate youth smoking.
plos-pone-0347839:
Jialing Zhang and colleagues compared a prized Chinese medicinal herb, Ligusticum chuanxiong, grown in its classic Sichuan home with a distinct variety cultivated in Gansu. Buyers prize origin, so the team measured everything: plant size and colour, scent through an electronic nose, and chemistry through chromatography and mass spectrometry, hunting for what separates the two.

The Gansu plants grew bigger and browner, with a different scent profile. Sichuan material carried more of several key active compounds, though one ran higher in Gansu stock. The volatile analysis found eighty-two scent compounds in Gansu plants against sixty-two in Sichuan, with altitude threading through the differences. The study maps a quality case for the Gansu variety.
plos-pone-0348139:
Frances Charlotte Butcher, Patricia Kingori, and Michael Parker sort the moral views hidden inside global health security, the field that handles disease outbreaks crossing borders. Experts disagree about whose safety the field serves. Their 2026 study interviews thirty-eight professionals and groups their views into four models of what the work is really for.

One model treats outbreaks as threats to stop, another as shared risks to manage together. A third tries to reframe the field's terms entirely, and a fourth puts relief of suffering first. Naming the models gives negotiators a map of why talks stall: partners often argue from different moral maps without knowing it. Clearer terms could make outbreak agreements faster and fairer.
plos-pone-0348239:
Yunbo Gao and co-workers build a forecasting method for rail freight volumes that admits uncertainty instead of hiding it. Freight data are fuzzy and nonlinear, and point forecasts often miss badly. Their 2026 study first compresses nine years of monthly records from a Chinese freight center into low, central, and high fuzzy bands, then trains a tuned support vector model on each band.

The hybrid method posted the smallest errors of the models compared, for every band. It also drew the narrowest honest forecast interval around future volumes. An improved swarm search kept the training from settling too early on weak settings. Rail planners gain not just a number but a believable range for staffing, wagons, and warehouse space.
plos-pone-0348339:
Rangsima Lolekha and a Thai team followed 149 young adults born with HIV, cared for at two Bangkok hospitals. They wanted to see how schooling and working lives turned out in the treatment era. Their 2026 report draws on a youth development program the participants joined as teenagers. Annual follow-up ran for five more years, into 2020.

The picture is largely encouraging. Nearly all stayed on antiretroviral therapy. Most had healthy immune counts and suppressed virus. More than eight in ten finished at least secondary school, and three quarters were employed. Marriage and frequent drinking predicted skipping university. Having no disability and attending individual program sessions predicted pursuing it. The cohort shows perinatal HIV is now a condition people build adult lives around.
plos-pone-0348439:
Koki Tsuda and colleagues cast a wide net over lifestyle and thinking skills in healthy Japanese adults aged forty and above. Their dataset held roughly eighteen hundred measurements per person, from body composition to daily habits, alongside a standardised cognitive test battery. Seven hundred ten participants fed the 2026 exploratory analysis, which used strict corrections to avoid false alarms among so many comparisons.

Twenty-eight factors passed the filter. Walking pattern, blood vessel function, grip strength, and oral health stood out, while ordinary blood markers did not. The authors stress these are candidates, not conclusions: the snapshot design cannot show cause, and long-term studies must check whether these factors truly track mental sharpness.
plos-pone-0349239:
Cirque Gammelin and Daniel Schindler reconstructed sixty years of habitat conditions for young sockeye salmon in Alaska's remote Chignik Lakes watershed. The local salmon fishery collapsed in 2018, and the team asked whether the nursery lakes themselves had deteriorated. Different parts of the watershed change on their own clocks, which can mask or mimic decline.

Overall rearing capacity had not fallen. A shallow lake grew warmer over the decades while a deep lake stayed stable, the deep lake's plankton food supply actually improved, and young fish production shifted between habitats. Variability, not collapse, was the story. For managers, the result redirects the search for the fishery crash away from the nursery habitat and toward other stages of the salmon's life.
plos-pone-0349339:
Marek Weis and Wojciech Dawid trained a machine learning model to pick good locations for bike-sharing stations, a planning problem with many tangled factors. The model learned from land cover and population data around existing successful stations, comparing several learning methods including neural networks. It reached very high accuracy in identifying suitable spots.

Predicted stations matched the real network's logic and suggested sensible expansion points, clustered near big intersections and transit stops. As a harder test, the model was turned loose on Rzeszów, a Polish city with no bike system yet, and proposed a coherent starter network. Cities weighing a launch could use such a model to argue site choices with evidence instead of hunches.
plos-pone-0349439:
Khalid Awad Al-Kubaisi and colleagues asked drug shop staff across Jordan what they know about gene-based drug choice, and how ready their shops are to use it. A person's genes change how drugs work in the body, so gene tests can make drug choice safer. The poll reached staff in all three parts of the land and scored their know-how next to world rules.

It also scored their views, their sense of what blocks the change, and how set their shops are in staff, funds, and gear. Most people in Jordan get their drugs from shops like these, so shop readiness will decide if gene-based choice stays a hospital extra or turns into day-to-day care. Each gap needs its own fix: more training, more trust, or more funds.
plos-pone-0349939:
André Hajek and Hans-Helmut König surveyed adults in Germany in early 2026 about wearable health devices. More than a third already used one, and the authors also asked non users what might persuade them to start.

Smartwatches dominated use, with fitness bands a distant second and rings, glasses, and smart clothing rare. Among non users, future medical need was the top reason that would move them, followed by lower prices and interest in watching their own health. Age, income, and health shaped answers in the modelling. The results help firms and health services time their offers to life events.
plos-pone-0350039:
Prachi Singh and colleagues ran a small pilot trial of an herbal drink for insomnia, testing it against a placebo in a crossover design. Ten healthy adults over fifty with significant insomnia drank either the supplement, built on chicory and green tea extracts, or a dummy drink for a week, then switched after a two-week break. Sleep was measured by questionnaires, wrist movement tracking, and one lab sleep study.

Herbal sleep aids are popular but rarely put through blinded trials, so even ten participants add real evidence. Subjective sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue were tracked alongside the objective recordings. Pilot results of this kind cannot prove a supplement works; they show whether a larger, definitive trial is worth running and how it should be designed.
plos-pone-0350639:
Caifang Qiu, Hui Wang, and Ran Liu compared dance students with other women students in China in 2026, looking at body makeup and gut microbes. Dance training shapes bodies intensely, and whether it also shapes the gut community was unknown.

Seventy students, half from dance majors, gave body scans and stool samples for gene based microbe profiling. Dance students carried less fat by many measures and more favourable muscle and water ratios, while gut communities differed across several microbe groups. Some microbes tracked fat and muscle in opposite directions. The links are correlations, but they sketch how training, body, and gut travel together.
plos-pone-0350739:
Young basketball players need both raw strength and springy power, and a simple ratio can show which one lags. Casado-Martínez P and colleagues built a four-week in-season training plan around that ratio for twenty-one players averaging about sixteen years old, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Players were grouped by their starting ratio and given different emphases: heavy strength work, a mix, or jumping drills. Everyone trained three times a week beside normal practice. Jump height, squat force, and estimated lifting maximum were measured before and after. The strongest-looking group gained notably in squat force, showing short tailored blocks can shift muscle profiles mid-season.
plos-pone-0350839:
