Maja Hemberg and colleagues tested a key defence protein against flu in human airway tissue grown in the lab in 2026. The protein, MAVS, relays alarms from virus sensors inside cells, and animal work suggested it was vital, but human airway proof was missing.

Using gene editing, the team removed MAVS from primary airway cultures grown at an air surface. Infected with flu, the edited tissue made far less of the main antiviral signals and let the virus grow more freely. The result confirms MAVS as a non backup part of human airway defence, a fact that matters for judging risk in people born with faults in this pathway.
plos-pone-0350939:
Rasmi Abu-Helu and colleagues at a Jerusalem hospital compared two ways of finding bacteria in urine and spinal fluid samples. Standard lab culture is slow and can miss germs that grow poorly or are present in tiny amounts. Alongside culture, the team ran a sequencing test that reads a shared bacterial gene to name what is present.

In urine, both methods found common infection germs such as E. coli. Sequencing also picked up several kinds of bacteria in samples that culture had called negative or unimportant, and it did the same for spinal fluid, where missing an infection can be deadly. The authors conclude that sequencing catches more of what is really in a sample than culture alone.
plos-pone-0351139:
Curi-Quinto and colleagues set a cutoff for insulin resistance in Peruvian teenagers in a 2026 study. A common index based on fasting sugar and insulin lacks agreed cutoffs for teens, and values differ by population. Records for more than three hundred seventy teens from a long-running study supplied the data.

The team found the index value that best matched metabolic syndrome signs. They also weighed habits and body measures that families can change, plus early-life weight and family history. A local cutoff helps school and clinic screening flag risk earlier in this population. Borrowing cutoffs from other countries could mislabel many Peruvian teens.
plos-pone-0351439:
Sai and Aleithan improved a promising solar cell type with a two-part surface treatment in a 2026 study. Perovskite cells are cheap to make but lose power through surface defects. A blend of two protective salts formed a thin layered skin where the light-absorbing film meets the next layer.

Treated cells reached notably higher voltage and efficiency than single-salt versions. The skin was smoother and shed water better, which shields the fragile film. Cells also lasted longer under humid air and steady light. Dual surface care like this pushes perovskite cells closer to rooftops, where durability has lagged behind their strong lab efficiency.
plos-pone-0351539:
Shaoxing Chen and colleagues tracked cancers that affect women in China from 1990 to 2023 using a world disease burden database. Breast, cervix, womb, and ovarian cancers were counted for new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost. Trend tools split change into ageing, population growth, and true risk shifts, with forecasts for the next fifteen years.

Adjusted rates fell for most of these cancers, a sign of better control. Breast cancer was the exception, with its adjusted rate rising and new cases nearing three hundred and forty three thousand in 2023. Total counts rose for all four cancers as China aged and grew. Planning must hold both truths: rates can fall while clinics still face many more patients.
plos-pone-0351639:
Zhang analyzed persuasion in a Chinese government short-video account in a 2026 study. The account, promoting a province on a popular video app, supplied three hundred sixty top-liked videos from one year plus their public comments. Texts were mined for word patterns and feelings, then read closely for rhetorical appeals.

Emotional appeal led, filling posts with family warmth, collective pride, and urgency. Appeals to credibility came second, built through official voice and achievement claims. Reasoned argument played a smaller role. Knowing which appeals dominate helps explain what audiences reward with likes, and how official accounts tune messages to local pride.
plos-pone-0351739:
After leg amputation, many people feel pain in the missing limb, and Sneha Vidyasagar and colleagues reviewed whether the hormone calcitonin, given as an add-on drug, eases it. Their 2026 PLOS One paper looked back at thirty-five patients treated for at least three days between 2017 and 2023.

Patients rated pain strength, distress, and how much pain blocked activity before and after treatment. All three ratings improved, and patients reported feeling meaningful relief. The pattern held for people with and without diabetes, whose foot problems caused many of the amputations. As a backward-looking review without a comparison group, the study can only suggest promise.
plos-pone-0351839:
Marika Mariano and colleagues tested whether a virtual body that copies your movements makes you feel, deep down, that you caused what happens in virtual reality. Seventy adults switched on a virtual light bulb with real or guided hand movements while wearing a headset. The team measured agency two ways: what people said, and a timing illusion, intentional binding, that betrays felt control without asking.

People always claimed more control when they moved actively, whether or not the avatar mirrored them. The timing illusion appeared only when the avatar's hands moved in sync with the real hands, and only at the shortest delay. So a responsive avatar feeds the gut sense of acting, not the spoken one. Designers of rehab in virtual reality, where patients must feel ownership of movement, should note the split.
plos-pone-0351939:
Siviero and colleagues examined bite marks on dinosaur bones from Wyoming in a 2026 study. The bones came from a crowded burial site holding the plant-eating dinosaur Edmontosaurus, in rock from near the end of the age of dinosaurs. Marks on fossil bone are often called tooth traces, even when other causes fit better.

Out of more than three thousand bones checked, only twelve held marks the team could link to teeth. Fine grooves in two kinds of traces matched the tooth edges of Tyrannosaurus rex found at the same site. One set of holes turned out to have a different cause, which shows why close context checks matter.
plos-pone-0352239:
Nicholas G Mellor and colleagues coaxed brain cancer cells taken directly from patients to grow in neat grid patterns. The cells sat on a coated silicon surface. Their 2026 laboratory study used the mesenchymal form of glioblastoma. This is the most common and deadly adult brain tumor. The team fine-tuned pattern size, cell density, and growth conditions. Five scoring measures of their own design guided the tuning.

Two patient cell lines patterned with high fidelity. The arranged cells still behaved like living tumor cells. They flashed calcium signals when stimulated. Patterned networks matter because glioblastoma cells communicate through calcium waves as they invade. A tidy, repeatable grid lets researchers watch that signaling cell by cell. The platform is a first step toward testing drugs that might jam the tumor's internal conversations.
plos-pone-0352339:
Mohammad Alipour-Vaezi and colleagues used a huge United States health records network to ask which comes first in people with back, neck, and spine pain: mental illness or fading cognition. The two often arrive together in older pain patients, and each could feed the other. Matched groups were followed for three years in each direction to test both paths.

Both directions held. Pain patients with mental health conditions faced a higher risk of later cognitive impairment, steepest for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, with depression, anxiety, and other conditions also raising risk. Patients with earlier cognitive problems likewise faced higher risk of new mental illness, again led by bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. The authors recommend joined-up screening in pain clinics, since catching one side early may be the best chance to slow the other.
plos-pone-0352439:
Cao and colleagues, in a 2026 study, improve concrete made from recycled rubble so it can resist the salt attack that rusts steel inside bridges and sea walls. Recycled lumps carry old paste and cracks, weakening the mix. A baked mineral additive was tested as the fix, at several doses and several rubble replacement rates.

Strength and salt resistance both rose with the right pairings. One mix gained about a tenth in strength over the plain reference, and another cut salt passage by about a fifth, reaching a low permeability grade. Under the microscope, the additive and rubble together grew denser gel, filled pores, and delayed cracking, so failed samples showed no through-cracks. A scoring model that blends two weighting schemes then ranked the mixes fairly. The authors say recycled concrete, long the weaker cousin, can be engineered up to demanding jobs.
plos-pone-0352639:
Nima Rezvani Kakhki and five co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of melanoma cell chemistry. They compare melanoma lines that spread aggressively with one that spreads little. Normal skin-support cells serve as a baseline. The team profiled the cells' small molecules with nuclear magnetic resonance. They hunted for chemical signatures tied to spreading ability. Melanoma's deadliness comes mainly from spread.

Melanoma cells differed from normal cells across several energy and amino acid pathways. They stockpiled energy carriers and the antioxidant glutathione. They held less glucose and glutamine. The highly spreading line leaned further into antioxidant defense and altered amino acid use. It had more glutathione and glutamate, but less of a key energy cofactor. The authors read this as a shift toward resisting oxidative stress. That shift may help traveling tumor cells survive.
plos-pone-0353139:
Christina Artemenko and Mine Avcil test in 2026 a long held claim that brain activity for mental arithmetic shifts from front to back areas as children grow into adults. Their registered report measured brain activity with light based sensors in children, younger adults, and older adults doing two digit sums with carrying or borrowing steps.

Harder sums raised activity across the front and back network in every age group. Behaviour signs of struggle eased with age, yet the brain pattern stayed broadly stable, and back area activity did not rise as front activity fell. The claimed shift may hold only for single digit sums, the authors conclude.
plos-pone-0353739:
Hassan Ugail and Newton Howard introduce a free software toolkit for checking whether quantum machine-learning circuits keep the symmetries they promise, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Such circuits are usually graded on expressiveness or entanglement, but those scores never ask whether the circuit actually respects the symmetry built into its design. Their toolkit audits a circuit before training, reporting how it spreads across symmetry sectors and whether it stays coherent between them.

Tested on five circuit families with repeated random trials, the tool caught circuits whose symmetry machinery was silently inactive and separated designs that standard measures judged identical. Catching such faults before expensive training could save quantum researchers substantial wasted computing time.
plos-pone-0353839:
Debora Hashiguchi, Ana Luiza Dias, and Rodrigo Neves Romcy-Pereira study stress responses in young rats used to model autism, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The rats were exposed before birth to valproic acid, a treatment known to produce autism-like traits. The team measured bodily and behavioural stress signs — freezing, vocal calls, and defecation — during handling, mild electric touch, fear learning, and watching another rat in distress.

Exposed rats showed stronger and longer-lasting stress reactions across nearly every test. Their fear responses also fell out of their usual timing with bodily reactions, and distress at a companion's suffering lingered. The authors argue the model captures the stress vulnerability that often accompanies autism, making it useful for testing calming treatments.
plos-pone-0353939:
Dogbla and colleagues, in a 2026 study, count how many French workers leave occupational health visits with limits on their work, or ruled unfit altogether. Such verdicts shape lives and labor supply, yet they are rarely counted together on a large scale. The team analyzed more than seventy thousand visits in one department over two years.

About nine in ten workers were passed fully fit. A small share received temporary limits, a slightly larger share permanent limits, and about one in seventy-five was ruled unfit. Age over fifty-five roughly doubled the risk of both kinds of limits, and having a disability raised it similarly. Longer service and mid-sized companies also raised risk. Unfitness, by contrast, grew less likely the longer a worker had been with the company. The authors give employers and doctors a rare population picture of work capacity decisions.
plos-pone-0354139:
Msilikale Walter Manyiri led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of child brain development in Bagamoyo, Tanzania. Nearly six hundred children from six months to ten years old took age-appropriate development tests, and family wealth was scored from household assets. The team compared scores across wealth groups at each age band.

Rich and poor children started out alike, then a gap opened around age two and widened into a substantial preschool and school-age disadvantage for the poorest. Manyiri suggests programs aimed at the preschool years could blunt the divide.
plos-pone-0354239:
Canfield and Miller present a 2026 protocol for a trial that layers two early-childhood programs into regular pediatric visits for low-income families. Poverty in the first years of life is linked to lasting gaps in health and learning. Both programs coach warm, steady bonds between parents and babies; one adds a focus on play and reading talk.

About three hundred fifty parent and child pairs will be assigned at random to the combined program or the standard one alone. Support comes at each checkup from birth to age two, with measures at the start and at one and two years. Main outcomes are the parent-child bond, how much parents stimulate learning, and the child's social and emotional growth. A small early phase tests how well clinics can deliver the combined model.
plos-pone-0354339:
Quitterie Lostie de Kerhor leads a 2026 PLOS ONE audit of antibiotic choices in severe lung infection at a French intensive care unit. Severe community-acquired pneumonia, caught outside hospital, needs fast antibiotic treatment. Whether a narrower or broader drug should be first choice is debated.

Reviewing one hundred and four patients with confirmed target bacteria, the team found the narrower drug, amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, would have covered most cases. The broader third-generation drugs were chosen in a fifth of cases, and that choice was unjustified in most of them. Narrowing treatment later happened in only about a quarter of cases. Broader drugs seem overused, the authors say, pending wider confirmation.
plos-pone-0355339:
Wenyan Zhu, Xiaowei Wu, and Rongkui Hu published this 2026 genetics study of gestational diabetes, the blood sugar disorder that appears in pregnancy. Standard gene studies blend all tissues together, hiding which cells matter. Merging Finnish genome data with gene activity data from a dozen immune cell types, they searched for genes whose activity ties to the disease in specific cells.

Fourteen genes surfaced, strongest in helper T cells and monocytes, and several help present foreign material to the immune system. Whole-blood analysis found almost none of them. Zhu argues cell-level views reveal biology that bulk studies miss.
plos-pone-0355739:
Nabila Masud and co-authors blasted lab-grown brain precursor cells with shockwaves to model blast brain injury. Explosions can injure the brain without any blow to the head, and the cell-level mechanics stay poorly mapped. Their 2026 study applied single and double shockwaves from two directions and probed the cells with atomic force microscopy and staining.

Double shockwaves travelling one way softened the cells, roughened their surfaces, and tore up their internal scaffolding. The same double dose from the opposite direction cut the numbers of support-cell offspring and young neurons instead. Direction, not just dose, changed the damage pattern. Masud and colleagues argue injury models must account for wave direction when judging harm.
plos-pone-0355839:
Jessica Trico and colleagues track what happens across the whole balance system after one inner ear is chemically destroyed in rats. Balance loss is common in people, yet the brain and the surviving ear's joint response is poorly mapped. Over a month, the team measured posture and behavior, hearing, immune-style cell reactions in the brain's balance center, and the tiny sensory endings in both ears.

Posture problems began at once, while restlessness and anxiety-like behavior appeared later and lasted. Alarm cells in the balance center surged early, with one cell type staying raised all month. Sensory endings vanished on the treated side, dipped briefly on the untouched side, then recovered there, while hearing damage stayed one-sided. Trico and colleagues say recovery is a whole-system negotiation, not just brain compensation.
plos-pone-0355939:
Zainab Shirazi and co-authors used detailed three-dimensional scans to check a fine point of root canal work. How precisely do modern motors stop at the right depth inside a tooth? Their 2026 laboratory study shaped sixty extracted single-root teeth. Two motors with built-in length sensors were compared against a standalone sensor used before shaping. The team then measured the gap between the finished canal and its natural narrow point.

No motor drilled past the canal's end. All three approaches landed within the accepted tolerance about equally often. Still, the standalone sensor's canals ended closest to the ideal point. Both motor groups finished similarly to each other. For dentists, the message is reassuring but nuanced. Built-in sensors are safe, though a separate measurement may hold the endpoint slightly truer.
plos-pone-0356139: He and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on reading stock market reactions with large models. They paired large language or AI models with time series forecasting tools. The aim was to judge how markets respond to news or events. Blending text-savvy models with price history may sharpen market analysis, a task where timing and tone both move money.
plos-pone-0356239:
Amjad Bani Hani and seven colleagues compare two ways of counting antibiotic use in a Jordanian hospital's intensive care units, in this 2026 study. Stewardship programs track antibiotics to fight resistance, but the standard measures can disagree. One counts standardized daily doses set by the World Health Organization; the other simply counts each day a patient receives a drug. The team pulled a year of records for just over six hundred ICU patients who received antimicrobials.

The two measures tracked each other closely overall, yet differed meaningfully for individual drugs. Counting treatment days, the authors argue, gives clinicians a clearer picture of how long patients are actually exposed in intensive care, where doses are often adjusted. Standardized doses remain better for comparing hospitals. Their conclusion is that the measures complement each other and should not be treated as interchangeable.
plos-pone-0356539:
Christopher Whelpley and three others test whether standard hiring tools treat autistic applicants fairly, in this 2026 study. Interviews are known to disadvantage autistic candidates, so employers often turn to tests as the objective alternative. The researchers gave autistic and neurotypical adults three widely used selection tools, covering general mental ability, personality, and situational judgment, situations in which applicants choose what they would do at work.

All three tools produced real score gaps against autistic adults. That gap persisted even with ability held equal, personality, age, and gender. The authors caution this is early work, but the pattern suggests that tests billed as neutral can carry the same adverse impact as interviews. They call for hiring methods built to capture job-relevant strengths in neurodiverse applicants rather than quietly screening them out.
plos-pone-0356739:
Jaqueline S Angelo and colleagues added a smart alert layer to SISS-Geo, Brazil's free wildlife health reporting platform. The platform has collected georeferenced reports from professionals and the public since 2014. Their 2026 paper introduces the Z-Alert index. Reports are first grouped into clusters in space and time. Each cluster is then scored on weighted factors. These include the share of dead animals, the time span, and the geographic spread.

Weights were tuned by optimization, and managers can adjust the thresholds that trigger action. The team validated the system against historical Brazilian yellow fever data from the health ministry. That is a fitting test, since the disease spills from wildlife to people. Sharper alerts help surveillance teams spend scarce investigation budgets where an outbreak is likeliest.
plos-pone-0358039:
Zhiyue Xu and partners published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on whether stomach infection with Helicobacter pylori goes with high uric acid, a condition tied to gout. The bacterium has been linked to metabolic troubles beyond the stomach, but earlier studies were small and often ignored body weight and kidney function. Drawing on a huge health examination database of close to sixty-eight thousand adults, they adjusted step by step for metabolic, kidney, and inflammation factors.

At first glance the link looked clear: infected people had more high uric acid. But each adjustment layer shrank it, until in the fullest model the association was tiny and statistically uncertain. A very small rise in uric acid levels remained, and patterns held for men and women separately. Most of the apparent connection, they conclude, reflects the company infection keeps, body size and metabolic health, rather than a strong effect of the bacterium.
plos-pone-0358239:
Quynh Hoa Truong and Xuan Khanh Truong show that a nanoparticle's surface floppiness can flip how cells respond to its charge, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Charge is the usual dial for predicting whether immune cells swallow a nanocarrier. The authors instead measured the diversity of shapes the particle's surface ligands can adopt, an information based score. They scored one hundred five gold nanoparticles from a benchmark dataset. Then they watched the charge rule break at a threshold.

Below the threshold, more positive charge meant more uptake, as textbooks say. Above it, the relationship reversed: charge predicted less uptake, consistent with floppy ligands shielding the surface. Adding the entropy score improved prediction across several model types, with the gains concentrated in the floppy regime. A second dataset of over six hundred mixed particles supported the pattern. Drug designers gain a descriptor that tells them when their dial stops working.
plos-pone-0358439:
Bhavana Rhythm and three colleagues translate and validate a listening effort questionnaire for Kannada speakers with hearing loss, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Extended Effort Assessment Scale measures how hard people must strain to follow speech, a burden hearing tests miss. No checked version existed for Kannada, a major language of southern India. The team translated the scale both ways, reviewed it with experts, and tested it on one hundred native speaking adults.

Nine of the ten items behaved well in statistical checks; the telephone item misfitted, likely because phone listening mixes several demands at once. Overall consistency and repeat reliability were excellent, and scores tracked a simple effort rating scale as expected. Two items behaved differently by age or gender, so the authors advise care comparing those across groups. Clinicians now have a tested Kannada tool for a complaint patients voice often.
plos-pone-0358539:
Matthieu Lebrat leads a team of six measuring what happens to prescriptions when a hospital's specialists review them together, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Multi professional medication reviews bring doctors, pharmacists, and nurses around one table to prune drug lists, and psychiatry, where patients often carry heavy sedative loads, had little evidence. The French university hospital study compared stays before and after reviews began across four psychiatric wards, spanning 2017 to 2023.

After reviews started, patients left hospital with about one fewer prescribed drug on average, a small but statistically firm shift. The cuts concentrated where they matter most: psychotropic medicines fell furthest, led by benzodiazepines, with antipsychotics and anticholinergic drugs also down, and even laxatives, often prescribed to counter drug side effects, declined. No drug class rose to compensate. The authors read the pattern as reviews doing quiet, compounding good in a high risk prescribing environment.
plos-pone-0358739: Mumtaz and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how two small RNA molecules tune a gene that drives blood vessel growth. The gene, ERG, is a transcription factor for vessel lining cells. The two regulators are named miR-6756 and miR-3190. Knowing which small RNAs dial a vessel gene up or down can guide work on diseases where vessel growth helps or harms.
plos-pone-0358839:
Manal Nhili leads a team of eight measuring how fast a devastating goat disease spreads through a herd, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Peste des petits ruminants sweeps through goats and sheep in much of Africa and Asia, and control plans need hard numbers on transmission. The researchers infected goats experimentally while ultra wideband collars logged the distance between every pair of animals minute by minute, alongside clinical and virus checks.

Density proved decisive. At low density a healthy goat needed nearly two days of exposure near sick animals to catch the virus; packed tightly, four hours sufficed. Each infectious goat was estimated to infect roughly four to nine others, depending on how long it stayed contagious, and incubation ran about two weeks. Crowded livestock markets stand out as danger points where brief mixing can seed outbreaks across regions.
plos-pone-0359339: Sun and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on turning Chinese Braille documents into text. Their decoding method is aware of uncertainty, so it can weigh doubtful readings instead of forcing a guess. The structure of the document guides those choices. Better transcription opens printed material to blind readers and helps digitize Braille archives that now sit unscanned.
plos-pone-0359439:
Yuanyuan Tang and colleagues examined in 2026 how changing land use has reshaped the movement of carbon through soils in northern China. Soil holds enormous amounts of carbon, and converting land between farming, grassland, and forest changes how much carbon the soil stores or releases. The study focuses on that region's soil carbon dynamics under such changes.

Tang and co-authors trace how the shifts in land use altered carbon inputs, storage, and loss over time. Their subject sits at the crossing of farming practice and climate policy, since soil carbon is one of the largest levers in the land carbon budget. Findings of this kind inform decisions about which land conversions help climate goals and which quietly undo them.
plos-pone-0359639:
Masawa Nyamuryekung'e, Kokila Lakhoo, and Salome Maswime published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It sets out a study protocol, in several phases with mixed methods, assessing whether Tanzania's health system can care for babies born with major structural defects. The tracer condition is anorectal malformations, birth defects of the bowel opening that need early surgery.

A tracer condition stands in for a wider service: if the system handles this defect well, it likely handles similar newborn surgery too. Assessing surgeons, equipment, and referral paths shows where children born with defects lose their chance of timely care. Tanzanian health planners and children's surgery teams are the audience.
pmc-13174139:
Jamie C Thuan is first author on a 2026 chemistry study of making a cyclic dehydroalanine peptide at larger scale. Dehydroalanine is an unusual amino acid building block that readily accepts other molecules, making it valuable for attaching labels to proteins and for building new compounds. Scalable, repeatable synthesis was an unmet need.

The team optimized a joining reaction between a cyclic glycine dimer and a formaldehyde source, run through an acyl transfer mechanism, meaning a group swap inside the molecule. Grinding the mixture with a little liquid, called liquid-assisted mechanochemistry, proved important for efficiency and repeatability. The work targets preparative amounts rather than the small scales of earlier studies.
pmc-13192239: Gopal Agarwal and co-authors published a correction notice in 2026. The review compares four delivery routes: viral carriers, RNA in fat particles, non-viral DNA, and gene-writing tools. Each route trades off on targeting, lasting effect, repeat dosing, and safety. pmc-13198639:

Over six months, eleven percent had a related emergency visit. Patients whose thoughts resolved trended toward fewer visits, though the gap was not firm proof. Splitting by early change also trended the same way. Larger studies must confirm the hint.
pmc-13202139:
Teenage girls in poor city neighborhoods often eat narrow diets, and a 2026 study headed by Fahmida Dil Farzana tests whether education sessions plus supplements can widen them. Nutrition knowledge and hemoglobin levels improved significantly in the intervention group compared with the comparison group. Dietary diversity itself did not change, and parents told researchers that rising food prices limited what they could buy.
pmc-13202639:
Breathlessness has many causes that are slow to separate, and a 2026 proof-of-concept study by Daniel M Neville tests whether the shape of exhaled carbon dioxide can help. One angle measure tracked moderately with lung function in asthma and with heart pumping strength in heart failure patients. pmc-13203939:

Her history already included prolapse found after a youthful faint, heart MRI signs of scarring, and frequent abnormal beats on earlier monitoring. pmc-13209139: A retraction notice issued in 2026 withdraws a 2021 OncoTargets and Therapy article claiming the citrus compound bergamottin damages DNA and slows melanoma through a microRNA pathway. A third party raised data honesty concerns in 2026, and the journal's probe found unexpected matches across staining images, flow cytometry plots, and Western blots meant to show separate samples. The authors checked their data, found basic errors, and themselves asked for the retraction with an apology. Only the retraction notice itself survives here.
pmc-13210239:
Swallowed vaccines keep failing because the gut is built to tolerate, and a 2026 essay led by Avan Antia argues makers should start from that obstacle. The article rethinks oral vaccine growth around gut immune science itself, rather than blaming delivery platforms for weak gut uptake.

Prior infections and resident microbes further tune the local immune tone that any vaccine must overcome on arrival. By studying how real pathogens naturally defeat these defenses, the authors propose design rules for the next wave of mucosal vaccines.
pmc-13238239:
Zhou and colleagues vaccinate mice against toxoplasmosis using DNA that codes for two parasite proteins. The two target proteins, TgGRA47 and TgGRA72, are shed by the parasite inside its host cell and help shape its survival there.

The team gave BALB/c mice DNA vaccines carrying each protein's gene, then challenged them with the parasite. They measured immune responses and survival to judge protection. pmc-13240639:
Huang and co-workers at Jilin University tested Nintendo Switch exergaming as support for adults with subthreshold depression. Half played active games two or three times weekly for eight weeks.

The gaming group did better on depressive symptoms at every follow-up through week sixteen. Sleep quality also got much better, and anxiety eased at several points. Interviews with seventeen players told of immersion and habits that helped them stick with it. No adverse events took place, and the authors pitch commercial exergames as accessible early support.
pmc-13242339:

Effort was rated against three anchors: the same task's max, another task's max, or a personal lifetime max. Sessions rotated the three anchors in mixed order.

Task-matched anchors kept producing the highest ratings; self-set anchors the lowest. Gaps widened near maximal force, at eighty to one hundred percent effort. Rankings survived every anchor tested, keeping rough scale match. The team urges clear anchor rules in training research and coaching practice.
pmc-13242439:
Sakine Yılmaz and colleagues examined how stressful gender expectations relate to mental distress in women treated for breast cancer in Türkiye. Their study appeared in Supportive Care in Cancer in 2026. It surveyed 264 women who attended a state hospital's surgical oncology clinic after mastectomy. Because the breast is tied to feminine identity and body image, the team expected the stress of gender expectations to weigh on mental health after surgery.

Both gender role stress and distress ran high in this group. Women with university degrees, those in nuclear families, and those whose husbands held degrees reported especially high levels of both. Surprisingly, gender role stress itself was not significantly linked to distress in the analysis. The authors still urge nurses to assess both together, along with coping strategies, when caring for women after mastectomy. The findings show distress after this surgery has social roots, not only medical ones.
pmc-13244139:
Tristan Burgess and co-authors report a case where bedside ultrasound sped the diagnosis of an ischemic finger. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. A finger starved of blood can come from clots on either side of the circulation, and the cause decides the cure. Point-of-care ultrasound let the team check arteries and veins directly at the bedside, without waiting for formal imaging, and to map how far the blockage reached.

The workup landed on a rare double diagnosis. The patient carried two clotting disorders at once: polycythemia vera, a blood cancer that thickens the blood with extra red cells, and antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune clotting condition. Each alone can explain a blocked digit; together they compounded the danger. The authors remind clinicians to keep both on the checklist for limb ischemia. Rare pairs do occur, and missing one leaves half the problem untreated.
pmc-13245839:
León-Herrera and co-authors reviewed digital health tools for the mental and thinking problems of long COVID, in this 2026 scoping review. The reviewers searched four databases for studies of app-based and online programs aimed at these symptoms.

From nearly nine hundred records, only twenty-five studies qualified, most testing multi-part programs that combined exercises such as cognitive training, therapy, and symptom tracking. Results pointed to promise, especially for combined programs, but the evidence stayed preliminary, with few strong trials. The authors call for randomized studies, standard outcome measures, and attention to digital access.
pmc-13247039:
Gandjour evaluated Germany's drug stockpiling law in this 2026 Scientific Reports health-economics study. A recent legal change made six-month inventory reserves the government's main defense against medicine shortages. Working from the German social health insurance perspective, the author examined a public database of nearly two thousand eight hundred recorded shortages since 2012. The author modeled how many a reserve of a given length could have prevented.

A six-month reserve would have prevented roughly seventy percent of shortages. Each extra month prevented fewer additional shortages, so value for money thinned as stockpiles lengthened, with an estimated cost-effective ceiling near two and a half years under stated assumptions. The author concludes the six-month mandate is very likely cost-effective, while flagging warehouse practices as a key uncertainty.
pmc-13248739:
Nguyen and co-authors describe a rare surgical emergency in this 2026 case report. A sixty-two-year-old woman was having an infected keloid scar removed when she began bleeding uncontrollably during the operation. Tests confirmed disseminated intravascular coagulation, a dangerous state where clotting runs wild and then leaves the blood unable to clot.

Her preoperative clotting tests had been normal, though the scar had been inflamed for years. Doctors gave blood products, strong antibiotics, and kidney support, and her clotting recovered within fourteen hours. She recovered fully. The authors warn that chronic infected tissue can, rarely, trigger this crisis mid-surgery, and that fast teamwork saves lives.
pmc-13250839:
Adel Alsharei and a large team report a double gene puzzle in this 2026 case report. A seven-year-old Syrian boy kept breaking bones and had marked facial features pointing to a rare growth disorder called geleophysic dysplasia.

Scans and standard lab tests were mostly normal, though his bone density matched that of a 92-year-old. Gene testing found two altered copies of a gene called LTBP3, tied to this disorder. The team backs gene testing for children with repeated breaks.
pmc-13252039:
Kristianto and colleagues group patients by metabolic and body profiles linked to the ankle-brachial index, a leg blood flow test. Their 2026 Vascular Health and Risk Management study covers more than one thousand people seen at clinics and hospitals around Malang, Indonesia, between 2023 and 2025. Trimming the inputs to seven features sharpened the grouping, with belly fat, resting metabolism, and body mass leading. The authors stress the clusters describe patterns rather than diagnoses or predictions. They suggest the approach could help nurses and clinicians think about leg circulation risk, pending validation.
pmc-13254339:
Mohammed Ali and co-authors solve a wave equation for optical fibers in a 2026 mathematics study. Their model is a high-order stochastic nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which describes how solitons, self-keeping wave pulses, travel in fibers under noise and higher-order effects. They used a wave transformation and a mapping method with symbolic computing.

The method produced many exact solutions, including bright, dark, singular, periodic, and rational soliton types. A stability analysis showed the solutions stay stable under small disturbances. Graphs under varied settings display the dynamics, and the authors say the method handles this equation class reliably.
pmc-13261039:
Julia S Etkin and Vincent Joralemon wrote a 2026 legal analysis of who bears liability when AI chatbots give bad prescribing advice. Chatbots increasingly give patients prescribing-level guidance without a physician involved. The authors discuss the learned intermediary doctrine. That rule has long governed drug makers' duty to warn through doctors. They argue it operates differently in two emerging pathways: AI working behind the clinician, and AI advising patients directly, with no intermediary at all.

They cite studies in which ChatGPT wrongly reported no interaction between Paxlovid and verapamil, a dangerous error, and gave incomplete or wrong answers to nearly three-quarters of drug questions. Surveys show about a fifth of United States adults have used ChatGPT for health information, and nearly a third of those changed medications based on it. The authors warn clinicians may need to screen patients for AI-sourced prescribing advice under ordinary malpractice law.
pmc-13263139:
Francesco Compagnoni and Michele A Riva revisit a nineteenth-century Italian doctor's experiments on sugar and tooth decay in a 2026 historical article. Paolo Mantegazza, a physician and anthropologist, addressed the question in his 1864 hygiene manual, one of Italy's most influential public health books. People had long blamed sugar for rotten teeth, but the mechanism was disputed.

Mantegazza tested whether sugar chemically attacks tooth enamel in the laboratory. He concluded sugar does no direct chemical harm, and that damage instead comes from fermentation, in which microbes break sugar down. That reading anticipated the modern germ-based account of decay by decades. The authors credit his hands-on method and his push to spread science for public health.
pmc-13263339:
Helene Ackermann and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how failure feedback from a robot tutor affects adult learners in real time. Ninety adults aged eighteen to fifty-nine completed a learning task. A humanoid robot gave feedback in three styles: fixed, frequency-adaptive, or personalized to each learner's errors.

Both thinking-focused and planning-focused failure feedback raised the chance of a correct next answer in all three styles. Making feedback frequency-adaptive added no clear benefit. pmc-13263539:
Noah S. Brown and co-authors present a 2026 case report with a literature review on a rare spread of a pancreatic growth into the belly cavity. A 65-year-old woman had a large cyst in the tail of her pancreas, a mucus-producing tumor called an IPMN. She underwent removal of the pancreatic tail and spleen.

During surgery, doctors found two separate deposits of cell-free mucin in her pelvis. That pattern is pseudomyxoma peritonei, a condition where mucin collects in the abdomen, usually from appendix or ovarian tumors. Pancreatic cases are extremely rare, reported only nineteen times before. Both deposits were removed, she recovered well, and the authors recommend expert centers and scan-based follow-up.
pmc-13263639:
Ting Zhao and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a natural compound, D-chiral inositol, in rats modeling polycystic ovary syndrome. This common hormone disorder disrupts ovulation and metabolism. The compound is known to help insulin work better. The team induced the syndrome with letrozole, then treated the rats for four weeks.

The authors describe the compound's effect as multi-target and body-wide rather than limited to a single pathway.
pmc-13263739:
Zelong Tang and colleagues test a plant coumarin as a guard for brain stem cells after stroke-like injury. Their 2026 lab study mimics the hostile zone around a stroke with hydrogen peroxide on mouse cells.

Bergapten fought the oxidative stress and calmed the inflammation in their assays. Guarded stem cells lived on better and chose nerve-cell fates more readily under stress. The authors frame the compound as a hope for mending the stroke-damaged brain's own nursery.
pmc-13264439:

A scope exam found a narrowed, ulcer-like growth in the sigmoid colon, the last part of the large bowel. Lab study showed a poorly formed cancer with signet-ring cells, a harsh type. The cancer had not spread. Surgeons removed the affected part, and the boy recovered well. The authors urge early scope checks for such signs.
pmc-13264939:
Miriyala Gaayathri and co-authors published a 2026 study on improving how trainee emergency doctors document bedside ultrasound scans in a busy Indian emergency department. After the program, 35.1 percent of scans passed the bar and the median score rose to 69 percent. Gains stalled early on workflow snags, then jumped when a single user-designed form and game-like incentives arrived. pmc-13267039:
Ting Wang and colleagues present a 2026 cell study on a gum disease bacterium and liver cancer growth. pmc-13267939:
Maojiang Lyu and colleagues present a 2026 case report on rebuilding a teenager's thigh bone after infection. Their patient was a 14-year-old girl whose right thigh bone broke in a car crash. pmc-13268139:

pmc-13268639:

pmc-13269839:

pmc-13270339:
Li Yuhong and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 presenting a method to measure carbon isotope ratios in airborne volatile organic compounds, gases that help form ozone and particles. Seven compounds were validated, including benzene, toluene, and styrene. Best sampler settings were 300 degrees for five minutes. pmc-13271139:

Lying pressures matched almost exactly between the professional and home devices, with very strong agreement, and sitting agreement was also strong with only small average differences. The authors say trained patients' home readings, in both positions, are reliable for clinical decisions.
pmc-13271439:

From the day before treatment to day seven, average pain intensity fell from 6.41 to 5.24, pain distress fell from 5.85 to 4.81, and reported relief rose. pmc-13272239:

pmc-13273439:

pmc-13273639:

pmc-13273739:

The authors describe growth in online courses and meetings. They also stress support for doctors in low-resource settings. The vision aims to raise standards of blood care worldwide. Education, they argue, is the lever that moves practice.
pmc-13273839:

pmc-13274039:

pmc-13274139:

pmc-13275539:

pmc-13275739:

pmc-13276339:

pmc-13276539:

pmc-13278239:

pmc-13279439:
