pmc-13279739:
Luca Cavagnaro and colleagues report a 2026 study of hip shape after a spacer step in two stage hip revision. Two stage revision is a top route when a hip implant gets infected. Stage one swaps the implant for a joint like spacer. If leg length and offsets, the side reach of the hip joint, stay off, the joint can slip or fail. The team read X rays for how well shape was restored.

Charts covered patients who got one articulating spacer type at one centre from 2020 to 2022. Measures held leg length gap, thigh bone offset, socket offset and global offset. Hip scores by two standard forms were logged as well. The team also checked if offset shifts linked with mechanical side effects between stages. Sound stage one shape may cut slips and ease stage two work.
pmc-13279939:
Enrique B. Hernandez and colleagues report a 2026 greenhouse study of three Brazilian folk medicine plants grown in German soils. Cultivated medicinal plants supply raw drugs, yet acts in non native soils were little known. The three species were Scoparia dulcis, Physalis angulata and Porophyllum ruderale. Two German soils were used: a clay rich silt and a sandy loam. The team weigh plant yield, element profiles and anti swelling strength.

Soil and plant tissue were read for major, minor and rare earth elements by two plasma based lab methods. Crude extracts were tested on human immune cells driven by a bacterial toxin. High detail mass scans profiled the extract chemistry as well. The design shows how soil type can shift both drug plant growth and the mix of elements a patient dose would carry. Such checks matter as folk plants move to new farm lands.
pmc-13280639:
Carlo Foppiano Palacios and colleagues published a 2026 study on yearly testing for sleeping tuberculosis in people with HIV. Sleeping tuberculosis means the germs are in the body but cause no illness yet. The team worked in places where tuberculosis is rare. They tracked test results over five years at two large city health centers.

Of close to nineteen hundred patients tested at least twice, only twelve picked up a new infection. Yearly testing for everyone thus found very few cases. The authors say clinics should test the people most at risk, as current guidelines advise. That approach would save time and cost with little loss in safety.
pmc-13280939:
Syed Saad Ali Chishti and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a belly button lump that fooled doctors. A thirty-seven-year-old woman came in with belly button pain, swelling, and constipation for a week. She had a small, dark, firm lump there that hurt to touch. She also told of pain at the spot that came with her monthly cycle for five months. A sound scan pointed to a trapped hernia, a bulge of tissue through a weak spot.

Emergency surgery found a small hernia with only fat inside and no trapped gut. Beside it sat a firm lump under the skin. Lab checks showed the lump was womb lining tissue growing in the wrong place, a rare form of a common female condition. She healed well and stayed free of pain at four months.
pmc-13281639:
Kimia Bagheri and colleagues reviewed brain drainage systems and migraine in a 2026 paper. Migraine brings severe head pain, and its roots stay unclear. Two drainage webs have drawn fresh interest. One clears waste from the brain through fluid channels, and one lines the skull's cover. If drainage lags, waste may build up and stir pain circuits. The team searched three databases for human and animal studies. Ten of more than four hundred papers fit their rules.

Six human studies used scans, and four used animal models. Scan studies found changed drainage signals in both brief and long-term migraine. A second scan method gave mixed results, with clearer flaws in frequent attacks. In animals, migraine triggers slowed the brain's waste inflow. Fluid outflow through the skull lining also fell. The authors call the proof early but suggestive. They urge larger human studies that track drainage and pain together.
pmc-13282039:
Elad I Stotland and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for a scoping review, a broad mapping of past studies, on a gut parasite in Southeast Asia. The parasite, Cryptosporidium, spreads through water, animals, and food. It causes diarrhoea that hits young children and people with weak immune systems hardest. The review uses a One Health lens, meaning human, animal, and environmental health are treated as linked.

Searches of five databases through September 2024 found eight hundred eighty-nine records. After screening, one hundred seventy-six studies from nine of the eleven countries in the region were kept. The protocol itself reports no new health findings, since it mainly lays out the mapping work. Its value lies in showing where proof is thin, how tests differ, and what joint surveillance across farms, clinics, and water systems might fix.
pmc-13282339:
Alexandre Carvalho Costa and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a maned wolf infected by two urinary parasites at once, a first for the species in the wild. The maned wolf is a threatened South American wild dog that eats fish and frogs, which can carry parasite larvae. One parasite is a giant kidney worm, the other a bladder worm found in wild and domestic dogs and cats.

The adult male wolf arrived at a Brazilian wildlife centre after a train accident in an urban area. Ultrasound showed signs of the kidney worm in and around his right kidney. Urine sediment held eggs of both parasites, measured to confirm each type. The authors stress that simple urine checks can reveal hidden parasites in wild animals. They call for more study of the bladder worm in wild dogs, since knowledge of it remains poor.
pmc-13282439:
Robert M Kaplan and co-authors present a 2026 national survey on what employees want from employer health plans in the United States. Employer insurance covers over sixty percent of Americans under sixty-five and costs employers heavily, yet worker preferences are understudied. The team surveyed one thousand two hundred adults with employer coverage, weighted to match the population, about trade-offs between pay, benefits, and provider network size.

Nearly half preferred keeping the current balance of salary and benefits. Yet about forty-six percent would accept a narrower provider network for higher pay. About thirty-one percent backed narrow networks if savings funded other benefits. Views varied by age, sex, race, parental status, and politics. Three quarters trusted employers to pick plans, and most said savings should return to employees. Many also backed excluding costly providers without proven quality gains.
pmc-13283139:
Red and near-infrared light as a sleep aid is pooled across five trials in a 2026 meta-analysis led by Wellington Marcos Vital de Azevedo. The method uses red or near-infrared light without drugs or surgery. Poor sleep is rising and is tied to brain strain and inflammation.

Five trials with 240 people in total met the review rules. Pooled results showed better sleep quality scores with light therapy than with sham care. The effect size was modest and the range was wide, so precision was low. Brain scans and lab work suggest better cell energy and calmer brain support cells. The authors advise caution and call for larger trials with shared methods and longer follow-up.
pmc-13283439:
Ultrasound textures plus slide patterns forecast node spread in ovarian cancer in Ge Yan's 2026 multicenter model. Spread status guides whether node removal surgery is worthwhile. The model joins ultrasound traits, slide image traits, and clinical facts.

Records covered 157 patients who had node removal with confirmed spread status. Groups split into 91 for training, 38 for internal checks, and 28 for outside tests. Ultrasound features were cut from over a thousand down to 11 key traits. Slide features were cut to a small refined set by learning methods. Combined models beat single-source models on accuracy checks in the study. Surgery planning could use such pre-op risk estimates.
pmc-13284039:
A rare kidney tumor with flipped cell polarity is detailed for a 64-year-old man by Yu Wang and colleagues in 2026. Fewer than one hundred such cases have been reported since its 2019 definition. Clearer case records help pathologists separate it from look-alike tumors.

The mass was found by chance in the left kidney on imaging scans. Heart disease and left leg numbness formed his background history. Surgeons removed part of the kidney, and tissue tests confirmed the diagnosis. Marker tests showed a characteristic positive and negative pattern set. Recovery was excellent, and no further treatment followed surgery. Phone checks and ultrasound over three months stayed reassuring.
pmc-13284439:
Raunak Lohar and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study of implant coatings made from harmless commensal microbes. Medical devices often grow bacterial biofilms that resist drugs and evade immune attack. The team heat-fixed commensal flora onto titanium to form a stable layer, then checked its surface traits and safety with human cells.

The coating did not harm red blood cells, boosted macrophage killing through reactive oxygen species, and cut biofilm growth by a gum pathogen. It also balanced immune signals and raised bone-forming signals in stem cells. In a 3D human model with mixed biofilms, the coating kept tissue cover intact under harmful challenge. The work points to living-inspired coatings that fight biofilm while aiding bone growth.
pmc-13285739:
Shengnan Cui and colleagues examine mucosal involvement in bullous pemphigoid in a retrospective cohort study from 2026 from Beijing. The blistering skin disease rarely touches the mouth and other moist linings, and doctors suspect those cases run a harsher course. The team compared patients with and without such lesions to test that view.

The cohort held 265 patients treated between 2013 and 2022, and 71 of them had mucosal lesions, most often in the mouth. Those patients were younger at onset, needed higher steroid doses, and faced more hospital stays and infections within a year. Lesions on the head, neck, hands, and feet, plus higher disease scores, marked the group in adjusted models. The pattern can help staff spot patients who need closer checks and stronger care.
pmc-13285839:
Ana Carolina Izurieta-Pacheco and colleagues track heart health after spine radiation in child tumor survivors in a 2026 cohort study. Radiation aimed at the brain and spine can scatter a modest dose to the heart, and its late effects stay poorly mapped. The team followed ultrasound measures of pumping strength over years of survivorship.

The cohort held 129 survivors treated between 2000 and 2024, first diagnosed at a median age of eight years. Standard pumping measures slid downward over time, though ejection scores stayed in the normal range for all. Strain measures rose at first, then fell as years passed, and filling measures held steady throughout. Older age at treatment and hormone problems shaped the slide, which argues for heart checks across adult life.
pmc-13285939:
Chiteng Zhou and colleagues build a web tool that flags swallowing trouble in COPD patients in a 2026 model study. Breathing and swallowing share the same airway, so lung disease can let food or drink slip the wrong way. Records from one hospital were used to train smart models that sort patients by risk before harm follows.

The records covered 710 patients admitted across about a year, and close to three in ten had swallowing trouble on a water test. Five traits drove risk most: years of disease, body weight index, past breathing tube use, muscle strength, and breathlessness grade. Among eight models tried, one boosting method sorted patients best and held its accuracy on repeat checks. The team placed the model online as a free calculator, so ward staff can score risk in seconds and act early.
pmc-13286139:
Ahmad Al-Bitar and colleagues survey pornography use among medical students in Syria in a cross-sectional study published in 2026, the first of its kind from that country. Private habits on such a taboo topic stay almost unmapped across the Middle East, even as phones put explicit content within easy reach. An anonymous online form asked students about first contact, current use, quit tries, and felt effects.

The form drew 960 students from medical schools across Syria in late 2024. About three in four reported some contact in their lives, with first contact near age fifteen on average. Higher family income and having a private room each raised the odds of contact, while sex showed no clear link. Half of current users had tried to quit, and most of them reported rough effects after stopping, while early first contact stood as the strongest tie to feeling hooked.
pmc-13287239: Editors of the International Journal of Nanomedicine retracted a 2021 study in 2026. The study used a modified polymer carrier. It delivered gene-silencing material in a rat model of liver scarring. Concerns raised in 2023 led to checks. Those checks found overlapping tissue images shown as different samples. Further problems appeared in blot data and in supplementary figures shared with an earlier article. The authors supplied original data for one figure but could not resolve the other concerns, so the article was withdrawn and will remain online marked as retracted.
pmc-13287839:
Bohdana Doskaliuk and colleagues ran a blinded contest in 2026 asking four large language models to write short social media posts promoting 36 open-access public health articles. One rater, kept unaware of which model wrote what, scored each post on accuracy, clarity, rule following, call to action, and structure.

Every model stayed accurate and broke no rules. Top scores tied between GPT-5 and Perplexity Pro, with Gemini close behind and Grok-3 lower, chiefly for weak calls to action and shorter posts. Reading ease varied by model. The authors say editors can pick a model by audience, since quality is high across the board.
pmc-13288439:
Hanlu He and co-authors tracked 72 people in 2026 across three multi-day group trips to New York City. Heart rate, location, and sound levels were recorded around the clock. The test asked whether hearts fall into step during real social life, not only in labs.

Hearts did sync when people stood close together, even without direct interaction, so shared surroundings alone can drive the effect. Sync ran higher among familiar peers and during shared attention, and faded in scattered contact. Moderate sound levels helped; heavy noise cut sync to loner levels. The authors propose heart sync as a workable sign of social engagement in daily settings.
pmc-13288539:
Mingxuan Xie and colleagues track two blood measures and kidney risk in 2026. Their study holds 7,541 adults. All had three or more yearly health checks. One measure is a ratio of uric acid to good cholesterol. The other is fasting blood sugar.

In all, 558 people got kidney disease. That is 7.40 percent of the group. High ratio levels stayed tied to risk. The sugar link faded after full checks. Four joint paths were found. The high-ratio path faced about four times the risk. That was versus the lowest path. The joint pattern may flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13289139:
Andrea M Patey and colleagues weigh a Canadian program to cut wasteful lab tests in 2026. The program is called Using Labs Wisely. It links hospitals in a learning group. Sites share data and run fix-it projects. The team spoke with staff at cohort hospitals.

Thirteen of fifteen invited hospitals took part. Staff praised the program's national weight. Peer learning and shared tools helped buy-in. Lab teams gained a bigger voice in quality work. Pulling data proved hard for many sites. Staff time was tight, more so in the pandemic. Calls rose for more training and outcome tracking. Harder, pricier tests need joint work, staff said.
pmc-13289339:
Tiemei Li and colleagues present a 2026 biomarker study on blood sugar stages in Tibetan adults on the Qinghai Plateau. High altitude life may shape diabetes risk in distinct ways. The team compared healthy controls with pre-diabetes and diabetes groups to find chemical signs that separate the stages early.

A total of 904 participants gave data on body fat, blood tests, body measures, and 332 metabolites, which are small chemicals in blood. Hundreds of metabolites differed between groups in first checks. Machine learning methods then narrowed the list to a compact set, mixing body measures, fat levels, inflammation, and lipid ratios. Combined panels sorted sugar stages well, offering leads for early screening in plateau clinics.
pmc-13289639:
Yantao Fu and coauthors review a 2026 set of advances aiming to break the ceiling of chemoembolization for liver cancer. That procedure, called TACE, blocks tumor blood flow while delivering chemotherapy and remains standard for middle-stage disease. Low oxygen after blocking sparks new vessel growth and high return rates, capping long-term gains for many patients.

Pairing TACE with targeted drugs, immune therapy, or ablation improves some outcomes, the review finds. New smart blocking materials also turn a passive plug into active tumor environment control by design. Some triple regimens extend time without worsening, yet proof of longer overall survival is still missing in key trials. Mixed study designs urge caution, and team-based selection is proposed.
pmc-13290939:
Long exposure to methylmalonic acid inflames and rewires astrocyte-like cells, Rômulo Almeida and colleagues show in a cell study from 2026. Methylmalonic acidemia is an inherited disorder where this acid builds up in the brain. Patients worsen over time, yet most lab models expose cells only briefly. This study prolonged the exposure in C6 astroglial cells.

Sustained exposure switched on inflammation genes: cyclooxygenase 2, interleukin-1β and its receptor, and IL-6 all rose, while the calming IL-10 fell. Glutamate handling shifted too, with uptake and the enzyme glutamine synthetase up, and the nerve-support factor GDNF down. Stress and energy pathways, among them NFκB, p38 MAPK, and Nrf2, also shifted. Almeida and colleagues say the pattern may explain the lasting glial damage behind the disease's brain symptoms.
pmc-13291039:
Diego Pinheiro and Anabelle Silva Cornachione write a 2026 narrative review on how obesity harms skeletal muscle from the inside, beyond the familiar idea that muscle simply shrinks with age. Fat stored inside muscle, cell power problems, and long-running low-grade inflammation all feature in their account of why strength and metabolism suffer.

Signals shared between fat and muscle tissue, including interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor, can blunt insulin action and raise oxidative stress in muscle fibers. Power-producing structures inside cells also work less well under these conditions. Taken together, the evidence frames muscle as both a victim of obesity and an active player in its metabolic fallout, which opens fresh angles for treatment and prevention research.
pmc-13291139:
Immune maps inside colon tumors are built by Cunen Wu and colleagues in a 2026 study. Colorectal cancer helps only some patients with immunotherapy. Gene patterns that track drug response are needed. Single-cell and spatial data were joined here.

Cells numbered 27,414 from tumor and normal tissue. Natural killer T cell types were mapped in detail. Spatial data showed them beside Th1 helper cells. Tumors rich in these cells fared better. Drug sensitivity also ran higher in such tumors. A gene score was built from both cell types. Nine cohorts tested that score with care. High scores marked distinct tumor traits.
pmc-13291239:
Running a modern power grid grows harder each year. Hanjiang Dong leads a 2026 review on using large model agents in control rooms. Solar, wind, and electric cars make grids fast-changing. Human teams must watch data and act in minutes.

Tailored agents could help track grid state. They could also aid teamwork across grid jobs. Safe rollout needs task-ready data first. Agents must ground answers in true grid knowledge. Checks, staged trials, and close human watch are vital. The review maps a careful path into live use. Done well, agents support operators rather than replace them.
pmc-13292439:
Yu Liu and co-authors uncover a 2026 immune side to Nrf2, the antioxidant master switch, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Radiation resistance plagues this cancer, and the team asked whether Nrf2 also dulls the immune alarm that dying tumor cells should raise. They built mice whose esophageal tumors lack Nrf2, profiled the immune landscape by single-cell sequencing, and ran co-culture tests with dendritic and T cells.

Without Nrf2, tumors lost the antioxidant enzyme GPX2 and grew easier to kill with radiation, spilling classic immunogenic death signals such as ATP, HMGB1, and surface calreticulin. Dendritic cells responded by releasing IP-10, which proved essential for recruiting and firing up CD8 T cells. Living-animal tests confirmed stronger radiation response and deeper T cell infiltration. The authors pitch the Nrf2-GPX2 axis as a way to heat up cold tumors.
pmc-13292639:
Renata Bacila Morais dos Santos de Souza and co-authors feed a 2026 novelty to beagles: protein grown from the fungus Paecilomyces variotii as a single-cell ingredient. Three experiments tested five diets carrying 0 to 16 percent of the protein, a palatability contest between formulas, and a substitution trial to value the ingredient itself. Gut microbes and fermentation products in feces were also tracked.

The fungal protein itself digested reasonably, with crude protein digestibility of 83.9 percent and metabolizable energy of 3843.3 kilocalories per kilogram in the estimates. Still, whole-diet digestibility and energy slid steadily as inclusion rose. Fermentation shifted toward more short-chain and branched-chain fatty acids, and the 4 and 8 percent diets enriched Lactobacillus in feces. The authors conclude moderate inclusion, 4 to 8 percent, buys gut benefits without heavy digestive cost.
pmc-13292939:
Yanfen Zheng and colleagues show, in a 2026 study, that root bacteria called pseudomonads help soybean plants handle salty soil. Salt harms crops worldwide, and roots gather microbes that can either help or hinder growth under stress.

Across many soils and crops, pseudomonads grew more common on roots of salt-stressed plants, and their genes carried salt coping traits such as sodium pumps. Strains taken from stressed plants settled on soybean roots and improved growth in greenhouse and field tests. Benefit ran through stronger lignin building in the plant, not through sodium balance. Plants unable to make lignin lost the benefit entirely.
pmc-13293439:
Bora Lee, Soojin Im, and Sungho Won refine, in a 2026 study, how body weight, smoking, and blood fats are measured when judging death risk. Loose definitions can mislead large health studies, so sharper measures may change who looks at risk.

Two Korean cohorts were used, one with 659,494 people and a second with 10,477 for outside checks, both tied to death records. Being underweight raised death risk in all age groups, above all when paired with belly obesity in younger adults. Heavy smoking load relative to age also raised risk, as did one or more risky fat ratios. Time-based checks matched the main pattern.
pmc-13293839:
Meitong Guo and coauthors offer a 2026 narrative review on why pancreatic cancer starts and how it advances. The disease is uncommon but deadly, now ranked as the sixth leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and standard surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation have barely moved survival. The authors sort causes by strength of evidence and likely value for care.

Topics include smoking, alcohol use, obesity, diabetes, and long-term pancreatic inflammation, plus inherited mutations and key signaling pathways. Later sections cover early lesions, changes around the tumor, and how cancers evade immunity. The aim is clearer targets for earlier detection and more precise treatment.
pmc-13293939:
Chi Ma leads a 2026 quasi-experimental study on game-based basketball training that uses changing constraints instead of drills first. Forty-eight male college players split evenly into a constraints-led group and a technique-then-scrimmage control group. Both trained three times weekly for 8 weeks at matched intensity, with load, feelings, and game skill tracked.

The game-based group gained more in shooting accuracy and assist-to-turnover balance, and covered more distance with more accelerations. Fatigue fell while enjoyment rose. Statistical pathways showed mental readiness carried part of the gain from load to performance, with stronger indirect effects among lower-skill players. Fit and engaged practice appears to be the driver.
pmc-13294339:
Jasper Crokaert, Yasmine Bouayed, Clara Daher, and Gerard Calzada use film to teach psychiatry in a 2026 article from a University of Geneva course. Students in Psychiatry in Cinema study the American film Brothers, where soldier Sam returns from war and cannot settle back into family life, developing posttraumatic stress disorder. Scene signs are matched against diagnostic manual criteria.

Beyond diagnosis, the class judges how staging conveys Sam's inner state and whether the portrait matches patient experience. Social meaning gets equal time: does the film stigmatize the disorder, and how might that shape public views? Concrete images make abstract symptoms teachable before ward rotations.
pmc-13294539:
Guo-hui Gao and colleagues report an overlap of two rare nerve diseases in a 2026 case with literature review. One patient carried both antibody-positive myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune attack on muscle control, and Kennedy disease, an inherited motor neuron disorder. Clinical notes, lab results, and electrical muscle tests were set against all prior overlap reports the team could find.

Electrical findings plus androgen receptor gene testing confirmed Kennedy disease alongside the antibody disease. Only four past cases showed myasthenic features with Kennedy disease, and every one lacked the defining antibody, making the new case stand apart. Dual testing prevents one diagnosis from masking the other.
pmc-13294839:
Carlos De las Cuevas examines the hidden psychology behind psychiatric prescribing in a 2026 essay. Psychiatry often works without firm biological markers, leaving diagnoses and likely outcomes uncertain. Prescribing is usually presented as a calm, evidence-led reply to patient need, yet the clinician's own feelings also shape choices.

Drawing on work about thinking biases and tolerance for ambiguity, the essay asks whether writing a prescription can also ease the prescriber's own discomfort. Waiting and watching, by contrast, demands comfort with not knowing for longer. The piece roots the pattern in system pressures such as short appointments and patient expectations, not in personal failings alone.
pmc-13295239:
Matias F Schrauf and co-authors simulate breeding choices that protect rare gene variants in a 2026 study. Genomic selection speeds genetic gain but can quietly lose rare helpful variants and brand-new mutations. Five strategies were compared over 50 simulated generations for three kinds of trait control.

Populations of 1,000 individuals were bred under plain truncation choice, contribution-limited choice, two rare-variant boosting schemes, and a new loss-limiting scheme. Boosting rare variants gave an efficient balance, matching or beating plain choice on both long-term gain and kept diversity. Contribution limits also saved diversity, showing breeders need not trade tomorrow's variation entirely for today's gain.
pmc-13295839:
Zhenfeng Cheng and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study of heart damage that follows restored blood flow after a blockage. Their focus is USP20, an enzyme that removes ubiquitin tags, and whether heart muscle cells use it to limit injury.

Work in mouse hearts and cultured cells showed USP20 levels fall after injury, and mice lacking it in heart muscle fared worse, while extra USP20 protected the heart. The enzyme was found to act on GRP78, stripping one type of ubiquitin chain and easing stress inside the cell. The team propose USP20 as a possible drug target for this kind of heart injury.
pmc-13296039:
Alex S F Kwong and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for tracking depression moment by moment inside two long-running British cohorts. About 700 young adults with known depression histories since childhood will answer phone surveys three times daily for six weeks.

Questions cover mood, sleep, activity, substance use, diet and social contact, with fuller questionnaires every two weeks. The team will model how daily factors and mood push each other around, and whether patterns differ by earlier life-course path. The aim is to spot who is at rising risk and which daily habits could be targeted to prevent episodes.
pmc-13296439:
Vivien Resch and co-authors design, in 2026, altered estrone molecules meant to block enzymes that make or activate oestrogen inside tissues. Hormone-driven cancers of breast, womb and ovary depend on those enzymes, so selective blockers could slow growth with fewer side effects.

Several ring-modified versions blocked one target enzyme, and some blocked two at once, hitting both production and activation routes. One glowing version can light up its target inside cells, giving researchers a tracking tool. The authors present the set as leads for new treatments and for studying steroid handling in hormone-driven cancers.
pmc-13296839:
Rebeck and co-authors propose a new explanation for fat droplets inside activated microglia in this 2026 hypothesis paper. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. When they switch on, they round up, pull in their branches, and fill with lipid droplets. The authors link that shape change to the cell's outer membrane.

Drawing on their own slice experiments and published work, they note microglia extend some processes toward a stimulus within minutes while retracting others. Chronic amyloid exposure in mouse models cut microglial surface area two to three fold. Activated cells also switch on fat building genes. Rebeck proposes that membrane fats are first reshuffled during quick responses, then converted into stored droplets during chronic activation. Drug and genetic tests could confirm or refute the idea.
pmc-13297239:
Aurélien Riou and co-authors show, in 2026, that support cells donate their powerhouses to struggling neurons carrying a faulty tau protein. Tau diseases drain neuronal energy, so lab co-cultures of neuron-like and astrocyte-like cells, confirmed in human stem-cell models, tracked the donations.

Transfer rose when mutant tau was present and ran mainly through direct contact, with more tiny tubes linking the cells. Donated powerhouses joined the home network, were recycled, or sat solo, and breathing capacity in recipient cells improved. The authors call the donation a built-in rescue worth exploiting therapeutically.
pmc-13299739:
Mosquito-borne viruses are gaining ground in Saudi Arabia as cities grow and the climate warms, warn Shuaibu Abdullahi Hudu and colleagues in a 2026 review. Dengue is the established threat, concentrated in Jazan and the western cities of Makkah and Jeddah where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes thrive.

Rising temperatures, shifting rainfall, urban heat islands, international travel, and mass religious gatherings all widen the transmission window. Chikungunya and Zika have not yet shown sustained local spread, but conditions increasingly suit them. The authors catalog gaps in surveillance, diagnostics, and insecticide resistance monitoring, and they propose climate-informed early warning, risk mapping, and a One Health program joining human, animal, and environmental data.
pmc-13300639:
Pairing two immune checkpoint blockers woke up ovarian cancer T cells far better than one alone, Maitreyee Parulekar and colleagues found in a 2026 dish-based study. T cells taken from ovarian tumors were treated with a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor by itself or alongside blockers of LAG-3, TIM-3, or CTLA-4. Flow cytometry and ELISAs measured cell ratios and cytokines.

Single treatment barely moved the CD8/CD4 ratio, while adding CTLA-4 blockade lifted it to 3.69 against 1.41 for the lone drug. Tumor necrosis factor alpha rose only under that pairing, and interferon gamma gains also led the field. The authors present the CTLA-4 pairing as the leading candidate for deeper functional testing.
pmc-13301339:
Cold-seep mud from the South China Sea yielded fresh chemistry in a 2026 natural-products study by Ziyi Wu and colleagues. From the fungus Aspergillus strain SCSIO 41331, they isolated two new anthraquinone derivatives and one new diphenyl ether, alongside six known compounds. Structures were solved with NMR, mass spectrometry, and chiroptical checks.

The newcomers include a mirrored pair of chlorinated averantin relatives and a chloroaverythrin, all mapped atom by atom. Screening against tumor cells found one known compound, numbered 4 in the series, moderately slowed HT29 colon cancer growth and colony spread. The work adds deep-sea fungi to the hunt for anticancer leads.
pmc-13304439:
Francesco Maffìa and co-authors review jaw joint fluid as a source of precision markers in a 2026 synthesis on temporomandibular disorders. Standard exams often miss the chemistry driving pain, disc shifts, and joint wear in these conditions.

Studies of human joint fluid proteins and related markers were gathered from PubMed. Fluid drawn from the joint sits beside the tissues at fault, so it can carry signs of inflammation, cartilage breakdown, poor lubrication, oxidative stress, and new vessel growth. Patterns differed between disc shift types and arthritis forms. Such fluid profiles could one day guide care matched to each patient's biology.
pmc-13305139:
Zaki Alwatban and co-authors present a 2026 case report with literature review on red ear syndrome, a rare condition of sudden ear reddening and burning pain. Attacks often ride along with migraine, and the condition is easily mistaken for infection.

A 35-year-old man with poorly controlled migraine had repeated attacks in both ears, mainly the left, set off by migraine, heat, and touching the ear, and eased by cooling. Exams, labs, and scans all read normal. A pain drug plus magnesium ended the attacks fully. Careful history and ruling out other causes spare patients wrong treatments.
pmc-13306239:
Shansen Peng profiled a mismatch between nuclear and mitochondrial gene activity in clear cell kidney cancer in a 2026 multi-omics study. Bursts of mitochondrial DNA gene output against the nuclear background marked fast-growing tumour groups and reshaped tissue layout.

Data combined single-cell gene reads, spatial gene maps and imaging of tissue chemistry from a Tongji hospital cohort. Clustering and cell-state tools picked out malignant groups carrying the asymmetry and traced their neighbourhoods across tumour space. Follow-up checks backed the pattern, which the authors link to spread of aggressive cells and resistance to treatment.
pmc-13306439:
Hao Zhang compared muscle control during squash forehands between world-level and national-level players in a 2026 sensing study. Wearable surface electrodes recorded arm, leg and trunk muscles while athletes hit standardised strokes.

Factor methods extracted shared muscle groupings, their weights and timing, while time-frequency checks measured coupling between body regions across three bands. Group gaps in basic grouping counts were small in the reported results, shifting attention to finer timing and coupling markers. The authors offer sensor-derived signs to guide training and ongoing athlete monitoring. The team says such sensor signs may help coaches spot top level control.
pmc-13307539:
Sheng Wang and co-authors review in 2026 how grapevines react in body and chemistry when downy mildew, caused by Plasmopara viticola, infects them. The germ enters through leaf pores and can ruin leaves, shoots, and young fruit, with heavy losses in bad years for growers worldwide.

Resistant vines tend to sense attack early and mount a fast defence, while weaker vines respond late or weakly. The review weighs leaf traits, photosynthesis, oxygen stress enzymes, and defence chemicals, and it notes where studies clash on sugars and key enzymes. Gene editing, microbe based control, and multi sign scoring tools stand out as next steps for breeding and field care.
pmc-13308539:
Valeriya Kostyukova and co-authors screen in 2026 bacterial germs on sick apple leaves near Almaty, Kazakhstan, where fire blight and related ills threaten both farm fruit and wild apples. Quick gene scans hinted at Erwinia amylovora and Pseudomonas types, so full genome reads were run on five isolates.

Two isolates proved to be the fire blight germ, kin to a widespread group found in many lands. Three fell in the Pseudomonas syringae group, and two of those types had never been logged in Kazakhstan before this work. Genome tools beat look alike traps that fool simpler tests, which should sharpen orchard watch and control choices.
pmc-13309139:
Lisa D Burry and co-authors study in 2026 whether new sedative scripts filled soon after hospital discharge link to falls and other harms in older adults in Ontario. Their cohort held 1,868,484 adults aged 66 years and up from 2003 to 2023, and 13.2 percent filled such a script within seven days.

Falls struck 1.6 percent within 30 days, while urgent visits, readmission, and death all ran far higher in raw counts. For adults new to sedatives, each harm ran about a fifth higher in tuned models, and death ran higher still. For past users, only death ran higher. Drug class split the risk, so discharge review must weigh each new script with care.
pmc-13309939:
Jingjing Xiang and co-authors test whether thyroid function causes blood-forming cancers using genetics in a 2026 study. Thyroid problems often coincide with blood changes, but cause and effect stay murky. Inherited variants that shift thyroid traits can act as natural experiments to probe cause.

Thyroid trait data were paired with Finnish cohort data on myeloproliferative diseases, excluding one leukemia type. Variants tied to hormone levels and to overactive or underactive thyroid served as instruments, chosen under strict strength rules. Several analysis methods cross-checked the main result, with tests for bias and direction. The authors weigh whether any thyroid trait truly moves disease risk, rather than merely traveling with it.
pmc-13310039:
Haitao Lu and co-authors combine gene and protein profiling of keloid scars in a 2026 study. Keloids are stiff skin growths where scar tissue overbuilds and keeps spreading past the wound edge. They return often after removal, so deeper molecular clues are needed for better treatment.

Twenty keloid samples with nearby normal skin underwent gene sequencing and protein analysis. The scan found 4,994 genes and 828 proteins differing between keloid and normal tissue in the reported counts. Changed genes clustered in growth and matrix pathways, including PI3K-AKT and TGF-beta routes. Network analysis named hub genes tied to excess matrix buildup and broken skin barrier. The authors offer the paired profiles as targets for drug testing.
pmc-13310639:
Shreya Barnawal and co-authors describe an older man whose tuberculosis masked a second disease in a 2026 case report. Tuberculosis fills over a quarter of the world caseload in India, and its many forms tempt doctors to credit every sign to it. This patient carried brain tuberculosis plus advanced chronic liver disease at once.

Liver damage limited the usual strong tuberculosis drug choices, complicating care from the start. High blood calcium appeared and could easily have been blamed on tuberculosis, a known cause. Further workup instead found a parathyroid adenoma, a small gland growth that drives calcium up, whose treatment was deferred given his state. The authors warn against single-diagnosis thinking when several diseases coexist.
pmc-13310739:
Norma Carolina Hernandez-Bautista and co-authors review HOX genes in head and neck cancer in a 2026 mini review. HOX genes guide body pattern in early life and control cell growth, movement, and survival in adult tissue. When their activity goes wrong, cancers of the mouth and throat may grow, spread, and resist drugs.

Humans carry 39 HOX genes in four clusters across four chromosomes. The review sums up how each gene can act as a growth driver or a brake, based on context. It also weighs use as warning signs and drug targets. Gaps remain, and the authors call for tests that prove which changes truly drive disease.
pmc-13310939:
Xindi Liu led a 2026 study that builds a living eyelid support tissue from a zoned gel scaffold. The tarsus plate gives the eyelid its shape and holds oil glands that guard the eye surface. Loss of the plate harms both support and oil flow, and current substitutes fail to copy both roles.

A light printed gel copied the layered build of natural tarsus, then salt and stretch steps raised its strength and flex. Human oil gland cells, matured with a drug cue, were seeded to form the tissue. Grafts placed in rat eyelid gaps gave support and aided regrowth. The joint plan may improve eye surface health.
pmc-13311639:
Po-Huang Chen and colleagues present a 2026 emulation study on whether COVID-19 mRNA shots raise immune side effects in cancer patients on checkpoint drugs. The shots may boost the drugs' power but could also stir more immune harm.

Using a global records network, the team matched 3609 vaccinated patients with 3609 unvaccinated patients starting checkpoint therapy for spread cancer. Vaccination within 100 days before treatment start defined the exposed group. Immune side effects over 36 months formed the main outcome, with severe events, deaths, and ICU stays also tracked. Bias checks used a negative-control eye outcome. Vaccinated patients showed higher overall immune event risk.
pmc-13311939:
Tessa Fayers and co-authors report a 2025 randomized trial comparing two suture materials in eyelid skin. Polypropylene and polyglactin 910 threads were tested for tissue reaction and scarring around the eye.

Forty-seven entropion patients were assigned one material for both a first stitch procedure and later definitive surgery. A masked pathologist measured the inflammation ring around the thread in removed tissue. Mean ring width was 0.39 mm for polypropylene and 0.56 mm for the rival in this trial. Foreign body giant cells were clearly fewer with polypropylene, the one firm statistical gap. Scar ratings by patients and masked judges are also reported.
pmc-13312239:
Ulhas Vasave and Amit Paroha assess, in a 2026 study, whether a tailored antimicrobial stewardship program could improve antibiotic use across 11 Indian hospitals. Resistance is rising fast in low-income settings, yet stewardship there must work with thin staffing and budgets, so the team built hospital-specific tools rather than importing a fixed package.

From January 2022 to June 2023, the program introduced local antibiograms, written antibiotic policies, consumption monitoring, and tracking of multidrug-resistant organisms, backed by staff training and audit with feedback. Antibiotic compliance climbed from 10 percent at baseline to 71 percent, and surgical prophylaxis compliance improved sharply where it had lagged. Prescribing shifted toward safer first-line drugs. Resistant organism rates stayed uneven between sites, which the authors flag as the next frontier.
pmc-13312539:
Phui Chyng Yap and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, two harmful bacteria carried by urban rats in Malaysia. City rats live close to people and can shuttle zoonotic germs, including drug-resistant Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae, yet their strain variety and virulence in tropical settings were barely known.

The team trapped 277 rats at wet markets across four states and grew samples from lung tissue, yielding 19 E. faecalis and 7 K. pneumoniae isolates. Every E. faecalis strain carried several virulence genes, a few tetracycline-resistant ones held three resistance genes, and five sequence types were wholly new. All Klebsiella isolates carried the SHV resistance gene, and two new types showed up there as well. Family trees spread the strains among global lineages. The authors urge adding urban rats to One Health resistance surveillance.
pmc-13312839:
Qing Zhang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, three cheap blood-based scores used to predict survival in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease whose course varies wildly between patients. Inflammation, immunity, and nutrition all shape progression, so scores blending those elements might forecast outcomes better than lung tests alone.

The team reviewed 240 patients treated at a Chinese university hospital between 2011 and 2020, computing the prognostic nutritional index, the CRP-to-albumin ratio, and the lymphocyte-to-CRP ratio at baseline. Patients who died had a lower index and lymphocyte ratio and a higher CRP-to-albumin ratio than survivors. All three scores split outcomes on simple analysis, but the nutritional index predicted both overall and disease-related death best, and it alone held up in adjusted models. The authors back it as a practical tool for clinic use.
pmc-13314439:
Bin Xue and colleagues test a five-sign model for guessing who gains from CAR-T cell therapy in a hard lymphoma, in a study from 2026. CAR-T care has reshaped treatment of returned or drug-proof diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, yet who gains for long stays hard to foretell.

The team studied 92 patients given CD19 CAR-T at four centers in China from August 2021 to November 2024. The model scores five signs: double-expressor status, TP53 changes, poor fitness grade, bulky disease of at least 5 cm, and four or more past therapy lines, as listed in the report. Median follow-up was 14.6 months as stated, and outcomes such as response rate and survival were checked against the model. A simple bedside score that holds up in real-world data could guide who should get this costly therapy.
pmc-13315439:
Minh-Hoang Phan and colleagues study in 2026 how to make para-menthane-3,8-diol, a plant-based insect repellent, from citronellal with help from ultrasound. The compound, found in Eucalyptus citriodora oil, is a proven repellent against mosquitoes and ticks and exists as eight mirror and shape forms with different strength.

The work follows the Prins ring-forming reaction and checks which forms are made. The cis forms work better than the trans forms, likely due to how they bind scent receptors and how fast they evaporate. Computer modeling supports the shape analysis. Better control of form could raise repellent quality without new raw materials.
pmc-13315639:
Mohamad Mortada and colleagues ran two feeding trials in 2026 to compare how well male broilers can use zinc from four sources. The sources were zinc sulfate, zinc glycinate, a zinc amino acid hydrate, and a zinc methionine hydroxy analog. They were tested first in a depletion and refill design, then under normal corn and soybean diets.

Added zinc changed weight gain, feed intake, feed conversion, and zinc stored in the shin bone. Growth leveled near an intake of about 11.7 milligrams per kilogram, while bone zinc kept rising. The two organic sources raised bone zinc by 11 to 12 percent and beat sulfate on feed conversion and estimated availability.
pmc-13316139:
Muniz and co-authors study how a mother's diet in pregnancy reshapes gene activity in her offspring's muscles in this 2026 paper. The work concerns long non coding RNAs, RNA strands that regulate genes without making proteins. Goats were underfed either early or late in pregnancy, at half their maintenance needs. The team then sequenced RNA from the back muscle of the kids.

Comparing the two restriction schedules turned up three differently expressed long non coding RNAs. One rose in the early restriction group and sat near genes for fat burning and cell signalling. Two fell, near genes tied to protein turnover and cell structure. Muniz suggests that prenatal underfeeding leaves marks on muscle regulation that could shape growth, a process called fetal programming.
pmc-13316639:
Emily-Rose Martin and co-authors report 2026 cell work on CYFIP1, a gene in the chromosome 15 stretch whose duplication is a common inherited cause of autism. Extra copies of the region were already tied to oversized immune signal responses in nerve cells, and CYFIP1 was a prime suspect.

Raising CYFIP1 levels in human kidney and nerve-like cells lowered amounts of two signal proteins, STAT3 and STAT1, yet made their gene-switching response to immune messengers IL-6 and interferon stronger. Nerve cell branches also grew less at rest and answered IL-6 oddly. The pattern suggests CYFIP1 tilts immune signaling in ways that could feed brain inflammation linked with autism, a lead for deeper study.
pmc-13317439:
Fatma Abdou Eltaib and colleagues ran a 2026 before-and-after study in Arar, Saudi Arabia, on whether structured foot care teaching helps patients with diabetic nerve damage protect their feet. Nerve loss hides injuries that can fester, so daily habits matter.

Forty adults at a specialist diabetes center learned the international diabetic foot guidelines between October 2023 and September 2024, answering questionnaires before and after. The group averaged 65.35 years of age, and women made up 65 percent of the participants. Knowledge of prevention and daily self-care habits improved clearly after teaching, and reporting of nerve symptoms rose too. The authors urge ongoing training programs rather than one-off lessons.
pmc-13317539:
Yvxi Zhang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 walking study, how brains and muscles coordinate in older adults who practice Tai Chi long term versus brisk walkers and non-exercisers. Falls strike many older people while walking, and neural teamwork may be part of the protection.

Sixty-two older adults walked while light-based sensors read brain activity and electrodes read leg muscles. Tai Chi practitioners showed stronger links among movement and sense areas of the brain than non-exercisers, and stronger brain-to-muscle coupling in shin and calf pairs. One brain link also beat the brisk walkers. Richer coordination may underlie Tai Chi's known balance gains, offering a target for fall-prevention programs.
pmc-13318539:
Mrityunjoy Saha and K Sharat Vishwanath write a 2026 letter to the editor. They comment on a study by Zambetti and co-workers about psychological help during cardiac rehabilitation. That earlier work followed 181 inpatients. It compared group education, muscle relaxation training, and one-to-one counselling.

The letter praises the real-world setting and the low dropout rate. Dropout was 16.6 percent among participants in the study discussed. Standard scales covered anxiety, depression, and illness perception. The central worry is the lack of random assignment. Counselling went to those scoring worst at entry. Their later gains may reflect natural settling of extreme scores. Without a similar untreated group, benefit cannot be separated from expected recovery.
pmc-13318639:
Kevin R Zhang and co-authors offer a 2026 survey study of eye problems in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of inherited connective tissue disorders whose eye effects are poorly mapped. An anonymous online survey reached patients through social media and advocacy groups.

Altogether 766 completed surveys were analysed, and most respondents, 83.3 percent of them, had the hypermobile form. Short-sightedness was commonest, with severe short-sightedness reported by about 40 percent of respondents, above general population estimates. Dry eye, squint, and blue-tinted eye whites were also frequent, and glaucoma and retinal tears appeared younger than expected. Eye surgery was generally tolerated, though lasting pain afterwards was often reported, so the authors back stronger screening.
pmc-13318939:
Pauline N. Wekesa leads a large team exploring, in 2026, online shopping for self-care contraception in Kenya. E-commerce is growing fast, but women's views on buying contraceptives online were little known. The study ran in two phases. First came 61 in-depth interviews with women of reproductive age.

Many women liked the convenience but feared fraud. Limited digital skills and internet access also held them back. In phase two, eight Nairobi women tried a women's health shopping site with guidance. Afterwards they viewed online buying far more positively. Privacy, convenience, and personal control stood out, especially for contraception. The authors recommend in-person introductions to build trust and skills when launching such platforms.
pmc-13319039:
Zhaodi Yu, Zhenxiang Xu, and Jiangang Qi offer a 2026 policy text analysis of China's smart pharmaceutical regulation. They coded 90 policy documents issued between 2007 and 2026. A two-part framework sorted tools by type and by policy stage. The NATO scheme classified instruments into information, authority, money, and organisation types.

Information-based tools formed the largest share of the texts. That reflects a strong push toward data-driven oversight and information sharing. Money-based tools centred on digital infrastructure and technical capacity. Authority tools remained important beside the new digital ones. Organisation tools lagged, especially on coordination between agencies and shared governance. Over time, policy shifted from basic computerisation toward lifecycle and intelligence-oriented regulation. The authors urge stronger coordination and stakeholder participation.
pmc-13319539:
Vahid Sadeghi and co-authors compare two orders for spine surgery steps in a 2026 study from two hospitals in Tabriz, Iran. Surgeons often free the spinal cord by cutting bone and then hold the spine firm with screws. Whether screws should go in before or after the bone cut, and how that order shapes risk, was the open question.

Records for 104 patients from 2017 to 2020 were split evenly, with 52 in each order group. Blood loss and drain output ran higher when the bone cut came first, while surgery time ran shorter in that group. Infection and transfusion gaps between groups were small and could reflect chance. Order alone did not settle safety, so surgeon judgment still rules.
pmc-13319639:
Kelsey Barrett and co-authors review fair scale up of finger oxygen sensors for sick children in a 2025 article on global child care. The clip on tool is now seen as a core part of front line child care, with project proof showing it can be used well and helps staff follow care rules. World guidance and post COVID focus on oxygen have added push.

Most lands have updated child care rules and scale up plans, yet cash still leans hard on donors. Busy clinic staff face time strain that could wear down daily use in packed front line sites. Fair reach will need home grown funding, lighter work loads, and supply chains that keep sensors and spare parts in stock.
pmc-13319739:
J. García-Talegón and co-authors age granite stone in the lab in a 2026 study of cold climate wear near Ávila, Spain. Day night swings there can top thirty degrees, which cracks stone grain by grain over time. Three local granite types were put through 90 rounds of lab aging that mimic frost, heat, and salt attack.

Sound speed through the stone and weight change were tracked on all three faces before, during, and after each aging run. All aging types shifted both measures next to fresh quarry stone. The combined frost, heat, and salt run did the most harm, and one flecked granite type wore most. A grey granite held up best, which helps guide stone choice for cold sites.
pmc-13320039:
Pin-Heng Tiao and co-authors scope past work on web health searching by people with diabetes in a 2026 review. Daily self care drives a steady hunger for clear, usable health facts, and search now runs through smart feeds that rank what each person sees. Past reviews had not joined tech change, layered causes, and fairness for this illness in one map.

Five databases were swept for real world studies of searching habits across all diabetes types, with no start date limit. Findings were charted in a shared form and sorted by a layered model that runs from the person out to policy. The map covers what facts people seek, what drives the search, and how habits shifted across eras of digital health.
pmc-13320539:
Christian A Long and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study on stress signals in midlife Latinas going through menopause. Hair cortisol, a hormone measure built up over weeks, was compared with mood, social strain, and menopause symptoms. The women took part in a community heart health pilot called Menopausia, Salud, Corazón.

Baseline data from 45 women, with a mean age near 47 years, showed a median hair cortisol level of 4.3 units. Having hot flush type symptoms in the prior two weeks was tied to higher hair cortisol after checks for age and schooling. The link softened once felt stress was added, which shows how hard chronic stress is to pin down.
pmc-13320639:
Hadeel Zaghloul and a large team survey digital health skills in a 2026 study of Arab adults in Qatar who live with long-term illness. Participants had diabetes, high blood pressure, rheumatoid arthritis, or a mix of these. Skill in finding, judging, and using online health advice matters more as care moves online, yet regional proof was lacking.

Clinic surveys of 405 adults, with a mean age of 53.8 years, gave a mean skill score of 24.9, and 53.1 percent scored in the high range. Adults aged 60 and over had much lower odds of high skill than younger adults, while those with an advanced degree scored higher. Training aimed at older patients is a clear need.
pmc-13322839:
Majid AL Busafi and colleagues survey how sports stakeholders judge coach education in Oman, in a study published in 2026. A nationwide online survey drew 159 responses between September and November 2024, from people in varied roles and with varied experience.

Most respondents, reported as 75.7 percent of the group, backed reform, and the current programme was judged underdeveloped and weak in effect. Views on private provision differed modestly by role and experience. Private delivery could add flexibility and income, yet raises concerns about fairness, oversight and lasting funding. The authors favour a mixed system, with public oversight joined to private and digital methods, plus reform of governance, teaching and local fit.
pmc-13323139:
Yu Ning, Wei Gao and Yan Gao hunt for a new diagnostic and drug target in Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 multi-omics study of the substantia nigra. That brain region loses dopamine cells in Parkinson's, and current treatments remain limited for older patients.

Starting from public gene datasets, the team combined differential expression, network analysis and Mendelian randomisation to nominate risk genes tied to the disease. Three machine learning methods then picked a central factor, MMRN1, whose diagnostic strength was checked across several independent datasets. Single-cell data mapped its molecular and immune patterns, and network screening with docking searched for drugs that might act on it. The authors present MMRN1 as a candidate for testing.
pmc-13323239:
Vinay Modgil and co-authors study system drivers of outpatient antibiotic use in Bihar, India, in a 2026 multicentre study of three public tertiary hospitals. Prescription data from 2023 to 2025 held 8,822 outpatient records, matched against state supply records and catchment population data.

Prescriptions averaged four or more drugs each, leaned heavily on empirical choices, and used culture testing in only a tiny share of cases. Broad-spectrum products dominated, led by amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, azithromycin and cefixime in the reported shares. The authors link prescribing to central supply and catchment pressure, and judge alignment with stewardship goals and the WHO AWaRe scheme to guide tighter antibiotic policy.
pmc-13324439:
Weiqi Hu and co-authors present a 2026 study on why pressure inside an inflamed tooth makes pulpitis worse. Pulpitis causes severe tooth pain, and swelling inside the pulp raises pressure, but the effect of that pressure was unclear.

The team built rat models of pulpitis and measured pressure-linked signals at 0, 24, and 72 hours. They also grew inflamed pulp tissue and immune cells under set pressures, including 180 kPa. Higher pressure tracked with worse disease and stronger macrophage responses. Pressure and bacterial signals acted together through the TRAF6 pathways, and blocking the Piezo1 sensor eased inflammation. The work points to pressure control as a possible treatment angle.
pmc-13324839:
Mamata Modak and colleagues pin down one amino acid that the enzyme Pks13 needs to build mycolic acids in a 2026 study. Those waxy acids armor the mycobacterial cell wall, and Pks13 runs the final joining step in making them.

Using a switchable pks13 mutant of Mycobacterium smegmatis, the team swapped single residues in the ketosynthase domain. Changing Asp264 to alanine crippled growth and nearly wiped out mycolate output, including the lipids TDM and TMM. Other swaps did little harm. Modeling suggests losing Asp264 squeezes the active site pocket and shifts a loop near the catalytic Cys267. The residue seems to hold the working shape of the site.
pmc-13326939:
Luke Bransom and colleagues compare drug pairs against methylphenidate for cognition in rats in a 2026 study. The standard ADHD drug lifts dopamine and norepinephrine broadly, with uneven benefit between patients.

Animals took methylphenidate, a D1 dopamine agonist, the alpha2A agonist guanfacine, cannabigerol, or paired agents. Tasks measured order memory, flexibility, and spatial working memory. Pairing a D1 agonist with an alpha2A agonist beat methylphenidate, but only in rats that started with poor scores. Strong starters gained nothing extra. The authors suggest tailored receptor pairs deserve study for people with clear cognitive deficits rather than as a blanket swap.
pmc-13331239:
Rumei Li and colleagues trace how a bile acid helps liver cancer return after heat ablation in a 2026 study. Incomplete burning leaves a setting that favours regrowth. The team used liver tumour models with partial ablation, bile profiling, and immune cell counts, plus human leftover tumour tissue checks.

Ablation raised lithocholic acid in the liver, tied to suppressive macrophage states and fewer natural killer T cells inside tumours in the reported data. The acid switched on the vitamin D receptor in macrophages, lifting a suppressor gene and cutting a T cell drawing signal. Removing either gene link restored the signal. A bile acid modulator countered the pathway in living models, the authors report.
pmc-13333539:
Xinmei Pan and colleagues cross-check the safety record of the HIV drug Biktarvy in a 2026 pharmacovigilance study, setting a hospital's charts against the United States national adverse event database. The once-daily combination tablet is a mainstay of HIV care, and spontaneous reports plus real-world records can surface harms that trials were too small or too short to catch.

Together the two sources yielded 10,424 adverse event reports, 6,850 from the FAERS database and 3,574 locally. Statistical signal methods flagged 343 events as associated, 263 nationally and 80 in the hospital data. The hospital records raised signals absent from the label, including eye disorders and results such as raised urinary vitamin C, triglycerides, and uric acid. The national data instead pointed at vascular danger, flagging stroke, heart attack, and heart enlargement. The authors present the picture as complementary evidence for watching both the eyes and the arteries in patients on the drug.
pmc-13334139:
Min Ho Lee and co-authors described a scalp salvage operation for exposed deep brain stimulation hardware in a 2026 case report. Repeated scalp breakdown over DBS implants, especially with chronic infection and prior revisions, often forces removal of working hardware.

Their strategy layered acellular dermal matrix over the exposed device as a biological reinforcement, then closed a rotational scalp flap without tension after debridement. They also recessed the skull surface slightly to reduce how far the hardware protruded. Follow-up imaging confirmed the lower profile, and the wound healed stably with no return of breakdown or infection during follow-up. The combined approach offers reconstructive surgeons a way to save functional neuromodulation hardware instead of explanting it.
pmc-13336439:
Jin Wang and co-authors pinned cigarette smoke's lung damage partly on premature aging of alveolar macrophages in a 2026 study. Smoking injury is usually blamed on airway lining and blood vessels, but the lung's resident immune cleaners age too.

Single-cell sequencing of human lung wash fluid, combined with macrophage models bathed in smoke extract, showed smokers' macrophages enriched for senescence markers and inflammatory secretions. Smoke raised mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and DNA damage, weakened bacterial eating, and pushed cells toward death. A gene called GEM emerged as a causal driver. It rose in smokers, tracked with the aging marker CDKN1A, and when perturbed changed the whole phenotype, acting by suppressing the SIRT3/SOD2 defense axis. Activating SIRT3 pharmacologically reversed the defects, and a mouse smoking model backed the pathway.
pmc-13336739:
Huichan Xue and co-authors trace why lung tumors resist combined radiation and immune therapy in a 2026 study. They finger an enzyme called UBE2O, which tags a partner protein, CDKL1, for breakdown. Losing CDKL1 frees a pathway that raises PD-L1, a shield tumors use against immune attack.

Silencing UBE2O kept CDKL1 stable, lowered PD-L1 writing, and let killer CD8 T cells enter and activate in tumors. Blocking UBE2O alongside radiation and anti-PD-L1 therapy worked better in lung cancer models. The known drug arsenic trioxide, which jams UBE2O links, also lowered PD-L1 and boosted the combined therapy in early animal tests. The axis offers a fresh target for resistant lung cancer.
pmc-13336839:
Yun Ji and colleagues build a closed-loop brain device for nerve pain in a 2026 study. Nerve pain lacks clear objective markers and good treatments. The team found stronger theta-band activity, at 4–8 Hz, in the front brain area as a specific marker in patients. Their soft hydrogel electrode records brain signals gently and steadily.

In rats the gel held stable recordings for 28 d and beat screw electrodes, confirming the theta shift in nerve pain. Built into the loop, it triggered brain stimulation when theta rose, raising pain thresholds and easing anxiety- and depression-like behavior. Gene maps showed stimulation tuned inflammation and pain pathways both ways. Marker-guided, self-adjusting stimulation could make pain care more precise.
pmc-13336939:
Debarani Devi Khumujam and co-authors grow a self-rebuilding catalyst for zinc-air batteries in a 2026 study. Air cathodes need many active sites and fast, reversible oxygen chemistry. Their hollow carbon nanotubes, rich in sulfur and nitrogen, host a cobalt sulfide starter phase distorted by tiny manganese sulfide particles.

In use, the starter rebuilds into active cobalt phases that open and heal oxygen vacancies in a working cycle, confirmed by live Raman and isotope-labeled gas analysis. The catalyst beat platinum for oxygen intake and iridium oxide for oxygen release, lasting over 5000 cycles in stability tests. A full zinc-air cell reached an energy density of 993.8 Wh per kilogram and held voltage through 250 charge-discharge cycles in the reported build.
pmc-13337839:
Kunfu Wang and a large team build a solar edge AI system for rice pests in a 2026 study. Fast pest control cuts crop losses and chemical use, yet watching large fields by hand is hard. Their prototype spots pests, triggers a trap, and links multiple field nodes.

Training used 1,500 field images of 12 rice pests from paddies in Fujian, China. A lightened vision model runs on the device with fast inference, while small controllers handle trapping and long-range messages. Lab loop tests and simulated placement in split paddies tested cost and coverage. Early outdoor checks add a first look at performance under real weather and light.
pmc-13338239:
Yuxi Chen and a large team study prostate symptoms, aging complaints, and partner support in a 2026 survey. Enlarged prostate is common after age 50 and overlaps with body, mood, and sexual complaints of aging. A responsive partner might soften that burden, attachment theory suggests.

A total of 412 men aged 50 or older with confirmed enlargement completed symptom and partner scales. Worse prostate symptoms tracked with worse aging complaints in the reported models. Partner responsiveness rose with prostate severity only in the severe group and did not carry the link for moderate cases. Support alone therefore does not explain how prostate burden becomes broader aging strain.
pmc-13339239:
M. Cassandra Witt and co-authors trace energy sources for surgical treatment of atrial fibrillation in a 2026 review. Drugs and catheter methods lose strength in long-standing cases, while surgery controls rhythm better but seems daunting. Energy choice for making ablation lines has changed the field.

Bipolar radiofrequency and freezing remain the proven standard with decades of results as reviewed. Both carry heat-related limits and technical demands. Pulsed-field energy, which kills heart cells by electric pulses while sparing neighbors, is the rising option. Early lab and catheter data show fast, deep lesions, setting up surgical adoption questions.
pmc-13339639:
Jayabrata Das and a large team release a dataset of more than 50,000 carbon-nitrogen coupling reactions in a 2026 study. These couplings build medicines and farm chemicals, yet outcome prediction lacks overlapping training data. Palladium, nickel, and copper conditions were varied in a shared grid.

The 50,688-reaction set lets catalyst classes be compared directly for the first time at this scale as presented. Some ligands performed well across all three metals. Metal-free controls revealed hidden paths, including an aryne route likely common yet overlooked. Standard prediction tasks are included so other groups can benchmark models on the same ground.
pmc-13339739: Huawen Song and Yanping Liu published a 2026 correction touching only the ethics note of their nursing intern survey on stress and leave-taking. The approval details were wrong as printed. The correct number is E20260410001. It comes from Linfen People's Hospital. Voluntary consent wording stands as restated. All findings stand unchanged.
pmc-13340939:
Digital tools reshaping skin medicine are surveyed in a 2026 review led by Lea Henkel with a large German author group. Artificial intelligence fed by big image datasets now sharpens classification and prognosis from clinical and dermoscopic pictures, though synthetic training data still needs clinical validation.

Teledermatology, through video visits and store-and-forward images, has become routine and helps close care gaps in underserved regions. Apps and platforms support adherence and self-monitoring. Against these gains stand open problems in data protection, system compatibility, and regulation. The authors stress that doctors remain central for judging data quality and interpreting what digital systems produce.
pmc-13341439:

pmc-13398739:
Chiara Galli and colleagues map exactly which cells answer a weight-cutting hormone signal in mouse organs. Their 2026 study gives ciliary neurotrophic factor, a protein that curbs appetite and body weight and improves blood sugar and lipid control in animals and humans. The factor works through a three-part receptor and switches on the transcription factor STAT3, but which cell types in gut, pancreas, liver and fat actually respond was unmapped.

Receptor part levels were measured across those organs in adult male mice, and staining then located the switched-on STAT3 cell by cell. Knowing the true target cells sharpens hopes of copying the factor's benefits, weight loss without its side effects, in future obesity and diabetes drugs.
pmc-13398839:
Evandro José Cesarino and co-authors discuss, in a 2026 piece in Portuguese, how well the MAGGIC risk score performs for Brazilian heart failure patients. Heart failure is the leading cause of cardiovascular hospital admission in Brazil, especially among older adults, and repeat admissions strain the system. Scores that forecast risk guide treatment planning and honest talks with families.

The discussion centres on a validation study in a specialist clinic cohort, where MAGGIC showed good discrimination with an AUC of 0.72 in the results described, plus sound calibration matching international validations. Performance held similar in men and women, a stratified check the authors highlight. Imported scores need local proof, they argue, and this one passed its Brazilian test.
pmc-13399039:
Antonio Maria Zacarias Araújo Monteiro and colleagues published a systematic review in 2026 on catheter ablation for people who have both atrial fibrillation and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Their central question was whether the procedure raises the left ventricular ejection fraction, a measure of how well the heart pumps, more than drug treatment does.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched five databases in March 2025 and kept only randomized trials that compared ablation against medication. The trials showed better ejection fraction after ablation. One trial, CAMERA-MRI, recorded an absolute gain of 18.3 percent at six months, while CASTLE-AF linked ablation to fewer cardiovascular deaths and fewer heart failure hospital stays. The authors pooled no results in a meta-analysis, so they caution that the mixed evidence should be read carefully.
pmc-13399339:
Mi Chen reads Tan Twan Eng's novel The Garden of Evening Mists through the twin lenses of personality psychology and functional linguistics, in a 2026 literary study. The analysis combines the Big Five personality model with systemic functional linguistics, which treats grammar choices as meaning-making. Chen's guiding idea is emotional polarity, how a passage leans positive or negative through its wording, tracked across three phases.

Obligation-laden wording and compressed syntax mark the trauma recollection phase. Balanced, descriptive language takes over during the apprenticeship at the garden of Yugiri. More open, relational phrasing closes the book. Chen maps those shifts onto trait changes. High conscientiousness and neuroticism tie to trauma control early on. Steadier conscientiousness with growing openness follows in the middle, and openness rises as neuroticism falls at the end. The author offers the combined framework as a transparent method for studying personality change in postcolonial fiction.
pmc-13399439:
Nayara Luiza Henriques and co-authors followed Brazilian families caring for young children with chronic conditions across the arrival of the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 study. Twenty-four family caregivers of children aged two to four were interviewed twice. The team read the interviews through the Family Management Style Framework, which treats the family's own perspective as the steering wheel of daily care.

Before the pandemic, caregivers described a view centered on their children's strengths. Their routines aimed at promoting development and keeping the child well. Once the pandemic took hold, the same families' perspective swung toward frailty and vulnerability, organized around fear of the virus. Daily care tightened accordingly, with intensified watching, stricter hygiene, and shrunken support as services and schools closed. The authors conclude that the family perspective both guides care management and bends under pressure. Professionals should remember that in health crises, the authors say.
pmc-13399639:
Marouane Bouloudhnine describes an all-suture method for stabilizing a dislocated acromioclavicular joint, the small joint where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade, in a 2026 technical note. Such dislocations tear both the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments, and rebuilding only one leaves the joint unstable. The technique is designed to avoid metal implants and fluoroscopy-guided tunnels, with their risks of hardware trouble and nerve injury.

Working arthroscopically with the patient in a beach-chair position, the surgeon places unicortical, self-punching all-suture anchors at the base of the coracoid without piercing its lower cortex. Eight suture tapes are prepared, then routed through four slim tunnels drilled in the clavicle and acromion. Crossed tapes rebuild the coracoclavicular ligaments, while the remaining limbs reconstruct the acromioclavicular ligament, giving three-dimensional stabilization. Nothing metallic is left behind. The author reports the steps as safe and cost-effective.
pmc-13399839:
Molly N. Jones and colleagues describe pinning a loose osteochondral fragment back onto the inner femoral condyle with sutures instead of screws, in a 2026 technical note. The example patient is a 14-year-old girl with three years of medial knee pain that conservative care had failed to settle. MRI showed a fragment measuring 1.2 by 1.2 centimeters with fluid beneath it, the signature of instability. Fixing it promised to preserve her own cartilage rather than discard the piece.

A double-loaded PushLock anchor at the defect's inner apex sends suture strands across the fragment in a bridge pattern to a second anchor in the notch. A crisscrossed superficial row to a third anchor below completes the net, squeezing the fragment onto its bed without any metal crossing the cartilage. The authors argue the suture bridge avoids the fragment-splitting and removal operations that screws can cause.
pmc-13400039:
Edward T.C. Dong and colleagues asked whether a shot of heparin during DIEP flap breast reconstruction prevents the clotting complications that can kill a free flap, in a 2026 retrospective analysis. The team reviewed all such reconstructions at their institution from January 2018 to June 2024. They compared patients who received a single intraoperative bolus of 2,000 units of unfractionated heparin with those who did not.

The series covered 114 patients and 141 breasts, split into 66 patients in the heparin cohort and 48 controls. Complication rates did not differ in any window: intraoperative events, acute complications within four days, and delayed ones beyond that point were statistically indistinguishable. Thrombosis and hematoma risks specifically were comparable. The authors read the results as reassuring on safety but negative on efficacy: the heparin bolus neither reduced clotting events nor provoked bleeding. The single intraoperative dose, as given, is not where clot prevention succeeds or fails in this operation.
pmc-13400639:
Metodi V Stankov and co-authors examine, in 2026, how a COVID-19 booster matched to the JN.1 variant reshapes immune memory in people already heavily exposed. A worry was that boosters mostly recall old memory cells tuned to the original virus, leaving new variants poorly covered.
