Forty-two adults, most with several prior vaccinations and at least one infection, received the updated shot. Antibody binding and neutralization of JN.1 and its descendants rose. Memory B cells tuned only to JN.1 grew modestly, while cross-reactive cells stayed dominant. Deeper analysis showed accumulated mutations within existing cell families sharpened binding to the new variant. The booster, in short, refined old memory rather than recruiting much that was new.
pmc-13400839:
Scott Potter, Margaret Williams, Timothy M Hanley and Kalyani Sen present, in 2026, a patient whose severe folate deficiency looked like a bone marrow cancer. Folate, vitamin B9, is essential for DNA copying in fast-growing marrow cells. Severe shortage usually causes a distinctive anemia, but rarely it produces low counts across all blood lines with marrow changes mimicking myelodysplastic syndrome or leukemia.

Their patient had normal vitamin B12 levels, yet the blood and marrow picture initially suggested high-risk marrow disease. With folate replacement, the abnormalities resolved. The authors warn that careful nutritional assessment is essential before labeling such cases as cancers needing toxic chemotherapy, since the mimic is reversible.
pmc-13400939:
Vineet Kumar, Luke Sang, Wyatt David and Nirav Pandya examine, in 2026, workload patterns before Achilles tendon ruptures in NBA basketball players. The injury sidelines players for nearly a year and can shorten careers. A record seven ruptures in one recent season sharpened interest in whether heavy recent workloads raise risk.

Using public league data across eleven seasons, the team identified nineteen in-game ruptures in players averaging about twenty-eight years old. Minutes played across the ten and fifteen games before injury ran significantly higher than each players season average. Longer league experience also correlated with heavier total workloads. The exploratory analysis cannot prove causation, but it flags the weeks before rupture as a window worth monitoring.
pmc-13401239:
Berta Munné Barellas and co-authors ran a 2026 survey in Catalonia, Spain, on how women view medicines, vaccines, and other therapies during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Evidence on safety and choices in these stages is thin, and doubt can shape health behaviour.

The survey reached 889 pregnant and recently delivered women at public sexual and reproductive health services in 2024 and 2025. It asked about use, opinions, information sources, and choices. More than half reported a health problem needing medication during pregnancy. Most women, just under 85 percent of those who answered, followed health staff advice and prescriptions. About half felt safe and sure using medication, and vaccination in pregnancy also came up often in the answers.
pmc-13401539:
Abdullah Al-Jeffery and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of a first-in-class IKKalpha inhibitor, SU1349, in prostate cancer models, with close attention to bone. IKKalpha sits in the NF-kappaB signalling system, which is implicated in both prostate cancer growth and bone metabolism.

The team first confirmed that selected inhibitors slowed human prostate cancer models. SU1349 is potent and highly selective for IKKalpha. It reduced how well PC3 cancer cells migrated and invaded in dishes. It also cut their ability to dissolve bone in lab-grown samples and limited trabecular bone loss in mice. Oddly, treated mice also lost cortical bone. Detailed bone measurements and cell tests showed the drug suppressed osteoclast formation, the cells that break bone down, yet both raised and lowered osteoblast numbers and activity depending on context.
pmc-13401839:
Chan and colleagues pool the evidence on adding platelet concentrates to gum regeneration surgery. The surgery treats deep pockets where bone has been lost beside a tooth root. The concentrates release growth factors and are used, yet whether they add anything over a bovine bone graft plus a guided tissue membrane was unsettled. Their 2026 review searches five databases for randomized trials in adults with defects deeper than three millimeters and grades risk of bias.

Five trials survived the screen. Platelet groups gained more gum attachment and shallower pockets at twelve months, by fractions of a millimeter. The differences never reached statistical significance, and only one trial leaned positive. Every study carried bias concerns, missing pre-registered protocols, and only one followed patients past a year. The verdict is a shrug: the add on is popular, but the trials cannot show it works, so bigger, cleaner, longer studies must decide.
pmc-13402239:
Achilleas Mandalos and co-authors describe a 68-year-old man who developed two kinds of unwanted tissue growth inside the eye after difficult cataract surgery. Surface cells had crept inward, a problem called epithelial downgrowth, alongside fibrous ingrowth. The mix was first misread as malignant glaucoma, and treatment for that gave only brief relief.

Removing a piece of the abnormal tissue and studying its cells settled the diagnosis. Stubbornly high eye pressure and a swollen cornea then led to a drainage implant, followed by a full-thickness corneal transplant. Eighteen months after the transplant he saw 20/30, the graft stayed clear, and no regrowth had appeared. Downgrowth is rare but relentless, the authors note, and their case shows staged, team-based surgery can still save useful sight.
pmc-13402939:
Bharti Jain, Savita Kulkarni, and Nawab Singh Baghel present an in-house DNA biochip built to flag extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis fast, by reading resistance mutations directly. Standard culture testing for such strains can take 16 to 20 weeks in sequence, during which patients spread infection and receive the wrong drugs. The World Health Organization 2024 report counts tuberculosis again as the top single-germ killer, with 1.25 million deaths in 2023.

Current definitions set extensively resistant disease as multidrug resistance plus fluoroquinolone resistance and resistance to bedaquiline or linezolid, the backbone drugs of modern regimens. A chip that profiles the mutations behind those failures could compress months of waiting into a rapid laboratory answer. The authors position their device for settings where sequencing is out of reach but resistant tuberculosis is common.
pmc-13403039:
Ozgur Basal and co-authors systematically review what decides success after hip labral reconstruction, the grafting of a new rim cushion when the original labrum cannot be repaired. Searching PubMed and Scopus through December 2025, they pooled 32 studies covering 2252 hips, with bias checked by ROBINS-I. Patient-reported outcomes improved broadly after surgery, but keeping the native joint varied with joint condition and technique.

Across studies, 8.8 percent of reconstructed hips converted to total hip replacement in the pooled analysis. More high-grade cartilage damage in the socket predicted more conversions, and longer follow-up raised conversion risk month by month. Ring-shaped reconstructions and donor grafts looked better than segmental repairs and own-tissue grafts, but surgeon experience and case mix tangle those comparisons. The authors stress study-level caution: advanced cartilage wear and visible arthritis flag the patients likeliest to fare poorly.
pmc-13403439:
Yuxuan Huang and colleagues built a computer model in 2026 for a balloon that partly blocks a large vein below the liver during surgery. Blocking the vein can cut bleeding, yet fast swelling of the balloon makes pressure below it spike. Surgeons now judge the pace by feel alone.

The model paired blood flow with balloon stretch and tested control plans on the data. A standard smooth swelling plan pushed pressure about 46 percent past its target level. Their tuned plan held the spike near 6 percent while still blocking most flow. Bench and animal tests come next before any use in real operations.
pmc-13403639:
Roberto Corrêa Leite and co-authors studied in 2026 how six families manage mental illness in a teenage member. Interviews ran from July to November 2022 and were read with a family management framework. Teen mental illness brings stigma and daily strain that reshape home life.

Families saw their teen as swinging between normal and fragile, so care leaned toward safety and calm. Routines bent to handle sudden swings in mood and behavior. Hopes for the future centered on the teen's freedom and steady mental health. The team backs coaching that builds family strengths, teaches facts, and eases the hardest parts of home care.
pmc-13403739:
Rongxuan Lu and co-authors surveyed in 2026 a young idea: using ferroelectric materials, whose inner charge can flip, to speed hydrogen making. Splitting water for hydrogen now leans on costly rare-metal catalysts. Ferroelectric charge may steer surface reactions in helpful ways.

The piece sorts such catalysts into four build types, from plain single-phase solids to single-atom tweaks and layered pairs. Worked examples show how each type has been tested on the hydrogen reaction. Future angles include metals that are ferroelectric by nature and links between charge and spin. The authors hope the map spurs fresh catalyst hunts.
pmc-13404339:
Shujie Wang and a team of twelve studied a rice gene in 2026 that moves plant hormones around and, when overactive, worsens heat harm. Rice feeds half the world, and hotter spells cut yields hard. The gene, OsPUP1, carries growth hormones called cytokinins from place to place.

Plants with extra gene copies grew poorly under heat and piled up cell-damaging compounds. Their defense enzyme activity dropped, based on the team's measures. Moving hormones thus reshapes where protection sits inside the plant. Heat tolerance in rice may hinge on that hormone map, which breeders could tune for warming fields.
pmc-13406339:
Olivia Tania Hernández-Hernández, Dora María Velázquez-Hernández and Ignacio Camacho-Arroyo review how nerve growth factors and ovarian hormones interact in endometriosis, in a 2026 narrative article. In the disease, womb-like tissue grows outside the uterus, resisting progesterone while oestrogen dominates. That imbalance fuels inflammation, pain and infertility.

Hormones adjust levels of nerve growth factor and BDNF, which in turn encourage nerves and blood vessels to grow into lesions, a process called neuroangiogenesis. More nerves may mean more pain, linking the chemistry to symptoms. The review gathers evidence on this two-way control and its treatment implications. Gaps in human data are noted across the fast-moving field.
pmc-13407439:
Yücedağ Gündoğdu and Paslı measure, in 2026, the navicular bone of the foot in anatomical detail, giving fracture surgeons dimensions for placing screws and implants without breaching the joint surfaces. They examined 55 dry navicular bones without deformity, using calipers and thickness gauges to map the tuberosity, the body at several levels, and the concave surface that meets the talus.

The body's mean mediolateral width measured 37.69 millimeters, with anteroposterior dimensions stepping down from 18.01 millimeters at one level to 12.56 millimeters at another across the planes. The tuberosity, the bone's medial bump, had a narrowest width of 6.59 millimeters, a groove depth of 2.05 millimeters, and distances to the medial cuneiform joint surface of 21.86 millimeters at the nearest point and 29.65 millimeters at the farthest in the series. The authors argue these level-specific values define safer fixation corridors and should inform preoperative planning and future implant design for this keystone midfoot bone.
pmc-13407939:
Pedro Azalim-Neto and co-authors review, in 2026, how time, temperature, and shape-shifting complicate measuring a classic drug family's grip on its target. Cardiotonic steroids bind the sodium-potassium pump, a membrane machine, and act through both classical and signalling routes; how fast they bind and release shapes their real-world potency and selectivity.

Binding studies often ignore that the pump changes conformation during its cycle, which can distort both kinetic and heat-based measurements of the interaction. The review compares workhorse assays based on enzyme inhibition, including a dephosphorylation readout, against gold-standard methods and their limits. Statistical advice for fitting such data closes the piece. Better characterisation, the authors argue, will sharpen drug discovery aimed at this pump, whether the goal is blocking or activating it.
pmc-13408339:
Famoussa Dembélé and a large Ghana-based team measured in 2026 how much carbon dioxide soils breathe out across different land uses. Ghana's farm and forest sector is a major emission source, and soil respiration is a big, poorly baselined part of it. Four land types in the semi-deciduous forest zone were compared: forest, fallow, maize, and rice.

Closed chambers captured soil emissions twice a month for thirteen months, alongside moisture, temperature, and soil chemistry readings. Fallow and cropped plots released the most carbon dioxide, while forest soils released the least, held back mainly by persistent moisture limits rather than temperature. Organic matter, acidity, moisture, and silt content predicted emissions best. The authors back forest conservation, reforestation, and gentler soil management as practical ways to cut these losses.
pmc-13408439:
Kwanwoo Song and co-authors report a 2026 machine-learning hunt for lead-free ceramic materials. The goal was ceramics that hold their electric traits steady at high heat. Such relaxor materials matter for the electronics in cars and aircraft. Yet their best recipes hide in a huge chemical space with harsh trade-offs. The team mined past papers in several formats to train their models.

A physics-guided model set screened more than 150 million candidate mixes. It singled out one simple family built on strontium, sodium, and bismuth titanate with a touch of tin. Lab samples at the two flagged mixes kept their key trait high. They also stayed stable enough to pass several industry heat grades. Atomic-scale imaging tied the results to a stretched framework that creates polar patchiness. The checked pipeline offers a shortcut for finding heat-stable ceramics of this kind.
pmc-13408539:
Qiang Zhang, Yungang Sun, and colleagues trace in 2026 a message in a molecular envelope that helps lung cancer spread. Macrophages of the tumour-friendly M2 type release tiny vesicles called exosomes, and lung cancer cells swallow them readily. What the vesicles deliver, and why it makes the cancer nastier, was the open question.

The cargo turned out to be rich in a small RNA, miR-491-3p, which on arrival silences a gene called UBE2D3 inside the cancer cell. Treated cancer cells grew, migrated, and invaded more aggressively in dishes and in animals, while blocking the small RNA reversed the effect. Restoring its target tells the same story from the other side. The pathway offers oncologists a candidate drug target and a possible marker of macrophage-driven progression in lung tumours.
pmc-13409039:
Ashraf Hantouly and colleagues report early safety results in 2026 for a knee reconstruction strategy adapted to teenagers whose skeletons are still growing. Eighty-four patients averaging under fifteen years had their torn anterior cruciate ligament rebuilt with an over-the-top technique plus a reinforcing strip of tissue on the outer knee, all by one surgeon. Tunnel placement was tailored to how much growth each child had left.

Most patients also had meniscus damage repaired during the same operation. Over follow-up averaging twenty months, and at minimum nine, no major complications occurred, and minor problems were limited. The authors caution that the window covers rehabilitation rather than the return to sport, when new injuries typically strike. Still, the clean early record supports the growth-sparing design for skeletally immature athletes.
pmc-13410539:
Qi Wu and a large team report in 2026 on heart health during pregnancy in China and how it relates to outcomes for mother and baby. Pregnancy offers a key window to check and improve heart health. Six measures, from smoking and weight to sleep, were scored at 24 to 28 weeks.

Among 2,775 women, roughly a third each fell into high, moderate, and low heart-health groups. Each added point on the score tied to lower risk of bad outcomes for both mothers and newborns. Women with fully ideal scores faced notably lower risk than those with any poor measure. Weight, blood sugar, and sleep stood out among the single measures, yet two thirds of women missed the ideal mark.
pmc-13410739:
Yoko Arai and colleagues survey in 2026 how Japanese centers treat high blood pressure in the lung arteries, a rare disease that strains the right side of the heart. Guidelines urge combined drug therapy, yet real practice varies. Their web survey asked doctors what they actually prescribe and what holds them back.

Oral drugs were widely stocked and commonly used across centers. Inhaled and drip treatments were scarcer and used less often. Doctors at specialized centers prescribed drip therapy and double or triple drug mixes far more often than peers elsewhere. Experience with high-risk patients at those centers widened the gap further. Bringing intensive therapy beyond specialist walls is the clear unmet need.
pmc-13412139:
Beaugard and colleagues investigate how residential addiction treatment in the United States can serve Black patients better, in 2026 qualitative health research. Black patients fare worse in addiction treatment than White peers, and residential programs require living inside the treatment setting, which can feel unsupportive. Building on a community-engaged project, the team first interviewed seven experts with experience as patients or providers in programs focused on Black patients. They then ran five focus groups at one short-term residential facility.

Patients, staff, and leadership generated recommendations in five domains for policy and practice. The first calls for stronger representation of Black people and people with lived recovery experience among treatment staff. The second calls for staff training that effectively supports Black patients in daily care. Remaining domains address program culture and accountability in similar practical terms. Beaugard presents the framework as directly usable by facilities auditing their own equity.
pmc-13412539:
Fadi Aljamaan and colleagues survey in 2026 how Saudi medical students feel about generative AI joining their training. The cross-sectional study gathered 1,039 undergraduate responses nationwide with a pilot-tested questionnaire on familiarity, perceived usefulness, and attitudes toward technology-led teaching. Most respondents were men, and the median age was 22 years across the group surveyed.

About 70 percent backed adding these tools to the curriculum, and 86.4 percent expected them to reshape medical education in coming years. Support ran stronger for basic science teaching than for clinical skills training, where only 41.6 percent saw clear utility in the responses. Distrust of output reliability troubled over half, and 64 percent knew the tools can invent references. Students saw AI as a complement, not a replacement.
pmc-13415239:
Mesude Seda Aydoğdu and Zarife Ekici Gök examine whether routine blood counts can flag active eye inflammation in ankylosing spondylitis, in 2026. Their retrospective study covered 140 patients, split by whether uveitis, inflammation inside the eye, was present. Several combined indices were computed from blood values, including the HALP and CALLY scores.

Patients with uveitis showed higher neutrophil, platelet, and system wide inflammation ratios. Their HALP and CALLY scores ran lower, and those gaps survived correction for multiple testing. Two other indices lost significance after that correction. Curve analysis gave the scores only moderate power to spot uveitis, so the authors frame them as supportive markers, not stand alone tests.
pmc-13415339:
Di Pentima Melania and a large team test cattle herpesviruses as cancer killing agents for dog tumors, in 2026 laboratory work. Two aggressive dog cancers, bone osteosarcoma and histiocytic sarcoma, have poor outlooks and few options. Cell lines from both cancers, plus normal dog skin fibroblasts, were infected with two bovine viruses.

The engineered virus BoHV4EGFPΔTK infected and killed tumor cells strongly while sparing fibroblasts comparatively. The plain type 1 virus infected normal cells most heavily instead. Engineered virus infection triggered apoptosis and raised gasdermin D, a cell bursting protein. Tumor cell movement also changed under both viruses. The engineered candidate earns further study, the authors conclude.
pmc-13416139:
Shuowen Guo and colleagues boost a nickel catalyst with zirconia to turn maleic anhydride into gamma-butyrolactone, in 2026. Their carbon coated nickel grains bind strongly to added zirconium oxide. When woken, part of the zirconia loses oxygen, leaving surface gaps that work with live hydrogen.

A two to ten mix of zirconium to nickel did best, turning all feedstock with about 98 percent selectivity at 210 degrees under hydrogen. Thirteen reuse rounds showed no clear loss of power. Tests from diffraction to infrared checks back the gap based path they set out.
pmc-13418239:
Jyoti Kumari, Adarsh Singh, and Ashok Kumar Gupta build a composite catalyst that destroys resorcinol in water under visible light, in a 2026 study. Resorcinol is a common ingredient in personal care products and can disturb hormones. The composite joins a bismuth based material with carbon coated iron oxide made from a metal organic framework.

The best mix, at five percent iron oxide phase, removed about 99 percent of the pollutant in three hours of light. Wider surface area, a narrower energy gap, and slower charge recombination explain the gain. It survived five reuse cycles, showed no bacterial toxicity, and its breakdown products were predicted less harmful.
pmc-13418539:
Alejandro Ortigas-Vasquez and colleagues sequence 65 strains of Marek's disease virus, a chicken herpesvirus, to find genes behind virulence and vaccine escape, in a 2026 study. The virus has grown more virulent over a century, breaking through successive vaccines. Each strain had a standard virulence rating from a United States Department of Agriculture assay, enabling genome wide comparison.

Ten genome regions linked significantly to virulence, including a tandem repeat built from two versions of a short repeating motif. Repeat and between gene variants contributed alongside protein changes. Virulence is a complex trait, the authors conclude, and monitoring these loci could warn of vaccine breaking strains.
pmc-13418739:
Jason O. Matos and colleagues report the structure of benzaldehyde synthase, the petunia enzyme that makes a key scent compound. Benzaldehyde gives almond-like aroma notes and helps plants draw pollinators and fight fungi. The enzyme works in two unlike parts, both from the same broad protein family, and the final step of its pathway stayed unclear for years.

Crystal work showed the parts pair up as a four-unit complex with two copies of each subunit. One subunit type holds the active site, while the other has lost that role yet stays vital for holding the complex together. A tail from the quiet subunit reaches across to shape the pocket where the starting compound binds. Swap and mixing tests confirmed that the units add their efforts rather than acting as one switch. The layout offers a model for building custom enzyme teams.
pmc-13420339:
Menghi and colleagues report a 2026 study of the brain signals behind continuous error correction in movement. Most studies test single, sudden errors, but daily actions need constant small fixes. Twenty-three adults held a steady grip force, with or without live visual feedback, while scalp electrodes recorded brain activity.

With feedback, grip force wobbled at about six cycles per second, a rhythm of active correcting. That rhythm tied to brain waves across theta, beta, and alpha rhythms, linked to monitoring, updating, and attention. Without feedback, force drifted steadily worse and the brain signatures faded. Constant feedback thus runs a live loop in the brain, not a series of separate alarms. The finding helps explain how people steer smooth actions, and what may fail in movement disorders.
pmc-13420739: The International Journal of Cell Biology issued this 2026 correction to a 2019 paper by Devocelle and co-authors. The paper covered how the immune signal IL-15 blocks kidney cell changes driven by TGF-beta1, a process involved in renal scarring. During figure assembly, the image of untreated cells in Figure 3c was accidentally duplicated from the IL-15-treated group, so the two panels wrongly shared features. The notice supplies the corrected figure and caption and apologizes for the error.
pmc-13420839:
Barroso and colleagues argue in 2026 that the rectus femoris tendon deserves consideration as its own graft for rebuilding torn knee ligaments. The tendon is the front thigh tendon, usually treated as part of the quadriceps. Surgeons need graft options beyond hamstring and kneecap tendons.

The narrative review gathered 35 articles found through searches running to June 2026. Cadaver studies showed a consistent tendon about 30 centimeters long, yielding grafts 8 to 11 millimeters wide. Strength tests placed the doubled graft within the range of standard ligament grafts. The tendon has served for front and rear cruciate ligament repairs and for revision surgery. Early patient series matched hamstring graft results, with little harm at the harvest site. The evidence so far is limited to weaker study designs and about three years of follow-up, though.
pmc-13421239:
Ezgi Mamus, Mounika Kanakanti, Sho Akamine and Aslı Özyürek report, in a 2026 study, that people blind from birth gesture differently from sighted speakers when describing motion. Using computer vision, they tracked the hand movements of Turkish speakers during an audio-based motion description task: 20 blind from birth, 21 blindfolded sighted people and 21 sighted controls.

Only gestures tracing the path of movement were analysed, for how closely they matched the real trajectory, plus their size and duration. Blind speakers' gestures matched the true paths more precisely, and their movements were larger and longer. The authors read the result as evidence that a lifetime without vision sharpens spatial tracking, and that bodily experience shapes the very form gestures take.
pmc-13421539:
Kosch and colleagues imaged in 2026 a model brain aneurysm using magnetic particle imaging, a method that tracks magnetic tracer particles. Aneurysms are weak bulges in brain arteries that can burst and cause deadly bleeding. The team built an artery model from a real patient's CT data, complete with aneurysm, and filmed a tracer bolus passing through it.

The method resolved the bolus location and movement with millisecond timing in each part of the model. Flow patterns inside the aneurysm sac differed clearly from those in the main artery channel. After a flow-diverter stent was inserted, the imaging showed changed flow through the aneurysm region. The authors present the results as a step toward using this imaging for vessel checks in living patients.
pmc-13422639:
Fanny Indra Warman and three colleagues review, in a 2026 meta-analysis, surgery for piriformis syndrome that refuses to settle. The piriformis muscle sits deep in the buttock. It can squeeze the sciatic nerve and send pain down the leg. Most patients recover without surgery. Yet refractory cases face a choice between open release and a newer keyhole, endoscopic approach.

No study had compared the two directly, so the team pooled each separately under reporting guidelines. Twelve studies qualified, nine endoscopic and three open. Across six pooled endoscopic studies, pain scores fell sharply and hip function scores rose strongly, with complications uncommon and minor. Open-surgery evidence was too thin for firm pooling. The authors present endoscopy as promising while the comparison stays indirect.
pmc-13422839:
Mwenda-Ng'uni and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for a realist review on teaching people with type 2 diabetes in poor communities to understand and use health information. Programs that work in one place often fail in another, and this method asks why.

A realist review builds theories about how context triggers mechanisms that produce outcomes, rather than averaging results. The team will define the scope and draft initial program theories. It will then search databases spanning health and education, select papers for relevance and rigor, and extract and synthesize the evidence. Their framework tracks intervention, context, actors, mechanism, and outcome together. The goal is to explain which educational strategies improve health literacy, for whom, and under what local conditions, so future programs in low-income communities can be designed to fit.
pmc-13423139:
Teodora P Staeva heads a 38-author consortium introducing Lupus Nexus, a shared registry, sample bank, and data platform built to speed research into systemic lupus erythematosus. Lupus varies widely between patients, its causes stay unclear, and the authors argue that progress needs one deep, well-curated dataset that any qualified team can use.

The centrepiece, the Lupus Landmark Study, will enrol up to 3,500 adults into four cohorts and follow them for five years. Records combine medical data with clinician and patient reports, while the bank stores blood, urine, saliva, stool, and tissue. By March 2026, 705 people had enrolled, spanning new-onset disease, flares, active kidney involvement, and long-standing cases. All raw analysis data return to the platform, deepening it over time.
pmc-13423439:
Masakatsu Fukuzawa and eleven colleagues pilot an improved buffer for stool sampling bottles used in faecal blood testing, where heat and storage time can distort results. The team compared the new buffer with the standard one on how closely readings matched and how well three stool markers survived a week at 37 degrees.

Across 130 patient samples collected between 2021 and 2024, the buffers agreed strongly on blood, transferrin, and calprotectin readings. After the hot week, blood-marker reactivity held up significantly better in the improved buffer, especially at higher levels. Transferrin stayed stable in both, while calprotectin faded in the standard buffer but kept better in the new one, easing transport worries.
pmc-13423739:
Julia Messerman, Callia Nickels, and Nigel James scope the literature on why low-income women in the United States miss mammography screening, arguing the story is wider than cost alone. Their review followed standard scoping guidance, searching three databases for peer-reviewed work from 2010 to 2025 and keeping 47 studies.

Barriers sorted into five domains: financial, structural, informational, cultural and social, and systemic. Structural hurdles, transport problems and scarce clinic slots, were reported most, followed by money and information gaps. Fear, stigma, mistrust, provider bias, and fragmented follow-up care added further drag. Rarely did one barrier act alone; instead they stacked, limiting both first screening and follow-up after an abnormal result.
pmc-13424139:
H R Heba and three colleagues isolate a slime-making bacterium from naturally fermented Egyptian cucumber and give a first profile of the sugar polymer it gives off. Gene sequencing named the microbe Bacillus tequilensis, part of the Bacillus subtilis group, and such glucan-type polymers from fermented plants remain little studied.

Lab tests showed a structure matching a glucan, a chain of glucose units. The liquid grew thicker step by step as more polymer was added, proving a genuine large molecule. The strain also broke down sucrose, tying sugar use to polymer output. Human and animal cell lines handled low and middle doses well, though survival fell at high doses. The authors present the polymer as a possible food or materials input needing deeper study.
pmc-13425039:
Stéphanie Boutin and colleagues follow children over time to ask whether heavy use of indirect aggression predicts later problems on its own. Indirect aggression means social tactics such as spreading rumours or excluding someone, rather than hitting or shouting. Their 2026 study separates its effects from general conduct problems.

Data came from a long-running Quebec project with 744 children, including 434 recruited from eight school boards for conduct problems. Parents and teachers rated aggression and conduct from about age 8 to 13, and outcomes were self-reported at about 17. Children on a high, stable indirect aggression path reported more problematic substance use and delinquent behaviour, and faced a higher risk of dropping out of school. This held after accounting for conduct problems, so the authors urge screening for indirect aggression itself.
pmc-13426039:
Mhando and colleagues survey fungal foot infections among footballers in the Tanzanian Premier League. Sweaty boots, shared showers, and nail knocks make players prime targets for athlete's foot and nail fungus. Their 2026 study examines 314 players from thirteen clubs, nine men's and four women's. It uses skin and nail checks, a fungal test under the microscope, and questionnaires on habits and exposures across the 2024 to 2025 season.

More than a third of players, thirty seven percent, carried a foot fungus. Nail infection led at seventeen percent, skin infection of the feet followed, and some players carried both. The commonest signs were soggy skin between the toes, thickened nails, and itch. Risk clustered on fixable habits: communal shower use nearly tripled the odds, sharing socks and a family history of fungus raised them, and toenail trauma doubled them. Screening and hygiene coaching, the authors argue, belong in club routines.
pmc-13427239:
Yupeng Wang and colleagues built EndoTac, a small touch sensor that gives surgeons a sense of feel during keyhole surgery. Keyhole surgery works through tiny cuts, so surgeons lose the direct touch that warns them how hard they press tissue.

The sensor slips through a standard surgical port and uses an endoscopic camera plus a curved mirror to watch a wide soft pad deform. That design keeps the device slim while covering a large sensing area, unlike earlier bulky or narrow tools. Tests showed it could detect forces as light as about 20 thousandths of a newton, a very gentle touch. It also estimated vessel squashing reliably in palpation tests, a step toward safer handling of fragile tissue.
pmc-13427439:
Fengming Yang and coauthors describe purifying retinal pigment cells grown from stem cells in a 2026 protocol aimed at macular degeneration therapy. Induced pluripotent stem cells can be steered into retinal pigment epithelium, a promising transplant source for the leading cause of vision loss in older adults, yet cultures need cleaning before use. Their method digests cells sequentially with different enzymes and then sorts by the natural autofluorescence of mature pigment cells.

Sorting by glow avoids fixation and antibody staining, keeping cells alive and pure at low cost. Transplant programs and laboratory researchers gain a gentle purification route preserving viability for grafting studies.
pmc-13427539:
Mayuri M. Mungale and Ashish A. Thatere present a 2026 case report on Ayurvedic care for irritable bowel syndrome. Their patient was a 71-year-old woman with three years of frequent loose and formed stools, belly pain, bloating, weakness, and poor sleep. Standard drug treatment over those years had brought her little relief. In Ayurvedic terms her illness matched Grahani Roga, a disorder of digestion.

She received a medicated enema treatment for 16 days, then calming herbal medicine for four months. Scores for symptom severity, adequate relief, and quality of life all improved during that care. A single case cannot prove a treatment works for everyone. Still, the report gives clinicians a detailed example to weigh when standard care falls short.
pmc-13428539:
Grace Johnston and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, blood chemistry in green sea turtles feeding at two Ecuadorian sites. One group forages in a protected bay in the Galápagos, grazing mostly on algae. The other feeds off the mainland near Puerto López, where fishing is heavy and turtles pick at discarded catch. Blood drawn from 24 turtles was tested on site with a portable analyzer.

Mainland turtles showed clearly higher blood urea nitrogen, blood sugar, and total protein than the island group. The pattern fits a richer, protein-heavy diet built on fishery waste rather than seaweed. Human food sources, in other words, are reshaping wild turtle physiology. Wildlife managers gain a measurable signal of how fishing activity leaks into the diets and bodies of a protected species, even across a short stretch of coast.
pmc-13428839:
Boonthanakorn and colleagues run a pilot trial of medical cannabis oil for stubborn muscle stiffness after spinal cord injury. Many patients keep severe spasticity, painful involuntary muscle tightening, despite top doses of standard drugs. Their 2026 study is a double blind crossover. Sixteen patients with chronic injury take a one to one THC to CBD oil and a placebo oil for a month each, in random order. Stiffness is scored by clinicians and by patients themselves.

Clinician scores on the Ashworth scale, the standard stiffness rating, did not budge with the oil at the dose used, about twelve milligrams of THC a day. Patient self ratings told a different story: stiffness scores fell clearly during the oil phase and not during placebo. No one dropped out. The authors suggest future trials test higher doses and make the patient's rating the main outcome, since that is where relief showed.
pmc-13429139:
Yongqiang Jiang and co-authors package, in a 2026 study, an experimental breast cancer drug inside a gel that melts at body temperature. The drug, called FTA, is their own aspirin-modified compound with stronger anti-tumor activity than its parent. Delivery was the problem they set out to fix. Tiny fat bubbles called liposomes first carried the drug, and a poloxamer gel then held those bubbles in place after injection near a tumor.

The plain liposomes leaked their cargo within hours, while the gel version released steadily over a longer stretch. Against breast cancer cells in dishes, the gel killed far more effectively than the free drug and slowed cell movement sharply. In tumor-bearing mice, a shot beside the tumor held it back by about 64 percent, beating both the free drug and a standard comparison drug. Body exposure lasted longer, and safety checks stayed clean.
pmc-13431239:
Doria and co-authors interviewed 30 people who had medication abortions fully through telehealth. They asked how bodily sensations shaped the choice of remote care. They also asked what made people feel the abortion had worked. Medication abortion now makes up most abortions in the United States. Fully remote supply has grown quickly since 2021.

Those interviewed judged success through embodied experience, such as cramping and bleeding patterns. Many did not rely on clinical proof alone. Stigma ran through the interviews. Many wanted to avoid sitting in a clinic in the role of abortion patient. One person summed it up as not wanting to be in the energy of that situation. Choices for telehealth were therefore partly about handling being seen. They were not only about ease or privacy at home. The authors call on providers and leaders to weigh these embodied, social, and cultural sides of care.
pmc-13432839:
Yenan Yang and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a giant protein crew that helps switch genes on, viewed from fresh sharp images of its build. The crew bridges far-off gene boosters to start sites and touches each phase of gene reading, from set-up to wrap-up. Cold-scope images have now mapped its parts and how they flex.

The review walks through jobs at each phase: building the start crew, freeing stalled readers, speeding the read, splicing the draft as it forms, and capping the end. New work shows signal flow through the crew's shape, sticky multi-grip factors, loop pullers, and droplet-like clumps. Faults in the crew tie to cancer and growth disorders. Future work aims at live speed reads and at drugs that hit its kinase parts.
pmc-13433139:
Lim, Kim, and Huh scoped the young literature on digital twins in nursing, virtual replicas of patients built from real-world data that can simulate, predict, and guide care. Following a five-stage scoping framework, two researchers searched six databases in April 2026 without year limits and ultimately included 15 studies on nursing applications.

The applications clustered into three domains: clinical care centered on patients, education and training, and decision-making and workflow management across nursing services. Clinical uses analyze multimodal patient data with artificial intelligence to build a virtual persona supporting real-time personalized care and patient self-management at the bedside. In education, twins create realistic, safe practice environments where nursing students can train without risking real patients during learning. The authors conclude digital twins hold substantial potential for predictive, personalized nursing, while noting the evidence base remains small and varied.
pmc-13433539:
Takuma Nishimaki and Keiko Sato put forth a fresh yardstick in 2026. It grades family trees built from gene data. The grade rests on how much news a tree passes along the line of descent. Picking the best tree build method has long lacked a shared scale, since each route bakes in its own growth model. Their frame first rebuilds the shared root strings of a tree.

With root strings in hand, the yardstick counts the news held as strings split and shift down each branch. Trees from rival methods can then face one count on the same scale. The authors say the count can crown the tree that best fits the flow of gene news through time. The frame aims past tree craft, at a wider read of how life stores and ships its code.
pmc-13434639:
Paola V Figueroa-Delgado and Shaul Yogev watch nerve branches being pruned in a tiny worm in 2026. Sense cells grow lush branches during a rest stage, then cut them back when growth resumes. Each branch rank turns out to need its own gene set for removal.

A kinase named SAX-1 drives removal of the second and third branch ranks, but not the fourth. It works with two partner proteins shared across species. Two traffic proteins help only with second rank branches. SAX-1 also boosts the cell eating of its own membrane during cleanup. Branch level rules may guide repair after nerve harm.
pmc-13435339:
Park and colleagues solve a supply problem for neutron science: making paracetamol, the common painkiller, with nearly every hydrogen atom swapped for deuterium, its heavier twin. Neutron scattering tests on disordered materials need grams of such fully swapped samples, yet most lab recipes make milligrams at a few sites only. Their 2026 synthesis starts from 4-aminophenol and swaps its hydrogens under acid with microwave heating.

The unstable middle product was purified by sublimation, turning it straight from solid to vapor and back, which dodged dark impurities that otherwise ruin the batch. A final acetylation step, adding the acetyl group that completes paracetamol, ran at a 75 percent yield on the batch reported. The team made more than ten grams of final product. Deuterium sat at over 93 percent of sites on average, with no site below 78 percent, pure enough for neutron work.
pmc-13437639:
Magnus Ueland Nygaard and Audun Havnen studied how beliefs about one's thinking relate to anxiety before and during soccer matches. Such metacognitive beliefs, ideas about whether worry helps or harms and whether thoughts can be controlled, drive anxiety, but sport research has barely touched them. Their 2026 survey covered 150 Norwegian players at elite and amateur levels, using standard scales for these beliefs, competitive anxiety, and depressive symptoms.

Amateurs reported more competitive anxiety than elite players, and women more than men. Positive beliefs about worry tied to bodily anxiety, the racing, tense side. Negative beliefs about worry, plus a habit of watching one's thoughts, tied to the worry part of match anxiety. The authors suggest drills challenging these beliefs, borrowed from a therapy model built on them, deserve trials in sport. They frame the findings as a first map in Norwegian soccer, not a finished case for treatment.
pmc-13438539:
Gin Hoong Lee and colleagues validated a faster way to scan muscle: reading the thigh from the front in long slices instead of many cross-sections. Muscle MRI spots swelling and fat replacement in inherited and inflammatory muscle diseases, yet the standard method eats scanner time. Their 2026 study used the new coronal protocol on 102 people, patients with either disease kind plus healthy volunteers, scoring swelling and fat by eye.

Side-by-side checks on the same thighs showed the front view agreeing with the standard view almost perfectly. In inherited disease, more fat on the scan tracked with weaker muscles and older age. In inflammatory disease, more swelling tracked with weakness. Under the microscope, fat scores matched fat seen in tissue samples, and swelling scores matched fiber death, repair, and scarring. The authors pitch the protocol as a high-throughput stand-in covering wide anatomy in less time.
pmc-13439439:
Nikita Kolosov and colleagues launch a public browser for polygenic scores, numbers that sum many small gene effects into one risk estimate, reporting in 2026. Such scores can flag high-risk people years before illness, yet comparing scores built by different groups was messy. The team benchmarked more than three thousand score models, mostly from a public catalogue, in nearly half a million FinnGen participants, a Finnish health genetics resource. Every model was placed on one shared performance scale.

Reference charts, adjusted for ancestry, let users read where a personal score falls in the population. Phenome-wide scans linked scores to hundreds of thousands of trait associations. Combining several scores improved prediction for most complex diseases. Eleven leading time-to-event models are offered interactively on the open site, aimed at easing careful clinical use of genetic risk.
pmc-13439939:
Medina-Quintana and colleagues build a fly model for human muscle disease. Their 2026 paper studies Zasp52, a protein that helps organise the Z-disc, the boundary of the sarcomere, the muscle's basic contracting unit. The human counterpart, LDB3, carries mutations that cause heart and skeletal muscle disease, but Zasp52's full role was unclear because no complete knockout existed.

The team deleted most of the Zasp52 gene in fruit flies. The mutants lived but could not fly, and their flight muscles showed badly damaged fibres. Removing a partner protein as well collapsed muscle organisation further, revealing backup overlap between the two. Engineering the fly version of a human disease mutation produced enlarged sarcomeres and stronger binding, matching a gain-of-function pattern. The authors propose the fly as a testbed for disease variants.
pmc-13440439:
Mouna Jameleddine and a large regional group report a policy dialogue on health technology assessment across the Middle East and North Africa, published in 2026. Health technology assessment weighs evidence to guide fair, value-based coverage choices, yet systems in the region vary widely in maturity. The talks, led by the global body HTAi, met in person in Tunisia in 2025 beside a regional meeting. Survey answers from experts in twelve countries joined discussion input from policymakers, practitioners, scholars, and global groups.

Participants valued the process for fairer resource allocation, openness, and access to worthwhile technologies. Named obstacles included scarce quality data, thin staffing, split governance, and weak legal footing. Top priorities were formal legal mandates for assessment work, stronger technical depth, and better health data systems. The report maps shared ground for regional cooperation.
pmc-13441839:
Alanah Pike and colleagues lay out a pilot trial testing combined brain and body training for men on hormone therapy for prostate cancer, publishing the protocol in 2026. Men on androgen deprivation often report foggy thinking beyond age-matched peers. Training thought and movement at once may protect cognition better than either alone, judging by older adult studies. The pilot aims first at acceptability and feasibility against preset progression bars, then at early effect estimates on cognition, fatigue, and quality of life.

Seventy-six men are the recruitment target. Four arms split them among combined cycling-plus-computer training, cycling only, computer training only, and a wait-list. Sessions run twice weekly for eight weeks, building toward an hour. Recruitment, adherence, harms, and a no-cognitive-harm check headline the feasibility readout. The authors present the pilot as the gatekeeper for a full trial in this population.
pmc-13442039:
Liang Yue and a large team chart where proteins sit across the human body and its cancers, assembling a mass-spectrometry atlas in a 2026 report. Gene maps alone cannot show the working molecules of each tissue. Their resource profiles more than thirteen thousand proteins across 2,856 samples, spanning fifty-eight major tissue types, hundreds of subtypes, and twenty-five cancers. States covered include fetal tissue, tumours, tissue beside tumours, and healthy adult organs.

Side-by-side protein quantities trace how tissues diverge through development and how cancers depart from their home organs. Those contrasts spotlight organ-specific toxicity risks for drugs, surface repurposed cancer drug candidates, and rank fresh therapeutic targets. The authors establish the atlas as a navigational resource for human biology and oncology, free for other teams to mine. Protein-level geography, they argue, is the missing layer between genome maps and medicine.
pmc-13442439:
Aditya Chakraborty and A. K. M. Raquibul Bashar compare five math models that flag current asthma in children in a 2026 study. Their data came from a United States phone survey call-back set for 2011 to 2020, with 9,813 children in all. Models learned from one split of the records and faced a held-out split for fair scoring.

The XGBoost model scored best overall, with an AUC value of 0.95 that marks strong sorting of cases from non-cases. A random forest model caught the most true cases, with a sensitivity score of 0.9786 that suits first-pass screening. Score fixes made the stated risks match real rates more closely on held-out data. Charts that split credit among risk factors showed which traits pushed each call. The authors frame the forest as a screen and the boosted model as the sharper judge.
pmc-13444439:
Fatou Kiné Top and colleagues characterize SARS-CoV-2 strains in brain inflammation cases in Senegal in a 2026 study. The virus mostly hits lungs and heart, yet it can invade the brain and spark encephalitis. A national encephalitis watch system fed cases from the pandemic years.

Spinal fluid checks by PCR and sequencing, plus blood antibody tests, confirmed brain entry. Gene reads named Delta-like and Eta-like variants in the encephalitis cases. Three protein changes were flagged by computer checks as likely to bend protein work, a hint at brain tropism. Among 11 patients, 30 percent held virus antibodies in blood, and 20 percent held them in spinal fluid. The authors add Senegal data to the thin map of viral brain disease.
pmc-13446039:
Tommaso Amato and colleagues report a newborn with a rare birth condition in which the bladder swells hugely, the colon stays tiny, and the gut barely moves, published in 2026. Scans before birth had already shown the swollen bladder. Gene testing found a fresh change, not inherited, in ACTG2, a gene for gut muscle protein.

After birth the baby's belly swelled and feeding failed, and scans showed wide bowel loops with a narrow colon. Surgery on day five confirmed the pattern with no physical block. Surgeons placed a stomach port and a bowel outlet, then fed the baby by vein before shifting bit by bit to gut feeding with stool recycling. Bladder drainage by tube and infection cover completed the care plan.
pmc-13446139:
Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study forming carbon-nitrogen bonds at a remote position of a molecule, a long-standing challenge in synthesis. Their trick uses light: a strained four-membered ring, methylenecyclobutane, springs open under photochemical conditions. Nitrogen partners then attach at the far end in a 1,4-pattern while a second group adds at the near end.

Using pyrazole or the solvent acetonitrile as the nitrogen source, the method produced a range of bishomoallylic amines, versatile building blocks for medicines. The same ring-opening also worked with carbon partners, including pyrroles, indoles, and naphthol, extending the idea to carbon-carbon bonds. Remote functionalization matters because chemists usually must build such patterns step by step. A light-driven ring opening that installs two groups at once shortens routes to complex molecules.
pmc-13447139:
Hilal Karabag Citlak and colleagues describe four children with Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome in a 2026 case report covering two unrelated families. The rare inherited condition is best known for thick skin on palms and soles plus severe early gum disease. These cases show a wider range, including deep infection as the first sign.

In one family, a girl presented with a large abscess deep in the hip area, while her identical twin had only mild skin and dental signs. In the other family, a boy had repeated soft tissue abscesses and years of delay after his skin changes were mistaken for psoriasis. Gene testing confirmed two different gene variants, and screening found affected siblings early. The report argues for prompt testing and checks of relatives.
pmc-13447739:
Lee, Kim, and Lee published a 2026 study on eating habits among teen athletes in Seoul. Young athletes need fuel matched to their sport, yet many eat too little. The study compared 76 track athletes with 68 athletes in weight-class sports. Food records and surveys covered intake, knowledge, and daily habits.

Both groups ate well below sports nutrition advice for energy and carbohydrates. Weight-class athletes ate higher-quality meals yet skipped breakfast and fasted more often. Those habits tied to cutting weight fast before weigh-ins and matches. Track athletes kept steadier habits but scored lower on diet quality. Both groups knew little about sports nutrition, so tailored lessons are needed. Coaches and parents share a role in fixing these habits early on.
pmc-13448239:
Hwangseon Ju and colleagues report life-threatening coughing of blood caused by a calcified catheter sheath that broke loose into a lung artery in a 2026 case study. Long-term central vein catheters grow fibrin sleeves that can stay behind when a catheter is removed. A forty-five-year-old man with kidney failure and heart failure arrived bleeding heavily from the lungs, two months after a catheter exchange.

Chest CT showed long filling defects in a left lung artery with chalky rims and a wedge of dead lung tissue beyond. The picture suggested either a calcified clot or a broken catheter tip. Emergency surgery removed the left lower lobe and cleared the artery, and tissue study proved the embolus was the retained fibrin sheath itself. Such sheaths belong on the suspect list when calcified lung clots appear in catheter patients.
pmc-13448839:
Drummond McCulloch and colleagues test in 2026 whether the many published measures of brain entropy actually agree when a psychedelic drug is given. Theory holds that psychedelics raise the entropy, or disorder, of brain activity. Thirteen earlier studies each used a different measure, so the team applied the full set to one shared dataset.

Their data came from 28 healthy volunteers with 121 brain scans taken before and after psilocybin. Five measures rose consistently with drug effects, including Shannon entropy of the spatial pattern and short-scale sample entropy. Eight of fourteen measures showed no dependable effect, and the rest behaved inconsistently. The measures also correlated weakly with each other, leading the authors to conclude that brain entropy is not one single thing these tools all capture.
pmc-13449939:
Lin Wang and a large engineering team build in 2026 a self-driving system for a single hydrostatic transmission crawler tractor, the tracked workhorses of hilly Chinese farmland. Tracked machines steer awkwardly, and earlier systems traded accuracy against stability. The team modeled the chassis motion and wrote a path-tracking controller that weighs sideways and heading errors together. They also designed a steering strategy that switches smoothly between differential steering and one-sided braking by modulating the steering cylinder.

Field trials ran at the national precision agriculture demonstration base in Beijing, over soil and cement. On curved paths the system held an average sideways deviation of 4.25 centimeters, a third better than braking-only steering, with tight consistency. Back-and-forth field passes kept row spacing errors near six centimeters. The authors judge the three-layer design, perception, decision, and execution, ready for wider use on similar terrain.
pmc-13450139:
Renz and Werner comment on a multicenter analysis of more than 1,100 distal pancreatectomy patients that established postoperative hyperamylasemia, persistently raised blood amylase after surgery, as an early warning of pancreatic fistula. Fistula, leakage from the pancreatic stump, remains the chief source of complications after this operation for left-sided pancreatic lesions.

The underlying study, by Perri and colleagues across three high-volume European centers, found the enzyme signal independently predicted both the occurrence and the severity of fistula after distal resection. The commentators stress the marker reflects genuine early pancreatic injury rather than a harmless laboratory blip after surgery. That matters more as enhanced recovery pathways push toward early drain removal, which demands reliable early risk flags to stay safe. Prior work from Verona and from the authors' own group after the larger Whipple operation points the same direction, strengthening the case for acting on the signal.
pmc-13451439:
Cappuzzello and a very large team revisit in 2026 a classic atom probe, firing helium nuclei at each other to test nuclear force models. Recent electron work on an excited state of helium-4 raised doubts about how well those forces are known. The new runs brought unmatched care in reading the shape of the scattering signal.

Their study of the full set of readings found a fair match with current nuclear force models. That match uses the same atom density maps as the electron work, so the puzzle does not break the models outright. The authors say the gap points instead to a need for better models of small open quantum systems, and for more work on this helium state.
pmc-13452239:
Xu and colleagues profiled in 2026 how antibody defenses against a wide range of respiratory germs changed across the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic reshuffled which germs circulated and whom they infected, leaving gaps and surpluses in population immunity. The team used a chip carrying pieces of 56 germ proteins to read blood antibodies in one pass.

Serum came from 287 people sampled before, during, and after the pandemic, with a second group of 175 used to confirm the patterns. Antibodies from COVID-19 exposure reacted strongly with the earlier SARS virus but barely with MERS. Protection aimed at older virus strains faded toward newer Omicron forms over time. Antibodies against several cold coronaviruses, flu B, and RSV fell, while flu A held steady and another virus rose. The authors call for ongoing blood surveillance.
pmc-13453439:
Bittner and colleagues present a 2026 educational case on medulloblastoma, a malignant brain tumor of childhood, written as a teaching tool for pathology courses. The fictional case sits inside a national framework of pathology competencies for medical education, organized into disease mechanisms, organ system pathology, and diagnostic medicine. Each section ties the case to named learning objectives.

The primary objective asks students to compare and contrast common brain tumors by location, age pattern, cause, molecular basis, appearance, and outlook. Medulloblastoma suits that exercise because its modern classification is molecular: tumor groups defined by gene pathways carry different prognoses and treatments. Working one case in depth teaches the classification habit better than lists. The format also shows teachers how to write cases that map cleanly onto national objectives, a practical template beyond this single tumor.
pmc-13454139:
Melony Dilshad, Giulio I Lampronti, Thomas D Bennett, and Xavier Moya report a porous crystal that cools and heats strongly when squeezed, with a working point tunable by gas loading. Solid state cooling with such barocaloric materials could replace gases that harm the climate. Their 2026 study uses ZIF-4, a zinc based zeolite like framework that flips structure under pressure with a large volume change.

Loaded with nitrogen, the framework gave entropy changes over 38 units and temperature swings over 10 degrees near 190 kelvin, driven by about 1 kilobar. Dried out, the same framework pointed to far larger effects, up to about 60 degrees near 137 kelvin. The catch is that guest mass must be counted honestly, the authors note. They present the findings as a benchmark for green solid refrigerants with a tunable dial.
pmc-13454839:
González-López and Selmer froze in 2026 the step where a germ's protein mill splits for reuse, and caught how a stock drug jams the split. The mill, the ribosome, must break in two at each build's end. Two helper parts drive the split. The drug fusidic acid locks one helper to the mill, and mills stall. No one had caught the stall in the act. The pair used cold scope shots to fix mills mid act in a staph germ.

The shots show the helpers pry the mill's links in joint work. The small half rolls back, and the spent code cart is nudged to the exit slot. Most stalls, though, showed the lock with no first helper yet in place. The drug bars the pair from ever forming. New jam aims may copy that bar.
pmc-13456639:
Çiray and co-authors survey Turkish nursing students about microplastic pollution in this 2026 cross-sectional study. Microplastics are tiny plastic fragments now found throughout the environment, and nurses will be expected to teach communities about such health risks. The study included 356 undergraduates sampled across all study years between March and June 2023, using scales for microplastic awareness and for overall environmental literacy.

Average awareness scored about 23 points and environmental literacy about 85 points on their respective scales, and the two measures rose together in a positive correlation. Students who had heard of microplastics before, or who wanted environmental education, scored higher on both. Even so, a considerable share had never encountered the topic. Yet 94.4 percent still showed high environmental literacy overall in the survey results. The authors say curricula should close that gap.
pmc-13456739:
Feng and Zhang ask whether a heart health score tracks with bacterial vaginosis, a vaginal condition caused by an upset in the bacteria mix. The score, Life's Simple 7, grades smoking, activity, diet, weight, blood pressure, blood fats, and blood sugar. Their 2026 study uses a national survey from 2001 to 2004. It covers 1,203 women aged 18 to 49, of whom 382 had the condition, with data weighted to stand for the wider population.

Women with the condition scored lower on the heart health scale than women without it. Each one point rise in score came with about a tenth lower odds of the condition in adjusted models. Women above the cutoff score had far lower odds than women below it. The dose pattern was smooth and steady across subgroups. Because the survey captures one moment, the authors stress the link is an association, not proof of cause.
pmc-13457039:
Julia Belone Lopes and four colleagues review, in a 2026 article, care for older adults whose lung cancer has spread to the brain. Brain spread is a leading source of suffering in non-small cell lung cancer, and better body-wide drugs mean more patients live long enough to face it. Older patients are scarce in the trials that set practice, so clinicians often extrapolate.

The review argues that birthdays mislead. Frailty, other illnesses, thinking problems, and thin physical reserves vary wildly at any age and should drive choices instead. Structured geriatric assessment can sort who tolerates aggressive care. The authors then weigh brain-directed options, from focused radiation to surgery, against modern systemic drugs that cross into the brain. Their through-line is personalization: match the plan to the person's reserves and goals, not to an age cutoff.
pmc-13457539:
Yuvnik Trada and co-authors systematically reviewed whether scans taken halfway through radiotherapy can predict how head and neck cancers will respond. Their 2026 meta-analysis gathered studies from 2005 to 2023 that measured imaging features from CT, MRI, or PET scans during treatment for these cancers. The key question was whether changes during treatment predict local tumor control better than measurements taken before treatment started or single mid-treatment snapshots.

Forty-one studies covering 1,654 patients met the criteria, and seventeen studies with 612 patients supplied data for pooled analysis. Measures of change during treatment performed best, reaching a pooled accuracy score of 0.796 on the standard curve measure used, ahead of both baseline and single mid-treatment values. Diffusion MRI changes and PET measures of tumor volume and activity were the most consistently predictive, supporting treatment plans that adapt mid-course.
pmc-13459239:
Jiao Yi and co-authors studied how often new mothers develop diastasis recti, a separation of the two front abdominal muscles along the midline after pregnancy. Their 2026 study compared 594 women diagnosed with the condition after births between February 2023 and February 2024 against 205 postpartum women without it. The team measured the widest separation point and used statistical modeling to find which factors raised the risk on their own.

The condition appeared in 56.6 percent of the 1,050 women in the overall sample examined. The widest gap sat at navel level most often, and that pattern grew stronger as severity increased across mild, moderate, and severe groups. Having given birth before and C section delivery both correlated with the condition. Interaction analysis singled out C section as the strong independent contributor. Vaginal delivery showed no such increase, so the authors suggest controlling unnecessary C sections could reduce cases.
pmc-13459639:
Qiman Zeng and co-authors compared wild and farmed Angelica sinensis, a prized Chinese medicinal herb, to learn why wild roots are considered superior as wild stocks run scarce. Their 2026 study paired chemical profiling of the roots with gene-expression analysis, hunting for the compounds and genes that differ between mountainside and cultivated plants. The approach links what the plant contains to the genetic switches controlling its chemistry, knowledge growers need if farming is to close the quality gap.

Chemistry separated the two clearly: 131 metabolites differed significantly, concentrated in fatty acid metabolism, amino acid production, and secondary compounds, and wild plants held higher levels of these substances. Gene analysis found 18,993 differentially expressed genes. Nine structural genes, including PAL, 4CL, and CCR from the phenylpropanoid pathway, were flagged as the core drivers of the chemical differences. These genes are breeding and cultivation targets, the authors say.
pmc-13460139:
Jian-Di Li leads a team that mapped in 2026 the burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis in China, India, and Russia using Global Burden of Disease 2023 estimates. The three countries hold the world's largest counts of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant cases. Trend, decomposition, and forecasting methods separated how rates moved over thirty years and what drove the movement.

China's age-standardized rate for multidrug-resistant disease fell sharply while India's and Russia's climbed, driven mainly by epidemiological change. For the extensively resistant form, recent burden eased in China and Russia yet stalled in India, and forecasts see prevalence rising again in India and Russia. Men carried more disease everywhere, with peak ages differing by country. The authors call for country-specific strategies plus joint action.
pmc-13461439:
Huang and co-authors probed a 2026 mouse study of kidney damage in obesity, centred on podocytes, the cells that wrap the kidney's filtering units. An enzyme called acid sphingomyelinase drives a fat signalling pathway already tied to obesity related kidney disease. The question was whether it also triggers pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death.

Mice engineered to overproduce the enzyme in podocytes showed stronger inflammasome activation and more pyroptosis on a high fat diet, Huang found. Blocking the enzyme, the inflammasome, or the pore forming protein gasdermin D each eased the kidney injury in obese mice. In isolated podocytes, a fatty acid mimicked the effect and jammed the cell's waste clearing system. Deleting the enzyme gene protected the cells instead.
pmc-13461539:
Marta Waliszewska-Prosół leads a 2026 study of brain responses to sounds in people with different forms of migraine, tested between attacks. The team recorded two brain waves, called N200 and P300, that show how fast the brain notices and sorts information. They compared migraine with aura, migraine without aura, and aura without headache. Scores for disability, sleep, anxiety, and mood were collected alongside the brain tests.

The study held 173 people, including 55 healthy controls, and all patients also had a brain scan. Every migraine group showed slower brain responses than controls, with the aura group slowest of all. People without aura also had weaker P300 signals. In the group with aura but no headache, brain measures tracked closely with anxiety, low mood, and poor sleep. That pattern points to a strong link between mental health and brain processing in that group.
pmc-13461839:
Toshiaki Ito asks, in a 2026 commentary, where robots add value in keyhole heart surgery. The prompt is a report of two patients who had valve surgery and a bypass graft through one right-sided approach under the arm, using a robot. Doing both from the right side was long thought to need a full chest opening or a second cut. Ito calls the work a proof of what is possible.

Still, he presses a wider point. For routine valve work, skilled teams reach fine results through small chest cuts with long tools, without robot cost and complexity. Sewing a valve ring, trimming leaflets, or fitting a valve sits within normal human skill. The robot's edge, he suggests, shows where tasks near or exceed what hands and tools can do, such as combining procedures through awkward access. Value should be judged case by case, not assumed from the machine's presence.
pmc-13462039:
Mohamad Bakir and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how to model the harsh setting cancers find when they spread to bone. Lesions are not just tumor cells among bone cells. Low oxygen, acidity, hard mineral, pressure, and poor blood flow all shield the cancer, help it sleep and wake, and blunt drugs. Simple cultures copy only parts of that setting, often making drugs look better than they are.

The review tours richer platforms: mineral-coated scaffolds, mixed cultures, living bone pieces outside the body, mini tissue models, bone-on-a-chip devices, and animal and computer models. Rather than ranking by complexity, the authors propose picking the platform that fits the question. They show how tuning oxygen, acidity, pressure, stiffness, and vessel flow can guide treatments aimed at the niche. The goal: models mirroring lesion states closely enough to predict which patients and drugs do well.
pmc-13462839:
Samia Allaoua Chelloug and colleagues present, in a 2026 computing study, a light data-cleaning method for sensor networks that work underwater or underground. Such networks lose packets, drain batteries fast, and resend readings, so data arrive with holes and duplicates. Their hybrid method pairs a Kalman filter, which estimates missing values from the stream's pattern, with a sliding window check spotting repeats by distance between readings.

Simulations modeled harsh links losing twenty to forty percent of packets, across 1,200 sensor nodes and twenty thousand recordings. The method estimated missing values with low error, filtered out a fifth of packets as redundant, and lifted delivery success to 88 percent. Network life stretched to over twice the best rival method, while average delay stayed near eleven milliseconds. No training data or cloud help is needed. The authors target deep-sea observatories, buried infrastructure, and mines where batteries cannot be swapped.
pmc-13463639:
Han and co-authors tested in 2026 whether SH003 can fight colorectal cancer by blocking two immune checkpoints at once. SH003 is a three-herb formula from traditional East Asian medicine. Checkpoints are brakes cancers use to hide from the immune system; PD-L1 and CD47 are two of them. The team used patient-derived organoids, miniature tumors grown from patient tissue, plus cell lines and a mouse model.

SH003 slowed organoid growth and cut their energy and proliferation markers. It lowered both PD-L1 and CD47 by reining in a growth-driving protein called c-Myc. Inflammatory signals such as VEGF and TNF-alpha fell too. In dishes, T cells killed more cancer cells when SH003 was present. They also produced more of the activating messenger IL-2. In mice, the formula shrank tumors and lowered both checkpoints. It drew in more CD8 killer T cells as well.
pmc-13463939:
Alfaqeeh and co-authors mined a national Indonesian family survey from 2014 on stunting. Stunting is the growth failure from chronic undernutrition that leaves children far shorter than they should be. Their 2026 analysis covered 4,570 children under five. A child counted as stunted when height fell more than two standard steps below the age reference. Child, mother, and vaccination factors were weighed together.

About 24 of every 100 children were stunted. Low birth weight stood out sharply, roughly tripling the odds against normal-weight newborns. Incomplete immunization raised the odds by about half. Children of underweight mothers faced about double the odds. Children of overweight mothers fared better, as did children whose mothers received tetanus shots in pregnancy. Older toddlers were far less likely to be stunted than infants. The authors point to maternal nutrition, full vaccination, and good early feeding as the levers that matter.
pmc-13464039:
Arkadeep Dhali, Jyotirmoy Biswas, Ali Shan Hafeez, Sajjad Ahmed Khan, Dushyant Singh Dahiya and Saikat Mandal published this 2026 study of United States death records. They focused on records listing both pancreatic cancer and cerebrovascular disease, conditions such as stroke. Each disease is well studied alone, but deaths naming both together had not been tracked. The authors examined national mortality data from 1999 to 2024 and modelled future trends.

They counted 22,085 deaths among adults that recorded both conditions. The age-adjusted rate rose from 0.32 to 0.56 deaths per 100,000 people over the period studied, with a sharp turn upward after 2013. Men had higher rates than women, and non-Hispanic Black or African American individuals had the highest rates of any group. The authors stress that death-certificate patterns describe populations, not any one patient's stroke risk. They call for studies with linked clinical data to explain the rise.
pmc-13464439:
Romano and co-authors review how starter yeasts make or break fermented fruit drinks. Their 2026 paper surveys how Saccharomyces yeasts, and non-Saccharomyces ones, are chosen and used for juices and fruit wines, a sector pulled by health-conscious consumers and demand for low-alcohol products. Yeasts, the authors stress, decide much of a beverage's sensory, chemical, and functional character.

The review walks the pipeline: isolating candidate strains, screening them by phenotype, and identifying them precisely with genomic and metabolomic tools. Inoculation strategy gets detailed treatment, comparing single strains, sequential additions, and co-fermentation for their effects on quality and complexity. A final thread covers re-evaluating fruit processing by-products as fermentation feedstocks. The authors frame modern strain selection, increasingly engineered rather than merely found, as the route to sustainable and diverse new beverages.
pmc-13464539:
Swetha Kodhandaraman and three co-authors present FedAD, a learning system that trains medical image models across hospitals without pooling patient data. Three walls block such work: privacy law, scarce expert labels, and scans that shift style between sites. Their design joins federated training, self-teaching, and domain-proofing in one frame.

One part of the system splits image traits into meaning that travels and style that stays local, using a rule that keeps the two apart without a fight between models. A second part, a teacher-student pairing, adjusts pressure as the shared model settles or wobbles. Tests on public medical sets beat prior methods on unseen sites. Hospitals gain a path to shared AI that keeps records home.
pmc-13464939:
Hetta and colleagues review in this 2026 article the full landscape of point-of-care testing for SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, meaning tests run beside the patient rather than in a central laboratory. Their structured search covered studies published from January 2020 to January 2026 across three major databases.

The review sorts the technology into five families. Molecular tests, including rapid PCR, a constant-temperature method called LAMP, and CRISPR-based assays, deliver the highest accuracy and increasingly work outside laboratories. Antigen tests trade some accuracy for speed and low cost, performing best at high viral loads. Antibody tests serve mainly to map past infection. Biosensors and AI-assisted readers look promising but remain mostly prototypes. Their conclusion is that no single format wins everywhere, so the modalities should be deployed as complementary tools.
pmc-13465039:
Yun and co-authors told in 2026 how a routine gallbladder operation at another hospital nearly killed a 45-year-old woman.
