Such licences aim to improve access for public health needs, yet hard proof of market effects has been scarce. The team used sales and price data from 11 countries for 2002 to 2022.

They focused on 21 HIV drugs that faced at least one such licence. After licences began, retail and hospital sales rose and prices fell by clear margins. Readers should note the study cannot rule out added access through public imports or aid supply.
pmc-13534639:
Ruofei Liu and colleagues identify in 2026 RAD54L as a coordinator of DNA repair in the nucleolus, the cell zone that builds ribosome parts. Heavy gene copying there creates stress and break risk for ribosomal DNA. Cell tests tracked where the protein goes after breaks were cut at those sites.

The protein sits in the nucleolus normally and rushes to repair caps after damage. Without it, repair marks lingered, damage signals rose, and faulty nuclei formed more often. Hybrid RNA-DNA loops also aided repair setup, so the work maps a key guard of genome stability.
pmc-13534739:
Muhammad Irfan and colleagues apply in 2026 machine learning to molecular graphs of two ring compounds used in industry. Number summaries drawn from a graph can predict material traits, yet a fair comparison for these rings was missing. The team computed several indices based on atom links and nearby links for both structures.

Those indices fed models that link molecular shape to measured physical traits. Learning-based fits then judged how strongly each summary tracks real property data across both rings. Readers gain a fast way to estimate traits and a base for models of larger polymer networks in future work.
pmc-13535739:
Biel Garcias and colleagues sequence in 2026 Klebsiella germs from European hedgehogs and compare them with human hospital strains from the same region. The germ causes hospital infections and resists many drugs, and urban hedgehogs meet people and livestock often. Whole-genome reads mapped strain types, resistance genes, and mobile DNA rings.

Hedgehogs carried high resistance levels, including a key enzyme that defeats last-line drugs. Two globally spread hospital clones appeared in both hedgehogs and humans, and shared plasmid types suggest gene spread across settings. Direct transmission was not proven, yet wildlife monitoring is urged.
pmc-13536539:
Veronika Hatlova and colleagues test in 2026 knotless scleral fixation with a durable suture material in rabbit eyes after lens removal. When natural lens support is missing, implants must be stitched to the eye wall, and early hold strength matters. Two knotless patterns were placed in each eye and pull strength was measured over 30 days.

Both patterns needed more force to pull out as days passed, showing growing early stabilisation. The Z pattern ranged slightly higher than the chain pattern across time points. Findings are exploratory yet support further preclinical and clinical checks of both methods.
pmc-13536639:
Ross P. Wohlgemuth and colleagues test in 2026 whether collagenase injections can clear muscle scarring in a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Scar tissue stiffens muscle and blocks repair, and it is often viewed as hard to reverse. Enzyme shots went into leg muscles of normal and dystrophy-model mice.

The enzyme digested scar matrix well, yet muscle grew weaker with bleeding within a day and a thickened support layer after a week. No functional gain appeared in strength or lab tests. The team urges scar-specific enzymes plus paired therapy work in future trials.
pmc-13538239:
Joseph Amihere Ackah and colleagues compare long-standing high blood pressure with pregnancy-induced high blood pressure in a 2026 systematic review. Both conditions complicate many pregnancies and threaten mothers and babies, yet their timing and course differ. Searches of three databases gathered observational studies, screened for quality and combined in narrative form. Outcomes, risk factors, and diagnostic tools were contrasted across the two conditions.

Major harms in both groups included fetal death inside the womb, slowed fetal growth, low birth weight, and newborn and maternal deaths. Pregnancy-induced pressure often worsened suddenly and severely without close watching, while long-standing pressure favored early steady surveillance. Older age and other illnesses raised risk in both groups. Ultrasound flow checks helped early risk sorting. The authors urge tailored monitoring by condition type.
pmc-13538339:
Shilin You and co-authors review oncolytic virus therapy for liver cancer centered on hepatocellular carcinoma in a 2026 synthesis. Engineered viruses infect and burst tumor cells while sparing normal tissue and waking anti-tumor immunity. Lab and clinical studies across five virus families were weighed for benefit, safety, and delivery hurdles. Special attention went to viruses rebuilt to carry immune boosters or checkpoint blockers.

Herpes and vaccinia viruses showed strong benefit and safety signals, while rebuilt adenovirus and Newcastle disease platforms also showed promise. Better engineering and delivery lifted tumor targeting and immune activation. Standing hurdles include host antiviral defenses clearing the virus, weak delivery to tumors, and choosing the right patients. The authors present virus therapy as a rising partner for standard liver cancer care.
pmc-13538539:
Solomon Oyebisi and colleagues test oil palm stem fibers as concrete reinforcement in a 2026 materials study. Natural fibers promise greener building while easing resource strain. Palm midrib fibers, untreated or soaked in lime solution at varied strengths and times, replaced small shares of concrete volume. Workability plus compression, splitting, bending, bond, and rupture tests ran after curing at three ages.

Lime soaking at a mid strength for a full day gave fibers their best pulling strength. Workability dipped slightly as fiber share rose. Treated fiber lifted compression and splitting strength at low dosage and bending strength at a slightly higher one. Bond strength and rupture resistance beat untreated fiber versions after a month of curing. The authors endorse treated palm fiber for quality sustainable concrete.
pmc-13538639:
Julie Gosez and colleagues model brain electric fields from scalp stimulation in obsessive-compulsive disorder in a 2026 patient-specific study. Response to the stimulation varies widely in treatment-resistant cases. Forty-two trial patients who received active stimulation had personal head models built from scans, and symptom change was scored on a standard scale with responders clearing a set threshold. Current direction and strength maps were compared voxel by voxel.

Greater inward current in two frontal zones tracked with symptom improvement. Outward current in a lower frontal zone also linked to gains. Field strength alone showed no such links, spotlighting direction as the active ingredient. The authors argue that tailoring stimulation to personal anatomy and current direction could sharpen results in psychiatric care.
pmc-13540839:
Zijiao Zhang and six colleagues review, in a 2026 meta-analysis, whether machine learning predicts a first stroke in community primary care better than older statistical models. Stroke prevention depends on spotting high-risk people early in ordinary clinics.

Forty-three studies holding ninety-three models met the criteria. Traditional Cox regression was the commonest approach, and its pooled accuracy matched or beat the machine learning entries, including random forests and gradient boosting. Three quarters of the studies carried a high risk of bias, and applicability to real community care raised concerns in a fifth. The authors conclude that machine learning's clinical value here remains unproven.
pmc-13540939:
Michelle C Paulus and colleagues compare two protein dosing schemes in 2026. The patients were critically ill adults in intensive care. One scheme set protein by total body weight. The other set it by fat-free mass. Body impedance scans measured that mass. Weight-based dosing may overshoot in heavier patients.

Six hundred twenty patients took part, half in each era. The main outcome was death within ninety days. Mortality did not differ in a clear way between schemes. Fat-free-mass dosing linked to shorter intensive care stays. It also linked to fewer ventilator days. The weight-based era showed faster muscle loss. Big baseline gaps urge caution, the authors note.
pmc-13541239:
Hayden Carlton and eight colleagues describe, in a 2026 engineering study, a radiofrequency head coil that heats magnetic nanoparticles inside brain tumors while fitting inside a magnetic particle imaging scanner. Pairing the imaging with the heating promises better treatment planning and dose control than either alone.

The coil was designed for a human head, a uniform field along its centre, and scanner compatibility. Bench tests produced fields above the design target and heated tumor phantoms to therapeutic temperatures. In a prepared canine cadaver with particles implanted in the brain, imaging signal differences matched later temperature rises at the same spots. A computer simulation of a human glioma treatment suggested clinical feasibility.
pmc-13543539:
In a 2026 study, Megha Mehrotra and colleagues tested whether the drug alpelisib, which blocks the growth-signalling protein PI3K, can make cisplatin chemotherapy work better in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. This cancer is usually found late and often becomes platinum-resistant. The team used tumour cells grown from patients' abdominal fluid, established cell lines, and patient-derived tumours in mice, and profiled mutations to learn which cancers respond.

The combination killed cancer cells in about a third of patient samples, and most responders carried extra copies of the PIK3CA gene even without mutations in it. Certain mutant forms of the p53 protein proved to switch PIK3CA production up after cisplatin exposure, handing the combination its opening. In mice, the pairing halted tumours carrying one such p53 mutant but not tumours with normal p53. Mutation type, not just the target gene, may therefore decide who benefits.
pmc-13543639:
Tayyeba Ali and colleagues published a 2026 study of destroying para-chlorophenol in water using ultraviolet light and persulfate, a strong oxidiser. The toxic chemical serves in preservatives and as a building block for farm chemicals. Three setups were compared: light alone, light with persulfate, and light with persulfate plus iron. Breakdown speed, the radicals responsible, the products formed, and the cost and toxicity of the leftovers were assessed.

Light alone removed well under seventy percent of the chemical in twenty-five minutes. Adding persulfate pushed removal to ninety percent in acid water and complete removal at neutral and alkaline levels. The iron version achieved complete removal even in acid conditions within the same time. Mineralisation to harmless end products ran deeper with iron, reaching about eighty-six percent over two hours. Natural organic matter and common ions slowed the process, and software judged the breakdown products' toxicity.
pmc-13545139:
Miriam Casares-Lopez and co-authors reported in 2026 on whether tear film tests agree when students new to the task perform them. Sixty-one young volunteers, most of them women, had tear volume and break-up time measured by manual, automated, and fluorescein methods. Symptoms were recorded with a standard eye discomfort questionnaire.

Agreement between the methods proved poor, except that the manual and fluorescein readings matched each other moderately well. Repeating a measurement three times did not improve consistency, and symptom scores barely tracked any test result. The authors caution that automated readings cannot replace careful clinical judgment, especially when examiners have little experience.
pmc-13546539:
Yang Xu and co-authors studied in 2026 a chromosome-packaging protein called NCAPH in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer with few effective drug targets. Across several public datasets, NCAPH levels ran high in tumors and tracked with worse features and poorer survival. Single-cell data helped show which cell types carried the protein.

Silencing NCAPH in two esophageal cancer cell lines cut their growth, colony formation, movement, and invasion, and tumors grown from silenced cells stayed smaller in mice. Molecular profiling pointed to the Wnt and beta-catenin signaling pathway, a growth route that quieted after silencing. The authors suggest NCAPH could serve both as a warning marker and as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13547339:
Sruthi Sundharram and co-authors went beyond yes-or-no lie detection in 2026, asking whether brain and body signals can reveal what kind of secret a person is hiding. Ten volunteers took a concealed information test while dense brainwave recordings and body measures like skin response and temperature were captured. The hidden items belonged to three classes: an object, a person, or a place.

Machine learning that fused both signal types classified the hidden category with about 94 percent accuracy, far above brainwaves alone or body signals alone. Eight well-chosen electrodes matched the full headset, with the most useful sites over the front of the head, matching regions tied to recognition and attention. The authors frame the pilot as a step toward wearable tools for forensic screening.
pmc-13548539:
Tomasz Grzyb and Justyna Szulc screen six soil bacteria as possible helpers for farm crops, in a 2026 genomic and safety assessment. The strains came from fields after maize harvest, and earlier bench work showed they could promote plant growth. The authors read their genomes for nutrient and stress traits, enzymes that break down crop residue, chemical factories inside the cells, and any signs of danger to people.

Each strain carried well over a thousand growth-promotion genes, shaped strongly by how closely the strains were related. One Paenibacillus strain held the richest enzyme set for digesting plant fiber. Safety screening flagged one Bacillus cereus strain as toxin-producing and unfit for use. Two strains showed no virulence factors or resistance genes at all, marking them as the leading candidates for farm preparations once living tests confirm the predictions.
pmc-13549339:
Andrey A. Sapronov, Dmitry E. Doronkin, and Jan-Dierk Grunwaldt use a smart search algorithm to tune the theory behind X-ray absorption spectra until calculations match experiment, in a 2026 methods paper. The near-edge part of these spectra reveals an atom's oxidation state and surroundings, and two established programs simulate it, yet their settings are usually adjusted by hand and eye. The team let Bayesian optimization, which learns from each trial, adjust both packages.

Tests used the K-edge spectra of nickel, iron, and palladium metals, scored by several different similarity measures between theory and measurement. Automated tuning improved the match for both simulation codes. The authors present the approach as a way to make spectrum interpretation less artisanal and more reproducible for catalysts, batteries, and other materials where local atomic structure decides performance.
pmc-13550439:
Julie Bania and colleagues survey urinary tract infections among women's-health patients in Northeast India, in a 2026 tracking study. Nearly nine hundred women took part. Their urine samples were cultured by standard methods. The bacteria found were then challenged with antibiotics under current guidelines. About thirty-one percent of participants had confirmed infections.

E. coli caused nearly two thirds of cases, followed by Klebsiella. Risk clustered with being eighteen to thirty-nine, a previous infection, high blood pressure, earlier antibiotic use, and pregnancy, each raising the odds. The main bacteria resisted several common antibiotics heavily, including two widely used classes. They stayed sensitive to fosfomycin, certain injectables, and stronger reserve drugs. The authors push for local resistance tracking and tighter prescribing habits, so treatment matches the region's actual patterns.
pmc-13550539:
Hao Hu and colleagues redesign a compact electron injector so its beam stays even from the first pulse to the last, in a 2026 accelerator engineering paper. The injector feeds a high-power terahertz free-electron laser. At high duty cycles the beam itself drains the accelerating fields unevenly. That effect, transient beam loading, spoils energy and timing uniformity across the pulse train.

Their fix splits the radio-frequency power feeds so the two accelerating structures can be timed independently, and makes the first cavity's coupling adjustable. A many-objective genetic algorithm then tuned four settings jointly: injection time, radio phase, coupling, and the delay between structures. Single-knob tuning could not balance energy and phase together, but the global search settled the macropulse near fourteen million electron volts with minimal spread. Simulations support the design for similar compact machines.
pmc-13550639:
Jiangbo Wang and Jiafeng Wu published a 2026 study of how population has shifted inside flood-prone parts of China's Pearl River Delta from 1985 to 2024. Most earlier work looked only at the 100-year flood, the event with a one percent yearly chance. The authors mapped six flood levels, from frequent 10-year events to a rare 1,000-year event, and matched them to population data and flood control upgrades.

Outside the mildest scenario, population grew fastest in the extreme high-risk zone, and growth inside risk zones outpaced the region as a whole. Eight cities besides Shenzhen showed the same pattern in high-risk areas. The authors argue that prevention planning should differ by city and flood level rather than treating the delta as uniform.
pmc-13551839:
Zakaria Zakariaei, with six colleagues, published a 2026 study of a parasite and obsessive-compulsive disorder in northern Iran. The parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, can reach the brain and shift its chemistry. That trait fuels a theory that infection may play a role in the disorder. The team compared 120 patients with 135 healthy controls. Groups matched on age and sex. Blood tests checked for antibodies, and a DNA test hunted the parasite itself.

Long-term antibody rates were nearly the same in both groups. No one showed signs of fresh infection. Parasite DNA turned up slightly more in patients, yet the gap was not firm. Antibody rates rose with age in both groups. The team concludes that latent infection does not drive this disorder here.
pmc-13556039:
Qiong Shen and four colleagues compared pumpkin seeds with and without hulls in 2026, looking for what makes the seed coat differ in Cucurbita moschata. Hull-less seeds are easier to eat and trade is growing, yet most earlier work covered a sister species. The team examined one hulled wild line and three hull-less mutant lines at two points during seed development, measuring anatomy, chemistry, and gene activity.

The hulled coat formed five distinct layers, while mutant coats stayed thin and papery with only two layers present. Chemistry diverged from the sister species: mutant coats held more pectin, and three lignin-building genes switched on late rather than fading. Some features matched the relative, others did not. Breeders gain a clearer map of which coat traits to select when developing hull-less varieties of this species.
pmc-13558339:
Wei Kang and a large group of colleagues compared in 2026 two blood-thinning strategies for clots caused by cancer. Patients can take daily oral anticoagulant pills or receive heparin injections, and guidelines leave room for either. Their systematic review searched three databases to mid 2025 and pooled results at the six-month mark that guidelines emphasise, separating randomised trials from observational cohorts.

Across five trials and sixteen cohorts covering nearly fifty thousand patients, the oral drugs cut clot recurrence by roughly a third compared with injections. Major bleeding was not clearly higher in the trial data and looked slightly lower in the cohorts, while death rates matched between strategies. The authors read the balance as favouring pills for most patients, with individual bleeding risk still guiding the final choice.
pmc-13559139:
Sui, Wang, and Liu published a 2026 study on a protein that worsens pneumonia lung injury in children. Childhood pneumonia resists control as germs grow drug-resistant and inflammation rages. Single-cell data flagged a protein, FBXO11, running high in lung immune cells. The team tested its role in mouse and cell models of the disease.

Silencing FBXO11 eased lung injury in the mouse pneumonia model. The protein pushed immune cells toward a fiery self-destruct mode. It did so by chewing up a brake protein that calms that mode. A plant compound curbed the fiery death in their lab tests. Aiming at FBXO11 may calm lung inflammation in sick children. Two inflammasome paths fed the damage the protein helped drive.
pmc-13560439:
Gyu Tae Park and colleagues test whether a cardiac surgery program run by a single surgeon, operating without another surgeon assisting, matches outcomes of team-operated surgery. Their 2026 propensity-matched study reviews adults operated at Chung-Ang University Hospital between September 2016 and August 2021. A staffing shortage era, when one surgeon worked alone, is compared with an earlier team era.

Matching produced seventy-nine patients in each group. Major adverse events, including death, stroke, new atrial fibrillation, and low cardiac output showed no clear difference. Kidney injury, intensive care stay, hospital days, and bypass times also matched. The one clear gap was speed: team operations finished in a median of three hundred minutes against three hundred seventy-nine for solo work in the reported times. The authors call solo practice feasible on short-term outcomes while warning that their study's limits demand cautious reading.
pmc-13562339:
Ahmed ElZefzafy and Abdul Wasy Zia test whether patterned lattice materials could improve the plastic insert used in artificial knee joints. The insert sits between metal parts and wears down over time, partly because standard inserts are not matched to each body. Their 2026 study compares three lattice designs, called gyroid, square anti-chiral, and triangular, against a solid insert. Computer models predicted stress and bending, while printed samples were squeezed and loaded repeatedly on a testing machine.

The triangular design carried loads up to 20 kN, bent by 2.3 mm without failing, and weighed about a third less than the solid part. Such lattices spring back after impact and let engineers tune stiffness for different body weights. The authors argue the approach could make knee implants safer and longer lasting.
pmc-13563739:
Kyung Han Kim and twelve colleagues test whether adding a verticalising robot to inpatient therapy speeds walking recovery after stroke. Regaining gait and trunk control early shapes independence. Their 2026 randomised trial enrolled patients in the subacute phase with severe walking impairment. Everyone received conventional rehabilitation five times a week for four weeks. The study group trained on the R-BoT PLUS device, which holds patients upright and rehearses stepping, for twenty sessions of thirty minutes.

The robot group improved more on a scale of walking independence, and the gap survived checks at the end of treatment and three months later. Trunk control gains matched the control group, yet patients starting with the weakest trunks gained most from the robot in a subgroup analysis. Thinking, balance, daily activities, and leg strength rose in both groups alike. The authors back the device as an add-on for gait, not a replacement.
pmc-13563839:
Annabel van der Weide and six colleagues lay out the protocol for a trial asking whether brain imaging can replace the tuning of brain stimulators in Parkinson's disease. Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus eases motor swings, but picking contacts and settings by bedside testing takes hours. Their 2026 protocol describes a single-centre randomised trial of 132 patients, split between imaging-guided programming and the threshold-based review. Assessors who score the outcomes will not know which arm each patient sits in.

The imaging arm builds a 3D model from MRI and post-surgery CT, simulating which tissue each contact would activate. The main measure is change in a motor score, off medication, six months after programming. Secondary measures cover daily life, side effects, satisfaction, care use, and how long programming takes. The design tests non-inferiority: imaging need only match the standard to win on speed and stability.
pmc-13569839:
Wael A. Mahdi, Adel Alhowyan and Ahmad J. Obaidullah published this 2026 study on a hidden weakness in computer models that predict chemical toxicity. Standard tests shuffle compounds randomly into training and test sets, letting near-duplicates appear in both, which inflates scores. The authors re-ran toxicity modelling on 1,792 organic molecules under a stricter protocol that holds back whole shape families. They tested whether invariance methods, which force models to ignore family quirks, restore performance.

Baseline neural models that scored around 0.91 to 0.94 on random splits dropped sharply once shape overlap was removed. Invariance methods, including invariant risk minimization and contrastive alignment, reduced the cross-family error and steadied the pattern of mistakes. Inspection of the learned features showed cluster-specific signals fading while toxic structure survived. The authors argue that trustworthy prediction needs both family-aware testing and invariance built into the model design.
pmc-13571339:
Javier Escober-Torres and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a 17-year-old woman whose failing thoracic duct caused both milky fluid around the heart and casts blocking her airways. The thoracic duct is the main lymph drainage channel. She arrived in obstructive shock with a large fluid collection squeezing the heart, and emergency drainage confirmed the fluid was chyle, leaked lymph.

A surgical window in the heart sac was needed after repeat collapse. Worsening breathing led to a camera exam that found chyle casts in the bronchi, a condition called plastic bronchitis. Lymph imaging showed widened lymph vessels without one clear leak, and blocking the thoracic duct through the skin resolved everything. The case argues for early lymph system checks in complex chyle disease.
pmc-13572339:
Wenxiang Liu and colleagues profile, in a 2026 multi-omics study, mouse skin inflamed by a chemical that mimics atopic dermatitis, the eczema driven by a leaky skin barrier plus immune imbalance. Gene, protein, and metabolite layers were measured together and woven into networks to find changes that agree across all three.

Inflamed skin thickened and filled with T cells, macrophages, and mast cells. Barrier building programs broke down across layers, with two molecules, FLG2 and KRT6B, sitting at the network center. Energy and fat-handling pathways shifted in step with barrier genes. The coordinated map gives eczema researchers shared targets where barrier repair and metabolic correction might meet.
pmc-13576139:
Wanbin Li, Jiayun Shao, and Yueqi Zhu follow stroke risk in older Chinese adults in a 2026 longitudinal study. High blood pressure, body fat, and low mood often travel together, yet they are usually studied one at a time. The team used the national CHARLS survey, which tracked adults from 2011 to 2020.

Among 15,992 people aged 45 and over who began stroke-free, 1,246 first strokes were reported during follow-up. High blood pressure carried the largest risk rise, at 1.80 times the baseline rate. Diabetes, heart problems, higher body mass, and larger waist size each added risk. Depressive symptom scores also mattered: every extra point nudged risk up slightly. The authors caution that strokes were self-reported and body measures had gaps, so the links describe patterns rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13576239:
Cristiana Almeida and three colleagues count the cost of fainting workups at a private hospital in Lisbon in a 2026 study. Syncope, a brief loss of consciousness, sends many people to emergency care, and testing habits vary widely. The team reviewed every case through 2023 and costed care patient by patient.

The cohort held 375 patients with a mean age of 49.4 years. A cause was found in 41.1 percent, with reflex fainting the most common, while 58.1 percent stayed unexplained. Total cost reached nearly 662,000 euros, a mean of 1,765 euros per patient, and diagnostic tests took 63.3 percent of the spend. Age over 80, male sex, more illnesses, and a heart cause each raised costs. The authors estimate guideline-based testing could have saved about 214 euros per patient in the emergency phase.
pmc-13578439:
Samantha Castro Teixeira, Geraldo da Rocha Castelar-Pinheiro, and Jaqueline de Carvalho Rodrigues study anxiety in rheumatoid arthritis. Their 2026 study, set in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, asks how anxiety, body felt symptoms, and coping weave together. Ninety seven patients at a public clinic filled out scales for anxiety, physical symptoms with no clear cause, and ways of coping. Most were women, with an average age near sixty.

More than four in five showed severe anxiety symptoms. Most leaned on emotion based coping, such as seeking comfort or reframing, over problem solving steps. In a network map anxiety sat at the center, tied to most body symptoms. Gut complaints, pain, and nerve like symptoms each predicted anxiety most strongly. The authors urge clinics to treat mind and body as one problem here.
pmc-13579839:
Jianing Qiu and colleagues chart where lung cancer hides in lymph nodes after drug treatment before surgery, in a 2026 study. The treatment pairs chemo with immune therapy and has become standard for operable disease, yet the node map after it was unclear. Records covered 394 patients treated at a Shanghai hospital from 2019 to 2022, all with full tumor removal after the drugs.

Node spread clustered at set stations near the tumor and at the central crossing station, with rates near one in ten at the top spots. Nodes near the tumor beat distant ones across all lung lobes, and lower right tumors reached high into the chest more than expected. Wider node clearing trended toward longer cancer free spans but missed firm proof. Tumor type and starting node stage steered survival most.
pmc-13580339:
Alcy Torres, Laurie Douglass, Phillip L Pearl, and Karl Kuban memorialize child neurologist N Paul Rosman, who died in Boston in March 2026 at age ninety one, in a 2026 obituary. Born in Ottawa in 1934 and trained at McGill, where he took his degrees with high honors, Rosman moved to Boston in 1963 and spent the rest of his career there. He founded the child neurology division at Boston City Hospital in 1969 and led it for seventeen years.

His pen produced over two hundred papers and chapters and drew more than thirty grants. Work on fever seizures and developmental disorders marked his name in the field. At a second hospital he co-founded a center for children with complex needs, and late in life he helped rebuild a residency program. Trainees from many states and countries gathered to honor him.
pmc-13580639:
Valérie Bourque-Riel, Bruce Crooks, and David Conrad argue in this 2026 essay that children with leukemia should be shown their own disease, not just told about it. They describe the Cellfie Project, a Canadian program where blood specialists sit with young patients and explore their cancer cells together.

The authors frame this direct teaching as advocacy: seeing the pathology behind a diagnosis can ease fear and return a sense of control to families. Adult clinics where pathologists meet patients have already improved understanding and trust, but no such model existed for children. They call on clinicians and policymakers to treat open, visible diagnosis as a core part of child and family centered care, not an extra.
pmc-13582339:
Ryosuke Saiki, Kan Katayama, Mutsuki Mori, and Kaoru Dohi map a rare overlap of two kidney filter diseases, in a 2026 scoping review. One disease is an antibody driven attack that scars the filters with crescent shapes; the other coats the filter wall with immune deposits. Three databases were searched to April 2026 for cases carrying both at once.

Seventy studies covering one hundred forty patients qualified. The typical patient was sixty, with kidney function well down and heavy protein in the urine. The team sorted cases into likely types: mostly attack led, some deposit led, many tied to another condition, and a few unclassifiable. Nine in ten began together. Case reports ruled the pile, antigen testing was patchy, and follow up reporting wandered, which the authors say future studies must fix.
pmc-13586239:
Ting-ting Yao and colleagues review smart delivery systems for a new class of drugs called PROTACs. A PROTAC does not just block a harmful protein; it tags the protein for the cell's own shredder, which opens targets once thought undruggable. Yet these molecules are big and awkward: they dissolve poorly, cross cell walls weakly, and can wander to the wrong tissues.

The 2026 review sorts the fixes chemists are building. Some PROTACs are masked as prodrugs that wake up under light, enzymes, or the chemistry of a tumor. Others ride in fat bubbles, plastic particles, mineral scaffolds, or fused to antibodies and aptamers that home to chosen cells. Self-assembling and membrane-hugging designs point to a more programmable style of drug making. The authors call for shared tests that track the whole path from dose to effect.
pmc-13589339:
İlknur Dolu and four colleagues ask what helps teenagers judge health information online. High schoolers swim in health claims on social media, and skill at sorting good from bad, called eHealth literacy, varies widely. Their 2026 cross-sectional study surveyed students at participating high schools between March and July 2025, scoring their online health literacy, everyday critical thinking, and social media addiction on standard scales.

Critical thinking marched closely with eHealth literacy, the stronger the thinking, the stronger the literacy. Social media addiction, by contrast, showed no meaningful link either way. In the final statistical model, hours spent online each day and critical thinking were the two factors that counted. Instagram was the most used platform in the group. The authors advise schools to build critical thinking rather than only policing screen habits.
pmc-13589939:
Yuanyuan Wang and four colleagues review, in 2026, a plan to pair two cancer tools: viruses that kill tumor cells and drugs that loosen tight gene control. The viruses infect cancer cells, burst them, and alert the immune system, yet many tumors resist them. Drugs that change gene tags can help the viruses copy themselves inside a tumor. The pair may thus do more than either tool alone.

Wang and the team survey which gene control drugs exist and how each has been paired with a virus so far. Gains include more virus growth, more tumor cell death, and a tumor site that welcomes immune attack. The review also flags hard limits, such as the blood clearing viruses too fast.
pmc-13591939:
Natalia Campo-Ortiz de Zárate and three colleagues review, in 2026, a fresh idea in lung biology: cells may remember past mechanical force. Lung tissue is soft, yet disease can stiffen it many times over. Cells sense that stiffness and change their gene activity, shape, and inner wiring. The review asks whether those changes persist after the force fades, locking cells into a sick state.

Such mechanomemory could explain why lung scarring feeds on itself and why tumors resist drugs, the authors argue. Stored signals in cell skeletons and gene tags may keep scar making cells active long past the first injury. Campo-Ortiz de Zárate and the team propose that erasing this memory could break the cycle, and they map the open questions for the field.
pmc-13592739:
Chao Liang and three colleagues compare food poisoning germ detection in Beijing before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Habits from the pandemic years changed dining, hygiene, and care seeking, but the mark on foodborne illness stayed unclear. Their single hospital diarrhea clinic records covered 1,064 patients, split between 2018 to 2019 and 2022 to 2023, with the disrupted middle years left out. Stool test methods stayed constant across both windows.

Positive results fell from about twenty eight percent before the pandemic to about sixteen percent after. One gut bacterium stayed dominant in both eras, while a seafood linked bacterium and norovirus dropped sharply. Students and young men formed the largest patient groups. Liang and the team caution that one clinic cannot speak for the whole city and call for wider surveillance.
pmc-13593539:
In a 2026 case report, Lucas H Oliveira and colleagues describe an 83-year-old man. His pacing lead was damaged while it was being placed deep in the heart wall for left bundle branch area pacing. When the team tried to reposition the lead, its tiny corkscrew tip unwound inside the septum, a problem they link to too much twisting force on a trapped lead.

Warning signs included the lead wrinkling and a loss of the turning resistance the operator normally feels. Rather than pulling the damaged lead out by force, the team left it in place and managed the patient cautiously. That choice held up well: across three years of follow-up the man had no adverse events from the abandoned lead.
pmc-13593639:
Sophie M. Sametinger led a study grading how well two AI chatbots answer patient questions about oral anticancer drugs, the cancer pills people take at home. In June 2024 the team put four typical patient questions about twenty such drugs to Microsoft's Copilot and Google's Gemini, three times each, and scored the replies against standard written patient information.

Accuracy was high for both systems, with median scores at the top of the scale. Completeness lagged, with Copilot covering a median of about three fifths of the relevant points and Gemini about three quarters. Readability was the weakest point, since both chatbots wrote at a level many patients would find hard going. The authors conclude that the tools are factually sound but not yet a full answer to patients' information needs.
pmc-13594039:
Haiyang Zhang and colleagues evaluated a fast synthetic MRI method for judging whether thyroid eye disease is active, a distinction that guides treatment. The technique, called MAGiC, produces several quantitative tissue maps from one quick scan, and the team applied it to 113 patients, forty-nine with active disease and sixty-four with quiet disease.

Several measured values from the eye muscles tracked the clinical activity score, and three measures each predicted activity on their own. A model combining two of them, T1 and proton density, separated active from inactive disease with the best accuracy in the study, and adding a third measure did not help. Repeat measurements proved highly consistent, and image quality matched a standard sequence. The authors present the combined model as an objective marker that could support staging and treatment planning.
pmc-13609839:
Xianli Tang and four colleagues build a radio filter whose bandwidth can be dialed continuously without giving up low loss. Phones juggling many bands normally need a shelf of fixed filters, which fights miniaturization. Their design hybridizes acoustic-wave resonators with lumped elements, using a varactor diode to retune a reconfigurable resonator module, in two ladder layouts. Equations derived for both layouts predicted performance before fabrication, and simulations agreed.

Measured results backed the math. The simpler Type I filter tuned its 3 dB fractional bandwidth across a wide span with insertion loss between 1.2 and 2.2 dB. The Type II version, with an extra shunt branch, tuned slightly wider while losing a bit more signal. Both figures beat the 3 to 10 dB losses typical of earlier tunable filters built on low-quality resonators. The authors present the hybrid acoustic approach as a favorable compromise for flexible 5G and 6G front ends.
pmc-13610739:
Maxim I. Suchkov leads a nine-author team testing whether gentle heat treatment makes expressed breast milk safe at home. Several viruses can ride in breast milk, and Holder pasteurization, 62.5 degrees for thirty minutes, is the milk-bank standard balancing safety against nutrition. The team spiked milk from four donors with a panel of RNA and DNA viruses and ran it through a portable home pasteurizer, measuring infectious virus and leftover genomes.

Enveloped RNA viruses, HIV-1, chikungunya, and SARS-CoV-2, dropped below detection. Respiratory syncytial virus did not. Non-enveloped enteroviruses and the DNA viruses tested fell only partly. Two enteroviruses also behaved inconsistently between donors' milk, a reminder that milk composition varies. The authors conclude that home Holder pasteurization is a partial shield, not sterilization. They suggest it could join a future pandemic preparedness toolbox, helping mothers keep breastfeeding through common infections.
pmc-13612239:
Monika Drobna-Sledzinska leads a thirteen-author team cataloguing circular RNAs in an aggressive blood cancer in 2026. T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia grows from immature T cells. Circular RNAs, looped molecules that can soak up regulatory microRNAs, are suspects in its machinery. The team fished out RNAs bound to the protein AGO2 in four leukemia cell lines, hunting for circles acting as microRNA sponges.

Circular RNAs were over-represented in the AGO2-bound fraction, 7.3 percent against 3 percent for linear RNAs, and a consistent enriched set emerged. One abundant circle, circN4BP2L2, also ran abnormal in patients. Knocking it down slowed cell proliferation, restored cell-death sensitivity, and shifted key leukemia pathways. Patient tumors with high levels of this circle showed gene-expression features overlapping the knockdown signature. The authors present circN4BP2L2 as a survival-promoting regulator, and the AGO2-bound catalog as a map for further targets.
pmc-13612939:
Natassia Brenman writes about voluntary mental health services in inner-city London and the staff who felt their services were turning into dumping grounds for a system in crisis. Charities in Britain have long provided flexible community care that eases pressure on public clinics and hospitals. Under years of austerity funding cuts, Brenman found through fieldwork at three sites that these groups were stretched well past what they could hold.

Brenman offers the idea of threshold work to explain how staff decide, day by day, who and what they can take in. Staff manage limits in two linked ways: the physical thresholds of their buildings and the shifting line of how unwell a person must be to qualify for help. Readers see how care is shaped as much by doors, rooms, and cut-off points as by goodwill.
pmc-13614639:
Charles J. Gerardo leads a large team testing whether a drug called varespladib, given after antivenom, helps hospital patients bitten by venomous snakes. Snakebite kills an estimated 81,000 to 138,000 people each year and leaves more than 400,000 with lasting disability, mostly in poor regions. Antivenom is the only approved treatment and must be dripped into a vein, so an added drug that blunts venom could save tissue and lives.

In this phase II trial at many centres, patients were randomly assigned in a double-blind design to receive varespladib by vein then by mouth, or a placebo, on top of standard antivenom. Neither patients nor staff knew who got the drug. Trials like this decide whether a promising add-on earns a place in emergency care, where hours matter and stock of antivenom is often short.
pmc-13615039:
Yildiz Ucar, Caner Incekas, Keziban Ucar Karabulut, and Meltem Karacan Golen compare in 2026 how obstructive sleep apnea looks in men and women. They draw on 230 patients diagnosed by overnight sleep studies between 2020 and 2026. The condition, where the airway keeps closing during sleep, was long treated as a mostly male problem. In this group, 68.3 percent were men and 31.7 percent were women.

Women were older at diagnosis and had a higher body mass index. Their average and lowest oxygen levels during sleep were worse, and they showed higher pressure in the lung artery and a weaker heart pumping score. Blood inflammation scores built from white cell types ran higher in men. The contrast suggests women's disease is being caught later, after more harm, and that doctors should not wait for the classic male picture before testing women.
pmc-13615339:
Yue Chen leads a team reviewing how lactate, a by-product of sugar use in cells, and a chemical tag it adds to proteins, called lactylation, steer programmed cell death in human disease. Lactylation was found only recently, and it mirrors a cell's metabolic state while helping control which genes are read. Programmed cell death is the body's orderly way of removing cells under stress, in several distinct forms.

Once treated as separate topics, the two are now shown to be linked: the lactate tag can switch key gene and signal paths that drive various forms of cell death. The review gathers the fresh findings across diseases where this link may matter. Drug hunters gain new targets, since blocking or boosting the tag could change whether diseased cells live or die on cue.
pmc-13616239:
Huanhuan Yang, Yee Sin Ang, Sheng Meng, and Xiao Jiang study double-layer altermagnets. These form a new class of magnetic materials with no overall magnetisation. Stacking two layers with coupling between them lifts those rules and switches on a current type that was forbidden before.

Using a simplified model of electron orbits, the team showed two current types moving in opposite directions as the layer coupling grows, each ruled by a distinct mechanism. Detailed calculations on a real candidate material, a manganese phosphorus telluride bilayer, backed the predictions. Such light-driven, spin-sorted currents could serve future low-power devices that read information from spin rather than charge alone.
pmc-13618039:
C. Ruth Le Sueur, James F. E. Croft, and Jeremy M. Bound states, the energy levels of weakly joined systems such as van der Waals complexes, appear where a matrix eigenvalue crosses zero. Older search methods were fiddly to program and could lose track of the eigenvalue across an energy range.

Their algorithm tracks the needed eigenvalue of the matching matrix across the full energy span where it exists, making implementations much simpler. They give practical guidance on choosing the matching distance, the point where two halves of the calculation are joined. It should sit in the classically allowed region for every channel of interest, but not too close to a node in the wavefunction. The result is a more robust tool for spectroscopy and weakly bound systems.
pmc-13618839:
Kristina Shkirkova and eight colleagues report a 2026 secondary analysis of the FAST-MAG trial, testing whether a neuroprotectant started by paramedics can bridge stroke patients to clot treatment. Thrombolysis followed at about one hundred fifty minutes, and patients carried a median of ninety-three minutes of study drug exposure before reperfusion. Ninety-day disability did not improve significantly. A subgroup with the most severe strokes hinted at benefit, which the authors label hypothesis-generating only. They frame the contribution as proving the early-exposure model for future protective agents.
pmc-13624039:

Both questions were checked against a broad flourishing battery covering happiness, health, meaning, character, financial security, and relationships. Life satisfaction tracked every one of those domains more strongly than the ladder did, and the pattern held in all twenty-two countries. The ladder did lean hardest toward the financial side of life, matching its rung-climbing image. The authors conclude that when only one question fits, the plain satisfaction wording gives the fuller summary of how people judge their lives.
pmc-13625039:
Sintayehu Eshetu Abebaw and Tadla Guadie Feleke gather the research record on how climate change threatens food in Ethiopia. Following standard review rules, they screened the literature and kept 232 studies on climate risks, weak points in the food system, and ways to adapt. Farming there leans on rainfall, which leaves harvests exposed when rains fail or shift.

Drought, heat, and erratic rain stood out as the chief risks, with drought blamed for roughly sixty percent of crop losses in the studies. One degree of warming was tied to a tenth less output of main staple crops, and rural homes lost ground faster than city homes. The reviewers point to hardier farming methods, wider irrigation, and plans fitted to each region.
pmc-13625439:
Souvik Chaudhuri and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, hunt for early chemical warning signs in community-acquired pneumonia. The infection's course is hard to predict at the door, so the team took blood from seventy patients and thirty-five healthy controls at one center between January and November 2025. A scanning method measured small molecules in the serum, keeping ninety-three for study after cleaning.

Patient blood differed most in a set of organic acids, led by malic acid, and the disturbed pathways covered energy production, amino acid handling, and the body's rust-defense balance. A smaller contrast between sixty intensive care patients and ten milder cases fingered fats, cholesterol, and a vitamin E form. Early metabolic fingerprints may one day help doctors spot which pneumonia will turn severe.
pmc-13626339:
Kate Duchowny and colleagues map where America's essential workers lived during the COVID-19 pandemic. More than fifty-five million people kept working in person while others sheltered, yet little was known about their home neighborhoods. The team linked a national neighborhood database with census survey estimates from 2016 to 2020. Every tract was sorted into five bands by its share of essential workers. Access to food shops, health care, and parks was then compared across the bands.

Tracts dense with essential workers actually held more grocery stores than quieter tracts. The same tracts, though, had significantly fewer health care facilities and less park and green space. The people asked to absorb the most exposure, the authors conclude, went home to places least stocked with the resources that protect health in a crisis.
pmc-13629139:
Kritchavat Ploddi and three colleagues mapped the known methods for building health prediction models. Such models must keep working when moved to new groups of people.
